artigo.texto: A recent study in PRX Quantum from the University of Oulu identifies key limits on quantum battery reliability and shows how different charging protocols can balance high power output with steady, predictable energy and power delivery. The findings help clarify what “dependable” performance will require in practice, bringing usable quantum energy-storage systems a step closer. Quantum uncertainty imposes a fundamental trade-off in quantum batteries, limiting their ability to deliver steady power and reliable energy simultaneously. Quantum batteries are an emerging area of research, with progress coming from theoretical work and early proof-of-concept experiments in small quantum systems. Unlike the chemical batteries used in everyday devices, quantum batteries store and transfer energy using quantum states. Researchers are exploring them as potential power sources for quantum processors and other quantum technologies. Much of the early work has focused on how quickly and efficiently these batteries can be charged. In their recent study, the team identified fundamental limits on fluctuations in both the energy a quantum battery delivers and the rate at which it supplies that energy. A quantum battery ideally should not only be fast and powerful but also needs to charge or deliver energy in a reliable and stable manner at the same time. Our work shows that quantum mechanics places fundamental limits on the reliabilities of quantum batteries. Brij Mohan, Study First Author and Postdoctoral Researcher, University of Oulu The researchers show that a familiar cornerstone of quantum mechanics, the uncertainty relation, prevents energy fluctuations and power variations from being minimized at the same time. In other words, a quantum battery cannot be tuned to deliver both highly reliable energy transfer and perfectly steady power at the same time. Here, “stability” and “reliability” mean keeping fluctuations small relative to their average values. The trade-off arises because, in closed quantum batteries, work and power are represented by non-commuting operators, much like position and momentum in standard quantum mechanics. The team then examined how this trade-off relates to methods for charging multiple quantum battery cells. In parallel charging, the cells function autonomously. Collective charging involves all cells simultaneously. Hybrid charging represents a midpoint between these two approaches, in which groups of cells interact during the charging process. The findings indicate that more robust collective charging increases power but also amplifies power fluctuations, which reduces power reliability. This suggests that evaluating quantum-battery performance based solely on maximum power is inadequate. Our results show that there is a meaningful way to balance power enhancement and the reliability of work and power. Intermediate-range interactions based charging scheme can provide a useful compromise between high power and stable operation. Tanmoy Pandit, Research Scientist, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland The researchers further investigated quantum batteries with transverse Ising-type many-body interactions and found a similar qualitative trade-off between power and reliability. This finding suggests that the phenomenon is not limited to the most basic theoretical framework. The reliability limits connect quantum fluctuations with many-body quantum physics in a direct way. They provide useful charging strategies that are practically advantageous. Manabendra Nath Bera, IISER Mohali “Quantum batteries offer a fascinating link between quantum information, thermodynamics, and many-body physics. Understanding their fluctuations is essential if these systems are eventually to become useful technological resources,” added Maciej Lewenstein, ICFO, Spain. The researchers' next goal is to explore the limits of reliability in more practical environments, accounting for factors such as noise, energy loss, open-system behavior, and experimentally relevant quantum platforms. Quantum batteries represent an ongoing advancement stemming from the extensive research conducted by the Nano and Molecular Systems Research Unit at the University of Oulu. This research focuses on the theoretical and modeling aspects of quantum devices, including superconducting qubits and quantum processors. Journal Reference: Mohan, B., et al. (2026) Fundamental Limitations on the Reliabilities of Power and Work in Quantum Batteries. PRX Quantum. DOI:10.1103/fnv6-yqmk. https://journals.aps.org/prxquantum/abstract/10.1103/fnv6-yqmk.

artigo.texto: Ecopro BM and Samsung SDI Join Forces on All-Solid-State Batteries... Targeting Commercialization by 2027 Joint Development of Sulfide-Based Solid Electrolytes and All-Solid-State Cathode Materials Expanding Collaboration from Cell Development to Core Materials and Mass Production Systems Ecopro BM is joining forces with Samsung SDI in developing core materials and building a supply chain, aiming for the commercialization of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries next year. Ecopro BM announced on the 6th that it has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Samsung SDI for cooperation in developing materials for all-solid-state batteries. The two companies plan to strengthen collaboration from the early stages of development through quality assessment and mass production system establishment, with the goal of enhancing the technological completeness and business competitiveness of all-solid-state batteries. Image of all-solid-state battery materials unveiled by Ecopro BM at InterBattery in March. Ecopro BM View original image Under the agreement, Samsung SDI will be responsible for developing all-solid-state battery cells and advancing mass production technology. Ecopro BM will be in charge of developing core materials for all-solid-state batteries. The two companies will expand the scope of their cooperation to include not just cathode materials for all-solid-state batteries, but also electrolytes for cathodes and electrolytes for separators. All-solid-state batteries are next-generation batteries that use a solid electrolyte instead of the conventional liquid electrolyte. They are considered key technologies for future industries such as electric vehicles and humanoid robots, as they can improve energy density and safety. Ecopro BM has secured proprietary processing technology in the field of sulfide-based solid electrolytes, a core material for all-solid-state batteries, and operates a pilot plant with an annual capacity of 40 tons. Leveraging its powder control and quality management technologies, the company is enhancing its competitiveness in solid electrolytes while also developing cathode materials optimized for solid electrolytes using its high-nickel cathode technology. Based on its sulfide-based solid electrolyte technology, Ecopro BM was also selected in August for the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's "Super Eul Project." The Super Eul Project is an R&D support program designed to foster materials, parts, and equipment companies capable of leading global supply chains. The government plans to support each selected company with more than 20 billion won of long-term R&D funding per project over at least seven years. Last month, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy released the "Battery Industry Technology Roadmap," designating all-solid-state batteries as a key strategic technology for the future battery industry. The government plans to support the early commercialization of next-generation batteries by strengthening joint R&D and supply chain cooperation systems among cell and materials companies. artigo.texto: China’s industry ministry and six other agencies set 2030 as the date for the first large-scale use of all-solid-state batteries, though CATL’s chairman rates the technology four out of nine and calls million-vehicle use before 2030 very unlikely. ProLogium’s Dunkirk plant, the largest new European cell project since Northvolt went bankrupt, is staged at 0.8 GWh in 2028 and will be certified against a Chinese standard. China has set 2030 as the date for the first large-scale use of solid-state batteries. Its biggest battery maker rates the technology four out of nine. A plant in northern France broke ground in February. The plan came from the industry ministry and six other agencies on 28 September and covers 2026 to 2030, as CnEVPost reported. It also targets lithium cells good for 15,000 charge cycles. The ministry acknowledged weaknesses in innovation and imbalances between supply and demand. CATL is promising less than the plan does. Its chairman, Robin Zeng, put all-solid-state at four out of nine in June, on a scale where nine means ready for vehicle production. He called the chance of fitting it to a million cars before 2030 very small. CATL intends limited production in 2027. LG Energy Solution expects the technology to reach smartphones a decade before EVs. Its North America president says large cells are where manufacturers struggle. Europe is further along than that timetable suggests, though not by much, and not on its own technology. ProLogium already makes 6,000 packs a year in Taiwan, which is half a gigawatt hour, at 381 Wh/kg on TUV Rheinland’s measurement. That is roughly 30% above the cells in most electric cars today. The company is now building the same thing in France, with subsidies agreed in 2023 and permits granted the year after. The Dunkirk plant started construction in February beside the Gravelines nuclear station, staged at 0.8 GWh in 2028 and 12 GWh by 2032. Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Mercedes are separately working with Factorial on cells of their own. None of it is close to Chinese volume, and the gap is not narrowing. Chinese and South Korean makers supply 90% of Europe’s batteries, and Northvolt went bankrupt after raising $15bn. Dunkirk is the largest new European cell project since. The standard is Chinese as well. ProLogium’s cells are certified against GB/T 43568-2026, the all-solid-state specification Beijing introduced in July, and were separately tested by UL Solutions. China took 70% of global electric car production under the previous five-year plan. The new one says initial large-scale use rather than mass production, and even that is a target rather than a promise. artigo.texto: A Macau Internacional Troca de Emissões de Carbono Limitada, mais conhecida por MEX, pretende tirar partido das vantagens oferecidas por Macau para promover a negociação de activos ambientais – incluindo de créditos de carbono, certificados de energia verde e outros instrumentos similares – entre a China e os Países de Língua Portuguesa. Meng Meng, Directora-Geral da entidade, revela que a plataforma de negociação operada pela MEX já listou mais de 30 projectos ligados a países lusófonos e de língua espanhola, envolvendo uma redução total de emissões de carbono superior a 14,13 milhões de toneladas Como foi criada a Macau Internacional Troca de Emissões de Carbono Limitada (MEX, na sigla inglesa)? Quais são os seus objectivos estratégicos? A MEX foi criada a 30 de Outubro de 2024. Recorrendo a tecnologias de informação avançadas e padrões de referência no sector, integra produtos e oportunidades relacionados com o clima a nível global, proporcionando à China uma solução específica com características de Macau para se conectar aos mercados internacionais de finanças verdes. A Região Administrativa Especial de Macau (RAEM) é um porto franco, com regras financeiras alinhadas com as normas internacionais. Além disso, a cidade situa-se na confluência de duas importantes estratégias nacionais – o projecto da Grande Baía Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau e a Zona de Cooperação Aprofundada entre Guangdong e Macau em Hengqin. Neste sentido, possui um conjunto de vantagens intrínsecas que lhe permite posicionar-se como um “superconector” no mercado internacional de carbono. A nossa tarefa é transformar gradualmente esse conjunto de vantagens intrínsecas numa realidade concreta. A nível nacional, trabalhamos no sentido de apoiar as metas de “duplo carbono” estabelecidas pelo país [atingir o pico das emissões de dióxido de carbono antes de 2030 e alcançar a neutralidade carbónica antes de 2060], proporcionando um canal mais aberto para que o mercado de carbono da China possa estabelecer ligações com capital, tecnologia e regulamentações internacionais. A nível global, estamos a construir uma plataforma de cooperação no campo da acção climática, ao mesmo tempo que promovemos o alinhamento de padrões com as normas internacionais e a sua implementação prática, divulgando o progresso alcançado pelo mercado de carbono da China. Em paralelo, a MEX encara o comércio de carbono como um motor para alcançar a neutralidade carbónica e desenvolver as finanças verdes. Oferecemos também a diversos sectores-chave em Macau soluções ligadas à neutralidade carbónica, ferramentas associadas a certificados verdes de absorção de carbono e instrumentos de financiamento verde, transformando a transição para a neutralidade carbónica numa vantagem competitiva para as indústrias da RAEM. Qual é o modelo operacional da MEX? A nossa plataforma pode ser entendida como um mercado digital de negociação de activos ambientais. Os produtos listados na MEX incluem créditos de carbono, certificados de energia renovável e outros itens similares. Apoiamos a negociação de certificados verdes internacionais e chineses e somos a única bolsa do género na China a disponibilizar contratos padronizados de créditos de carbono de elevada qualidade com cobertura global. Nas áreas não directamente relacionadas com a negociação de activos, prestamos serviços de dados e estudos, formação, consultoria e outras soluções. Publicamos regularmente relatórios sectoriais para ajudar os participantes no mercado a compreenderem melhor tendências, a identificarem oportunidades e a mitigarem riscos. Além disso, disponibilizamos programas de capacitação que ajudam as empresas a aprofundarem o seu conhecimento sobre os desafios associados à acção climática. Prestamos igualmente serviços personalizados ao longo de toda a cadeia, desde o inventário de emissões de carbono e o planeamento de trajectórias de redução de emissões até à definição de soluções de compensação. Através deste modelo integrado, que combina actividades de negociação e serviços não transaccionais, procuramos criar um ecossistema sustentável de activos ambientais e serviços verdes, permitindo que as empresas que necessitam de soluções nesta área as encontrem na MEX. Quais os principais marcos já alcançados pela MEX? Em primeiro lugar, concretizámos o nosso posicionamento estratégico de utilizar Macau como ponto de apoio para ligar a China ao mercado internacional de carbono. Macau tem vindo, gradualmente, a afirmar-se como um centro activo do mercado de carbono na Ásia. Até Agosto deste ano, o volume acumulado de créditos de carbono negociados através da MEX tinha ultrapassado 1,17 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO2-e). Já o volume de certificados de energia renovável negociados ascendia a 2,07 milhões de certificados. Contamos actualmente com 146 membros registados na nossa plataforma. Logo no dia da nossa inauguração, concluímos as primeiras negociações envolvendo cerca de 870 mil toneladas de créditos de carbono, abrangendo uma dezena de sectores em cinco países. Esperamos que, através da adopção de um conjunto de normas rigorosas e de uma governação sólida, os produtos disponibilizados através da MEX se tornem sinónimo de elevada qualidade. Somos a única instituição de Macau que é membro da Associação Internacional de Comércio de Emissões. Estabelecemos igualmente parcerias com outros membros e organizações internacionais e mantemos uma cooperação aprofundada com diversas instituições académicas e industriais de referência a nível mundial no sector. Estas colaborações, ao promoverem o reconhecimento mútuo de activos, a integração de sistemas e a harmonização de normas, posicionam Macau como um verdadeiro pólo de ligação entre os vários mercados de carbono da Ásia e do mundo. A nível nacional, a MEX formou alianças e assinou acordos de cooperação estratégica com várias instituições, com o objectivo de promover conjuntamente o desenvolvimento de um ecossistema de finanças verd

artigo.texto: Uma das maiores empresas de auditoria e consultoria do mundo, a PWC, projeta US$ 11,4 bilhões em investimentos em data centers no Brasil em 2026. O valor é 49,3% maior em relação a 2025, que foi de US$ 7,6 bilhões. A informação foi publicada no jornal ‘Folha de S. Paulo’. No entanto, o mercado ainda aguarda a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenters (Redata), sancionado pelo governo no dia 15 de setembro. Há indefinições com relação a impostos estaduais na implantação de projetos de centro de dados. O cálculo é que o Redata abra caminho inicialmente para planos de investimento de R$ 20 bilhões no Brasil. Entre as empresas que devem fazer esse aporte incluem as americanas Ascenty e Scala, a britânica Terranova e a brasileira Takota. O Brasil é o quinto maior destino de recursos em datacenters no mundo em 2026. Os investimentos são liderados pelos Estados Unidos (US$ 448,4 bi), seguidos da China (US$ 48,9 bi), Índia (US$ 28,2 bi) e Alemanha (US$ 16,7 bi). No mundo, os investimentos devem chegar a US$ 828,4 bilhões só este ano. Um estudo recém-divulgado da FGV Projetos estima que a implantação de um único datacenter, incluindo a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, mobiliza cerca de R$ 25 bilhões em investimentos totais. A instituição calcula que aproximadamente 12.560 empregos diretos e indiretos são gerados durante a fase de construção e implantação. Desse total, cerca de 1.860 postos são permanentes, incluindo equipes de operação, manutenção e serviços de apoio ao empreendimento. O setor calcula investimentos de R$ 500 bilhões até 2030 em centro de dados. A capacidade atual dos datacenters no Brasil gira em torno de 730 MW, mas a previsão é de saltar para 3,2 GW em quatro anos, com foco em atender o processamento de inteligência artificial.

artigo.texto: Amazon abandona NDAs em data centers: o que muda na prática A AWS aboliu os acordos de confidencialidade com governos locais para tentar frear mais de 100 moratórias contra data centers nos EUA. A Amazon Web Services decidiu parar de usar acordos de confidencialidade (NDAs) nas negociações com governos locais para aprovação de novos data centers nos Estados Unidos. O anúncio foi feito por Matt Garman, CEO da AWS, em uma publicação que tenta responder à crescente resistência de comunidades americanas contra a expansão dessas instalações. A medida não é um gesto de boa vontade espontâneo. É uma reação calculada a um movimento que está ganhando corpo: mais de 100 moratórias contra data centers estão sendo discutidas em diferentes localidades dos EUA. O estado de Nova York já aprovou uma suspensão de um ano em licenças para grandes data centers. A Amazon está, na prática, tentando conter um incêndio regulatório antes que ele se espalhe. Por que as comunidades americanas estão rejeitando data centers A raiz do problema é a falta de transparência. A ativista ambiental Erin Brockovich resumiu o padrão que gera revolta: projetos anunciados depois que as licenças já estão garantidas, desenvolvedores que não retornam ligações e autoridades locais que assinaram NDAs antes que os vizinhos soubessem que um projeto estava sendo considerado. Esse ciclo corroeu a confiança pública. Como analisamos na cobertura de tecnologia do portal, a corrida por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial acelerou drasticamente a construção de data centers, mas as empresas trataram a expansão como uma operação sigilosa, e não como um projeto que afeta diretamente a vida de milhares de pessoas. O CEO da Anthropic, Dario Amodei, classificou a situação como “fundamentalmente uma crise de confiança”, em que as pessoas assumem que governos e big techs estão sempre tramando alguma forma de prejudicá-las. É um diagnóstico que vale para todo o setor, não apenas para a Amazon. Os quatro mitos que a Amazon tenta derrubar Garman tentou desmontar quatro críticas recorrentes aos data centers: consumo excessivo de água, aumento nos custos de eletricidade, poluição e ausência de benefícios para as comunidades locais. Sobre a água, a Amazon apontou que o consumo direto de seus data centers representa apenas 0,5% de todo o uso industrial de água nos EUA, volume descrito como “ordens de magnitude menor” do que campos de golfe ou o cultivo de amêndoas. A Nvidia, por sua vez, afirmou recentemente que seu novo sistema de refrigeração elimina “praticamente todo o uso de água” dentro dos data centers. Há um problema nesses números, no entanto. Tanto a Amazon quanto a Nvidia parecem ignorar o consumo mais amplo de água envolvido na geração de eletricidade e na fabricação de chips. Cientistas alertaram que precisam estudar o uso de água e energia dos data centers de forma independente, já que não existem exigências federais ou estaduais sobre como as empresas de tecnologia reportam esses dados. Em outras palavras: as big techs estão pedindo que acreditemos nos números que elas mesmas compilam, sem auditoria externa. Quanto à eletricidade, Garman argumentou que as tarifas só subiram em alguns estados com grande concentração de data centers, enquanto em outros caíram ou cresceram mais lentamente. Ele atribuiu os aumentos à falta de investimento prévio na rede elétrica. Mas um órgão de fiscalização independente apontou recentemente que os data centers foram os principais responsáveis por um aumento de 76% nos preços de energia, em base anual, na maior rede elétrica dos Estados Unidos. Os dados contam uma história diferente da narrativa corporativa. A questão da poluição e o caso Texas O ponto mais delicado talvez seja a poluição. Um data center planejado pela Amazon no Texas tem licença para emitir até 33 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono por ano, volume superior ao de qualquer outra usina de energia do país. Garman contra-argumentou dizendo que os geradores ficam ociosos 99,9% do tempo, funcionando em média apenas 10 horas por ano para testes de manutenção. A resposta, embora tecnicamente válida, não aborda o ponto central da crítica: se os geradores quase nunca funcionam, por que solicitar uma licença tão permissiva? O limite alto na licença cria uma percepção de risco que alimenta a desconfiança, como já discutimos ao analisar o impacto energético da IA. O caso do Texas é emblemático porque ilustra como o setor opera na prática: pede o máximo possível de margem regulatória, argumenta que usará uma fração mínima e espera que a comunidade confie nessa promessa. É uma estratégia que funcionava em um ambiente de baixa fiscalização, mas está sendo desafiada agora. Um bilhão em contribuições é suficiente? Garman também destacou que, nos últimos três anos, a Amazon contribuiu com mais de 1 bilhão de dólares para comunidades onde mantém presença significativa de data centers. É um número expressivo, mas que precisa ser colocado em perspectiva: a AWS gerou cerca de 105 bilhões de dólares em receita apenas em 2024. O investimento comunitário representa menos de 1% desse faturamento. O abandono dos NDAs é um passo concreto, mas provavelmente insuficiente para reverter o sentimento anti-data center. Como observou a escritora Jasmine Sun, quando opositores dos data centers são confrontados com os argumentos das empresas de tecnologia, a resposta costuma ser simples: “Eu não acredito neles.” Para a indústria de tecnologia como um todo, o episódio é um alerta. A expansão da infraestrutura de IA depende de licenças locais, apoio comunitário e redes elétricas que consigam absorver a demanda. Se as moratórias avançarem, Garman avisa que “os EUA podem estar escrevendo seu próprio bilhete perdedor nessa corrida, e as consequências durariam gerações.” O argumento de competitividade global pode funcionar em Washington, mas não convence moradores que veem seus custos de energia subir e caminhões de construção passarem pela porta todos os dias. artigo.texto: DeepSeek is close to raising at least 80 billion yuan, or about $12bn, in a new funding round, Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday. Tencent and the battery maker CATL have committed some of the largest sums, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg. The Chinese AI lab had first set out to raise about 50 billion yuan. Demand grew after the launch of its latest model, Bloomberg said, and the final total could approach 100 billion yuan. DeepSeek has not announced the round. At these levels, it would top the company’s first outside funding earlier this year. That round raised about 50 billion yuan at a valuation of $52bn to $59bn. Founder Liang Wenfeng was the largest investor in that first round, putting in about 20 billion yuan of his own money. Tencent added roughly 10 billion yuan and CATL about 5 billion yuan, alongside JD.com, NetEase and China’s national AI investment fund. Those same two backers now lead the new round. Tencent runs the WeChat messaging app and a large cloud business. CATL makes batteries for electric cars and is working on solid-state batteries. For Tencent, becoming more closely associated with DeepSeek could enable it to keep up with its domestic competitors. This was reported by Reuters in June when the first round of the comparison was being prepared. Last month, Reuters reported that DeepSeek had secured CITIC Securities to prepare for a possible initial public offering on Shanghai’s STAR Market, a market board for technology companies. However, they said that the timing, valuation and scale of the listing had not yet been determined. DeepSeek originated from High-Flyer, the quantitative hedge fund which Liang set up. The laboratory attracted widespread attention around the beginning of 2025 due to its R1 open-source model and launched its V4 models this year. artigo.texto: The tech industry would build data centers twice as fast without the supply constraints they face, the CEO of Nokia told CNBC, underscoring continued demand for AI even as top executives debate slowing down the pace of development. "I don't think you can say in any manner we're overbuilding today because reality is that if we could build 2x faster, our customers could build 2x faster, they probably would," Justin Hotard told CNBC's "The Tech Download" podcast. "So that gives me confidence that we're still in the early days" of the AI buildout, Hotard added. Shortages of key memory chips and energy are among the supply constraints facing the sector. Nokia, one of the world's biggest telecommunications equipment makers, has pivoted to become a key player within the AI infrastructure space. It sells the technology required to connect racks of chips within data centers as well as technology that interconnects data centers across different locations. Nokia's growing role as a "picks and shovels" player in the AI boom appears to have won over investors, with the stock up around 130% over the past year. But there's been continued debate over whether the industry is building data centers too fast and whether demand will be there to sustain it. Investments in the AI buildout from data centers to chips and related infrastructure will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032 — an average of 3.63% of U.S. gross domestic product per year, according to research presented at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity. Companies are using debt, joint ventures and other complex financing mechanisms to raise investment for these projects, which depend on sustained demand for AI services over the long term. Concerns about the pace of the AI buildout were exacerbated by safety worries sparked by an Anthropic researcher's warnings on the existential threat of the technology, which prompted the company's CEO Dario Amodei to call for a slowdown in the development of the most advanced models. That sparked a knee-jerk sell off in AI-related stocks last month. Hotard said that demand for AI is not just predicated on frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI releasing new models. "I think the reality is that we're even where we are today is so early in the deployment, and the power of these models is so massive that there's a lot of there's a lot of demand to run in just deploying," Hotard said. "Even if we didn't have another frontier model released in the next three years, we could probably make tremendous progress just deploying the technology that's there today."

artigo.texto: Créditos de carbono: Não olhe apenas para o preço. Os créditos de carbono não só abrem novas fontes de receita, como também ajudam as empresas a melhorar suas capacidades de gestão de emissões, atender às demandas do mercado e criar valor agregado à marca. O valor de um crédito corresponde a uma tonelada de carbono reduzida. O mercado de carbono vietnamita está entrando em uma fase operacional com muitas oportunidades, mas também com maiores exigências para as empresas. Investir em créditos de carbono requer custos com tecnologia, medição, inventário, verificação e gestão de dados, enquanto a receita da venda de créditos nos estágios iniciais pode não ser suficiente para fornecer incentivos financeiros diretos. No entanto, o valor dos créditos de carbono não reside apenas na receita das transações. O processo de criação de créditos também está ligado à melhoria da capacidade de gestão de emissões, ao atendimento aos padrões de mercado, à ampliação do acesso ao financiamento verde e ao fortalecimento da posição da empresa na cadeia de suprimentos. A história da Thanh Thanh Cong - Bien Hoa Joint Stock Company (AgriS) é um exemplo disso. A empresa registrou 4.375 créditos de carbono provenientes de seu projeto de fertilizante orgânico Verra (VCS), que segue padrões internacionais, e emitiu 25.000 certificados de energia renovável I-REC. A planta de Ba Tra, especializada no processamento de subprodutos agrícolas, deverá gerar aproximadamente 9.600 créditos de carbono anualmente. A AgriS também firmou um acordo bilateral de transferência de créditos de carbono com um parceiro de Singapura , nos termos do Artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris. Segundo a empresa, a receita direta proveniente da venda de créditos de carbono atualmente não contribui de forma significativa para sua estrutura financeira. O que motiva as empresas a continuarem investindo? Em sua apresentação no Fórum de Carbono do Vietnã 2026 “Da Política à Ação”, o Sr. Tran Tan Viet, membro do Conselho de Administração da AgriS, afirmou que a participação precoce no mercado de carbono contribui para fortalecer a reputação e o posicionamento das empresas no mercado internacional. Diversos fundos de investimento e instituições financeiras têm explorado essa possibilidade de forma proativa, abrindo assim mais oportunidades para que as empresas acessem fontes de crédito verde. O ponto crucial é que nem todas as atividades de redução de emissões geram automaticamente créditos de carbono. O Sr. Nguyen Tuan Quang, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente , afirmou que os projetos devem atender aos requisitos de complementaridade, integridade e sustentabilidade; a quantidade de redução de emissões deve ser mensurada, validada e comprovada por dados suficientemente confiáveis. Esse requisito estabelece a base para a qualidade do mercado de carbono. Quando os créditos são utilizados em transações domésticas ou em mecanismos de cooperação internacional, a capacidade de mensurar e verificar as reduções de emissões é um fator crucial para a aceitação no mercado. Quando a demanda do mercado impacta a produção Você também pode gostar A pressão para reduzir as emissões já não provém apenas das políticas ambientais. Os requisitos para o desenvolvimento sustentável, a responsabilidade ambiental nas cadeias de abastecimento e os novos mecanismos comerciais estão a impactar cada vez mais as atividades de produção e exportação. De acordo com o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong, Chefe Adjunto do Departamento do Mercado de Carbono da Agência de Alterações Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e do Ambiente, os processos relacionados com os créditos de carbono precisam de garantir transparência, rigor e conformidade com as práticas internacionais. No que diz respeito à cooperação internacional ao abrigo do Artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris, a Agência de Alterações Climáticas está a coordenar com os parceiros o desenvolvimento de formulários, diretrizes e procedimentos detalhados. O Dr. Nguyen Hung Minh, Vice-Chefe do Departamento do Mercado de Carbono da Agência de Mudanças Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, afirmou que o Vietnã está aprimorando seu sistema de políticas e leis de resposta às mudanças climáticas. A Lei de Proteção Ambiental de 2020, cujo Artigo 139 estabelece a base legal para a organização e o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono, juntamente com as regulamentações subsequentes, concretizou gradualmente o inventário de gases de efeito estufa, a medição, a comunicação, a avaliação, a alocação de cotas de emissão e a operação do mercado de carbono. Entretanto, as exigências dos mercados internacionais estão se tornando cada vez mais claras. O Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira (CBAM) da União Europeia impacta diretamente diversos setores, como aço, cimento, alumínio, eletricidade e hidrogênio. No setor da aviação, o CORSIA também gera demanda adicional por créditos de carbono. Essas mudanças tornam a capacidade de gerenciar e fornecer dados de emissões cada vez mais parte integrante dos requisitos para atividades de produção, negócios e exportação. Para empresas que participam de cadeias de suprimentos internacionais, a capacidade de demonstrar desempenho ambiental pode afetar sua capacidade de atender aos requisitos de parceiros e expandir a cooperação. Segundo estimativas, o Vietnã poderá enfrentar um déficit de carbono de aproximadamente 2,3 milhões de créditos de carbono até 2028, o que equivale a uma necessidade de financiamento de cerca de US$ 92 milhões, caso o preço por crédito se mantenha em US$ 40 por tonelada. Esses números demonstram que o mercado de carbono está cada vez mais integrado a diversos setores da economia , da produção industrial e exportações à aviação e finanças. Em nível empresarial, o planejamento antecipado pode, portanto, oferecer certas vantagens. O Grupo TH é um exemplo disso, tendo começado a medir as emissões de carbono em toda a sua cadeia

artigo.texto: Hyundai Motor, Toyota, BYD Intensify Race to Develop 'Dream Battery' Solid-State Technology Automakers are going all-in on developing solid-state batteries, the next-generation power source poised to reshape the electric vehicle landscape. With Hyundai Motor, Toyota, BYD, and other major global automakers simultaneously entering the development race, attention is focused on whether this "game changer" will become a reality. Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a non-flammable solid material. By dramatically reducing fire risk and boosting energy density, they can deliver over 1,000 kilometers of driving range on a single charge—earning them the "dream battery" label. Given that current lithium-ion batteries offer roughly 500–600 kilometers of range, the technology promises nearly double the performance. Manfred Harrer, president of R&D at Hyundai Motor Group, made the company's solid-state battery ambitions clear during a press meeting at the "HMG Tech Talent Forum 2026" held in San Jose, California, over two days starting on the 17th of last month. "We must absolutely participate in the solid-state battery development race," he said. "We will continue investing to secure leadership in this technology, which represents the biggest strategic bet in the automotive industry." Hyundai Motor is pursuing a "battery internalization strategy" in which it develops battery cell specifications and structures in-house while outsourcing mass production to external manufacturers. The rationale: if Hyundai can achieve breakthroughs in solid-state battery development ahead of battery makers, it gains leverage in price negotiations and a favorable position to expand EV sales. Hyundai Motor Group has built a solid-state battery pilot production line at its Uiwang research center in Gyeonggi Province and is targeting commercial mass production around 2030. Global automakers join the fray Hyundai Motor is far from alone in the solid-state battery race. Toyota, which has been cautious about EV development, is collaborating with energy company Idemitsu Kosan and others on solid-state battery research, targeting mass production as early as next year. Honda has also recently entered the fray, partnering with U.S. battery startup QuantumScape. Honda previously unveiled its own solid-state battery pilot line at its research facility in Sakura City, Tochigi Prefecture, in November 2024, and began cell production in January of the following year. The joint research agreement with QuantumScape was signed in June of this year. Nissan is also building a pilot production line at its Yokohama plant, targeting commercialization in fiscal year 2028 (April 2028–March 2029). This means all three major Japanese automakers—Toyota, Honda, and Nissan—now have their own pilot lines and collaboration frameworks in place, accelerating development. Notably, the 2027–2028 timeline cited by Toyota and Idemitsu refers to the commercialization stage, with full-scale mass production to follow—a different benchmark from Hyundai Motor Group's mass production target of around 2030. Chinese players are moving quickly as well. BYD, China's largest EV maker, announced a roadmap to begin pilot production of vehicles equipped with solid-state batteries in the first quarter of next year, enter mass production in 2028, and achieve mainstream adoption after 2030. BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li told local media in Valencia, Spain, last month: "We will unveil the first model featuring solid-state battery technology next year." However, Li did not specify a concrete mass production schedule or a timeline for consumer availability. Industry observers interpret the vehicle she referenced as likely a test vehicle for technology validation rather than a production model. Geely Automobile Holdings announced in its five-year strategy released earlier this year that it would complete in-house solid-state battery development and begin validation within this year. Some Chinese EV makers, including Li Auto, are reportedly already at the sample production stage. Taiwan-based battery maker ProLogium has already entered the mass production phase. On the 2nd of last month, ProLogium announced that its 3.5-generation lithium ceramic battery (LCB) had begun mass production at its gigawatt-scale plant in Taiwan. The large-format cell, with a capacity of 185.4Ah, achieved an energy density of 381Wh/kg by weight and 903Wh/L by volume in German TÜV certification, according to the company. ProLogium classifies this battery as solid-state and has identified data centers, marine, and aerospace applications as target markets beyond EVs. The company plans production bases in France and North America in addition to Taiwan. The solid-state battery timelines announced by major players are summarized below. Caution persists over commercialization timeline Skepticism remains about how quickly the battery market landscape will shift, given the high technical difficulty, demanding manufacturing processes, and the likelihood of elevated prices in the early stages of mass production. Zeng Yuqun, chairman of CATL, the world's largest battery maker, said at the World Economic Forum annual meeting in Dalian, China, in June: "If we divide battery technology maturity into stages 1 through 9, solid-state battery technology is only at stage 4." At the time, projections within China's battery industry suggested that solid-state battery manufacturing costs would exceed three times those of batteries offering 500 kilometers of range. Notably, CATL itself—despite Zeng's stage-4 assessment—is maintaining its plan for small-volume production in 2027. In response to investor inquiries in July, CATL stated it "expects small-scale production in 2027." The company is building a pilot line of approximately 2GWh capacity in Yibin, Sichuan Province, with equipment installation set to begin in the second half of this year. SMM, a battery

artigo.texto: BYD Sealion 6 Adds All-Wheel Drive in South Korea…Dual-Motor Setup Hits 100 km/h in 5 Seconds BYD Korea has added an all-wheel-drive (AWD) trim to its plug-in hybrid (PHEV) SUV, the Sealion 6 DM-i, and began taking pre-orders on the 6th. The strategy is to broaden choices beyond the existing front-wheel-drive (FWD) single configuration to respond to diverse driving environments and consumer preferences. The newly unveiled Sealion 6 DM-i AWD places electric motors with peak output of 150 kW (204 horsepower) on both the front and rear axles. The front motor produces 300 Nm of maximum torque, while the rear motor delivers 340 Nm, giving the rear axle greater rotational force. The vehicle accelerates from a standstill to 100 km/h in 5.0 seconds, a configuration that emphasizes the instant acceleration response characteristic of electric motors. Along with the AWD system, dedicated Mud and Sand terrain modes have been applied to ensure driving stability on rough surfaces such as unpaved roads. The goal is versatility that spans urban commuting as well as weekend leisure and outdoor activities. Battery and Charging Performance The vehicle is equipped with a 26.6 kWh BYD Blade Battery. It can travel 93 km in pure electric mode under South Korea's Ministry of Environment certification, allowing daily short-distance driving to be operated like a fully electric vehicle. On the charging front, it supports approximately 18 kW DC fast charging and features V2L (Vehicle-to-Load) capability with up to 3.3 kW of external power output. This allows the vehicle battery to power electronic devices during outdoor activities such as camping. Convenience features have also been upgraded compared to the existing trim. The audio system uses HARMAN's premium brand Infinity sound system, with a total of 10 speakers including a subwoofer. A head-up display (HUD), multi-color ambient lighting, metal door sill plates, and dynamic ceremony lighting have been applied to elevate the interior ambiance. The driver's seat supports 8-way power adjustment with memory function. Pricing and Market Strategy The Sealion 6 DM-i AWD starts at ₩41.9 million (approximately $31,000). BYD Korea stated, "By adding AWD, we have broadened the range of choices according to customers' driving environments and preferences," adding, "We plan to continue introducing products that consider the diverse lifestyles of South Korean consumers and to continuously strengthen product and service experiences." The addition of this trim is interpreted as BYD's intent to compete head-on with existing hybrid SUVs in the South Korean market not only on price competitiveness but also on driving performance and convenience features. The Sealion 6 was previously launched with a single FWD trim, and the addition of this AWD version has further thickened the lineup in South Korea's PHEV SUV market. In another statement, a BYD Korea representative said the AWD trim, which combines dynamic driving performance with premium convenience features, now allows the company to meet the expectations of customers seeking diverse PHEV options. As the presence of Chinese-made PHEVs grows in the South Korean market, the Sealion 6 AWD — offering dual-motor all-wheel drive and 93 km of electric range at a starting price in the low ₩40 million range (approximately $30,000) — is expected to appeal to value-conscious consumers. However, South Korea's PHEV market remains small compared to the EV segment, and factors such as consumer perception of Chinese-made vehicles and changes in government subsidy policies are expected to serve as variables in actual sales performance. artigo.texto: South Korea's Big Three Battery Material Makers Counter China with LFP, LMR, and Solid-State Push — Cathode Supremacy Battle Reignites Chinese battery makers are rapidly encroaching on the global market with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries as their weapon, forcing South Korean cathode material producers to overhaul their product strategies. POSCO Future M, EcoPro BM, and L&F — which had concentrated on high-nickel ternary chemistries — are now racing to close the gap with China by strengthening their LFP response while simultaneously broadening their portfolios to include lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) and solid-state battery materials. According to SNE Research on October 5, global EV battery usage excluding China reached 316.2 GWh in the first seven months of this year, up 25.8% year over year. During the same period, the combined market share of CATL and BYD climbed to 44.6%, up 7.0 percentage points from a year earlier. Chinese companies that once relied heavily on their domestic market are now rapidly seizing the non-China market by expanding supply to global automakers, establishing overseas production bases, and leveraging the price competitiveness of LFP batteries. By contrast, combined battery usage by South Korea's three major cell makers — LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Samsung SDI — in the non-China market fell 8.9% year over year to 86.1 GWh. Their combined share tumbled 10.4 percentage points from 37.6% to 27.2%. While the overall non-China market grew more than 20%, the South Korean trio actually contracted, widening the gap with Chinese rivals. The decline in North American usage was a particularly significant drag on their performance. South Korea's materials industry is strengthening its LFP response beyond its traditional high-nickel focus while preparing LMR and solid-state technologies as next-generation counteroffensive cards. The growing share of entry-level EV models and the explosive growth of the AI data center-driven energy storage system (ESS) market are creating structural demand for low-cost, high-safety materials. Defending with LFP, Counterattacking with LMR POSCO Future M is placing the most aggressive bet on LMR cathode materials. The LMR cathode jointly developed by POSCO Holdings' Future Technology Research Center and global automakers and battery companies has successfully completed pilot production, and the company is now working to secure mass-production technology. LMR reduces the use of expensive nickel and cobalt while increasing manganese content, lowering costs while maintaining high energy density. It also has the advantage of being compatible with existing NCM cathode production facilities, relatively reducing the burden of new factory investment. At the same time, the company is rapidly expanding its LFP footprint in Pohang. It plans to convert part of its existing Pohang NCM cathode lines to LFP and begin supply by the end of this year, while its joint venture CNP New Material Technology is building a dedicated LFP plant with a maximum annual capacity of 50,000 tons at the Pohang Yeongilman Industrial Complex, targeting mass production in 2027. It is a two-track strategy: defending the current market with LFP while targeting the next mid-to-low-priced EV market with LMR. SK Securities analysts Park Hyung-woo and Jung Young-hwan noted, "Precursors and anode materials are expected to become bottlenecks in the LFP landscape next year. POSCO Future M is well positioned to respond flexibly to this." EcoPro BM is raising its commercialization readiness on both the LMR and solid-state fronts. Its LMR cathode has entered the final validation stage targeting mass production for key customers. The company has optimized its processes so that existing ternary cathode production lines can be used as-is, enabling rapid conversion to mass production once orders are confirmed. For solid-state batteries, the company is operating a solid electrolyte pilot line, and its products are undergoing quality verification by major battery makers. The mass-production line design is also complete, with construction to begin once customer demand is confirmed, targeting mass production as early as 2027. Eugene Investment & Securities analyst Han Byung-hwa said, "Next-generation materials including solid-state and LMR have advanced to the stage just before mass production. Once the market recovers from the EV chasm, the company will be able to secure growth engines simultaneously in both existing high-nickel and new battery chemistries." L&F Builds the Broadest Portfolio L&F, based in Daegu, is pursuing the broadest portfolio strategy. Building on its experience as the world's first to mass-produce ultra-high-nickel 95% cathodes, the company has entered LFP mass production and is expanding its next-generation product lineup to include high-voltage mid-nickel, LMR, all-solid-state battery (ASSB), and sodium-ion battery (SIB) cathodes. It unveiled next-generation materials at major exhibitions this year and is in concrete discussions with select customers on mass production of solid-state battery cathodes. Its current primary focus is LFP. The company is pursuing commercialization of LFP cathodes at a level unprecedented in South Korea in the second half of this year, while developing proprietary iron phosphate (FP) technology and a precursor-free manufacturing process to build a supply chain with reduced dependence on China. The plan is to add LMR and solid-state cathodes going forward, transitioning to a structure that addresses everything from high-nickel to mid-to-low-priced and next-generation markets. L&F recently signed a mid-to-long-term LFP cathode supply contract with Samsung SDI worth 1.6067 trillion won (approximately $1.2 billion), followed by a 160 billion won (approximately $119.0 million) supply deal with SK On. artigo.texto: China’s Gotion High-Tech has secured 6GWh of battery storage capacity in Saudi Arabia’s first utility-scale battery storage programme, accounting for around 75% of the total tender. Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) awarded the company three core sites of Al Muwayah, Haden and Al Kahafa, under the G1 project. Each site will provide 500MW/2GWh, giving the project a combined capacity of 2GW/8GWh and a value of around $1.16 billion. The award represents the first international large-scale deployment of Gotion Grid, the company’s utility-scale energy storage system. Gotion says the system has been engineered for extreme environmental conditions, with an operating range from -30°C to 55°C. Its thermal management system is designed for desert conditions and maintains full output during sandstorms, while reducing high-temperature degradation by 40% compared with conventional systems. The ESS has a stated design life of 25 years, compared with an industry average of 15–20 years. The company says this can avoid mid-life equipment replacement, an important consideration for build-own-operate contracts requiring more than 20 years of operation. The system also incorporates an AI-powered battery management system for intelligent dispatch, proactive safety warnings and lifecycle diagnostics. All three Gotion sites can be remotely operated and connected to Saudi Arabia’s 380kV backbone grid. The award adds to the company’s growing presence across the Middle East and North Africa, where it says its regional footprint is around 9GWh. This includes a 1.5GWh BESS in Egypt alongside a planned 3GWh local manufacturing base, and a 1.2GWh project in Morocco with ACWA Power. Globally, the company’s cumulative system-level storage projects exceed 10 GWh, including a 281MW/843MWh solar-storage project under construction in Australia that is expected to enter commercial operation in the first half of 2027. With G1 awarded and G2 underway, the Saudi programme could provide further opportunities as renewable deployment and grid stability requirements increase. Image: Gotion BESS. Credit: Gotion

artigo.texto: Elon Musk's data centers are pushing out a family that's owned land since "before people of color were allowed to" On a 2-acre property in Mississippi, 52-year-old Krystal Polk's family lived off the land for generations, raising chickens and pigs, growing onions and herbs and trading their peaches for pears. The land, on the border with Tennessee in the city of Southaven, was her family's survival, Polk said. "We lived a very simplistic life," she told CBS News. While life there may have been simple in Polk's view, the circumstances surrounding her home rarely ever were. Her family acquired the property "before people of color were allowed to have land," she said, and it's been passed down for four generations. When Polk's parents first moved in, they discovered "KKK" scrawled at the bottom of the hill of their property, she said. Holding on to the land was made more difficult a year ago when a noisy neighbor appeared across the street — a power plant so loud, it drove the family away. Since then, the land has sat mostly empty, occupied only by an unrelenting hum. The plant, which is powering Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the Memphis area, has sparked backlash from Southaven residents concerned about noise and air pollution. A petition by the resident-run Safe and Sound Coalition calling to shut down the power plant has over 1,400 signatures. Polk said she remembers when she could hear the birds chirping at her family home. Now, she said the plant's "constant roaring" lingers in her ears even after she leaves. "It's like you're in the middle of the airport where the planes are taking off, but they never take off," she said. SpaceXAI, formerly known as xAI, recently said in a July press release that it is investing millions of dollars in sound walls and silencers with "advanced quieting technologies" around the plant. Southaven residents have told CBS News that one sound wall installed so far has provided little reprieve from the noise. "We gathered there" Over the course of two years, Musk has expanded his footprint in the Memphis region starting with the construction of his Colossus 1 data center just north of Southaven in 2024. By January 2026, two more data centers were announced. This July, Musk quietly confirmed the construction of another local data center, "Minihard," in a reply to a post on his platform X. Musk's SpaceXAI projects will total more than $20 billion in investments to Southaven, which Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves said in a press release will "bring amazing opportunities to its residents for generations." But for Polk, the development has meant a new kind of strain on her family. "We don't know the future," she said. "So we're not sure what to invest into it." Polk moved away from the family home after getting married, and for years, it bounced between relatives. It was where Polk churned her own ice cream as a child, held her rehearsal dinner when she got married and hosted the holidays each year. "We gathered there and we thanked God for what we had," she said. "It was always a celebration." She planned to return as a retiree and eventually pass the property down to her children. But now, those plans have been put on hold. Apart from the "24/7" noise, Polk said she and her family have asthma and are concerned about fumes from the gas turbines at the plant. "I'm afraid that we will be the ones that everyone looks back on and says, 'Hey, remember they tried to tell us that these things were hazardous to our health and causing harm,'" Polk said. "I'm afraid that we're going to be those casualties." The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and other groups sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in April, alleging that the plant "emits significant amounts of harmful pollutants." In June, SpaceXAI filed a motion to dismiss the case, and the Department of Justice also moved to intervene and dismiss the case. The Justice Department said in a statement that the matter "concerns national security and Mississippi's lawful action regarding permitting" and that the NAACP's lawsuit "could hinder the War Department's use of AI for national defense." CBS News reached out to SpaceXAI multiple times for comment and has not heard back. The company has entered into an agreement with the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality that includes removing the 69 temporary turbines at the plant and replacing them with 41 permanent turbines over the course of a year. But a study conducted by EmPower Analytics Group found that the plan to install dozens of gas turbines would increase air pollution in the area and would be concentrated in communities that are disproportionately Black. The study was commissioned by the Southern Environmental Law Center, which is co-counsel for the plaintiffs in the NAACP's lawsuit against xAI and MZX Tech. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality said in a statement that it doesn't comment on "third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation" and that it "remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations." MDEQ said that as part of the permitting process, MZX Tech was required to demonstrate that the proposed facility would not violate air quality standards. Still, residents are not convinced. Shannon Samsa, a 27-year-old physician assistant living in Southaven, is concerned about the plant's impact on her community's health. She's become an outspoken advocate against the plant, speaking up at city meetings and leading the Safe and Sound Coalition as its director. "It's not just my neighbors, it's not just my family and friends, it's my future patients," she said. "It's also a huge healthcare issue." artigo.texto: First Look: West Feliciana’s data center Parish president says tax revenue and transparency were priorities in deal WEST FELICIANA PARISH, La. — A data center under construction in West Feliciana Parish will serve as a processing hub for Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence model when it opens in just over a year. Water usage and energy consumption are top concerns as Louisiana positions itself for a national A.I. build-out. Size and scope The data center will measure roughly 10 football fields long once completed. Projects of similar size elsewhere in the country have raised concerns over groundwater usage and rising electric bills for nearby residents. Parish President Kenny Havard said protecting the community against those issues was part of his goal. The developer Hut 8 is partnering with Entergy for a new substation on site that will power the project, fully funded by the company. On top of that, the data center will be using a closed-loop coolant system that replaces the need for tapping groundwater. “One was water and the other was taxes, we wanted to make sure everyone in West Feliciana Parish pays the same taxes whether you’re big industry or the local grocery store,” Havard said. Tax revenue and community funding Havard said the data center will bring in $90 million in tax revenue every year. That money will go back into the community through funding, infrastructure projects and rebates on property taxes. “We would have to build 6,000 houses to pay for one mile of road the way the taxes are distributed so this allows us to keep the quality of life that makes West Feliciana such a special place,” Havard said. Transparency in the deal process The agreement was made without non-disclosure agreements or private negotiations, according to Hut 8’s Hailey Miller. “Working with the parish president and parish council, a deal was done in public view, in open, transparent and for everyone to have input and consideration,” Miller said. State and political reaction Gov. Jeff Landry has pointed to more than $200 billion in industrial development during his time in office. Landry pushed back against critics of transparency in deals, who say secrecy is sometimes necessary to attract large projects. “Everything we’ve done to change policy in this state has been in the public so the public gets to grade us on that, this just says when these companies come in we don’t tell anybody they are coming in. Why? Because we want to keep them here!” Landry said. Many of Hut 8’s data centers across the country mine bitcoin rather than power artificial intelligence models like the one at River Bend. That connection brought bitcoin investor Donald Trump Jr. to the site. “People understand generally that you need AI, its the space race of 2026, its a really big deal there’s another reason why China is funding 200,000 bots on Twitter trying to vilify AI, its not because its bad for America, its because America leading is bad for China and we need to do that while still addressing the needs of the community,” Trump Jr. said. Construction timeline About 1,200 construction employees are working day and night to complete the project. The data center is expected to be operational by the end of 2027. artigo.texto: Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig B. Johnson’s recent defense of data centers presents a fundamentally flawed economic development narrative (“When judging data center incentives, don’t ignore the revenue,” Sept. 30). While he touts short-term revenue, his ledger ignores the long-term, structural costs these facilities impose on local communities. First, using job creation to justify data center subsidies is a sleight of hand. While $1.2 billion in construction permits is impressive, they’re short-term bumps in revenue. This masks the reality that data centers are essentially ghost towns once operational. They consume prime industrial real estate but employ only a small number of permanent staff members, meaning taxpayers are often subsidizing millions of dollars per permanent job. Furthermore, major tech companies rely on specialized, traveling construction crews. The economic multiplier effect largely leaves town when the concrete dries. Second, the mayor’s claim that Class 6B incentives don’t harm homeowners ignores the basic math of Illinois property taxes. When a data center’s assessed value is artificially slashed, the local tax levy doesn’t shrink. The burden simply shifts onto everyone else, driving up residential tax bills for 12 to 24 years. This is compounded when tax increment financing districts are used, such as the one Elk Grove Village created for the Vulcan Construction Materials site in 2022. While the mayor suggests schools stand to benefit, it should be noted TIFs divert new tax revenue to pay for project costs for up to 23 years, meaning schools and municipal services wait decades for the promised windfall. Worse, once operational, these operators frequently deploy aggressive legal teams to appeal their property assessments year after year, forcing municipalities to spend taxpayer dollars defending their own revenue. Finally, while data centers don’t add students to classrooms, they place enormous, invisible strains on our infrastructure. Their construction increases wear and tear on local roads from construction vehicles. Once completed, they are massive consumers of municipal water for cooling and place unprecedented demands on the electrical grid. These upgrades are eventually paid for by everyday ratepayers. Subsidizing heavily automated server farms that hollow out industrial parks, generate negligible employment and strain our grid is not the “pro-growth” policy our region needs. — Donald Guisinger, Strong Towns Oak Forest Will data centers pay fair share? Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig B. Johnson in his op-ed completely ignores the higher cost of water and electricity that his constituents will face subsidizing these monstrosities. Will he demand that data centers pay their fair share for the high volume of water and electricity they use? Or is it too late? — Ken Perez, Wood Dale Department of Justice’s credibility I am hopeful that with the recent focus on the “Broadway Six,” in particular due to the reporting of Tribune reporter Jason Meisner, the public will begin to understand that when prosecutors go unchecked, victims face extreme consequences for which they have very little redress. In recent years, the credibility of the U.S. Department of Justice has fallen to all-time depths as it has been weaponized against those with whom it disagrees, both political and nonpolitical, taking up positions not supported by the facts or even the law. This is on full display in Chicago. U.S. District Judge April Perry is being asked to consider disciplinary action against the U.S. attorney’s office for alleged misconduct in the grand jury investigation and prosecution of the “Broadview Six.” No justice system can function effectively if there are components within it that disregard the rules and mechanisms of checks and balance. The public relies upon this system to keep prosecutors in line, to punish misconduct and to send a message that misconduct cannot be tolerated. Misconduct is anathema to justice. — Michael Segal, U.S. National Title Services, Chicago Celebrate parking meter deal? No. Regarding Chicago’s parking meter deal, what a demonstration of ineptness and buffoonery — this is the 2026 edition of the 2008 disaster. As a Chicago resident and motorist, I have one simple question: Will it cost me less to park? Nothing I’ve read about this deal — a transfer fee, percentages of a future sale and net income, a “city wallet” program and 25- to 50-cent-per-hour surcharges for non-Chicagoans — suggests that it will benefit the great majority of drivers in Chicago. And as for the City Council’s self-congratulation over the deal: same-o, same-o. A final question: Where’s Mayor Brandon Johnson? — John Mjoseth, Chicago I support the arts in the city Thank you for the editorial regarding suburbanite parking in Chicago ( “Chicago may charge suburbanites more to park. How neighborly,” Oct. 1). I am a suburbanite who supports the Joffrey Ballet, the Chicago Architectural Center and the Art Institute with subscriptions to their events. I do attempt to take public transportation when I can, but that is not always feasible, since as the editorial mentions, timing for public transportation is sparse on the weekends. For example, a friend and I have Joffrey season tickets for its Sunday matinees, but trying to coordinate Metra and “L” train times with that is difficult. Although driving into town is stressful, we brave it by going down early to enjoy a great lunch at Italian Village before the show. And yes, we look for cheap parking because we’re already supporting businesses and cultural events. Also, because we are both in our 70s, we cannot park too far from the venue just to find an extremely cheap parking lot; we would then need a taxi to get to the Lyric Opera House. In short, considering our generous monetary contributions to the city of Chicago, asking us to pay more for parking really takes the cake! — Dianne Casuto, Lake Forest Naperville’s welcoming vibe Thank you for say

artigo.texto: Evanston Councilmember Krissie Harris is proposing a formal one-year moratorium on data centers across the city following vocal backlash to a proposal in her Second Ward, telling the RoundTable she wants to complete “due diligence” to understand data centers’ potential impacts before any are approved. Harris’ plan calls for a one-year halt on any city-level zoning approvals and incentives for data centers “pending infrastructure and grid audits,” and will go to the council’s Referrals Committee on Monday, Oct. 12. The measure is co-sponsored by Councilmembers Clare Kelly (1st Ward), Bobby Burns (5th), Parielle Davis (7th) and Matt Rodgers (8th), immediately giving it majority support from the nine-member council. Property owner Reed Beidler submitted a zoning analysis application last month to establish a “computer processing center” at 1265 Hartrey Ave. in the Second Ward. Beidler proposes filling about 20,000 square feet of space in the former factory building and envisions a large organization renting out most of the data center’s processing power alongside other businesses with smaller needs. Like other data center projects around the country, the Evanston proposal drew intense backlash from residents and local organizations, including at Second Ward and City Council meetings last month. Harris said in a phone interview Sunday she hasn’t met with Beidler about his proposal, but that she felt the city could be “bombarded with requests” in the near future and feels an official pause is warranted. “I don’t want it to be one of those [situations] like we say yes because it’s small, looks like it’s … not a big deal, and then it just balloons into this thing that we cannot control,” Harris said. “I want to make sure … we’ve investigated that thoroughly.” While Beidler argued the data center should be approved as a permitted use under existing zoning, city staff disagreed and found it doesn’t fit under any use already listed in the city code, meaning a zoning amendment is necessary for approval. City Manager Luke Stowe called this a “de facto moratorium” during the last council meeting and invited council direction to “pursue an official moratorium,” which Harris is now taking up. previous coverage Harris said she’s particularly concerned about the center’s potential impact on water and power use, sharing that she has a stake in the outcome since she lives just a few blocks away. “If I get more information and we, as a council, feel good about it, we can change that moratorium,” Harris said. “But it gives us, at least, time to just breathe and figure it out.” She also referenced potential state legislation that could impact projects in Evanston and elsewhere. The Illinois General Assembly failed to pass a comprehensive data center bill during its spring session, and Gov. JB Pritzker is pushing hard for lawmakers to take action during the veto session, which will run from Nov. 17 to 19 and Dec. 1 to 3. Asked if the four councilmembers co-sponsoring her proposal feel the same as her, Harris said some are less sure a moratorium is needed but are trusting her judgment, especially since the current proposal is in her ward. “Some people are kind of like, ‘Oh, I don’t know, but I’ll follow your lead on this,’ and so I’m appreciative of my team members saying OK,” Harris said. “I’ve got to be accountable for this, and if it’s going somewhere else [in another ward], I got to trust if somebody says, ‘I need more time to really make a good decision.'” The moratorium will need to be approved by City Council before it can officially take effect. Depending on how much time staff need to develop the proposal into full legislation, it could advance as soon as the council’s next meeting on Oct. 12 or at a future meeting in the coming months. As of Oct. 1, staff are still waiting for Beidler to submit additional information about his proposal before directing him to propose a zoning amendment.

artigo.texto: Aplicações de inteligência artificial presentes no mundo físico, como carros autônomos, vão demandar baixíssima latência, o que deve incentivar a construção de pequenos data centers nas pontas das redes. Na opinião de Ivo Ivanov, CEO da DE-CIX, uma das maiores operadoras neutras de troca de tráfego de Internet, data centers modulares serão implantados por toda parte no futuro. Em entrevista para Mobile Time em Lisboa, durante o evento Atlantic Convergence, o executivo falou também sobre os planos da DE-CIX para o uso de satélites; processamento multiagêntico; capital digital distribuída; e a operação no Brasil. Mobile Time – Como a demanda por aplicações de IA física, de baixíssima latência, vai remodelar o mercado de data centers? Ivo Ivanov – Sim, a IA física, e especialmente a inferência de IA, ditará como a infraestrutura deve ser construída. Bilhões, provavelmente trilhões de dólares, estão sendo investidos mundialmente, não apenas em modelos de texto ou para produzir vídeos engraçados, mas em agentes treinados para realizar processos industriais em diversos segmentos. Eles têm uma característica em comum: são extremamente sensíveis ao tempo real. Isso significa que precisam de uma comunicação muito rápida entre o sistema de inferência e o dispositivo — seja um robô, um carro ou outro equipamento controlado por agentes de IA. A distância entre o sistema de inferência e o robô não pode exceder dois a três milissegundos. Isso equivale a cerca de 200 quilômetros. Essa é a realidade física; não podemos alterar a velocidade da luz. Portanto, a infraestrutura digital que atende a esses dispositivos precisa se aproximar deles. Os robôs não entrarão nos data centers; os data centers precisam se aproximar dos robôs, dos carros e das outras instalações. Teremos que desenvolver uma infraestrutura o mais próxima possível dos usuários, sejam eles seres humanos ou dispositivos. Então teremos mais data centers menores na borda (edge) das redes? Exatamente. Data centers modulares precisarão ser implantados literalmente por toda parte, suportados por tecnologias de transmissão como fibra ou redes móveis — o 5G Advanced já está em progresso e, em breve, esperamos o 6G —, além da conectividade satelital. Como a demanda por menor latência impactará o tráfego de internet, considerando que haverá mais agentes acessando a rede do que seres humanos? O tráfego será muito mais localizado. Ainda teremos deslocamento de tráfego devido ao treinamento e aplicações de interesse global — como telenovelas, que não podem ser restritas a um único país —, mas, na era da IA, o processamento precisa ser local. Isso é excelente para a soberania, pois mantém os dados protegidos dentro da jurisdição. Recentemente, a Anatel propôs para o leilão da faixa de 6 GHz, que as operadoras invistam em data centers de borda. Qual sua opinião sobre isso? É uma ideia excelente. Deve ser executada o quanto antes. Operadoras de telecomunicações frequentemente reclamam que a conectividade se tornou uma commodity, transformando-as em “dumb pipes”. Você acredita que elas poderiam reverter esse cenário com a IA? As teles poderiam ter um papel diferente nesta era da IA? Depende da gestão. É fácil reclamar; é melhor definir novas ideias. Os tempos de incumbência acabaram; hoje é a era da digitalização, dos serviços digitais, da colaboração e da parceria. O mercado exige ofertas complementares de valor agregado, combinando forças de diferentes parceiros. A ideia de que “eu sou o dono do mercado” era popular nos anos 70, mas não funciona mais. Clientes corporativos esperam agilidade e opções de conectividade de ponta que incluam inovações, novos provedores de serviços e de GPU. Um exemplo é a nossa oferta de acesso a provedores de GPU como serviço. Uma empresa automotiva ou um banco pode construir sua comunidade privada de GPU como serviço e treinar o quanto desejar, utilizando agentes em um ambiente privado. Chamo isso de “roteamento multiagente”, onde diferentes provedores de agentes podem ser combinados em um ambiente seguro com interconexão direta. É o novo multi-cloud. Você mencionou o roteamento multiagente em março. Essa solução já foi lançada ou implantada em algum lugar? O conceito e a tecnologia estão prontos e operacionais no Brasil. Estamos aguardando a entrada dos provedores de agentes e serviços. Estamos apenas no início desta nova era e queremos estar um passo à frente. Acredito fortemente que o Brasil possui todas as condições para se tornar um enorme universo de IA. Fale sobre os planos da DE-CIX para o uso de satélites. É uma nova esperança para aumentar a disponibilidade de serviços digitais, especialmente em regiões hoje subatendidas, onde é difícil implantar fibra. Acredito na conectividade via órbita também como uma solução redundante e complementar para mercados estabelecidos, protegendo a infraestrutura contra ataques ou desastres naturais, já que não há vento ou tsunamis no espaço. Além disso, é uma extensão relevante para soluções de defesa e segurança para governos e corporações que lidam com dados críticos. Nosso objetivo é construir o primeiro ponto de troca de internet no espaço, o “De-CIX Space-IX“, permitindo o roteamento entre diferentes operadoras em órbita, interconectando data centers espaciais com instalações de nuvem, inferência de IA e sinalização quântica. Quais satélites serão utilizados? Serão geoestacionários? Utilizaremos satélites em órbita baixa (LEO) e ultra-LEO. Não estamos falando de construir enormes fazendas de servidores no espaço, mas de módulos do tamanho de cabines telefônicas. Eles não servirão para treinamento de IA, mas são ótimos para inferência, que é mais leve, e para cache de conteúdo. A vantagem é a latência reduzida. Quando espera a primeira implantação? Dependemos da prontidão dos módulos de data center das empresas de satélite. Como há muitos projetos bem financiados, isso acontecerá muito em breve.
