artigo.texto: There's A Big Problem With Building Data Centers Underground Data centers have become the necessary evil we all have to deal with for the sake of rapid AI advancements. However, they're problematic, and most regular people are very much against them for obvious reasons. Data centers are so loud that their noise may carry for a mile, and they may also drive up local utility costs, take up precious land, and waste water reserves. So, why not put them underground? That would theoretically solve most of these issues. If only it were that easy. Though the UAE has considered fortifying its own data centers with guns and burying some underground, that's basically a means-to-an-end solution due to the dangers of Iranian attacks. In normal circumstances, the project would just end up costing more, as you'd need to create a strong shell that can take the weight of all the soil above. That's not even accounting for drilling, insulation, and waterproofing. Then, these facilities wouldn't be easy to scale up because it would require additional blasting or drilling, meaning companies are unlikely to put down the cash for something that will make people happy at an additional cost and loss of scalability. The biggest challenge, though? Maintaining solid air quality. When you're underground, complications with the air can add up quickly. As such, the data center would require some expensive systems to get the same environment that's practically a given above ground, so add the expensive humidity control and ventilation system to an already hefty bill. In the end, it's all much more feasible than making orbital data centers, but far too tricky for companies to seriously consider it. In which case can building underground work? The good thing about underground data centers, theoretically at least, is they'd save operators money on cooling because there's no sunlight. They could also resort to geothermal energy, so it wouldn't waste as much electricity. It truly seems like a magic bullet when you lay it all out — if only the construction costs weren't so high. Well, new AI data centers can be built inside existing underground structures, which automatically solves the brunt of the issues, and we have real-world examples that attest to how well it can work. For instance, there are a few data centers operating out of abandoned mines in the U.S., which makes them super secure by design. The best part is, they're not expensive to build and maintain. Plus, the temperature in the mines, and more importantly, the humidity, are sometimes bordering on perfection. Unfortunately, there aren't that many mines that are both close to a power source and already have the necessary connections, so it's not as if companies can move to the mines in droves, Fallout style. In a perfect world, profits would be secondary to preservation of our natural resources. Ultimately, the reason why there isn't a huge push to find better solutions is that it's simply more expensive than just taking a piece of land and constructing a data center. Plus, the alternatives we have so far are all difficult to pull off. Data centers aren't built in Antarctica because it's too remote and doesn't have a power grid, despite the naturally cool air making it seem like a perfect solution for the AI boom. Until we figure something out, we'll all probably have to contend with effects of new facilities popping up, sadly.

artigo.texto: AI infrastructure is reshaping more than the servers inside data center racks. As GPU-intensive workloads push rack densities higher, Eaton, NVIDIA, Google, Microsoft and others are advancing direct-current power architectures designed to deliver more power with fewer conversion stages and less physical infrastructure. For solution providers, integrators and infrastructure partners, that shift could broaden the scope of AI infrastructure projects. Moving from traditional AC designs toward rack-level 48/50V DC and, eventually, 800 VDC affects not only power distribution but also backup systems, cooling, rack design and serviceability â forcing partners to think about those systems as an interconnected architecture rather than separate infrastructure purchases Why AI is pushing data centers toward DC power The broader demand curve explains why power architecture is receiving so much attention. The International Energy Agency projects global data center electricity consumption will roughly double from 485 TWh in 2025 to approximately 950 TWh in 2030, with consumption from AI-focused data centers growing even faster. Inside the facility, higher density creates another challenge: current. Delivering more power at lower voltages requires greater current, which can mean larger conductors, greater losses, and more heat. Higher-voltage DC distribution can reduce current while eliminating some power-conversion stages between the utility feed and IT equipment. 48V, 50V and 800 VDC architectures take shape The transition is already visible at the rack level. Open Compute Projectâs Open Rack V3 ecosystem uses 48V DC busbar architectures, while Eatonâs upcoming 50V DC system is designed for both conventional 19-inch racks and 21-inch ORV3 racks, with power ratings ranging from 33 kW to 132 kW per rack. Eaton specifically identifies system integrator builds, enterprise and colocation environments, AI/HPC deployments and OCP migration projects among its intended applications. The next step could be significantly larger. NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft are collaborating through OCP to establish 800 VDC as an open architecture for next-generation AI data centers. NVIDIA says moving from todayâs lower-voltage rack architectures toward 800 VDC reduces current, copper requirements and cable bulk while allowing fewer power-conversion stages. More than 80 equipment and infrastructure companies are participating in the ecosystem. Eaton is among them and is developing 800 VDC infrastructure alongside its current ORV3 and 50V DC offerings. DC power creates a broader infrastructure role for partners That does not mean every enterprise data center is about to switch to 800 VDC. In fact, the emerging market is better understood as a continuum. Existing facilities can continue operating AC infrastructure while introducing DC closer to high-density compute. Rack-level 48/50V systems offer another path, while 800 VDC is being positioned for future AI environments with substantially greater density. NVIDIAâs own roadmap explicitly includes hybrid architectures designed to introduce 800 VDC power racks into facilities with existing AC infrastructure. For the channel, architectural knowledge is increasingly important. Partners accustomed to selling servers, UPS systems, racks and power distribution as relatively discrete infrastructure categories may need to approach AI projects more holistically. Power density affects distribution, backup requirements, cooling, physical rack design and serviceability, meaning infrastructure decisions become interconnected earlier in the design process. Eaton similarly argues that power and cooling need to be planned together as AI densities rise. The opportunity, then, isnât simply selling a different power product. It is helping customers determine when existing AC infrastructure remains sufficient, when rack-level DC makes sense, how to design hybrid environments, and when future workloads justify a more fundamental architectural shift. Hyperscalers may be setting the direction today. Channel partners should be watching closely for when their customers begin following it.

artigo.texto: Lightstar is doubling down on Illinois, expanding its community solar and battery-storage footprint across the state As the solar energy industry continues to advance, there is an abundance of companies that are looking to be involved in shaping the sector and future energy production strategies. The United States continues to be among the leading solar energy-producing countries in the world, competing with other powerhouses like China. The big advantage that the U.S. has over most nations is its access to great wealth and resources, which increases its chances of producing the most sophisticated energy projects. As of late, Lightstar expressed that it is doubling down on Illinois, expanding its community solar and battery-storage footprint across the state. Lightstar continues to advance the United States solar energy sector Lightstar’s approach to project execution means that it is in a position where it is likely to always be in the running to be appointed to spearhead massive projects. Its reputation and previous success also mean that it is in a good position to be selected by countries other than the U.S.A., where it is based. The company’s current commitment is to building sustainable, high-value assets that support local economies and farming legacies for decades to come. Lightstar is doubling down on Illinois, expanding its community solar and battery-storage A recent press release from Lightstar Renewables, a national leader in community solar generation, announced that it is set to continue the expansion of its active Illinois portfolio across three service lines: community solar, agrivoltaic solar, and battery energy storage systems (BESS). Lightstar is known for contributing to Illinois not just in terms of energy facilities but also toward the economic progression of the state. The company develops these projects on private land throughout Illinois, guiding landowners through an origination-to-cooperation process that preserves land ownership, delivers fixed long-term lease income, and keeps land in productive use. Lightstar’s permitted, market-ready project pipeline offers an answer for landowners, municipalities, and clean energy partners looking for companies that develop community solar and battery energy storage in Illinois. Interestingly, Illinois has become one of the most active clean energy markets in the Midwest, driven by the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) and its target of 100% clean energy by 2050. Supportive programs continue to quicken deployment: the Illinois Shines Adjustable Block Program opens its 2026-2027 cycle on June 1, 2026, and the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA) expands community solar while permitting co-location of projects up to 10 MW on a single parcel or adjacent properties. A general overview of Illinois’ clean energy landscape as of 2026 With the year now coming to an end, industry experts are expecting it to be a record-breaking year for Illinois, considering the number of projects that have materialized. In 2026, Illinois enacted statewide energy storage legislation establishing new storage projects, emphasizing demand for reliable, grid-responsive infrastructure. Lightstar actively monitors these programs and evaluates every Illinois project for eligibility. This track record has positioned the company as one of the state’s most determined and experienced community solar and battery storage developers. Gaining an insight into the future of community solar and battery storage There has been a common theme of community and battery storage projects leading the charge in the solar sector in recent years. Kyle McAdam, Senior Development Manager at Lightstar, stated the following: “We believe that clean energy development must work hand-in-hand with the local community. By protecting the land, engaging with incredible students right here in Fulton County, and now investing directly in the VIT athletic field, we ensure this project leaves a positive, lasting mark on the region for decades to come.” Lightstar is well respected as a trailblazing community solar developer that was founded on the principles of advanced design and strategic project development. As a proud American company, Lightstar is a trusted partner for landowners, focusing on community solar and agrivoltaics projects that preserve agricultural land while generating energy. artigo.texto: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said the measures establish rules covering the development, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon projects and lay the groundwork for a credible domestic carbon market. Environment Assistant Secretary for Integrated Management System and Information Systems Daniel Darius Nicer presented the policies at a high-level roundtable on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. Market roadmap The first policy adopts the Philippines’ Readiness in the Voluntary Forest Carbon Market Roadmap for 2026 to 2030. The roadmap sets the national direction for policy development, measurement, reporting and verification systems, data management and registry readiness—all considered important in determining whether carbon credits can be reliably measured and tracked. “To date, the Philippines, through its Department of Environment and Natural Resources, issued two major policy instruments that establish the foundations of a credible forest carbon market directly addressing private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways,” Nicer said. He spoke during the “Shaping High-Integrity Carbon Markets” session convened by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development during Climate Week NYC. Project safeguards The second policy establishes national guidelines for the creation, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon credit projects. The rules require environmental safeguards, compliance with Free, Prior and Informed Consent and benefit-sharing with communities. They also mandate transparent project registration, which the DENR said would help reduce reputational and delivery risks for carbon credit buyers. “For the Philippines, carbon markets—both voluntary and compliance pathways—are central to our strategy for accelerating mitigation and unlocking climate finance,” Nicer said. “But for markets to function, the private sector needs clarity, predictability, and confidence that the credits they purchase are real, additional, and backed by strong governance.” Carbon framework The forest policies form part of wider government efforts to develop the country's carbon market infrastructure. Nicer cited Department of Energy guidelines for renewable energy projects, the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework and the rollout of the Philippine National Carbon Registry. The registry is intended to provide accounting and traceability of carbon credits and prevent double counting. Nicer said Philippine policies are also being aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement through bilateral arrangements, including an implementation agreement with Singapore and the Joint Crediting Mechanism with Japan. Looking ahead to the COP31 climate summit, he called for stronger international guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. “High-integrity markets should not only accelerate global ambition, but also deliver real, measurable mitigation outcomes that directly benefit and reach the communities, ecosystems, and sectors that need them most,” Nicer said. — Ed: Corrie S. Narisma

artigo.texto: Origin plans a 500 MW, 4,942 MWh battery at Eraring Origin proposes adding a 500 MW storage system at the Eraring power station site. The project, which still has to clear the approval stages, would target commercial operations between early and mid-2031. Origin is proposing Eraring BESS North, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with a discharge capacity of 500 megawatts (MW) and an accessible energy storage capacity of approximately 4,942 megawatt hours (MWh). The project would require up to 22 hectares on Origin-owned land at the Eraring power station site in New South Wales. It is located in the suburb of Eraring, within the Lake Macquarie local government area. A combined facility of about 1,200 MW The project would operate alongside the existing Eraring BESS, part of Origin's generation portfolio. The existing project received State Significant Development consent SSD-15950052 on 10 May 2022. According to the project document, the two facilities together would provide a combined maximum registered active power capacity of around 1,200 MW and an accessible storage capacity of approximately 8,600 MWh, subject to detailed design. The storage sector is drawing other projects from Europe to Asia. ML System secured two energy storage contracts in Poland worth â¬4.1 million, while Vena Energy won a 46.8 MW battery storage contract in Japan. In power transmission, Iberdrola expanded its alliance with GIC in Brazil. Company Origin Energy: company profile ORG A regulatory pathway ahead Origin expects the project to qualify as a State Significant Development (SSD) under Section 2.6(1) of the 2021 Planning Systems state environmental planning policy. It would be subject to Part 4, Division 4.7, Section 4.36 of the 1979 Environmental Planning and Assessment Act, as an electricity generating works development whose estimated cost exceeds the set thresholds. An environmental impact statement will have to be prepared in line with the Secretary's Environmental Assessment Requirements. The existing BESS received a "not controlled action if undertaken in a particular manner" decision on 19 July 2021 under the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 [2021/8956]. The new project includes approximately 11 hectares of vegetation clearance outside the previously assessed disturbance area. Origin says it reviewed alternative locations and consulted key stakeholders and the community to limit impacts. Components and timeline The project covers construction, operation, decommissioning and rehabilitation as far as reasonably practicable. It would include transmission works to connect the BESS to TransGrid's switching station, along with an extension of the existing substation. It also provides for extended water supply infrastructure, new electricity buildings, internal access roads and new operation and maintenance compounds. Construction is expected to start in 2028 and last about 2.5 years, with commercial operations anticipated in early to mid-2031, subject to approvals. Operations would run for up to 25 years, with a possible extension. Works would be staged, including site establishment, then earthworks for the battery compound and transformer yard, and finally civil and foundation works. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 % Origin presents the project as a response to the National Electricity Market's shift from coal toward variable renewables, supported by dispatchable storage capacity. The New South Wales roadmap targets at least 12 gigawatts of renewable generation and 2 gigawatts of long-duration storage by 2030. artigo.texto: O setor elétrico brasileiro vive um momento de transformação acelerada com a crescente demanda por infraestrutura digital de alto desempenho. A aprovação do regime de incentivos fiscais (Redata) aqueceu o mercado, mas acendeu um alerta sobre a capacidade da rede em suportar a carga exigida pelos novos centros de processamento de dados. Segundo a redação do Imprensa 24h, o desafio atual não é a falta de geração, mas sim a eficiência no escoamento dessa energia para os polos de consumo. Resumo da Notícia - Investimento previsto de R$ 120 bilhões em linhas de transmissão até 2035. - Projetos de data centers somam 10 GW em contratos e pedidos firmes de conexão. - Brasil desperdiçou 33 milhões de MWh em 2025 por falta de malha para escoar energia. - Descompasso temporal: obras de transmissão levam 7 anos, enquanto data centers ficam prontos em 18 meses. Para quem acompanha as notícias de Sergipe, o estado se posiciona estrategicamente nesse cenário, dada sua relevância na matriz energética nacional. A integração de fontes renováveis, especialmente as vindas do Nordeste, depende diretamente da robustez do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). As informações de Aracaju reforçam que a estabilidade elétrica é o principal atrativo para indústrias que buscam se instalar na região, transformando a infraestrutura em um motor de desenvolvimento local. O papel estratégico da transmissão no cenário nacional A malha de transmissão é o elemento que conecta a abundância de energia renovável produzida no Nordeste aos grandes centros industriais e tecnológicos do Sudeste e Sul. Sem essa conexão, o potencial de geração solar e eólica acaba subutilizado. Em 2025, o fenômeno conhecido como curtailment — a limitação da geração por falta de espaço na rede — resultou no corte de 33 milhões de MWh, volume comparável ao consumo anual de todo o estado do Rio Grande do Sul. A expansão da rede é, portanto, a solução para evitar esse desperdício e garantir que a energia limpa chegue aos novos polos de tecnologia. O mercado de data centers, que exige alta confiabilidade e grandes volumes de carga, monitora de perto os leilões de transmissão. Para mais detalhes sobre como esses movimentos impactam a economia regional, acompanhe no portal Imprensa 24h. Descompasso entre demanda tecnológica e obras de infraestrutura Um dos pontos críticos identificados pelo setor é a diferença de ritmo entre a construção de um data center e a entrega de uma linha de transmissão. Enquanto uma unidade de processamento de dados pode ser erguida em cerca de um ano e meio, o ciclo completo de uma obra de transmissão — que envolve planejamento, licenciamento ambiental pelo Ibama e construção — leva, em média, sete anos. Esse intervalo exige uma coordenação fina entre órgãos como a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) e investidores privados. A sinalização antecipada da demanda é fundamental para que os traçados das linhas sejam definidos antes que a necessidade se torne uma urgência crítica, garantindo que o crescimento tecnológico não seja freado por gargalos logísticos de energia. Planejamento decenal e aportes bilionários na rede O governo federal, por meio do Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2035), já traçou a rota para mitigar esses riscos. A previsão é de que sejam investidos aproximadamente R$ 120 bilhões na próxima década. Esse montante será destinado à construção de 30 mil quilômetros de novas linhas e ao acréscimo de 82 mil MVA em capacidade de subestações em todo o território nacional. Onde há linha de transmissão, há crescimento econômico e geração de empregos. A consolidação dessa infraestrutura permitirá que o Brasil não apenas atenda sua demanda interna, mas se torne um hub global para serviços de inteligência artificial e armazenamento de dados em nuvem. Fique por dentro das últimas notícias em Sergipe e no Brasil acessando nossa página inicial. Mantenha-se atualizado com as principais movimentações do setor de energia e tecnologia. Continue bem informado navegando pelas editorias do Imprensa 24h, o seu portal de referência para notícias de Sergipe e do mundo.

artigo.texto: Carmakers, including Hyundai Motor, are pouring their efforts into developing Solid-state Battery. A Solid-state Battery replaces the liquid electrolyte (a substance that conducts electricity) in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a nonflammable solid, reducing fire risk, and can extend driving range with higher energy density, earning it the nickname "dream battery." According to the auto industry on the 4th, Manfred Harrer, head of R&D (president) at Hyundai Motor Group, told reporters at the HMG Tech Talent Forum 2026, held in San Jose, California, for two days starting on the 17th of last month (local time), that he would continue investing in the development of Solid-state Battery. Harrer said, "We must take part in the race to develop Solid-state Battery," and "We will continue investing to secure leadership in this technology, which represents the biggest game-changer in the car industry." Hyundai Motor has recently been pursuing a "battery internalization strategy," under which it develops battery cell specifications and architecture in-house while outsourcing mass production to external manufacturers. In particular, if it succeeds in developing Solid-state Battery, considered a next-generation cell, ahead of battery makers, it could gain the upper hand in price negotiations and is expected to significantly increase electric vehicle sales. A single charge of a lithium-ion battery provides a driving range of about 500–600 km. Because this battery fills the space between the cathode and anode with a liquid electrolyte, it is vulnerable to fire risk and has limits to increasing energy density. By contrast, Solid-state Battery uses a solid electrolyte to improve heat resistance and durability, and increases density to extend driving range to more than 1,000 km on a single charge. For this reason, Solid-state Battery is seen as a "game changer" that could shake up the electric vehicle market. China's battery manufacturers, which mass-produce low-cost LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries, are currently encroaching on the global EV market. However, if Solid-state Battery, which eliminates fire risk and dramatically improves energy efficiency, is commercialized, analysts say the strengths of China-made batteries that emphasize "value for money" could also fade. Hyundai Motor is not the only carmaker betting its future on Solid-state Battery. Toyota, which had been cautious about EV development, is working with energy company Idemitsu Kosan and others with a goal of starting mass production as early as next year. Honda has also teamed up with U.S. battery startup QuantumScape and recently embarked on Solid-state Battery development. Chinese carmakers are also joining the race to develop Solid-state Battery. BYD, China's largest EV manufacturer, said it plans to begin pilot production of vehicles equipped with Solid-state Battery in the first quarter of next year. It also unveiled a roadmap to start mass production in 2028 and move into full-scale popularization after 2030. Stella Li, senior vice president at BYD, said in an interview with a local outlet in Valencia, Spain, last month, "We will unveil the first model equipped with Solid-state Battery technology next year." However, Li did not mention a specific mass-production schedule or launch timing for general consumers. Because of this, the auto industry interprets the Solid-state Battery-equipped vehicle Li mentioned as a test vehicle to validate the technology, rather than a mass-production model. Geely Automobile Holdings, a major Chinese car group, said in a five-year strategy released early this year that it would complete in-house development of Solid-state Battery within the year and begin verification. Other EV manufacturers are also working on Solid-state development, and some corporations, including Li Auto, are said to have produced samples. Still, a "cautious view" is emerging in the battery industry that it is difficult to predict when Solid-state Battery will actually be commercialized. The technology is hard to develop and the manufacturing process is demanding, and initial mass production is likely to be priced at a high level, making it unlikely that the battery market landscape will change in a short period. Zeng Yuqun, chairman of CATL, the world's largest battery maker, said at the World Economic Forum annual meeting in Dalian, China, in June, "If we divide the maturity of battery technology into stages 1 through 9, Solid-state Battery is only now at stage 4." At the time, China's battery industry also projected that the manufacturing expense for Solid-state Battery would exceed three times the cost required to make a battery with a 500 km range. President Manfred Harrer also drew a line under mass-production prospects, saying, "I expect high-performance vehicles equipped with Solid-state Battery to hit the market within five years, but I do not think the issue of materials and supplies expense can be resolved within that period."

artigo.texto: Renewable energy company Zelestra has entered into two new power purchase agreements (PPAs) with EDP to add four-hours of battery storage to existing solar plants in Spain. The deals will bring about 462MW-hours (MWh) of battery capacity to 181MW-direct current (MWdc) of solar power across two sites, Pedroso in Seville and Valkyria in Castilla-La Mancha. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. Under the new agreements, Zelestra will install a 25MW battery energy storage system (BESS) with around 100MWh of capacity at Pedroso, which already operates a 31MWdc solar plant. At Valkyria, a 90.45MW (approximately 362MWh) BESS will be added to the existing 150MWdc solar facility. EDP serves as the current offtaker for both sites. EDP global energy management CEO Pedro Neves Ferreira said: “At EDP, innovation goes beyond deploying renewable generation. We are continuously developing new solutions that combine technology, market expertise and flexibility assets to unlock greater value from clean energy. “By integrating storage with renewable generation, we can enhance system resilience, improve efficiency and accelerate the electrification and decarbonisation of the economy.” With these transactions, Zelestra and EDP’s joint portfolio in Spain now comprises four hybrid projects, with more than 1GW-hour of contracted storage capacity. The companies’ cooperation began in 2025 with the country’s first combined solar and BESS PPA, involving a 170MWdc solar installation and 400MWh of storage at Trujillo, Extremadura. Earlier, in 2024, the companies signed another agreement for a 160MWh BESS at the 50MW Pizarroso plant in Cáceres, reportedly the first PPA in Spain to hybridise an operational solar plant. Zelestra Spain CEO Jaime Burguete said: “Zelestra and EDP have built something together that is unique in the Spanish market: a commercial partnership that is unlocking large-scale storage capacity that will benefit the wider energy system. “These four hybrid projects show that energy storage is bankable in Spain, and we expect this segment of the market to be the main growth area in the years ahead. “It also means that every megawatt-hour moved into the evening or early morning is clean power the system would otherwise have had to find elsewhere.” In July 2026, Zelestra and EnBW signed a long-term tolling agreement for a 300MW share of a planned battery energy storage project in Emilia-Romagna, Italy.

artigo.texto: CATL in Debrecen is expanding its workforce CATL’s Chinese battery factory in Debrecen is increasing its workforce: now that trial production of battery cells has begun following the ongoing production of modules, the workforce will be expanded from the current 2800 to 3300 by the end of the year. Qin Liang, the chief operating officer of the Debrecen battery factory, said at a press event showcasing the plant that the third production line has already been launched in the module manufacturing operation that began in 2024; since then, more than 500.000 modules have been produced, powering approximately 10,000 vehicles across Europe. Module production has generated 100 billion forints in revenue for the company to date, on which taxes were paid in Hungary, the director noted. The Debrecen plant is designed to meet the needs of European automakers, producing nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, the director said, adding that the Debrecen plant ensures long-term stability, jobs, and new business opportunities for the region. Qin Liang noted that the cell factory received its operating permit in August, fulfilled all the conditions specified in the permits, and began trial production of battery cells on the first two production lines on September 22. Production will expand soon Following a few technical adjustments, the company will begin cell production on the other two lines as well. During the trial run, CATL experts are continuously monitoring the equipment, the quality and safety of the products, and full compliance with regulatory requirements. The new cell factory has a maximum annual capacity of 40 gigawatt-hours, all of which has already been fully reserved by customers. It was also announced at the press conference that the first phase of the project has now been completed at a cost of approximately 900 billion forints, and that once full capacity is reached, 4000 people will be employed at the plant. In response to a query from MTI, however, they confirmed that the entire project is planned in three phases; the total investment of 3000 billion forints will provide jobs for 9000 people and have an annual capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours. They added that they are open to negotiations with the government regarding the project, noting that they had an agreement for 129 billion forints in state subsidies to implement the first phase. They plan to rely on local labor Shen Feng, CATL’s managing director responsible for European operations, said at the press conference that cell production began in Germany in 2022; initially, the ratio of Chinese to German workers was 40 to 60 percent, but today 90 percent of the workforce is German. In Debrecen, the ratio of Chinese to local workers is currently 50–50 percent; according to their plans, the proportion of Hungarian workers will reach 90 percent by 2030. Qin Liang added that they will launch a supplier campaign in October to increase the involvement of local businesses in production. He noted that they currently have more than 300 local suppliers, 80 percent of whom are from Debrecen and the surrounding region. The plant manager also addressed the Debrecen plant’s water consumption, which is a particularly sensitive issue in Debrecen. He noted that they have developed water-saving technology—specifically, a cooling tower—that drastically reduces the plant’s water requirements. It was announced at the press event that the company will continuously provide the authorities with information on the plant’s water and energy consumption as well as its emissions, and that monitoring data will be published every two months so that the public can also access it. artigo.texto: An experimental solid-state battery continues to work perfectly at −40 °C, a temperature at which cold normally severely reduces the performance of this type of battery. In a battery, tiny charged particles called lithium ions must move between two electrodes. This movement makes it possible to store and then release energy. In conventional batteries, the ions pass through a liquid. Solid-state batteries seek to replace this liquid with a solid material. The problem appears particularly when it is very cold. The ions then move much more difficultly through certain solid materials. The battery loses efficiency and may eventually stop working properly. Researchers at Tsinghua University in China therefore sought to facilitate this movement. To do so, they added a conductive substance called polyaniline to their material. Its role is to modify the distribution of electrical charges inside the battery. This helps more lithium ions move, even when the temperature drops sharply. The researchers also observed another effect. When in contact with lithium, the new material promotes the formation of a thin protective layer. This reduces certain undesirable reactions that progressively degrade the battery during charging and discharging. In practice, the small batteries made in the laboratory worked between −40 °C and 45 °C. This resistance to cold could be useful for devices used in winter, in polar regions or at high altitudes. However, these performances still need to be verified with much larger batteries. In another test, the cells exceeded 13,000 charge and discharge cycles. However, these impressive figures should be put into perspective, as laboratory conditions are specific and actual service life depends in particular on the battery's size and how it is used. The next step is therefore to manufacture cells more similar to those used in real devices. The researchers will need to verify whether their material retains its properties with larger batteries and more energy-storing material.

artigo.texto: In Festus, Missouri, a town that gave Donald Trump 67 percent of its vote, residents have filed to recall the mayor and three council members over a $6 billion data center. In New York, a Democratic governor has signed the first statewide moratorium on new ones. Across seven states, at least 33 recall campaigns are targeting as many as 58 local officials for the same reason, and the reason is not a party. It is a building. That makes data centers the rarest thing in American politics right now: an issue where the folding chairs in a red county and a blue one are filled with people saying the same words. They are not saying "no technology." They are saying the box across the road raises their power bill, drains their water, takes the farm, and was negotiated behind a nondisclosure agreement before anyone in town knew its name. In Luther, Oklahoma, the moratorium passed only after word leaked that the mayor had been in closed talks with a developer for months. The anger is not about servers. It is about being handed a decision that was already made. Here is what almost nobody in those rooms has been told, and what both sides would want if they knew it. Every data center is a furnace. Nearly all the electricity that goes in comes out as heat, and in every facility in America that heat is thrown into the sky through cooling towers, at the owner's expense. The newest liquid-cooled halls release it as warm water, exactly what a greenhouse wants in January. A two-and-a-half-acre greenhouse on that water grows on the order of 695,000 pounds of fresh produce a year with no boiler and nothing burned. Write into the rezoning that at least 15 percent of it is covenanted to the host community, to the schools, the food bank, the farm store on the road, and one building's waste feeds about 400 of its neighbors, year-round, in towns where the nearest winter tomato has traveled 1,500 miles. Put the fish house on the same loop and homes on radiant floors at the end of it, and the campus that was going to bury the farmland has built a farm. Notice what that covenant is. It is the opposite of an NDA. It is a promise, written into a public document, that a resident can read at the county clerk's office and hold the developer to at every hearing for the life of the project. The reason people in Festus and Luther and Prince William County feel the technology is being forced on them is that the terms were hidden. A heat covenant puts the terms on the wall. And it is the one proposal that does not ask either side to give up what it wants. Conservatives want the tax base, the jobs, and the AI race won; Loudoun County, Virginia, collected $1.2 billion in data-center property taxes this year and cut its residential rate for the tenth straight year, so the money is real. Progressives want communities protected, ratepayers held harmless, and food grown close to home; a farm on the fence line does all three. Michelle Obama and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. agree on almost nothing, but they agree that Americans should eat real food grown nearby. A data center that powers the cloud and feeds the town is not a compromise between the two camps. It is both of them, in one site plan. Virginia noticed first. This spring its General Assembly passed the first law in the country directing the state to put data-center waste heat to use, and the Senate vote was 39 to 0. In a legislature that spent the same session at war with itself over data-center tax breaks, that is what an issue looks like when it belongs to no one. Wall Street has noticed too. Lenders now weigh local opposition and permitting status before financing a campus, and local resistance blocked or delayed some $130 billion in projects in the first quarter of this year alone. The developer who arrives with a public covenant and a farm in the first phase of the site plan is not being generous. He is de-risking his loan. So, to the organizers running recall petitions and the officials facing them, to the governors weighing a pause and the developers hoping they don't: there is a yes here that both of you can sign. Put one question in every rezoning, in public, in writing: where does the heat go, and what share of what it grows stays here? A moratorium buys a town a year. A covenant buys it a farm. The fight in Festus and the fight in Albany are the same fight, and this is the same answer. Andrew Potter is the founder and CEO of Intelligent Harvest, a Lynchburg, Virginia company that develops greenhouses and community farms powered by data-center waste heat.

artigo.texto: Just days after Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman declared that a gigantic proposed data center in the city “must be stopped,” a spokesman for the company behind the project said the 860,000-square-foot facility should be “evaluated based on verified facts.” Coffman posted his thoughts about Vantage Data Centers’ Trident project late last week on Facebook, saying the project “must not go forward.” His post followed a City Council meeting last week during which hundreds of people living in neighborhoods near the site came out to decry the data center, which would be among Colorado’s largest. Residents voiced concerns about the facilities’ large water use and electric consumption, along with worries about noise. Several cities in the state, including Denver, Thornton and Commerce City, have imposed temporary bans on new data centers as larger and larger — or hyperscale — facilities have sprouted. Hyperscale data centers are engineered for large-scale workloads and are at the heart of the burgeoning data-hungry artificial intelligence sector. The Aurora council narrowly rejected a moratorium on data centers in August, but the city is hammering out rules for the facilities, including a just-passed ban on the use of water-hungry evaporative cooling systems by any business across the city. Aurora, Coffman wrote, “must explore every available option, to include my calling the proposed Trident data center up for a public hearing and then asking the members of City Council for a ‘no’ vote to stop it from being built.” The mayor said he would do this regardless of any litigation Vantage might level against the city. Mark Freeman, vice president of global marketing for the Denver-based company, wouldn’t answer a question from The Denver Post about whether Vantage might take legal action against Aurora should the city kill its project. Freeman said the company’s proposed data center on a 108-acre site just inside the E-470 beltway at East 48th Avenue would use a closed-loop system that would require one initial 600,000-gallon injection of water and 2,200 gallons a day as part of ongoing operations — “about half the amount used by a similarly sized office building.” It would be designed to use 334 megawatts of electric power, he said, to run both “cloud and (artificial intelligence) workloads.” By comparison, nearby Denver International Airport uses 45 megawatts of electric power. Freeman also said the site plan will comply with all noise ordinance standards in the city, with sound levels from the facility expected to be “similar to a typical office building or a dishwasher running in the next room.” Aurora Councilwoman Amy Wiles, whose ward covers the proposed Trident site, recognizes the city is in a tricky position given that Vantage has been following the city’s approval process for more than a year and the site where it wants to build its center is zoned for that use. “I wish this had been done sooner — I brought it up months ago,” she said Monday. “Ideally, when (the area) was first re-zoned, I wish it had been looked at a bit more closely to balance the need for business while also prioritizing our residents.” Wiles said she still has questions about low-frequency noise and vibrations from data centers and how those might affect nearby neighbors. Coffman, in his Facebook post, said the project received preliminary administrative approval without a public hearing “because a data center is a permitted use under the current zoning.” The parcel Vantage wants to develop was zoned “airport district” by the city four years ago — a designation that permits businesses like data centers. The mayor is not against data centers per se, but he said more scrutiny needs to be applied in terms of where they are built. “We need to update our development code so that we have realistic distances between residential developments and data centers,” he told The Post in a text response to questions Monday. “The city of Aurora has a land mass a little larger than Denver and about a third of our city is undeveloped, so there definitely are suitable locations for data centers that are far enough away from homes.” Get more Colorado news by signing up for our daily Your Morning Dozen email newsletter.

artigo.texto: A agenda climática deixou de ser um capítulo isolado dos relatórios de sustentabilidade e passou a orientar decisões de investimento, contratos com fornecedores e a reputação de marcas inteiras. Nesse cenário, dois termos se tornaram onipresentes nos comunicados corporativos — Carbono Neutro e Net Zero. Embora sejam tratados como sinônimos, eles descrevem compromissos com profundidade, prazo e rigor bem diferentes. Segundo o Monitor do Mercado, entender essa distinção não é apenas uma questão semântica: é o que separa uma meta climática consistente de uma promessa sem lastro ou, em casos mais graves, de greenwashing. O que diferencia Carbono Neutro de Net Zero Ser Carbono Neutro significa que uma empresa equilibra a quantidade de dióxido de carbono que emite com uma quantidade equivalente removida ou evitada em outro lugar. Na prática, funciona como uma conta que precisa fechar em zero: de um lado ficam as emissões medidas; do outro, as compensações. Essas compensações costumam vir da compra de créditos de carbono ligados a projetos de preservação florestal, energia renovável ou captura de metano, de investimentos em reflorestamento — que aproveitam a capacidade das árvores de absorver CO₂ durante a fotossíntese — ou ainda de aportes em fontes de energia limpa. O ponto central é que a neutralidade de carbono não exige, necessariamente, que a empresa reduza suas próprias emissões antes de compensá-las. Ela pode manter o nível atual de emissão e simplesmente pagar pela compensação em outro ponto da cadeia. Trata-se de um modelo mais acessível e mais rápido de alcançar, o que o torna útil como primeiro passo, mas limitado quando tratado como meta final. Net Zero: escopo mais amplo e exigência de corte real O conceito de Net Zero representa uma evolução desse compromisso e parte de uma lógica bem mais exigente. Em vez de olhar apenas para o CO₂, a meta abrange todos os gases de efeito estufa, incluindo metano, óxido nitroso e hidrofluorcarbonetos. Além disso, a compensação só entra em cena depois que a empresa tiver cortado a maior parte possível de suas próprias emissões ao longo de toda a cadeia de valor. Isso envolve normalmente três frentes de emissão, conhecidas como escopos. O escopo 1 cobre as emissões diretas geradas por fontes controladas pela própria empresa, como frota própria, caldeiras e processos industriais. O escopo 2 está ligado à energia elétrica comprada. Já o escopo 3 abrange as emissões indiretas espalhadas por toda a cadeia de valor, da matéria-prima ao descarte do produto, e costuma ser a fatia mais difícil de endereçar. Só depois de reduzir drasticamente essas três frentes — e não apenas uma parte delas — é que se admite compensar a fração remanescente, considerada tecnicamente inevitável no estado atual da tecnologia. O que a SBTi considera uma meta Net Zero legítima A Science Based Targets initiative, conhecida como SBTi e principal referência internacional para validar metas corporativas de clima, reforça essa distinção. De acordo com a avaliação apresentada, uma meta Net Zero só é considerada legítima quando a empresa demonstra uma trajetória de corte real de emissões, geralmente entre 90% e 95% do total, antes de recorrer a qualquer compensação para o restante. O Carbono Neutro não segue esse mesmo nível de exigência. Esse padrão vem sendo continuamente aperfeiçoado. Em 2026, a SBTi atualizou seu padrão internacional de metas Net Zero corporativas, reforçando critérios sobre como as empresas devem comprovar, monitorar e reportar essa redução real ao longo do tempo — um sinal de que o mercado está fechando o cerco contra metas anunciadas sem lastro técnico. Hoje, milhares de empresas ao redor do mundo já têm metas climáticas validadas por esse tipo de padrão, número que cresce ano a ano à medida que reguladores, investidores e consumidores cobram mais transparência. Por que a diferença importa para quem investe É essa diferença de rigor, alcance e prazo que explica por que uma empresa pode se declarar carbono neutro já hoje, com relativa facilidade, comprando compensações suficientes para equilibrar suas emissões de CO₂ em um recorte específico da operação. Uma meta Net Zero, por outro lado, costuma levar décadas de reestruturação de processos, fornecedores e tecnologia para se tornar realidade. Justamente por essa diferença de complexidade e percepção pública, quanto mais a sustentabilidade influencia decisões de compra, contratação e investimentos, maior é a tentação de usar esses termos de forma solta. Uma empresa pode anunciar neutralidade de carbono comprando créditos de projetos de qualidade duvidosa, sem nunca reduzir de fato sua produção — o que, na prática, não resolve o problema climático, apenas o desloca no papel. O que observar além do rótulo Por isso, especialistas recomendam observar não o rótulo usado pela empresa, mas o plano por trás dele. Existe uma meta de redução real, com etapas intermediárias verificáveis? A compensação é usada como complemento ou como substituto da redução? Há transparência sobre os escopos 1, 2 e 3? Segundo a análise, essas perguntas dizem mais sobre o compromisso climático de uma empresa do que qualquer selo isolado. Na prática, os dois conceitos não são excludentes e costumam ser etapas de uma mesma jornada. Em um mercado onde compromissos ambientais se multiplicam, entender a diferença entre Carbono Neutro e Net Zero tornou-se essencial para interpretar o que as empresas realmente estão fazendo para enfrentar as mudanças climáticas. A neutralidade pode representar um ponto de partida relevante, mas o Net Zero é o que revela o grau de ambição e transformação envolvido. No fim, a pergunta mais importante não é qual termo aparece no relatório, mas quais ações concretas estão sendo implementadas para tornar essa promessa uma realidade. O texto é assinado por Renata G. Moreno, especialista em Direito Ambiental e Regulatório, sócia e fundadora do escritório Renata Franco Sociedade de Advogados, e por Luara Teixeira, estagiári

artigo.texto: Stevens Point starts data center conversation STEVENS POINT, Wis. (WSAW)— The city of Stevens Point added an item to Monday’s planning commission meeting for a public discussion on data centers, with city leaders saying they want the community to drive how the city reacts if or when a data center looks to move in. Current zoning rules “At this point, if a data center wanted to build one of those massive things, what safeguards would there be for the community?” said Alder Mary Kneebone, Stevens Point Planning Commission. The planning commission says there isn’t much. As of now, data centers can’t be built in residential or commercial zoning districts. They would be allowed in the city’s industrial zoning districts. Developer interest While the city hasn’t had conversations about constructing a data center, data centers have reached out to the city about interest levels. “It was a conversation that, we didn’t talk about it,” said Jarod Kivela, director of community development, Stevens Point. “They have been, I guess not responded to until we have this conversation.” Public concerns During public comment, many expressed concerns over the environmental impacts in a city built on the outdoors. “If I saw that there was a data center being built in Stevens Point and I was a prospective college student...like, if I went back to when I was looking just out of high school...I would’ve said no. I wouldn’t have come here,” Reemus said, an environmental studies student. Other concerns were lack of economic impact after data centers are built, as well as want of transparency between the city and the people if a project were to start. Federal candidates weigh in The issue of data centers is more of a city and state-level policy, but it can be influenced at the federal level. Both candidates for the 7th Congressional District are hearing from voters about them. “We are way behind in regulating this entire sector,” said Fred Clark, (D) 7th Congressional District candidate. “We need to treat AI like we treated nuclear energy in the 1950s. And, and the federal government is the only game in town to make that happen.” “This is where I think it’s so important to have young faces involved in this rise of AI,” said Michael Alfonso, (R) 7th Congressional District candidate. “You know, AI has the ability to put out of work so many workers. But I actually think if done properly, it can actually empower workers.” Clark says the state needs to regulate how they’re built. Alfonso adds that should include supplying their own power, not use up waterways and let local leaders make the decision. artigo.texto: Chinese battery giant CATL has reached a key milestone in proving the durability of its technology, demonstrating impressive laboratory analysis results. The prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells tested, which have been operating without interruption for almost fourteen years, have retained about 85 percent of their original energy capacity. The cells analyzed are part of the world's first large-scale energy storage facility, the 63 MWh Zhangbei, which began operation in 2011 and even provided clean energy for the 2022 Winter Olympics. The complete decommissioning of the facility in the summer of 2025 has allowed engineers to subject the components to detailed chemical and physical destructive testing. Over 50 samples taken from the original cells reveal remarkable material durability: the anode and cathode layers have retained perfect geometry, and the graphite shows no structural defects or critical signs of aging. An interesting detail is the fact that not a single cell from this manufacturer had to be replaced over the entire 14-year cycle. The test results open up new perspectives for the so-called “second life“ of industrial batteries. According to the company's experts, the retired cells have a resource for about 1,000 more complete charge and discharge cycles. This makes the components fully suitable for reintegration into smaller secondary storage systems for at least another decade. The current findings reconfirm the expectations from the control tests carried out on the ninth year of the facility's launch. LFP technology is also gaining in importance in the automotive sector. While these chemistries are inferior in specific energy density to nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) alternatives, they offer significantly lower manufacturing costs and unrivaled durability under extreme temperature and operating conditions. The achieved lifespan solidifies the technology's position as a key pillar for the future of sustainable mobility and green energy.

artigo.texto: Tech giants are trying to win over communities that oppose data centers as they pour billions into the infrastructure powering their AI ambitions. Amazon’s latest approach is to invest more than $1 billion over five years in job training, free community college, and energy efficiency upgrades. Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman announced the Built Together program in an Oct. 2 corporate post that also defended the company’s data center build-out. He compared the build-out to public benefit projects such as the interstate highway system, and wrote that Amazon understands communities’ “apprehension” about data centers. Still, he wrote, the more than 100 proposed data center moratoriums under construction could sideline the U.S. from the AI race. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman wrote. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.” Amazon isn’t the only hyperscaler trying to make the data center boom easier for host communities to accept. Microsoft pledged in January to cover the electricity and grid costs tied to its facilities, and Meta said it invested more than $550 million in water and wastewater infrastructure in its data center communities. What Amazon is offering Built Together targets common complaints dogging data center projects—that they raise energy bills, strain local infrastructure, and don’t deliver enough lasting benefits to residents. Those concerns have become harder for hyperscalers to ignore. New York imposed a statewide moratorium on new large data centers in July, and opposition spread to major data center markets like Virginia, where only 35% of people said in March that they’d be comfortable with a new facility being built there, according to a Washington Post and Schar School poll. Amazon itself is facing resistance in Loudoun County, Va., where officials are objecting to a proposed 800,000-square-foot data center project on the former George Washington University Virginia Science and Technology campus. Built Together is Amazon’s attempt to answer those objections with more direct benefits for host communities. Amazon said it will cover students’ remaining community college costs after financial aid for certain certificates and associate degrees, including programs in HVAC, fiber optics, and IT, and estimates more than 300,000 students could gain access over five years. The company also said its skilled trades centers plan to train up to 100,000 workers a year for jobs with Amazon and its construction partners by the end of 2028. The company also plans to fund energy efficiency upgrades for more than 30,000 homes and more than 300 schools and community buildings. Local officials and community groups will help steer funding toward projects such as roads, parks, fire equipment, affordable housing, and food assistance. “Working with county officials and trusted community organizations, we will identify the highest-impact investments and provide annual funding with transparent reporting on outcomes,” Garman wrote. “This is not Amazon deciding what communities need—it is Amazon providing resources and letting communities decide.” Amazon is also using the Built Together announcement to push back on some causes of the backlash. Garman wrote that data centers are unfairly blamed for higher electricity bills and water use, and that aging grids are at fault for rising energy bills in some states. “In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived,” he wrote. He also said Amazon’s average data center uses less than 13,000 gallons of water per day and said the facilities deliver tax revenue and construction jobs to host communities. In St. Joseph County, Ind., Amazon estimates it will pay more than $3 billion in taxes over the same period, compared with $1.2 million that the land’s previous use would have generated.

artigo.texto: Adani Green Energy Ltd. (AGEL), one of India’s largest renewable energy company, increased its operational battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity to 6.63 GWh at Khavda, Gujarat. The company expanded the capacity from 3.55 GWh in June 2026 and now accounts for more than half of India’s approximately 12.6 GWh of operational BESS capacity. According to AGEL, the milestone establishes Khavda as the world’s largest operational battery energy storage installation at a single location, with 6.63 GWh of operational capacity. BESS Expansion Supports Khavda Renewable Energy Project AGEL achieved the 6.63 GWh milestone within 14 months of starting BESS construction at Khavda. The latest capacity addition took just 10 months to commission from the beginning of construction. The battery storage system forms an integral part of AGEL’s renewable energy development at Khavda, where the company is developing a 30 GW renewable energy plant across 538 sq km of barren land. The company said its 6.63 GWh BESS can store enough clean energy to power around two million homes for a day. It can also support peak electricity demand in cities such as Nagpur, Patna and Vizag for several hours. Moreover, the storage capacity is equivalent to the battery capacity of more than 150,000 mid-sized electric vehicles and can store enough energy each day to meet almost twice the estimated daily electricity requirement of the Delhi Metro. Battery Storage Strengthens Renewable Power Reliability “Reaching 6.63 GWh of operational battery storage in just 14 months is a significant milestone for AGEL and India’s clean energy transition,” said Sagar Adani, Executive Director, Adani Green Energy Ltd. He added that storage at this scale can make renewable power firmer, more reliable and dispatchable when the electricity grid requires it. The BESS uses lithium-ion battery technology, supported by energy management systems (EMS) and automated telemetry. These systems manage charging and discharging, optimise battery performance and enable the facility to provide grid services. AGEL Targets More Than 10 GWh of BESS Additions Looking ahead, AGEL plans to add more than 10 GWh of BESS capacity during FY 2026–27. The company is also targeting 50 GWh of energy storage capacity over the next five years. In addition, AGEL is pursuing pumped storage projects (PSPs) as part of its broader strategy to develop large-scale renewable power that can deliver firm and dispatchable electricity. AGEL Expands Renewable Energy Portfolio AGEL develops, owns and operates utility-scale grid-connected solar, wind, hybrid and energy storage projects. The company currently has an operating renewable energy portfolio of 20.76 GW, along with 6.63 GWh of operational BESS capacity across 12 states. As reported by pv-magazine-india.com, AGEL aims to reach 50 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030, supporting India’s broader decarbonisation and clean-energy transition goals.

artigo.texto: Sistema de armazenamento de energia solar para varanda com duas tomadas de alimentação de reserva: análise do SigenMate 2700 Ultra Sistema complexo de armazenamento para varanda e casa. O SigenMate 2700 Ultra é um sistema de armazenamento tudo-em-um para instalações solares em varandas, oferecendo até 18,8 kWh e 4.000 Wp. A nossa análise revela o desempenho do sistema na prática e onde surgiram problemas. Marcus Schwarten (traduzido por DeepL / Ninh Duy) Publicado 🇺🇸 🇩🇪 ... Veredito do teste do SigenMate 2700 Ultra: Controle rápido, mas também problemas Com base nos nossos testes, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra da Sigenergy oferece uma interessante solução tudo-em-um para sistemas solares de varanda. No nosso teste, gostámos particularmente da elevada potência de entrada fotovoltaica distribuída por quatro MPPTs, da construção de alta qualidade e do assistente de IA na aplicação abrangente. O controlo da injeção na rede também é rápido e preciso - quando a ligação ao contador inteligente funciona. Também nos deparámos com alguns outros problemas menores, mas estes deverão ser corrigíveis com uma atualização de software. No geral, um sistema de armazenamento tudo-em-um mais do que sólido para sistemas solares de varanda, cuja capacidade pode aumentar até 18,8 kWh ao longo do tempo, mas que não oferece qualquer margem para além dos seus 800 W de potência de injeção na rede. Pro Contra Preço e disponibilidade Na Alemanha, o preço de venda recomendado do SigenMate 2700 Ultra é de 1.199 euros (com IVA de 0% na Alemanha). O preço de venda recomendado da bateria de expansão SigenMate BAT 2700 é de 899 euros. Os produtos estão disponíveis diretamente no fabricante, mas também podem ser encomendados em retalhistas como a Amazon ou a Tepto. Com o crescimento dos sistemas solares para varandas e dos pequenos sistemas fotovoltaicos, cada vez mais fabricantes estão a lançar no mercado soluções tudo-em-um que combinam inversores, MPPTs e armazenamento. Além dos nomes habituais, como Anker Solix, EcoFlow e Zendure, existem também soluções de fabricantes menos conhecidos. Entre estas encontra-se o SigenMate 2700 Ultra, que está disponível há alguns meses. A empresa por trás deste produto, a Sigenergy, não é uma recém-chegada, mas até agora tem atuado sobretudo na área dos sistemas fotovoltaicos de maiores dimensões. A nossa análise do SigenMate 2700 Ultra revela como o seu sistema compacto de armazenamento de energia para todos se comporta na prática e como se compara com a concorrência. Specifications Equipamento e instalação: Sistema de armazenamento para sistemas solares de varanda Uma análise das especificações acima mostra que o SigenMate 2700 Ultra tem muito em comum com o Anker Solix Solarbank 3 Pro do ano passado. Também oferece uma capacidade de bateria LiFePO₄ de pouco menos de 2,7 kWh (6.000 ciclos de carga, garantia de 10 anos). Se necessário, esta capacidade pode ser ampliada até 18,8 kWh com seis baterias de expansão BAT2700. Isso deve ser mais do que suficiente para a grande maioria dos lares - não só para sistemas solares de varanda, mas também para armazenamento de energia doméstico. Com uma potência de entrada fotovoltaica de 4.000 W, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra supera até ligeiramente o Solarbank 3 Pro, oferecendo também 4 MPPTs. Isto é vantajoso, pois não só permite ligar até oito painéis solares sem qualquer problema, como também proporciona condições ideais para painéis com diferentes orientações e sombreamento. A potência de saída é limitada a 800 watts, como é habitual num sistema solar de varanda. Além disso, estão disponíveis diretamente no dispositivo duas tomadas de alimentação de emergência com uma potência de saída contínua de 1,400 W e uma potência de pico de 1,800 W. Estas funcionam independentemente da rede elétrica e, por isso, também funcionam durante uma falha de energia (se a bateria estiver carregada). Quando ligado à rede elétrica, é possível atingir até 3,600 W (bypass). Além da entrada solar, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra também pode ser carregado a partir da rede elétrica com uma potência de até 1,400 W. Alguns outros sistemas no mercado oferecem potências máximas de saída e de entrada superiores. No entanto, estas capacidades são suficientes para um sistema solar de varanda. Tudo isto está alojado numa robusta estrutura metálica. A qualidade de construção da unidade que testámos é excelente e transmite uma impressão de produto de gama alta, inclusive em termos de design. Graças à classificação IP66 e à proteção contra corrosão C5-M o sistema está bem equipado para utilização no exterior. Foi concebido para suportar temperaturas entre -20 °C e 55 °C e pode ser aquecido através de uma manta de aquecimento, de acordo com uma programação ou automaticamente, se necessário. No entanto, já gera uma quantidade considerável de calor por si só sob carga. O dispositivo pesa cerca de 29 kg e exige alguma força para o deslocar até ao local de instalação. As duas pegas embutidas à esquerda e à direita facilitam o transporte. As dimensões de 46.0 x 27.5 x 22.5 cm são bastante compactas para um sistema com cerca de 2.7 kWh. Quando combinado com uma ou mais baterias adicionais, a torre torna-se proporcionalmente mais alta. O material de montagem para o fixar a uma parede não está incluído. A embalagem inclui apenas um cabo de alimentação com ficha Schuko, uma chave para desligar os painéis solares e um manual. To get started, simply connect the power cable to the corresponding port on the side of the SigenMate 2700 Ultra and to a power outlet. The system can then be switched on. To generate your own solar power, at least one solar panel must also be connected to the four inputs (MC4 sockets). These are located on the top under a somewhat cheap-looking plastic cover, rather than on the side (as with many competitors). This makes access and cable management easier (the cables run out toward the back). However, the spacing between the individual connectors is quite tight. App & operation: AI assistan

artigo.texto: Technology group Wärtsilä has secured an order to supply a 282 MW onsite power solution for a data center project being developed by a major US independent power producer in the United States. The power plant will operate with 15 Wärtsilä 50SG engines. The order demonstrates the growing need for fast-deployable onsite power solutions as grid constraints, lengthy connection timelines, and accelerating AI-driven electricity demand create power availability challenges for new data center developments. The order was booked by Wärtsilä in Q3 2026. The project further strengthens Wärtsilä's proven position in the rapidly growing U.S. data center power market. It marks the company's seventh data center-related order in the United States, bringing the total power capacity sold by Wärtsilä for U.S. data center applications to more than 3 GW. The customer selected Wärtsilä engine-based solution for its ability to provide large-scale power capacity on efficient timelines while enabling phased expansion as computing demand grows. The Wärtsilä 50SG engines provide high efficiency in demanding operating conditions, feature a closed-loop cooling system that minimises water consumption compared with conventional thermal power alternatives and offer flexibility to convert the engines to run on future fuels. For data center developers, these features translate into dependable power availability, scalable growth, and greater long-term optionality. “The U.S. data center market is moving faster than traditional power infrastructure can support,” says Risto Paldanius, Vice President, Americas at Wärtsilä Energy. “This order shows how flexible onsite power can help developers secure reliable power, reduce deployment risk, and scale their operations with confidence. Our growing portfolio of data center projects to date demonstrates the critical role flexible engine technology can play in solving one of the sector’s most urgent growth challenges.” The Wärtsilä equipment is scheduled for delivery in 2028, and the project is expected to become fully operational in 2029. artigo.texto: Crise energética nos EUA ameaça IA, mas poupa Nvidia e Broadcom Déficit de 34% na energia para data centers até 2028 pode travar a expansão da IA nos EUA, mas as duas maiores fabricantes de chips seguem blindadas, segundo análise do Morgan Stanley. O boom da inteligência artificial criou um problema que dinheiro, sozinho, não resolve: falta energia elétrica. Os bilhões de dólares despejados na construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos esbarram numa infraestrutura energética que não acompanha o ritmo da demanda. E o gargalo começa a redesenhar o mapa de vencedores e perdedores na cadeia de semicondutores. Um relatório do Morgan Stanley publicado nesta segunda-feira estima que os desenvolvedores de data centers nos EUA enfrentarão um déficit líquido de energia de 34% até 2028, o equivalente a 32 gigawatts. Para colocar em perspectiva, isso representa mais do que toda a capacidade instalada de geração eólica do Brasil. O número evidencia que o problema não é marginal: é estrutural. A conclusão central do banco, porém, surpreende pelo otimismo seletivo. Nvidia e Broadcom, as duas maiores fornecedoras de chips de alto desempenho para IA, estão relativamente protegidas contra esse cenário. O risco real recai sobre os elos secundários da cadeia: fabricantes de chips de memória, componentes ópticos, gerenciamento de energia e processadores analógicos. Por que Nvidia e Broadcom escapam do gargalo energético A lógica do Morgan Stanley é relativamente simples. Nvidia e Broadcom têm visibilidade privilegiada sobre a alocação de seus chips, a expansão geográfica dos clientes e a coordenação entre centros de dados, fornecedores e a cadeia de abastecimento de energia. Isso significa que essas empresas conseguem antecipar onde haverá capacidade de instalação e direcionar sua produção de acordo. Na prática, os maiores compradores de GPUs da Nvidia, como Microsoft, Google, Amazon e Meta, são justamente os operadores de data centers com maior poder de negociação junto a concessionárias de energia e governos locais. Esses hyperscalers já garantiram contratos de fornecimento de longo prazo e estão diversificando geograficamente suas operações, inclusive para fora dos EUA. O banco afirmou que não vê os gargalos energéticos colocando em risco as previsões de receita da Nvidia ou da Broadcom para 2027. A análise reforça uma tese que o mercado financeiro já precifica parcialmente: essas duas companhias operam num nível de demanda tão elevado que mesmo restrições de infraestrutura não reduzem a fila de pedidos, apenas redistribuem onde os chips serão instalados. Quem paga a conta: os elos frágeis da cadeia de IA Se a capacidade de produção de chips não puder ser implantada por falta de energia nos data centers, os clientes poderão adiar entregas ou cancelar pedidos. E os componentes mais expostos a esse risco são justamente os que dependem de volumes elevados para manter margens saudáveis. Fabricantes de chips de memória, como Micron e SK Hynix, operam com margens mais estreitas e dependem do ritmo de construção de novos data centers para manter a demanda aquecida. O mesmo vale para fornecedores de componentes ópticos, essenciais para a conectividade entre servidores, e para empresas de gerenciamento de energia e chips analógicos. Como analisamos na cobertura de tecnologia do portal, a cadeia de semicondutores funciona como um ecossistema integrado, e o atraso num elo propaga efeitos em cascata. O Goldman Sachs também sinalizou restrições crescentes à expansão dos data centers nos EUA, embora com uma leitura levemente diferente. O banco espera impacto limitado no curto prazo, em parte pela resistência política a medidas que freiem investimentos em IA. Já o Morgan Stanley enxerga desafios mais concretos, ligados a mão de obra, fornecimento de energia e entraves regulatórios. O déficit de 32 GW e o que isso significa para investidores O número de 32 GW de déficit projetado para 2028 não é apenas uma curiosidade técnica. Ele tem implicações diretas para quem investe em empresas de tecnologia e infraestrutura. A construção de novas usinas de geração, linhas de transmissão e subestações leva anos. Mesmo com o incentivo bilionário dos governos federal e estaduais, a oferta de energia não se expande na mesma velocidade que a demanda por computação. Esse descompasso já está gerando movimentos concretos. Empresas como Microsoft fecharam contratos para reativar usinas nucleares. Amazon investiu em geração solar e eólica dedicada a seus data centers. Google assinou acordos de compra de energia geotérmica. Como acompanhamos na editoria de finanças, o setor de energia virou talvez o maior beneficiário indireto do boom de IA, com ações de concessionárias e empresas de infraestrutura elétrica acumulando altas expressivas nos últimos 12 meses. Para o investidor, a leitura é que a tese de Nvidia e Broadcom permanece intacta no médio prazo, mas o risco migrou para a segunda e terceira camadas da cadeia. Empresas que pareciam apostas seguras no ciclo de IA, como fabricantes de memória HBM e fornecedores de equipamentos de rede, agora carregam um risco adicional de atraso na implantação que não estava no radar há seis meses. IA e energia: um gargalo que veio para ficar O cenário descrito pelo Morgan Stanley não é temporário. A demanda energética da IA generativa cresce exponencialmente a cada nova geração de modelos. O treinamento do GPT-4 consumiu estimados 50 GWh de eletricidade. Modelos futuros devem demandar ordens de magnitude a mais. E a inferência, o uso cotidiano dos modelos por bilhões de pessoas, adiciona uma camada contínua de consumo que não existia antes. A questão energética, portanto, deixou de ser um risco periférico e se tornou o principal limitador da velocidade de expansão da IA nos Estados Unidos. Países que conseguirem resolver essa equação primeiro, seja por abundância de recursos naturais, seja por agilidade regulatória, tendem a capturar uma fatia desproporcional dos investimentos em infraestrutura de IA.

artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›SECI Invites Bids for 800 MW/3,200 MWh BESS SECI Invites Bids for 800 MW/3,200 MWh BESS Solar Energy Corporation of India has issued a tender for supplying energy from 800 MW/3,200 MWh standalone battery energy storage system in India. Bid submission ends on October 30, 2026. October 05, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) has floated a tender for the supply of energy from 800 MW/3,200 MWh ISTS-connected standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in India. The projects must be set up under the build, own, operate (BOO) model. Bidders must pay INR 59,000 as a tender document fee. They also need to deposit INR 20,000/MW (plus GST) as a bid processing fee, subject to a maximum amount of INR 20 lakh (plus GST). Further, they need to furnish INR 7.184 lakh/MW as an earnest money deposit (EMD). Selected bidders must deposit INR 17.96 lakh/MW as a performance bank guarantee (PBG). The last date for submission of bids is October 30, 2026. The techno-commercial bids will be opened on November 4, 2026. The minimum capacity for bidding will be 50 MW/200 MWh. The BESSD must set up, operate, and maintain a BESS, with the primary objective of providing stored energy from the BESS to the buying entities on an “on-demand” basis. Identification of land, installation and ownership of the project, along with obtaining connectivity and necessary approvals and interconnection with the ISTS network/ STU or InSTS network (as applicable) will be under the scope of the BESSD. The charging power for the BESS project must be arranged by the BESSD such that at least 51 percent of the energy used for charging the BESS is procured from renewable energy sources. The BESSD must guarantee a minimum system availability of 85 percent on a monthly basis. The net worth of the bidder must be at least INR 71.84 lakh/ MW, as on the last date of FY26, or as on the day at least 7 days prior to the bid submission deadline. To demonstrate adequate financial capacity for the project, the Bidder must meet at least one of the following criteria: an annual turnover of at least INR 87.514 lakh/MW in FY26 or as of at least seven days before the bid submission deadline; PBDIT, excluding other and exceptional income, of at least INR 17,50,280/MW as of the end of FY26 or at least seven days before the bid deadline; or an in-principle bank/lender sanction for a working capital line of credit of at least INR 21,87,850/MW.
