artigo.texto: Vertiv Offers integrated leak detection as part of monitoring According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Water Leak Detection System For Server Rooms And Data Centers market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global market for Water Leak Detection System for Server Rooms and Data Centers is positioned for sustained expansion through 2035, underpinned by the relentless growth of digital infrastructure and the mission-critical need to protect IT assets from water damage. As data centers become denser and more distributed, the financial and operational consequences of even minor leaks escalate, elevating leak detection from a peripheral safeguard to a core component of facility resilience. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market, covering historical data from 2012 to 2025 and forecasting through 2035. It examines the market through multiple lenses, including product type, end-use application, integration level, and geography, offering a detailed view of demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, competitive landscape, and strategic opportunities. The analysis reveals a market evolving from standalone alarm systems to intelligent, integrated nodes within broader building and IT management ecosystems, with software, services, and subscription models gaining prominence. Key demand drivers include the proliferation of edge and colocation facilities, tightening insurance and compliance requirements, and the increasing adoption of IoT and wireless technologies for retrofit and new builds. The report is designed for component manufacturers, system suppliers, OEMs, distributors, investors, and strategic entrants seeking a commercially grounded understanding of this specialized market. The baseline scenario for the Water Leak Detection System for Server Rooms and Data Centers market anticipates steady growth from 2026 to 2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.2%, resulting in a market index of 182 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is supported by the accelerating construction of hyperscale, colocation, and edge data centers worldwide, coupled with the increasing value density of IT equipment and the stringent uptime requirements of cloud service providers and enterprises. The market is expected to bifurcate further: standardized, cost-competitive solutions will dominate high-volume edge and colocation builds, while highly customized, deeply integrated systems will prevail in flagship hyperscale and enterprise facilities. Revenue streams will shift from one-time hardware sales toward layered models including software licenses, integration services, and Monitoring-as-a-Service (MaaS) subscriptions. Geographically, Asia-Pacific will lead in new capacity additions, while North America and Europe will focus on retrofits and upgrades to meet evolving standards. Supply chain resilience, particularly for specialized polymer sensing materials and mission-critical electronic components, will remain a critical factor. artigo.texto: Data Center Design in the AI Era The unprecedented performance demands of AI workloads require a reimagined approach to data center design toward fully autonomous operations. October 5, 2026 Sponsored by HPE It wasn’t long ago that organizations thought their data centers would play a less central role in IT service delivery. Virtualized infrastructure, cloud computing, colocation, SaaS applications, and other factors pointed to more computing being done off-premises. But the rapid acceleration of compute-intensive workloads, generative AI, and ever-increasing network complexity is driving organizations to reimagine and, in some cases, completely re-engineer their data centers. The same is true for third-party data centers leveraged by so many organizations, often in tandem with their on-prem facilities. AI training and inference, combined with a rapid swing toward agentic AI, is intensifying pressure on data centers. Even with the impressive advances in compute and storage density, enterprises are realizing that incremental component refreshes cannot solve operational complexity; they require a modern fabric design and shift toward self-driving networks to improve IT agility, increase reliability, and optimize the end user experience. The trends have been exacerbated by huge demands for power and cooling, which data centers have struggled to meet. Research from Uptime Institute notes that 82% of data center operators report their highest-density racks are still below 30 kilowatts, a level unlikely to meet the growing demands of AI-level performance as rack densities increase. New Challenges Force Changes to Data Center Design The harsh reality is that traditional data centers were never designed for the performance, scalability, security, and resilience demands of the AI era. The massive growth in data volumes has created important opportunities for new insights, but also requires a fundamentally different approach to network design. Servers, networks, storage, end-user devices, cloud gateways, applications, security tools, and other sources generate unprecedented amounts of data, making it more difficult for networks to discern whether an alert indicates a potentially serious failure or a minor problem elsewhere. But it’s not just the proliferation of data sources that renders legacy data centers inadequate for the AI era. Traditional data center traffic usually had a fair amount of entropy, making it easier to design for capacity and accommodate occasional demand spikes that could impact network performance. AI has changed that in a big way. Modern AI workloads running on GPUs require deterministic, low-latency, higher-bandwidth networks, and massively scalable storage infrastructure, meaning that both existing and greenfield data centers need to support significantly higher performance. In addition, the traditional siloed approach to IT infrastructure that reflects organizational boundaries rather than end user needs—compute, storage, and networking—has given way to new design principles that promote tighter cross-domain integration for better overall data center and application performance. Shifting the Data Center to Autonomous Operations Although data centers have increasingly embraced automation, the next step is for data center design to progress toward autonomy. Data center personnel are simply too hard-pressed to address the increasing telemetry volume and complexity in real time without tools that provide full-stack, cross-domain visibility across the entire enterprise. AI agents should be an important element in the move toward autonomous operations because they enable lightning-fast assessments, analysis, and decision-making across the full spectrum of infrastructure and data sources. Management should focus not just on automating operations to reduce headcount, but on autonomous operations that improve the quality of application and user experience. The Importance of a Self-Driving Framework AI-era data centers now have the potential for unsurpassed levels of intelligence, autonomous operations, observability, and contextually aware decision-making. This is where self-driving frameworks coordinate data center operations with AI-era requirements. The emphasis has swung decisively away from historically fragmented management frameworks in favor of approaches that collect information from all available sources and put them into an actionable context across infrastructure. A key first step is intent-based networking, which defines the desired state of the network based on operator-intent and continuously validates its conformance to that standard. Problems are identified faster and with greater precision, relieving the data center team of tedious, time-consuming, and often inaccurate triage to avoid failures and downtime. A well-planned and meticulously executed approach to building the right data center architecture helps organizations establish validated topologies, automate deployment, improve visibility, automate remediation, and balance the strengths of AI tools with human experience. artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil: candidatos querem mais, EUA rejeitam Com propostas de redução de impostos e criação de polo nacional, candidatos a presidente mais bem colocados têm planos parecidos para data centers. Nos EUA, maioria é contrária à construção desses complexos em seus bairros. A divergência entre os dois países reflete diferenças estruturais e estratégicas no setor de tecnologia. Incentivos fiscais, fabricação local de componentes e IA brasileira: os candidatos à Presidência mais bem colocados nas pesquisas apresentam essas como algumas das propostas em seus planos de governo para atrair a construção de data centers no Brasil. A fonte não detalhou os valores ou prazos desses incentivos. Facilitar a construção de data centers é uma ação que alguns dos candidatos consideram importante para aproveitar o avanço da IA. Mas, enquanto o Brasil tenta atrair essas instalações, países como os Estados Unidos têm enfrentado protestos contra o avanço do setor. Manifestantes protestam contra expansão de centros de dados de IA nos EUA. O que é um data center? ❓ Um data center (“centro de dados”, em inglês) é um local que armazena e processa informações. Entre os modelos mais comuns, estão os de nuvem — cloud, para armazenar arquivos e operar serviços na internet — e de inteligência artificial, para treinar modelos de linguagem complexos. Essas infraestruturas são essenciais para a economia digital. Por que candidatos querem atrair? Com rejeição em outros lugares, por que candidatos no Brasil querem atrair mais data centers? Entre os motivos, estão as diferenças no tamanho dos mercados e nas matrizes energéticas dos países. O Brasil busca reduzir sua dependência de processamento no exterior. Com menos instalações, é preciso armazenar e processar muitos dados no exterior: o Brasil terminou 2025 com déficit de US$ 8 bilhões na balança comercial de Serviços de Computação e Informação, segundo a Brasscom, associação de empresas brasileiras de tecnologia. Esse déficit pressiona a economia e limita a competitividade das empresas locais. Energia renovável como diferencial E, enquanto os EUA dependem principalmente de energia gerada por combustíveis fósseis, incluindo petróleo e gás natural, a eletricidade no Brasil é gerada em larga escala por fontes renováveis, como usinas hidrelétricas. Essa matriz mais limpa pode atrair empresas globais preocupadas com sustentabilidade. O que há de comum no Brasil, nos EUA e em outros países é a discussão sobre o consumo elevado de energia e água por data centers: moradores de várias cidades americanas protestaram contra o avanço dessas instalações, e autoridades brasileiras questionaram os impactos desses projetos. A fonte não detalhou quais autoridades brasileiras se manifestaram. Especialistas pedem cautela Para Daniel Cordeiro, professor na Universidade de São Paulo (USP) e especialista em computação sustentável e de alto desempenho, o Brasil precisa aumentar sua capacidade computacional, mas deve tentar evitar problemas que estão sendo enfrentados em outros países. Ele não especificou quais medidas regulatórias seriam necessárias. Segundo Thais Ortega, coordenadora de pesquisa da consultoria Reglab, a atração de data centers é um consenso entre os principais candidatos, mas há diferenças nos modelos previstos para alcançar esse objetivo. “Todos convergem para atrair, mas como será a atração? O Brasil tem uma posição estratégica, com vários pontos positivos. Não temos como prever se teremos ou não os problemas dos EUA, mas temos como tentar mitigar com regulações”, destaca. Para empresários e comerciantes do noroeste paulista, a eventual instalação de data centers pode gerar empregos diretos e indiretos, além de demandar serviços locais. No entanto, os impactos sobre o consumo de energia e água devem ser monitorados de perto pelas entidades empresariais. Perguntas Frequentes Por que os candidatos à presidência do Brasil querem atrair mais data centers? Os candidatos querem atrair data centers para aproveitar o avanço da IA e reduzir o déficit de US$ 8 bilhões na balança comercial de Serviços de Computação e Informação, segundo a Brasscom. Quais são as principais propostas dos candidatos para atrair data centers no Brasil? As propostas incluem incentivos fiscais, fabricação local de componentes e desenvolvimento de IA brasileira, conforme os planos de governo dos candidatos mais bem colocados. Por que há rejeição a data centers nos EUA enquanto o Brasil tenta atraí-los? Nos EUA, a rejeição se deve ao alto consumo de energia e água e à dependência de combustíveis fósseis, enquanto no Brasil a matriz energética é majoritariamente renovável, o que torna a atração mais viável.

artigo.texto: EP Cube displayed its EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 for new or existing residential and Three-Phase Light C&I Solution for small commercial PV-plus-storage systems The residential system supports a maximum PV capacity of 15 kW and lists its storage capacity range of 5 to 40 kWh with a rated 10 kVA full-load power It also integrates with the company’s upcoming 7.4 kW AC EV charger, updated EP Cube App, and a new HMI for a connected and smarter home energy ecosystem EP Cube, an independent subsidiary and residential energy storage brand of Canadian Solar Inc., introduced its residential EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 and Three-Phase Light C&I Solution at Solar & Storage Live UK 2026 in Birmingham. The company's booth also displayed an EV charger, a Human Machine Interface (HMI) display, and a new dynamic tariff pricing AI mode as part of a smart home energy ecosystem. Both energy storage systems (ESS) feature an 'All-in-One' configuration, which combines a hybrid inverter and modular battery packs, stacked on one another. They use lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) battery units, each measuring 600 × 266 × 200 mm and providing 5 kWh of storage capacity at a 51.2 V rated voltage. While the configuration and battery pack are identical, their inverter and total storage capacities vary. The EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 features a 10 kVA hybrid inverter and a storage capacity range of 5 to 40 kWh by connecting to eight battery packs. With 4 built-in MPPTs, the inverter supports up to 15 kW of PV capacity with a 600 V maximum PV input voltage. In comparison, the Three-Phase Light C&I Solution combines a higher-capacity hybrid inverter (12 kVA) and storage capacities of 10 to 40 kWh using the same 5 kWh battery packs mentioned above. Its inverter lists a higher PV capacity of 24 kW and a maximum input voltage of 1,000 V, though the MPPT numbers remain the same. The product datasheets specify compatibility with new and existing PV arrays to make an AC-coupled PV-plus-storage system. The residential ESS supports up to 10 kVA (single-phase) emergency backup within 10 ms of a grid outage, while this function is optional for the C&I product. It switches to off-grid mode in less than 20 ms of a grid blackout and delivers up to 12 kVA (3-phase) backup power. Backup duration varies based on total connected storage capacity, rated discharge limit, and operational conditions, among others. EP Cube also introduced its new AC EV chargers in two variants – 7.4 kW single-phase and 11 kW 3-phase. According to the company, it planned to launch the 3-phase charger by the end of September 2026, while the launch of its single-phase counterpart is slated for Q4 2026. The single-phase charger supports direct connection with the EP Cube Single-Phase 2.0 through a dedicated built-in port, enabling a connected home energy ecosystem. These ESSs (mentioned above) integrate with the EP Cube App (installed on the user's device) and help monitor and support multiple applications, including PV self-consumption maximization and time-of-use (TOU) tariffs, among others. It also enables smart EV charging from excess PV generation during peak hours and use of low-priced electricity at night or during low solar generation periods. This increases PV self-consumption and optimizes charging costs. The company says it has updated the app with features that support the UK's dynamic electricity tariff management services. It added that these features will soon be embedded in a new Dynamic Pricing AI mode for more accurate low-price capturing and battery charging/discharging decisions. EP Cube is also expecting to include new Open APIs with the app. This will enable the home ESS platform to integrate with an existing third-party home energy management system (HEMS), like Home Assistant, to make the connected energy ecosystem smarter. In addition to remote monitoring and data visualization, the booth displayed the new 7-inch HMI for local data accumulation and visualization with local data storage, supporting data independence for end users.

artigo.texto: German Sodium-Ion Battery Tech Gains EU Funding Support ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: German startup Revolta AG received €264,200 in EU co-financing for its sodium-ion AC battery project, designed for grid-charging in residential apartments. - Why it matters: This development highlights the growing viability of lithium-free storage solutions that can operate independently of on-site PV generation. - Watch: The impact of new German grid regulations that allow storage systems to arbitrage grid power with reduced levies and fees. Background and Context As the global energy transition accelerates, the development of sodium-ion battery technology is emerging as a critical alternative to traditional lithium-ion systems. German startup Revolta AG has secured significant funding from the German state of Hesse, supported by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), to advance its “Highly Efficient AC Salt Battery” project. This initiative aims to deploy residential-scale storage systems that do not rely on lithium or cobalt, addressing supply chain vulnerabilities and material cost volatility. Key Details The project, which runs from August 1, 2026, to December 31, 2029, involves eligible costs totaling €660,545, with the EU providing a 40% co-financing rate of approximately €264,200. The core innovation lies in the system’s ability to connect directly to the grid, allowing users to charge during periods of low electricity prices and discharge when costs peak. This model is specifically targeted at rental apartments that lack the space or infrastructure for rooftop solar PV installations. Furthermore, the regulatory landscape in Germany has evolved to support this business model. Since October 1, the national grid regulator has implemented rules allowing storage systems to draw power from the grid and feed it back later, benefiting from reduced grid fees and levies. This shift effectively opens a new market segment for storage providers. Beyond Revolta AG, the ERDF is also supporting broader sodium-ion manufacturing, including a €2.52 million grant for a 1 GWh sodium-ion battery plant in Bavaria. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, the rise of grid-charging sodium-ion systems represents a shift toward decentralized energy management. While currently focused on the residential sector, the underlying technology—sodium-ion—offers a scalable, safer, and more sustainable alternative for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications. Developers should monitor these advancements as they provide a pathway to integrate storage in locations where solar generation is physically constrained. What Happens Next The industry will closely monitor the performance of these pilot projects as they move toward the 2026 launch window. As India continues to expand its renewable energy sector, the lessons learned from European regulatory frameworks—specifically regarding grid-charging arbitrage and non-lithium storage chemistries—will become increasingly relevant. India’s push for indigenous battery manufacturing under various PLI schemes may eventually incorporate these sodium-ion advancements to diversify the national energy storage portfolio.

artigo.texto: Nvidia e Broadcom se isolam de impacto de crise de energia em data centers dos EUA, diz Morgan Stanley Nvidia e Broadcom estão protegidas da crise energética em data centers nos EUA até 2027, segundo o Morgan Stanley, devido ao forte planejamento e alocação de chips. Contudo, o setor enfrenta um déficit de energia projetado em 34% até 2028, impulsionado pela alta demanda da inteligência artificial. Se a infraestrutura atrasar por gargalos elétricos, fabricantes de componentes secundários, como chips de memória, óptica e analógicos, serão os mais impactados por cancelamentos e adiamentos. Nvidia e Broadcom estão relativamente protegidas contra o agravamento da crise de energia nas centrais de processamento de dados dos Estados Unidos, afirmou o Morgan Stanley em relatório nesta segunda-feira. Porém, qualquer atraso resultante nas implantações de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial pode afetar os fabricantes de chips de memória, componentes ópticos e outros processadores secundários. O banco estimou no mês passado que os desenvolvedores de data centers nos EUA enfrentarão um déficit líquido de energia de 34% até 2028, equivalente a 32 GW. O boom da IA gerou bilhões de dólares em investimentos em data centers, mas as enormes necessidades de computação e eletricidade da IA generativa estão cada vez mais esbarrando nos problemas de fornecimento de eletricidade nos EUA. Tanto Morgan Stanley quanto Goldman Sachs sinalizaram restrições crescentes à expansão dos data centers nos EUA; o GS espera um impacto limitado no curto prazo devido à resistência política, enquanto o MS vê desafios relacionados à mão de obra, energia e política. O Morgan Stanley afirmou que não vê os gargalos colocando em risco as previsões da Nvidia ou da Broadcom para 2027, citando a visibilidade dessas empresas quanto à alocação de chips, à expansão geográfica e à coordenação entre centros de dados, fornecedores de chips e a cadeia de abastecimento de energia. Se a capacidade de produção de chips não puder ser implantada, os clientes poderão adiar entregas ou cancelar pedidos, sendo que componentes de memória, óptica, gerenciamento de energia e analógicos são os mais expostos a problemas de fornecimento, afirmou o Morgan Stanley.

artigo.texto: Data Center World estreia com foco em energia e Redata Edição brasileira começa nesta terça-feira, em SP, com debates sobre tributação, capacidade energética, financiamento e conectividade. A primeira edição brasileira do Data Center World começa nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro, no São Paulo Expo, com debates sobre os principais condicionantes para a expansão dos data centers no país. Tributação, disponibilidade de energia, financiamento, conectividade e aumento da demanda computacional estão entre os temas centrais do encontro. Realizado simultaneamente à Futurecom, o evento prevê a participação de mais de 2,5 mil líderes e 300 congressistas. Um dos destaques do primeiro dia será o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). O tema entra na discussão sobre competitividade, atração de investimentos e ambiente regulatório, ao lado dos efeitos do ICMS e de decisões do Confaz sobre a implantação de novos projetos. Oferta de energia concentra debates A disponibilidade de energia aparece como um dos principais fatores para a expansão do setor. O aumento da capacidade computacional exigida por novas aplicações amplia a demanda elétrica dos empreendimentos e afeta decisões sobre localização, escala e continuidade operacional. Os debates vão tratar de oferta efetiva, intermitência, geração, armazenamento e alternativas para reduzir riscos associados ao fornecimento. O crescimento da densidade dos racks também pressiona a infraestrutura elétrica e térmica dos data centers. Esse movimento tem ampliado a discussão sobre novas arquiteturas e sobre tecnologias de refrigeração, incluindo liquid cooling. Financiamento e viabilidade O acesso a capital será outro eixo do congresso. Representantes do Ministério das Comunicações, BNDES, Brasscom e Patria Investments participam de um debate sobre crédito, financiamento e condições para viabilizar novos empreendimentos. A análise de grandes projetos passa também por fatores como localização, custo, latência, segurança e continuidade dos serviços. Esses critérios serão discutidos sob a perspectiva de empresas que contratam infraestrutura de data center. Conectividade e capacidade A conectividade completa o conjunto de fatores que condicionam a expansão do mercado. O congresso terá discussões sobre rotas internacionais, latência e edge computing, relacionando a localização dos data centers ao desempenho das aplicações. O planejamento de capacidade por hyperscalers também estará em pauta, diante da dificuldade de projetar demanda em um ambiente de crescimento acelerado das cargas computacionais. A agenda inclui ainda debates sobre continuidade operacional, preparação para falhas e eventos extremos, além de investimentos e expansão da infraestrutura na América Latina. artigo.texto: Amazon investirá US$ 1 bilhão em comunidades de data centers em meio à pressão por consumo de energia e água A Amazon Web Services (AWS), divisão de computação em nuvem da gigante de tecnologia, anunciou que investirá mais de US$ 1 bilhão ao longo dos próximos cinco anos em comunidades locais nos Estados Unidos que abrigam seus data centers. O plano surge como resposta direta às crescentes preocupações públicas e críticas sobre a pressão que as estruturas exercem sobre o abastecimento de água e a rede elétrica local. Os centros de dados desempenham um papel indispensável no fornecimento do poder computacional maciço exigido para o treinamento e a execução de modelos avançados de Inteligência Artificial (IA). No entanto, o ritmo acelerado de construção dessas instalações tem provocado fortes resistências em diversos condados e municípios norte-americanos, gerando debates sobre o impacto nas tarifas públicas de energia e o equilíbrio ambiental das regiões vizinhas. Foco em capacitação, sustentabilidade e infraestrutura local O montante de US$ 1 bilhão será canalizado para iniciativas voltadas ao desenvolvimento socioeconômico e ambiental das regiões onde a AWS opera. O programa contempla: - Preservação e eficiência de água: Projetos comunitários para conservação de recursos hídricos e devolução de água tratada aos mananciais locais. - Acessibilidade e transição energética: Apoio a programas que ajudam a mitigar impactos nas contas de luz das populações vizinhas e investimentos em fontes renováveis. - Educação e qualificação profissional: Treinamento técnico e capacitação em tecnologia da informação e computação em nuvem para residentes locais. - Financiamento de prioridades comunitárias: Apoio a serviços essenciais, segurança hídrica e infraestrutura pública regional. Segundo a empresa, a AWS mantém o compromisso de alcançar o status de “positiva em água” (water positive) até 2030, o que significa devolver mais água às comunidades do que o volume total consumido pelas operações de resfriamento. A companhia afirma já ter atingido cerca de 75% dessa meta global. Corrida pela IA e os desafios regulatórios nos EUA Entre 2011 e 2025, a Amazon investiu aproximadamente US$ 276 bilhões em data centers nos Estados Unidos, com megaprojetos e expansões em andamento em estados estratégicos como Virgínia, Indiana, Carolina do Norte, Louisiana e Mississippi. A rápida proliferação dessas estruturas, impulsionada pelo boom da inteligência artificial generativa, levou mais de uma centena de municípios e governos locais a avaliarem moratórias e restrições para novas construções, tornando o consumo energético dos data centers um dos principais pontos de debate político e de infraestrutura no país. Em pronunciamento oficial, Matt Garman, CEO da AWS, ressaltou a relevância estratégica da infraestrutura para a soberania tecnológica: “Há urgência na construção desses data centers porque não somos o único país que vê os benefícios da IA para a economia e a segurança nacional. Os países que liderarem em inteligência artificial irão moldá-la e extrair o máximo proveito dessa revolução tecnológica.” Com o novo aporte bilionário, a Amazon busca equilibrar a expansão acelerada de sua capacidade de processamento em nuvem com o fortalecimento das relações institucionais e a sustentabilidade das comunidades que sustentam o ecossistema de IA.

artigo.texto: Chinese battery giant CATL has reached a key milestone in proving the durability of its technology, demonstrating impressive laboratory analysis results. The prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells tested, which have been operating without interruption for almost fourteen years, have retained about 85 percent of their original energy capacity. The cells analyzed are part of the world's first large-scale energy storage facility, the 63 MWh Zhangbei, which began operation in 2011 and even provided clean energy for the 2022 Winter Olympics. The complete decommissioning of the facility in the summer of 2025 has allowed engineers to subject the components to detailed chemical and physical destructive testing. Over 50 samples taken from the original cells reveal remarkable material durability: the anode and cathode layers have retained perfect geometry, and the graphite shows no structural defects or critical signs of aging. An interesting detail is the fact that not a single cell from this manufacturer had to be replaced over the entire 14-year cycle. The test results open up new perspectives for the so-called “second life“ of industrial batteries. According to the company's experts, the retired cells have a resource for about 1,000 more complete charge and discharge cycles. This makes the components fully suitable for reintegration into smaller secondary storage systems for at least another decade. The current findings reconfirm the expectations from the control tests carried out on the ninth year of the facility's launch. LFP technology is also gaining in importance in the automotive sector. While these chemistries are inferior in specific energy density to nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) alternatives, they offer significantly lower manufacturing costs and unrivaled durability under extreme temperature and operating conditions. The achieved lifespan solidifies the technology's position as a key pillar for the future of sustainable mobility and green energy.

artigo.texto: Opponents of a proposed Brighton data center development will push the City Council for a moratorium Tuesday night, as the populist backlash against the resource-hungry megacenters spreads across Colorado. Weld County data center opponents are also launching a signature drive to get a moratorium on a future countywide ballot. Questions about transparency from government officials, how much water and energy the data centers will use, and how much noise they will generate for nearby subdivisions are bringing unusual coalitions together to fight growth, said Jordan Forsyth, a Democratic Socialists of America activist in Adams County. “To see me, a very vocal member of DSA, and my neighbor who is very Republican and voted for Trump, being able to have a conversation on this issue and actually be united … it’s been really cool to see everybody be able to put politics aside and just engage for the good of the community,” Forsyth said. A nonpartisan Weld County group says it is circulating two data center petitions in coming weeks. One, requiring 10,000 signatures in 45 days, would petition the Weld County commissioners to refer their approval of Global AI’s proposed data center to all voters in a special election sometime after the November general elections. The second Weld County petition, also needing 10,000 signatures according to the coalition, would create a separate ballot measure that if approved would require a public referendum on any newly proposed data center or data center expansion. “This referendum puts power back in the hands of the people of Weld County,” said community advocate Patricia Garcia-Nelson, who also works as a fossil fuels transition advocate for GreenLatinos. “We have the right to decide what happens to our community, not just on this project, but on the ones that come next. Over the next 30 days, we’re going to make sure every voter in Weld County has that chance,” Garcia-Nelson said, in a statement announcing the petition drives. More chances for referendums on data centers arise as candidate positions on the controversial developments become a litmus test from city council races to U.S. Senate campaigns. Colorado Springs recently delayed approval of a proposed data center near Garden of the Gods after protesters were arrested at the public hearing. Aurora’s City Council rejected a moratorium on data centers but put in place new requirements on how much water projects might use. Seeking info in Brighton Activists in Brighton are organizing, and studying documentation filed with the city for a 2.5-million-square-foot, eight-building data center mapped out on farm land near 50th Avenue and Weld County Road 4, about 25 miles northeast of downtown Denver. The development would be in a portion of Brighton that is in Weld County, according to BizWest. Former Chicago TV anchor and current Brighton resident Stacey Baca has compiled the documents and explanations of the developer’s plans on her YouTube channel, and activists say they want answers from City Council on why the project has moved forward without public debate. Nondisclosure agreements or other proprietary negotiations might get in the way, Forsyth said, ““but I think they had the option for community involvement and input, and it doesn’t seem that they’re interested in it,” Forsyth said. Council members should have looked around Colorado and seen that data centers would be coming for the ample open space on co-op United Power’s grid, the activists say. A moratorium would give the community time to develop standards, from whether they want data centers at all, to whether they should be supported with tax breaks, to how water and power will be supplied, opponents say. Representatives of Dewberry engineers, the firm that has filed paperwork for the Brighton development, did not return calls seeking comment about the project. Activists say the developer is California-based Raeden, which did not return messages seeking comment. In addition to concerns about data centers’ cooling-water use amid historic drought conditions, activists also question how the centers’ massive power needs will be supplied. Data centers come with large fossil-fueled backup generators that emit pollution when fired up; their everyday needs require hundreds of megawatts of power. If the data centers are powered by new fossil-fuel generation such as natural gas, Colorado’s progress in switching to clean, renewable energy could stall further, opponents say. A United Power spokesperson said the co-op power supplier cannot talk about individual customer projects or proposals. United Power said it works with large-load prospective customers to ensure adequate supply will be available. Some Brighton City Council members have supported consideration of a 90-day moratorium on data center approvals. Forsyth said another council member will support a 180-day freeze at the Oct. 6 meeting. Weld County activists will be at the Brighton meeting, in neighboring Adams County, to gather signatures for their data center petitions, a campaign spokesperson said. Political leaders haven’t listened so far, said Matt Cheroutes, who is the campaign manager for the Weld County activists calling themselves Protect Our Water and Energy Resources, or POWER. “So now we’re taking this to the voters. The commissioners had their vote. Now it’s the people’s turn,” Cheroutes said.

artigo.texto: A Alibaba Cloud inaugurou seus primeiros data centers no Brasil em São Paulo em agosto de 2026, prometendo reduzir o tempo de resposta de sites e sistemas de pagamento. No entanto, especialistas do Grupo HRZ destacam que a infraestrutura só será útil se integrada a um planejamento completo de CRM, estoque e atendimento, evitando falhas em campanhas de alto volume. A Alibaba Cloud, divisão de computação em nuvem do grupo chinês Alibaba, anunciou em 27 de agosto de 2026 a inauguração dos seus dois primeiros data centers no Brasil, ambos localizados em São Paulo. A chegada dessa infraestrutura aproxima os servidores das empresas e dos consumidores brasileiros, o que pode melhorar significativamente o desempenho de sites, sistemas de pagamento, consultas de estoque e plataformas de atendimento. Essa expansão faz parte do compromisso global de US$ 53 bilhões da companhia com inteligência artificial e computação em nuvem. Com a chegada dos novos data centers da Alibaba Cloud no Brasil, a latência deve cair, mas será que a tecnologia sozinha salva uma operação de vendas instável Especialistas debatem o tema e analisam os desafios de integração de CRM, estoque e e-commerce para aproveitar ao máximo essa nova infraestrutura. - A Alibaba Cloud abriu dois data centers em São Paulo para reduzir o tempo de resposta dos sites brasileiros. - A infraestrutura faz parte de um investimento global de US$ 53 bilhões em inteligência artificial. - Especialistas alertam que servidores rápidos não resolvem falhas de estoque ou atendimento desatualizado. - Campanhas de grande volume, como a Black Friday, exigem estabilidade total de todos os sistemas. - É necessário diagnosticar a operação antes de migrar para garantir que os dados fluam entre canais. Proximidade de servidores reduz tempo de resposta Hugo Silveira, cofundador do Grupo HRZ, holding especializada em crescimento empresarial e estruturação comercial, avalia que a entrada de mais um grande fornecedor amplia as opções para empresas que dependem de sistemas digitais para vender. Ter servidores mais próximos pode diminuir o tempo que a informação leva para ir e voltar. Mas isso, sozinho, não resolve os problemas de uma operação. É preciso analisar o site, as integrações, o estoque, o atendimento e o CRM para entender onde a nova infraestrutura realmente pode trazer ganho, afirma o estrategista. Na prática, essa distância entre o usuário e o servidor influencia a chamada latência, que é o intervalo entre uma ação e a resposta do sistema. Quando um consumidor abre uma página, consulta um produto, tenta finalizar uma compra ou realiza um pagamento, diferentes sistemas precisam trocar informações em poucos segundos. Esse ponto ganha importância em operações que conectam loja física, e-commerce, aplicativo e WhatsApp. O Grupo HRZ atua em projetos nos quais estoque, vendas, CRM e atendimento precisam compartilhar dados para que o consumidor consiga iniciar uma compra em um canal e continuar em outro sem perder o histórico. A Alibaba Cloud informa que sua estrutura em São Paulo conta com duas zonas de disponibilidade. Em termos simples, são ambientes separados, com redes e fontes de energia independentes, criados para reduzir o risco de uma única falha afetar toda a operação. A própria companhia recomenda que as empresas utilizem estruturas próximas de seus usuários quando o objetivo é diminuir o tempo de resposta. Estabilidade é crucial em picos de vendas A capacidade de aumentar recursos rapidamente se torna especialmente importante em períodos que concentram muitos acessos em poucas horas, como Black Friday, lançamentos de produtos e grandes campanhas promocionais. Nessas situações, uma falha pode atingir diferentes etapas da compra, da abertura da página até a aprovação do pagamento. Iury Borges, estrategista de vendas e sócio-diretor do Grupo HRZ, afirma que uma infraestrutura mais próxima pode ajudar, mas precisa fazer parte de um planejamento mais amplo. Uma campanha com milhares de pessoas acessando ao mesmo tempo exige que toda a operação esteja preparada. Não adianta o site responder rápido se o estoque estiver desatualizado, o pagamento apresentar falhas ou a equipe não conseguir atender a demanda. A nuvem é uma peça dessa estrutura, ressalta. O desafio, portanto, não termina na velocidade do site. Sistemas de vendas, estoque, CRM e atendimento precisam trocar informações de forma organizada. Quando essa comunicação funciona, a empresa consegue atualizar a disponibilidade dos produtos, identificar a origem das compras e manter o histórico do consumidor ao longo do relacionamento. João Vinas, engenheiro e sócio do Grupo HRZ, onde atua em projetos de CRM, automação comercial e inteligência artificial aplicada a vendas, afirma que a migração para uma nova infraestrutura deve começar por um diagnóstico. O varejista precisa saber onde seus dados estão armazenados, quais sistemas dependem uns dos outros, quais serviços estão disponíveis no Brasil e quanto uma mudança custaria. Só depois desse levantamento é possível saber se a migração faz sentido, aponta. Privacidade de dados e diagnóstico prévio A presença dos servidores no Brasil também pode ser considerada por negócios que desejam manter parte do processamento de informações no território nacional. Isso, porém, não substitui as demais obrigações de proteção de dados. A Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados estabelece responsabilidades para empresas que coletam e utilizam informações pessoais, enquanto transferências internacionais seguem regras específicas da Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados. Antes de trocar de fornecedor ou transferir sistemas, a recomendação é medir o desempenho atual. O primeiro passo pode ser verificar, principalmente pelo celular, quanto tempo uma página de produto leva para abrir, como o checkout responde e em quais pontos o consumidor encontra demora. artigo.texto: Nevada data centers promise big power demand. Who will pay the bill? As Nevada faces unprecedented demand for electricity from the data center industry, developers are pushing back against some of NV Energy’s proposed safeguards designed to prevent the cost of serving their projects from shifting to other customers. But as the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada weighs agreements with future data center customers, confidentiality claims and redactions are preventing the public from seeing project-specific information needed to determine whether those safeguards are sufficient. Many data center developers currently seeking electric service from NV Energy are requesting 300 to 500 megawatts of electricity, six to 10 times the roughly 50 megawatts a major casino or mine might use, said Shawn Elicegui, NV Energy’s senior vice president of regulatory and resource planning. “What we see from data centers is unprecedented,” Elicegui said in a recent interview. “There’s really nothing comparable to data center load.” Unlike most customers — such as households or small businesses, which typically receive a monthly bill based largely on how much electricity they use — data centers typically commit in advance to how much power they expect to need. If they take service under terms approved by the PUC, they can be required to make minimum payments based on those commitments, even if they ultimately use less electricity. The stakes are significant. NV Energy’s plans for future electricity needs account for the enormous demand expected from data centers and other large customers, as well as the infrastructure needed to serve them. If a data center ultimately uses less power than expected, the utility could be left with costs it expected the large customer to help cover, potentially shifting some of those costs to other ratepayers. NV Energy wants some of its largest new customers to pay minimum charges tied to at least 90 percent of the power demand and energy use they sign up for. At least one data center developer, however, wants that minimum set at 70 percent, according to PUC regulatory filings. The disagreement is a test of NV Energy’s promise that Nevada’s growing data-center industry will pay the costs it creates rather than shift them to other customers. Guardrails — but not enough information to test them A Las Vegas Review-Journal investigation found several guardrails in regulatory filings designed to support NV Energy’s repeated promise that data centers will pay their own way. They generally include proposed minimum payments, charges for new generation, financial guarantees and penalties if a customer leaves early. But simply having those protections does not show whether they are sufficient to prevent the costs of serving data centers from shifting onto other ratepayers, energy and utility-regulation experts told the Review-Journal. Sarah Wang, a researcher who studies massive customers called large loads, said regulators can calculate the minimum revenue a customer must provide and compare it with the costs the utility would not otherwise incur. “Without modeling, or some set of calculations, it’s really hard to figure out what 70 percent or 90 percent really mean,” said Wang, a senior associate at energy policy research organization RMI. Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, said the key question is whether the service agreements between utilities and data center developers cover all the infrastructure costs created by the new demand, rather than only some of them. “I believe that large loads should be required to pay for 100 percent of the incremental costs,” Peskoe said. Utilities around the country are confronting similar questions as they plan new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure to accommodate rapidly growing data center demand. New large-load customer rules increasingly use minimum payments, long-term contracts, financial guarantees and exit charges to reduce the risk that other customers are left paying for infrastructure built for projects that arrive late, use less power than expected or never fully develop. The Review-Journal examined proposed agreements between data center customers and NV Energy, utility testimony and power plans, and submitted multiple public records requests to the PUC. The public filings and records obtained for several data center projects the newspaper reviewed do not contain enough project-specific information to compare the minimum revenue those data centers would provide with the costs NV Energy would not otherwise incur — and determine whether any of those costs could shift to other ratepayers. What 90 percent vs. 70 percent really means The minimum-billing dispute is playing out in a pending commission case over proposed large-load electric service agreements between NV Energy and industrial real estate company Prologis for at least one data center project under development in North Las Vegas. The agreements would govern how NV Energy supplies data centers’ enormous power needs. Prologis argues that a 70 percent minimum better reflects how data centers actually operate, saying their electricity use does not consistently reach 90 percent of capacity in every billing period and can vary as tenants move in. Prologis did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Wang said a 70 percent minimum could recover all new costs incurred by a customer if the underlying rates, direct cost assignments, contract terms and exit provisions enable a utility to collect sufficient revenue. The reverse, she said, is also possible: Even requiring minimum billing at 100 percent of contracted demand would not guarantee full cost recovery if the rates or the way costs are assigned are inadequate. The goal, Wang said, should be 100 percent recovery of the total cost to serve — both the properly assigned new costs and the large customer’s share of existing infrastructure it uses. artigo.texto: Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) has committed €1.2 billion to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ (CIP) sixth flagship renewable energy fund, CI VI. NBIM said CI VI will primarily invest in renewable power generation and energy storage projects across OECD countries in North America, Western Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region. The investment builds on NBIM’s partnership with CIP, following a €900 million commitment to CIP’s fifth flagship fund in 2024 (see Norway Commits €900 Million To CIP’s Renewable Energy Fund). In March 2025, CIP said its CI V fund exceeded the target of €12 billion to support grid connection of 30 of new energy capacity (see Danish Fund Manager Exceeds €12B Target For New RE Fund). The renewable energy business of Australia’s Igneo Infrastructure Partners, Atmos Renewables, has reached financial close on two projects backed by Australia’s Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS). The projects comprise the 400 MW/1,600 MWh Teebar Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Queensland and the 470 MW Parron Maam Marang Wind Farm in Western Australia. Together with the 100 MW/400 MWh Merredin BESS, which reached financial close in June 2025, Atmos says it has now taken 970 MW of CIS-backed capacity through financial close. Teebar BESS will provide 4 hours of storage, storing electricity when supply is abundant and dispatching it during periods of higher demand. Atmos will retain ownership of both projects through construction and operate them once completed. Austrian independent power producer (IPP) Renalfa IPP and Danish renewable energy developer Eurowind Energy have inaugurated the Tenevo hybrid renewable energy complex in southeastern Bulgaria. The project combines a 242 MW solar PV plant with two co-located BESS totaling 311 MW/773 MWh. The Tenevo complex is expected to generate around 332 GWh of clean electricity annually. The solar plant and the first phase of the BESS have been operational since 2025, while the project has now reached its full announced storage capacity. The duo calls it one of Europe's largest hybrid renewable energy projects. Financed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Raiffeisen Bank International, with support from an InvestEU guarantee, the project is located next to a coal region undergoing transition. The Tenovo site is planned to expand with more than 250 MW of wind capacity, with total investment across all phases expected to exceed €500 million. US-based developer and manufacturer of iron-sodium battery systems Inlyte Energy and CutPeak Energy have announced plans for an 80 MWh long-duration BESS at Berkshire East Mountain Resort in western Massachusetts. CutPeak Energy develops battery storage projects at ski resorts. The project is targeted to come online in 2028. The project is one of two long-duration storage demonstrations selected under Massachusetts’ $40.3 million Advancing Massachusetts Power (AMP) Energy Storage Grant Program. The battery will help the resort manage electricity demand from snowmaking, which can reach about 4 MW during peak periods, while also providing backup power during grid outages. Inlyte says the project is designed to charge during periods of lower electricity demand and discharge during snowmaking peaks. European BESS projects operator GIGA Storage has achieved ready-to-build (RTB) status for its 350 MW/1.4 GWh Albatross battery energy storage project near Neuenkirchen in Lower Saxony, Germany. It is developing the project with Isenau Projects and will connect directly to Amprion’s 380 kV high-voltage grid. The project will comprise 264 battery units and is expected to supply electricity equivalent to the daily consumption of approximately 193,000 households. With the development phase completed, GIGA Storage plans to take the final investment decision (FID) in Q4 2026, start construction in H1 2027, and commission the project in 2028. Albatross is GIGA Storage’s first large-scale energy storage project in Germany. It is one of three projects being jointly developed by GIGA Storage and Isenau, with the three projects together representing more than 1 GW of power capacity and 4 GWh of storage capacity. Global energy infrastructure manager Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) has taken the FID on the Kilmarnock South BESS in southern Scotland. The company is investing more than €270 million in the 350 MW/1,400 MWh lithium-ion project. Construction is already underway, and it is expected to begin commercial operations in Q1 2028. The 4-hour BESS will store surplus wind power and discharge electricity to the grid when network capacity is available. CIP said this project is its fourth transmission-connected BESS investment in Scotland. It has an optimization agreement with Shell Energy Europe, ensuring long-term contracted revenue. Together, CIP shared that its four Scottish projects are expected to provide 1.85 GW of power capacity and 4.4 GWh of storage when fully operational. Excelsior Energy Capital-backed Lydian Energy has closed a $300 million holding company credit facility with Infranity, an infrastructure asset manager. Lydian will use the proceeds for the development, construction, acquisition, and operation of its utility-scale battery energy storage and solar projects across the US. Lydian said its portfolio includes about 6 GW of operating, construction-ready and development-stage projects. In April 2026, Lydian acquired 1.5 GW Atlas North solar-plus-storage portfolio from Hanwha Renewables (see Lydian Energy Acquires Hanwha’s 1.5 GW Atlas North Portfolio).

artigo.texto: Reduce emissions to 'profit': New opportunities from the carbon market. (CLO) Officially operational from the end of June 2026, the carbon exchange in Vietnam is considered a significant step towards a low-emission economy. Although the market is still in its nascent stages, Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung - Director of VinaCarbon Investment Fund - believes that Vietnam has sufficient potential to transform emission reduction into a real source of economic value, attracting large capital flows into forestry, clean energy, and agriculture. The carbon exchange in Vietnam officially began operations at the end of June 2026. To date, the number of products and transactions on the market remains quite limited. However, the potential for development is considered significant as Vietnam is accelerating its emission reduction goals, promoting green transitions, and gradually improving the legal framework for the carbon market. Regarding this issue, a reporter from the Journalists and Public Opinion Newspaper had a private interview with Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung, Director of VinaCarbon Investment Fund, about the prospects of the carbon market in Vietnam. The Vietnamese carbon market has many favorable conditions for strong growth. + Sir, the official launch of the carbon exchange in June 2026 is considered the starting point for the carbon market in Vietnam. From an investment perspective, how do you view the opportunities and growth potential of this market in the coming years? - It can be said that the Vietnamese carbon market has many favorable conditions for strong development, especially given that our country is in a favorable position thanks to the convergence of four factors: international demand, natural supply, legal framework, and international institutions ready to cooperate. The pilot operation of the domestic carbon exchange, despite its limited number of products and transactions, is a significant step forward, as it lays the foundation for a transparent market, moving towards a low-emission economy and fulfilling Vietnam's climate commitments. The potential for growth in Vietnam's carbon credit market stems primarily from demand. Domestically, the need to reduce emissions and transition to green is being concretized through quota mechanisms, starting with high-emission industries such as thermal power, steel, and cement, and will be tightened to more industries in the future. Globally , the trend of greening supply chains is gaining momentum, with many new requirements for reducing emissions. From the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for Aviation (CORSIA), the net-zero commitments of multinational corporations, to the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), exporting businesses are being forced to manage their emissions more tightly. This creates a significant demand for high-quality and integrity carbon credits in the future. To meet that demand, Vietnam has potential supply sources in many sectors such as agriculture , renewable energy, waste management, and especially forestry, where there are clear and sustainable advantages. Vietnam has a large forest area, with planted forests accounting for a significant proportion, along with years of experience in forest management and established forest product value chains. Furthermore, forest carbon already has its own legal framework. Projects for forest protection, restoration, and sustainable management can both generate substantial emission reductions and support community livelihoods if appropriate benefit-sharing mechanisms are in place. And because forests are a long-term asset, with project cycles spanning decades, forestry is also best suited to the medium- and long-term development narrative of the market. However, having both supply and demand is not enough, because a market can only develop sustainably when it has the necessary infrastructure. In just about a year and a half, Vietnam has built almost the complete "framework" necessary for a carbon market, from a domestic emissions trading mechanism, an official exchange, a national registration system, to regulations for transferring credits internationally and a separate decree on forest carbon. Furthermore, Vietnam has also established bilateral cooperation channels with Japan and Singapore. In summary, Vietnam has all the necessary conditions for carbon market growth in the coming years. However, the pace of development will depend on the completeness of the legal framework and trading infrastructure, the quality and integrity of the credits, and the ability to meet international standards. You may also like + In your opinion, what are the biggest difficulties and challenges hindering the development of Vietnam's carbon credit market, in terms of credit supply, credit quality, trading mechanisms, and the ability of businesses to participate? - The biggest challenge currently is the limited supply of high-quality carbon credits. Generating a carbon credit requires a relatively long and expensive process, from project development and evaluation to registration, making it generally difficult for investors to access. Furthermore, buyers of carbon credits are becoming increasingly demanding regarding quality. Criteria such as complementarity, risk of reversal, and risk of double counting are receiving more attention. Therefore, the market will tend to prioritize credits certified by reputable standards. This requires Vietnam to improve its measurement, reporting, and assessment capabilities, while gradually harmonizing domestic standards with international practices. Another challenge lies in the legal framework and market infrastructure. Regulations, credit standards, data systems, and supervisory mechanisms still need further improvement to increase transparency, build confidence, and reduce uncertainty for investors. artigo.texto: SEATTLE — Amazon.com Inc. is pledging $1 billion or more over five years to communities where it builds and operates data centers. The company last week unveiled the “Built Together” investment framework for communities where the tech giant operates data centers across the United States. The increased investment will fund free community college for local residents, energy upgrades for homes and businesses, job training and protecting local water resources, the company said. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run,” Matt Garman, chief executive officer for Amazon Web Services, wrote in an October 2 post. “The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so.” Amazon is a leading player in the tech industry’s massive AI buildout that relies, in part, on finding communities willing to host data centers. Garman noted that there are more than 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the United States. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race,” he said, “and the consequences would last generations.” Added Garman, “There are clearly areas in which the technology and energy industries can be doing better (along with their government partners) but just like in the past when the country has banded together to accomplish something that’s critical for our national security and economic prosperity — we should approach this as a long-term mission that the private and public sectors pursue together.” Amazon said it is responding to apprehension over the data center buildout by codifying a series of tenets in what the company is calling its “Amazon Data Center Commitment.” The company commits to “protect and enhance communities,” “provide jobs and economic opportunities,” “engage communities,” and “build and operate responsibly.” Submit Your Press Release Have news to share? artigo.texto: Good morning. Andrew Nusca here, back in action after a week in New York for our inaugural AIQ Summit about putting AI to work in large companies. (Many thanks to Alexei Oreskovic for steering the ship while I was away.) Miss the AIQ festivities? No sweat—you can watch the entire thing here or view a session of your choosing here. If you’re in the business of deploying AI in the enterprise, there are lots of good insights to be had. And today’s tech news? Well, let’s get right to it. —Andrew Nusca Thoughts? Suggestions? Hot tip? Drop me a line. THE BIG STORY Meta is building one of the world’s biggest undersea cable networks While data centers dominate headlines amid mounting local opposition over electricity bills, water use, and zoning fights, Meta has been expanding its infrastructure somewhere far less visible: the bottom of the ocean. On Sept. 21, the company announced Petal, a roughly 4,300-mile subsea cable connecting the U.S. and France. Meta says the cable, expected to enter service in 2029, will be the first to deliver petabit-scale capacity across an ocean—double what today’s most advanced transoceanic cables can handle, thanks to “two-core fiber” that fits two light paths inside each strand. Projects like this rarely make headlines in an industry fixated on AI models and apps, but they’re what make those products run. Products like Meta’s personal AI agent Muse depend on moving enormous volumes of data between its data centers and its users around the world. Subsea cables aren’t new territory for Meta, which is now valued at roughly $1.85 trillion. The company has spent the past decade building its presence on the seafloor and says it has invested in more than 20 subsea cable projects. Taken together, those projects touch every continent except Antarctica. The most ambitious is Project Waterworth, announced in February 2025. Meta says the system will stretch more than 31,000 miles, longer than the Earth’s circumference. It will connect the U.S., Brazil, South Africa, India, and other regions across five continents. Meta hasn’t built all of this alone. Petal is being developed with Japan’s NEC and Sumitomo Electric Industries, and French telecom Orange is handling the landing on France’s Atlantic coast. Meta has even partnered with rivals: The MAREA cable between Virginia and Spain, completed in 2017, is jointly owned with Microsoft and telecom company Telxius. These projects don’t come cheap. TechCrunch estimates that the Waterworth project could top $10 billion. —James LaForge THE BLIND BOX “Just because you are using AI, that is not a proxy for your productivity or you doing a good job at work.” THE RUNDOWN —Trump forms “Super Intelligence Force” led by National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton. —OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” —Meta's Muse compiles “a page for every person in the user's life,” per Wired. —Firmus IPO: Investor demand far exceeds the offer size, one of Australia's largest. —Schneider Electric may buy PTC, the U.S. engineering software firm, for $20 billion. —Apple CEO John Ternus is in the design studio “several times per week,” per Bloomberg. —McKinsey: AI and automation will eliminate 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035 but add 41 million elsewhere. —U.K. neobank Monzo may sell a 15% stake to CVC and Advent after a Nubank deal fell apart. THE PARTING SLOP Sam told Mark not to say anything. Mark can't go in there, brazenly flaunt the rules and then think Sam’s gonna share his CUDA with him. Sorry! This is what comes from living under a Jensen regime.

artigo.texto: Cygni Energy and Indus Towers will explore BESS manufacturing capacity of up to 1.5 GWh for telecom applications The companies will evaluate higher-capacity and emerging battery technologies for telecom infrastructure Cygni currently operates a 4.8 GWh cell-to-container BESS facility in Hyderabad and plans to expand its overall capacity beyond 10 GWh Indian energy storage manufacturer Cygni Energy and telecom infrastructure company Indus Towers have joined hands to explore up to 1.5 GWh of battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing in India to serve telecom infrastructure. The duo has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) and plans to establish manufacturing capacity to meet the ‘evolving energy requirements’ of telecom infrastructure in India. The partnership will also evaluate advanced battery technologies for telecom applications. Formed by the merger of Bharti Infratel Limited and Indus Towers, Indus Towers Limited had over 267,611 towers and 432,250 co-locations as of June 30, 2026. It is present across 22 telecom circles. While Cygni's official statement does not reveal details about the MoU, telecom companies have been exploring energy storage as a backup power strategy to improve operational efficiency. According to Battery Council International (BCI), batteries can help provide stable power for data centers and telecom systems. Incubated at IIT Madras, Cygni Energy develops energy storage products for telecom, stationary energy storage, mobility, and other applications. Its battery portfolio currently includes 100 Ah solutions and could expand to higher-capacity systems, including 314 Ah. “We plan to develop capacity of up to 2 GWh, while building a portfolio that can evolve from today’s 100Ah solutions to higher-capacity 314Ah systems and emerging battery technologies,” said Cygni Energy Founder & CEO Venkat Rajaraman. In 2025, Cygni Energy opened a 4.8 GWh cell-to-container BESS Gigafactory in Hyderabad’s Maheshwaram, with plans to scale it up to exceed 10 GWh in the future. “Our ambition is to combine scale, reliability and Indian engineering to create future-ready energy storage solutions that can evolve alongside India’s rapidly expanding digital infrastructure,” added Rajaraman. According to Crisil, India could see up to 50 GWh of BESS installations by FY2028 as the technology helps improve power availability during peak demand. However, reducing reliance on overseas suppliers remains important to limit exposure to global supply disruptions and procurement uncertainties (see Crisil Projects India To Add 50 GWh BESS Capacity By FY2028).

artigo.texto: Just outside Toledo, Ohio, Meta is building an $800 million data center campus. Annually, the data center will use only as much water as two full-service restaurants using a technology known as a closed-loop system. The Great Lakes region offers an unmatched set of resources ripe for data center development, including an abundance of fresh water for cooling; longer, colder winters than the South or Sunbelt; and former industrial lands ready for redevelopment. But in Illinois, a polarizing data center debate has heated up in recent weeks. I agree with Gov. JB Pritzker’s recent statement at New York’s America is All in Conference. When asked whether we should be welcoming data centers into Illinois, he said that we need to ensure that data centers are bringing their own energy, and they are using their own closed-loop water systems. There are still very valid public concerns about letting these data centers develop projects untethered to government accountability. I hear them weekly on the campaign trail from Chicagoans who voice concern that we could damage Lake Michigan by exploiting its resources too heavily and that our electricity bills could skyrocket. I have two solutions for those main two concerns. Regarding the first concern — water usage — many Chicagoans I speak with hear “data center” and picture a server farm drinking up the lake. My vision is to build a massive geothermal heat sink coil system in Lake Michigan. This system is closed loop and filled with liquid coolant. This loop would be miles, perhaps tens or hundreds of miles, long and coiled far offshore at or near the bottom of the lake (the deeper, the better, as it’s colder). This system would consume water over time, thus taking a data center’s water consumption to virtually zero. The second concern I have heard is that with this new architecture, we would cook the lake. But Lake Michigan holds about a quadrillion gallons of water, so adding data centers is like setting a sealed coffee thermos in a swimming pool — it wouldn’t change. From a thermodynamics perspective, even with miles of coils and loops constantly cooling themselves in Lake Michigan, we likely could not even marginally increase the temperature or create an environmentally noticeable impact. But “it’s fine, trust me” is not good enough for a lake this city drinks from, so I propose a water and environmental study before a single pipe goes in, with the results and data published where anyone can read it. On top of closed-loop infrastructure at the bottom of the lake, data centers should have windows. It may sound basic, but right now, data center construction typically creates hard cases of primarily concrete with no ability to leverage the outside cold air. They are basically heat-trapping boxes, and, as we now know, they produce a massive amount of heat. When a house is hot, open the windows. When a data center is hot, open the windows. Chicago’s cooler fall, chilling winter and brisk spring climates all lend themselves to a basic idea of circulating cold air into the data center itself and hot air out. With windows open, they essentially have natural air conditioning three-quarters of the year. The marginal cost to put in windows and natural cooling systems in northern and colder climates such as Chicago far outweighs the risk of continuing to use billions of gallons of water and energy to sustain these operations. The potential savings are not marginal; they are massive. Cornell University has cooled its campus from a Finger Lake for 25 years and reports saving roughly 85% of the energy conventional refrigeration would burn. Toronto has cooled more than a hundred downtown buildings with Lake Ontario since 2004, saving about 90,000 megawatt hours a year, enough to power a town of 25,000 people. Its system is nearly full, and it is spending $100 million to expand it. A massive, closed-loop coil system in Lake Michigan could cool much more than data centers; it could provide air conditioning and cooling for hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of households and buildings across the city as climate change increases the overall temperature throughout the year. None of this is theoretical anymore because the demand is already here. Chicago’s data center vacancy rate is under 2%. There is not a single block of 5 megawatts or more available to lease anywhere in this market, and developers asking ComEd to connect new projects are being told 2032 and beyond, which is why they are now buying land based on where the power is rather than where they want to be. The real question is whether we shape our response or let it shape us. We are constantly told we have to pick. Jobs or the lake. Investment or affordable power bills. The artificial intelligence economy or the environment. I have never accepted that framing, and my entire plan for Chicago when I am mayor argues against it. This is not a “this or that.” It is both creating more jobs while protecting the lake and environment. Chicago has an answer, and it is sitting a few miles off Michigan Avenue at the bottom of the lake. Joe Holberg is a Chicago mayoral candidate. He was a math teacher on the West Side, then a small business owner and entrepreneur helping Chicagoans work toward financial goals. artigo.texto: [Photo: MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND CLIMATE CHANGE/ FACEBOOK] Fiji has launched a five-year $5.2 million plan aimed at preparing the country to enter international carbon markets by 2030. The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan was launched yesterday during the opening of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. The plan sets out the regulatory, technical and institutional systems Fiji needs before its first international carbon trade under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. It focuses on sectors including energy, transport, agriculture, waste and forestry, with strong emphasis on forests, mangroves, wetlands and other nature-based solutions. Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu says carbon markets must deliver benefits beyond the trading of carbon. “For Fiji, carbon markets must be about more than trading carbon. They must deliver real climate action, unlock new and sustainable sources of climate finance, and ensure that the benefits reach our communities and resource owners.” The plan places communities and resource owners at the centre, with provisions for fair benefit-sharing, social and environmental safeguards and Free, Prior and Informed Consent. Fiji will also establish a Fijian Transactional Registry and a National Carbon Market Inter-Agency Technical Working Group to manage and track carbon market activities. The Government will use the plan to engage development partners, donors and potential carbon buyers to secure the finance and technical support needed for implementation. Conservation International says the plan could help Fiji attract high-integrity carbon finance while protecting ecosystems and supporting resilient livelihoods.

artigo.texto: Tighter data center rules on Fort Smith Board agenda The Fort Smith Board of Directors is set to vote Tuesday (Oct. 6) on an ordinance that would give the city more oversight of any planned data center development within the city. The ordinance, if approved, also would require more information from utilities about energy availability and potential energy load. Board members on Aug. 11 asked city staff to craft new rules or amend existing rules around water use, zoning and other areas to discourage data center construction in the city and the metro. According to the city, there are no known data centers being considered in the Fort Smith metro. Tim Allen, president and CEO of the Fort Smith Regional Chamber of Commerce, said chamber staff are ânot actively working a data center project.â There are five large announced data center projects in the state. The facilities are either planned or in some stage of construction in Clarksville, Conway, Little Rock, Pulaski County, and West Memphis. The proposed ordinance the board will consider Tuesday would require a development plan review by the Planning Commission and then full board approval of a data center project in the cityâs industrial zoning districts. The ordinance also would require an eight-foot opaque wall surrounding the property, 500 feet setbacks from each property line, and âletters from applicable public utilities regarding capacity and proposed load.â The cityâs Planning Commission voted unanimously for the proposed ordinance, according to a memo from Deputy City Administrator Maggie Rice. The ordinance does not include any language about water rates and access to the cityâs regional water system. At the Aug. 11 board study session, Director Kevin Settle suggested the city consider significantly higher water rates for data centers. Settle also said he would support language that gives the board authority over certain water connections outside city limits. âTo me, the water, Iâve said many times, is our commodity, and we should be able to choose what is the price for it,â Settle said at the Aug. 11 meeting. BACKGROUND Arkansas officials, with support from Gov. Sarah Sanders, have restricted local government actions on data centers. Arkansas Act 851 of 2023 prevents local governments from banning data center development. The law does not prevent local governments from adopting rules that create delays or significant restrictions with data center projects. The cities of Fayetteville and Little Rock have approved more stringent data center development rules. The development of data centers nationwide and in Arkansas has become controversial, with pushback often resulting from local grassroots efforts. Concerns include the potential for massive water use, rising utility rates, excessive noise, and groundwater pollution. The state of New York recently implemented a one-year moratorium on data center construction. According to reporting from CNBC and other outlets, more than 500 local governments nationwide have enacted bans, moratoriums, and other restrictions on data centers. âData centers sit at the intersection of economic development, energy policy and state fiscal health,â according to a report from the National Conference of State Legislatures. âWhile 38 states currently offer dedicated tax incentives to attract data centers, lawmakers across the country are working to balance economic development priorities with sustainable development goals. These capital-intensive projects can generate significant tax revenue for localities, yet data centers also contribute to surging energy demand across the country.â
