artigo.texto: Amazon responde à reação contra seus centros de dados: fim das siglas e uma nova postura na era da transparência Recentemente, a Amazon Web Services (AWS) tentou acalmar as crescentes suspeitas e críticas relacionadas à operação de seus centros de dados, após uma forte repercussão negativa. Em uma resposta que surpreendeu muitos, a gigante do e-commerce declarou que não utiliza mais acordos de confidencialidade (NDAs) como ferramenta de blindagem, sinalizando uma tentativa de maior transparência. Este movimento é mais do que uma simples mudança administrativa: é um sinal de que gigantes de tecnologia estão sendo forçados a repensar suas estratégias de comunicação diante de uma sociedade cada vez mais consciente e questionadora. Rebatendo a desconfiança: a tentativa da Amazon de abrir os seus centros de dados O impacto da transparência na relação com o público Ao afirmar que não usa mais NDAs para esconder suas operações, a Amazon tenta reverter a narrativa de opacidade que assola a indústria de tecnologia. Essa postura pode ajudar a reconstruir a confiança dos consumidores e investidores, que hoje buscam mais do que apenas eficiência; querem responsabilidade e clareza. Em tempos de vigilância digital e debates sobre privacidade, a transparência deixou de ser um diferencial e virou uma necessidade. Por outro lado, essa mudança também pode ser vista como uma estratégia de marketing, uma tentativa de mostrar uma imagem mais aberta e ética diante de seus concorrentes. Afinal, a confiança não se conquista apenas com palavras, mas com ações concretas de transparência que comprovem a ausência de práticas questionáveis. A decisão da Amazon reforça a ideia de que, na era digital, informações são poder — e quem as controla, domina a narrativa. Por fim, essa postura pode influenciar toda uma indústria, levando outras empresas a adotarem uma postura mais aberta. Uma maior transparência pode criar um efeito dominó, promovendo uma cultura empresarial mais responsável e menos sigilosa, em benefício de toda a sociedade. O debate ético: confidencialidade versus transparência O uso de NDAs sempre foi uma ferramenta de proteção legal, mas também um método de esconder práticas que podem ser questionadas. A Amazon, ao anunciar que não utiliza mais essas siglas, coloca em xeque uma prática que há muito tempo é alvo de críticas na tecnologia. Afinal, quão transparente uma empresa precisa ser para atender às expectativas de uma sociedade cada vez mais informada? Por outro lado, há questões legítimas sobre segurança de dados, propriedade intelectual e estratégias comerciais que justificam certos níveis de sigilo. Equilibrar transparência e proteção não é uma tarefa simples, mas a postura da Amazon sugere que a balança deve pender mais para a abertura, especialmente em tempos de crise de confiança. Essa mudança de postura pode servir de exemplo para o setor, que frequentemente oscila entre sigilo e transparência. Por fim, essa discussão também revela uma mudança cultural: a sociedade está mais atenta e exige que as empresas sejam responsáveis e abertas. A ética corporativa, portanto, deixa de ser apenas uma questão de boas intenções e passa a ser uma estratégia de sobrevivência no mercado global. O futuro da comunicação corporativa na era digital A resposta da Amazon à reação contra seus centros de dados marca um ponto de virada na comunicação empresarial. Empresas que antes preferiam o sigilo agora precisam se adaptar a um cenário onde a transparência é cada vez mais esperada e exigida. Essa mudança pode impulsionar uma nova era de diálogo aberto, onde informações antes restritas se tornam acessíveis ao público. O impacto dessa postura pode se refletir em uma relação mais saudável entre corporações e sociedade, promovendo uma cultura de responsabilidade. Além disso, empresas que adotam uma postura mais transparente tendem a conquistar maior fidelidade e respeito, essenciais na construção de uma marca sólida e sustentável. Por outro lado, há o risco de que essa abertura excessiva gere vulnerabilidades e exposições desnecessárias. Assim, o desafio será encontrar um equilíbrio que permita transparência sem comprometer a segurança e a competitividade. O que a Amazon nos mostra é que, na era digital, a comunicação não pode mais ser uma via de mão única, mas um diálogo constante e sincero. Reflexões finais: a transparência como caminho para a credibilidade no mundo tecnológico A resposta da Amazon ao backlash, afirmando que não utiliza mais NDAs, é um passo importante na direção de uma maior transparência no setor de tecnologia. Essa mudança reflete uma sociedade que não aceita mais mistérios e busca entender melhor o funcionamento das grandes corporações que moldam seu cotidiano. A credibilidade, neste cenário, depende cada vez mais de ações que reforçam a confiança. Embora ainda existam desafios e limites para a abertura total, esse movimento sinaliza que o mercado está mudando. Empresas que adotarem uma postura honesta e transparente poderão se destacar em um ambiente cada vez mais competitivo e consciente. Para o consumidor, essa é uma oportunidade de exigir mais responsabilidade e ética de quem fornece produtos e serviços. Convido você, leitor, a refletir: até que ponto a transparência pode transformar a relação entre empresas e sociedade? Compartilhe sua opinião nos comentários ou compartilhe este artigo para ampliar o debate sobre o futuro da comunicação corporativa na era digital. artigo.texto: Voters in eight states have faced, or are soon to face, local ballot measures over data center development, as the infrastructure powering AI becomes an increasingly important issue in the midterm elections. According to the latest Ballotpedia count, at least 39 measures have been scheduled across California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin. Of those, 35 will be decided during the November 3 general election, while four were put to voters earlier in the year. The proposals range from outright bans on new data centers to advisory questions supporting the development. Others would require voter approval, introduce zoning protections or place conditions on companies receiving tax incentives. Data centers have become a major midterm issue because of concerns about their demands on electric grids, water supplies and land, as well as questions about tax breaks and whether residential customers could be left paying for infrastructure upgrades. At the same time, supporters argue that the facilities are essential to America’s AI ambitions and can generate construction work, investment and local tax revenue. The debate is affecting midterm races, even when data centers don’t appear directly on the ballot. Candidates are increasingly being judged on whether they do or don’t support tax incentives or projects, or whether they have or haven't called for restrictions and greater protections for ratepayers. In Ohio, for example, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has sought to make Republican Senator Jon Husted's role in the growth of the state's data center industry a central campaign issue, arguing that Husted was a leading advocate for the projects during his time as lieutenant governor. Brown told the Statehouse News Bureau in August: "I've made clear from the beginning that Jon Husted is the point man for these 230 or 240 new data centers in Ohio," labeling him “the face of data centers in Ohio.” During his time in office, Husted did publicly celebrate projects from technology companies including Google and Amazon Web Services, arguing that they would help establish Ohio as the "tech capital of the Midwest" and strengthen the state's role in the AI economy. More recently, however, Husted has emphasized consumer protections around data center growth, introducing the Ratepayer Protection Act, which seeks to ensure large electricity users such as data centers pay for the infrastructure needed to serve them rather than shifting costs onto households and small businesses. That evolution is reflected in Newsweek's AI Policy Scorecard, an interactive tool that evaluates where members of Congress stand on AI-related issues including regulation, data centers and energy, jobs and the economy, safety and privacy, and national security. Lawmakers are ranked from "AI Skeptic" to "AI Booster" based on their voting records, legislation, and public statements. While Brown continues to focus on Husted's previous support for bringing data centers to Ohio, the scorecard currently categorizes Husted as a "Lean Skeptic" on data centers and energy, indicating a more cautious approach to large-scale expansion and its impact on communities and utility customers than lawmakers classified as "boosters." Here are all 39 measures tracked by Ballotpedia, including the 35 scheduled for November and four decided earlier in 2026. California Voters in Alhambra will settle on a measure that would prohibit data centers within the city. It’s one of the most straightforward measures on the November ballot, as it simply asks residents whether the facilities should be banned rather than regulated through additional conditions. A second California measure has already been decided. In June, 88 percent of voters in Monterey Park supported a policy that amended the city’s land-use framework to prohibit data centers. Florida In Edgewater, voters will consider an amendment prohibiting new data centers from being approved, built, expanded, or operated within the city. The measure goes beyond preventing new projects by also addressing the expansion and operation of data center facilities, giving voters a broader choice over how they want the industry to operate within the community going forward. Illinois Seven measures are being put before Illinois voters, although several are advisory and would communicate residents’ preferences rather than automatically changing local law. In Bloomington, voters will determine whether to advise the city to impose a moratorium on the construction of large-scale data centers. Four measures are concentrated in Madison County. Voters in Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki, and Venice will be asked whether officials should permit the construction and operation of new data centers. In Joliet, in Will County, voters will consider an advisory question asking whether the city should approve the construction of AI data centers. Meanwhile, voters in Morgan County will decide whether to advise county officials to impose restrictions on the construction and operation of data centers. Together, the Illinois measures show that not every data center vote is designed to block development: Five ask whether officials should support or permit projects, while two seek a moratorium or additional restrictions. Kansas Three Kansas cities will vote on proposed data center prohibitions. In El Dorado, an initiative would prohibit the construction of “high-impact” data centers, as well as certain Type 2 and Type 3 battery energy storage systems. Voters in Emporia will also consider a measure prohibiting the construction of high-impact data centers within the city. In Ottawa, the proposed ban is tied to electricity consumption. It would prohibit data centers using more than 25 megawatts of power, a threshold also used by several measures in Ohio. artigo.texto: DENR sets forest carbon market regulatory foundations Nicer called for stronger global guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) recently disclosed that the Philippines has already established the regulatory foundations of a credible forest carbon market by issuing two major policy instruments designed to directly address private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways. Atty. Daniel Darius M. Nicer, DENR assistant secretary for integrated management system and information systems, spoke at the High-Level Roundtable convened in the sidelines of 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York last week, and declared that these regulatory milestones position the country to attract high-integrity private investments in nature-based carbon projects. Addressing international ministers, climate envoys and business executives at the session titled “Shaping High-Integrity Carbon Markets,” Nicer emphasized that corporate buyers require predictability and environmental rigor before deploying capital at scale. “To date, the Philippines, through its Department of Environment and Natural Resources, issued two major policy instruments that establish the foundations of a credible forest carbon market directly addressing private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways,” he said during the meeting convened by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development at Climate Week NYC. The first policy instrument is the adoption of the Philippines’ Readiness in the Voluntary Forest Carbon Market Roadmap (2026 to 2030). The strategic framework sets out national direction for policy development, measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) systems, data management, and registry readiness — key elements corporate investors evaluate when assessing market reliability. The second instrument is the national guidelines for the establishment, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon credit projects. These rules enforce environmental integrity, Free, Prior and Informed Consent compliance, and guaranteed community benefit-sharing, while mandating transparent project registration to significantly reduce reputational and delivery risks for corporate buyers. “For the Philippines, carbon markets — both voluntary and compliance pathways — are central to our strategy for accelerating mitigation and unlocking climate finance,” Nicer said. “But for markets to function, the private sector needs clarity, predictability, and confidence that the credits they purchase are real, additional, and backed by strong governance.” Beyond forestry, Nicer highlighted broader national carbon governance efforts, including the Department of Energy’s guidelines for renewable energy projects, the overarching Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework, and the rollout of the Philippine National Carbon Registry to ensure full accounting traceability and prevent double counting. He added that domestic policies are aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement through bilateral partnerships, such as the Implementation Agreement with Singapore and the Joint Crediting Mechanism with Japan. Looking ahead to the COP31 climate summit, he called for stronger global guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. “High-integrity markets should not only accelerate global ambition, but also deliver real, measurable mitigation outcomes that directly benefit and reach the communities, ecosystems, and sectors that need them most,” Nicer said. artigo.texto: A WEG prepara uma expansão industrial de US$ 165 milhões na América do Norte, com novas estruturas no México e nos Estados Unidos e uma meta de multiplicar por cinco sua capacidade global de geradores até 2030. A brasileira WEG anunciou um plano de investimento de US$ 165 milhões, aproximadamente R$ 840 milhões pela conversão divulgada pela própria companhia, para ampliar a fabricação de geradores na América do Norte. O projeto será executado em duas fases e pretende elevar a capacidade global da empresa dos atuais 10 para cerca de 50 geradores por dia, avanço relacionado ao aumento da demanda por infraestrutura crítica nos Estados Unidos, especialmente para data centers. Anunciada em 28 de setembro de 2026, a expansão combina uma nova operação no México e a construção de outras duas instalações industriais na América do Norte. A primeira etapa deverá entrar em operação já no segundo trimestre de 2027, enquanto a segunda está prevista para ser concluída até 2030. - Gigante chinesa prepara fábrica de R$ 200 milhões em Minas Gerais para dobrar produção de cabos ópticos - Brasil pode perder empregos e valor da sucata porque Repetro facilita operação de plataformas, mas deixa desmantelamento e reciclagem fora da mesma lógica tributária - Fábrica de semicondutores no RS recebe R$ 84,86 milhões para produzir memórias avançadas usadas em smartphones e inteligência artificial - Após 64 anos no Rio, Limppano investe R$ 50 milhões para ampliar fábrica, comprar novas áreas e modernizar produção O investimento ocorre enquanto grandes centros de processamento de dados ampliam a demanda por equipamentos capazes de sustentar operações que não podem ficar sem eletricidade. No caso da WEG, os geradores são destinados a aplicações críticas e podem integrar sistemas de energia de emergência e continuidade de fornecimento. O próprio presidente da companhia, Alberto Kuba, relacionou recentemente o movimento à aceleração desse mercado. Em entrevista à Exame, o executivo afirmou que a empresa “não imaginávamos que teria esse boom”, ao comentar o ritmo da demanda associada aos data centers. México receberá primeira etapa da expansão A expansão começará no México. Dos US$ 165 milhões previstos, US$ 24 milhões serão destinados à compra e adaptação de um prédio industrial localizado ao lado do atual Parque Industrial de Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula. A nova estrutura será voltada à montagem de geradores e deverá começar a operar no segundo trimestre de 2027. A escolha do local aproveita uma presença industrial que a WEG já mantém no município mexicano. Em janeiro de 2025, a companhia havia inaugurado a ampliação de uma fábrica de produtos de automação em Atotonilco de Tula, com aproximadamente 4,9 mil metros quadrados de área construída. A estrutura passou a concentrar atividades de produção, engenharia, projetos de painéis e treinamento. Segunda fase concentra US$ 141 milhões No novo projeto de geradores, porém, a maior parte dos recursos ficará para a segunda fase. A WEG prevê desembolsar US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais em território norte-americano. Até o anúncio, a empresa ainda não havia definido publicamente onde essas duas unidades serão construídas. Essa segunda etapa terá uma configuração mais verticalizada. Em vez de concentrar a operação apenas na montagem, as novas fábricas deverão incorporar processos como fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças. Segundo a WEG, a internalização dessas etapas busca aumentar a eficiência operacional e a competitividade da produção. O projeto também reduz a quantidade de processos industriais que precisam ser executados fora da nova estrutura antes da montagem final dos equipamentos. A diferença de escala entre as duas fases aparece também na distribuição dos investimentos. Os US$ 141 milhões previstos para a segunda etapa representam aproximadamente 85% dos US$ 165 milhões anunciados para todo o programa de expansão. Capacidade global pode saltar de 10 para 50 geradores por dia Quando o projeto estiver concluído, a mudança deverá ser significativa na capacidade industrial da companhia. Hoje, a WEG informa capacidade global de aproximadamente 10 geradores por dia. Até 2030, a previsão é alcançar cerca de 50 unidades diárias, considerando as fábricas localizadas no México, Estados Unidos, Brasil e China. Isso representa uma capacidade cinco vezes maior que a atual. O número, contudo, deve ser entendido como capacidade global de fabricação prevista depois da conclusão da expansão, e não como produção efetivamente realizada hoje ou como volume destinado exclusivamente aos data centers. A WEG também não informou que todos os 50 geradores diários serão produzidos nas novas instalações da América do Norte. A projeção considera o conjunto das operações da companhia nos quatro países citados. Expansão está ligada ao negócio incorporado com a Marathon O movimento industrial está ligado à Marathon, marca incorporada ao portfólio da WEG após uma aquisição anunciada em setembro de 2023. Na ocasião, a companhia brasileira fechou a compra dos negócios de motores elétricos industriais e geradores da Regal Rexnord por US$ 400 milhões, operação que envolveu as marcas Marathon, Cemp e Rotor. A transação trouxe para a WEG aproximadamente 2.800 funcionários e dez fábricas distribuídas por sete países: Estados Unidos, México, China, Índia, Itália, Países Baixos e Canadá. Também foram incorporadas estruturas comerciais em outros mercados. Três anos depois, a companhia associa diretamente os novos US$ 165 milhões ao crescimento desses negócios. João Paulo Gualberto da Silva, vice-presidente da Unidade de Energia da WEG, afirmou no anúncio que a expansão aumenta a capacidade produtiva e reforça a integração das operações incorporadas com a Marathon. artigo.texto: What does the data say about data centers? People everywhere are talking about data centers, the high-tech facilities that house our nations growing digital infrastructure. Illinois is a Top 10 state for data centers, with a history dating all the way back to the 1970s, initially as a central repository to meet the technology needs of state agencies. More recently, however, data centers have become the foundation of a global technology race in the private sector, housing large computer servers, storage, and networking equipment necessary to support cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI). In Illinois, they comprise 7% of total electricity demand (and climbing). Many rely on water for cooling. And new data centers often come seemingly out-of-nowhere, as major technology companies use of nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) with elected officials instead of committing to public transparency. All of which has contributed to a public backlash against construction of these facilities that is playing out in statehouses and electoral campaigns around the country. Developments have been canceled or postponed, and Gov. JB Pritzker paused Illinois tax exemption for data centers. But data centers now are a fixture of the modern economy. Understanding their costs and benefits and identifying the guardrails needed to mitigate risk to our communities is of paramount importance. It is with these factors in mind that the Illinois Economic Policy Institute and the Project for Middle Class Renewal at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign recently undertook the most robust analysis of Illinois data centers to date. Specifically, we looked at 75 completed and ongoing projects and related reports culled from state, county, and industry data, and integrated industry-standard economic modeling to forecast potential impacts of $57 billion in planned data center projects across our state over the next decade. Here’s what we found. First, data centers mean jobs. More than 120,000 of them over the next 10 years, to be exact. About a third of these will be in skilled construction occupations or IT, engineering, and operations jobs that pay well into the six figures, and the other two-thirds in the supply chain or as a result of related increases in consumer spending across the economy. This investment will grow the Illinois economy by $5 billion a year during the construction phase, and about $2 billion per year thereafter. The facilities would also mean $300 million in new property tax revenue going to local communities each year nearly two-thirds of which will support public schools. When it comes to protecting communities from potential costs, the picture is more complex. By 2035, new data centers could use the same electricity as 4.5 million Illinois homes. Without any sort of requirements that data centers produce or otherwise offset their power demands, this would increase average Illinois household electric bills by $12 per month. Water resources can also be strained, unless new data centers use the air-cooling or closed-loop systems which recycle water instead of constantly drawing on new resources that are becoming commonplace. In both cases, there are tools available to policymakers to mitigate the risk and ensure responsible development of data centers. First, they can be required to pay for 100% of their energy, transmission, and interconnection costs and to use closed-loop or air-cooling systems to reduce water usage. The currently suspended sales tax exemption could be reformed to promote stronger energy and environmental standards, rewarding only those facilities that install Illinois-based clean energy. New data centers can be required to have battery storage. And policymakers can improve public disclosure around energy usage, water usage, and contact with elected officials. Even though the data on data centers shows they can be a net positive for our economy and our communities, there is a trust deficit. With commonsense guardrails, Illinois can modernize our energy system, protect workers and ratepayers, and improve transparency around an industry that too many people believe has been operating in the dark. Frank Manzo IV, MPP is an economist at the nonpartisan Illinois Economic Policy Institute.

artigo.texto: By PACNEWS Fiji has launched a FJD$5.2 million (US$2.6 million) five-year plan to develop its carbon market and position the country to undertake its first international carbon trade by 2030. The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan 2026–2030 was launched by the Government on the opening day of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. The plan, developed by the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change in collaboration with the Ministry of Forestry and Conservation International, sets out the systems and frameworks Fiji needs to participate in international carbon markets. Carbon markets allow verified reductions in greenhouse gas emissions to be traded, creating opportunities for Fiji to attract climate finance for projects that reduce emissions and protect natural ecosystems. The Government said the plan could help attract new investment into renewable energy, sustainable forestry, waste management and the protection of forests, mangroves and other ecosystems. Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu said Fiji’s carbon market must deliver benefits beyond the trading of carbon. “For Fiji, carbon markets must be about more than trading carbon. They must deliver real climate action, unlock new and sustainable sources of climate finance, and ensure that the benefits reach our communities and resource owners,” Bulitavu said. The plan places communities and resource owners at the centre of Fiji’s carbon market development, with a focus on fair benefit-sharing, safeguards and resilient livelihoods. The Government said the framework would prepare Fiji to access emerging sources of climate finance while ensuring communities and resource owners share in the benefits. It has also called on development partners to support implementation of the plan. The plan forms part of Fiji’s broader efforts to mobilise climate finance and strengthen its capacity to respond to climate change while protecting the country’s natural ecosystems.

artigo.texto: Cheyenne and Arapaho tribal citizens voted Saturday to impose a three-year moratorium on data center construction on tribal lands. During the tribal meeting, the floor was opened for anyone to speak about the topic. The primary concerns related to environmental, economic and transparency issues. Key Takeaways - Cheyenne and Arapaho tribal citizens voted Saturday for a three-year moratorium on data center construction on tribal lands. - Of 351 votes cast, 261 supported the moratorium, 83 opposed it and seven abstained. - Tribal citizens raised concerns about water use, environmental effects, potential economic benefits and transparency surrounding future data center proposals. - Cheyenne and Arapaho Gov. Reggie Wassana said no data center agreement has been signed and said any potential project would undergo further study and community discussion. Environmental Concerns “We have a spiritual responsibility because we are Cheyenne and Arapaho people and our traditional values respect this water of life,” said Kyle Spotted Horse, a member of the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes. He brought up Mní Wičóni at Standing Rock, the location of a protest against an oil pipeline that crosses Sioux land in the Dakotas. In 2016, a vocal protest against the Dakota Access Pipe Line took place, creating the Mní Wičóni movement to protect water and tribal lands. Spotted Horse said a data center would require 300,000 gallons of water per day, adding up to 100 million gallons per year. RELATED: Oklahomans Gather In Downtown OKC In Support Of Standing Rock Sioux Tribe A group of Oklahomans gathered at downtown Oklahoma City’s Kerr Park to show support for the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe in their fight against the Dakota Access Pipeline. “Until we adjudicate our water rights, how do we move forward with such a massive amount of consumption of water?” Patrick Kincaid said. According to Oklahoma State University, water right adjudication is the process through which groups can establish who has ownership of which bodies of water. “You know what would be a dealbreaker for me is that through this whole process, there is 100% transparency. No NDAs and a full impact study, especially on our buffalo,” said another woman. “We’ve spent years building our herds. How will this affect our buffalo herd? And as good neighbors, what impact will this have on surrounding farms and farmland and animals? I want us to be informed all along the way.” Damon Dunbar raised the question of fracking and its comparable water usage to a potential data center. “They’re draining Canton Lake right now to feed Oklahoma City. That’s not funny, that’s very deadly. We’re not going to be having anything. We’re going to be looking like south Texas or the desert.” Another man was concerned about the effects of drought and further water usage on the community and environment. “I don’t get up and say much at these meetings, but this part is very important,” he finished, a sentiment echoed by another speaker. “Water is our way of life. If we don’t protect our lands, who’s going to? If we don’t stand up for our kids, who’s going to?” A woman said, supporting the moratorium. RELATED: How much water does AI really use? Governor’s Response Governor Wassanna responded to these concerns, saying a potential data center would use a closed loop system, challenging earlier estimates of 300,000 gallons of water per day being used. “The water usage has developed to where there’s little to none except filling it up because it’s a closed loop,” he said. Wassanna further clarified that data centers are now capable of using cooling coils which do not use as much water as previous facilities. “It won’t be 300,000 gallons a day. Actually, cities use more water on their golf courses than people would actually use probably for data centers.” Economic Concerns “I feel like it’s the old days of the old cattle barons, oil barons, people wanting to exploit our resources, snake oil salesmen,” Spotted Horse said of the economic impact of a potential data center. He questioned who would receive the profits from the facility. Governor’s Response “Data centers are huge profit making projects. They make over $1 billion a year. 20%, 30%, $200 million. Somebody told us the other day, ‘Reggie, we make $90 million a day.’ $90 million a day,” said Wassanna. “If you want to look at the tribe’s share, you look at elders, you look at per cap, you look at housing, renovations, all these things we talk about that we’re hurting. Food, gas, these things.” Wassanna further stressed that if a data center was built on tribal lands, those in the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes wouldn’t have to worry about financial issues. “You’d be comfortable, the most comfortable tribe around in western Oklahoma.” Transparency Concerns “We have a responsibility not only to ourselves and this water and Mother Earth, but we also have a responsibility to our community. How many have heard about Yukon voting out their mayor because he did an NDA? Kudos to them for doing that,” Spotted Horse said in reference to the recent recall motion against Yukon mayor Brian Pillmore in Aug. “How would they feel if we just ripped right behind their back in their backyard and did our own thing, potentially causing water pollution, air pollution, not to mention electrical grid cost impacts.” RELATED: Yukon certifies recall petition against Mayor Brian Pillmore “If we make this decision today, in 3 years, we’ll have a better idea of how this is going to impact our future, our children,” said a woman named Vera. The moratorium would halt any data center construction for three years. Governor’s Response “I just want to say something. Before, there was going to be community meetings. This resolution came up, but there was going to be community meetings. Nothing’s been signed, there is a feasibility study that was going to be done. The legislators all acknowledged it. We ain’t done nothing yet. This is up to you guys to say yes or no.” RELATED:

artigo.texto: I’ll admit that I’m the Computer Village Idiot when it comes to using technology like personal computers and smartphones; I still struggle. And I’m in over my head trying to figure out this whole AI (artificial intelligence) thing that some Anthropic research experts believe could ultimately destroy mankind. Are you thinking about artificial intelligence? AI is in the news everywhere these days, and the subject of AI data centers popping up in one’s town or city is enough to freak out most people. There are many unknowns about artificial intelligence, and we need to learn as much as we can about this new technology. Here in the Granite State, there are multiple traditional data centers, but they aren’t the same as AI data centers. There’s often confusion about the two, and unfortunately, AI has become the catch-all term for modern tech infrastructure. For instance, data center space is available for lease in Nashua Technology Park off Exit 1 near the NH/MA border. The campus offers dedicated data center space equipped with heavy-duty corporate infrastructure, but it lacks the capacity and available land for a huge hyperscale or large-scale AI build. And the same could be said for my city’s Millyard Technology Park in the historic district. The tech park leases general office space to companies of all sizes under one roof, featuring “software firms, various service businesses, more than one corporate headquarters, and a few computer hardware companies,” its website says. I know of no AI data center proposals in Nashua, and that’s good news to me. However, a warehouse-sized data center using 40 acres of land on Old Turnpike Road was proposed for the town of Nottingham last May. Residents were up in arms, blasting Granite State developer Tom Moulton. He later withdrew his application because of heavy community opposition. Nottingham residents recently voted overwhelmingly on a 12-month moratorium on any data center development within town limits. That enormous proposal wouldn’t sit well with most people. Massive data centers consume tons of energy, thereby placing a significant strain on water infrastructure and the power grid. These facilities are also seen as a threat to residents’ income, quality of life and the environment. In Bow, residents have come out fighting hard against Granite Shore Power, which owns the shuttered Merrimack Station. The owners had filed a request with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to discuss connecting a 350-megawatt project to the regional power grid for a potential hyperscale AI data center. No data center development proposal has been submitted to the town yet, but that was enough to draw outraged locals to the Bow municipal building. Some of us also wonder about the harm AI could do to the journalism industry. Generative AI is considered a time-and-money-saving newsroom tool that can handle diverse data types like documents, videos and social media at speeds unmatched by traditional processing. But it could also eliminate jobs. However, AI has limitations and cannot replace human reporting, as Mike Reilley explained in an essay for the Red Line Project. Reilley is a University of Illinois Chicago digital journalism professor and an expert in artificial intelligence and data visualization within newsrooms. “Specifically, AI cannot: physically enter a courtroom or interview a defendant behind bars; cultivate trust with a whistleblower; brave the front lines of a war zone; provide the critical thinking, original reporting and smart editorial judgment that humans do.” Innovation should always be welcomed with responsibility. On that note, here’s to a free press!

artigo.texto: Trending VANDALIA, Ohio --- President Donald Trump defended data centers that power artificial intelligence projects but have become a contentious campaign issue nationwide, as he took his midterm tour to Ohio this weekend to insist his party will keep its majorities in Congress despite steep political headwinds. Trump took several minutes during his campaign rally in southwestern Ohio near Dayton late Saturday night to promote his administration's action on data centers, saying he was seeking to ensure they "benefit local communities" and praising Republican Sen. Jon Husted for an ill-fated attempt to push forward legislation on the issue. "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China," Trump said, repeating his defense of data centers that he had made before. The massive warehouse campuses generating energy for AI projects have become a toxic political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies. It's become especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centers to Ohio when he served as lieutenant governor. Trump is embarking on what he says will be a 32-day blitz ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, hitting the deep red states of Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama last week before pivoting to Ohio, a battleground state once again that's home to one of the top-tier Senate races this cycle. Husted -- who was appointed to fill the Senate vacancy left by now-Vice President JD Vance -- is running to win the seat outright. There is likely no path to a Senate majority for Democrats without flipping Ohio, where former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown is trying to return to the Senate after losing to Republican Bernie Moreno two years ago. Polls show that race is extremely tight. Since last year, Democrats have listed Ohio, along with states such as North Carolina and Maine, as key races to win control of the Senate. And this past week, the head of the Senate GOP's campaign arm said Ohio is among 10 battleground races that are "within striking distance." "The good news for us is that Jon Husted is a closer," Sen. Tim Scott, the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told reporters. "We're seeing the gap that was there between the two candidates, which was just a few points, now it is right at a dead-even race. So this is as tight as ticks, as we say in South Carolina." DATA CENTERS At his rallies, Trump has been trying to convince voters that the economy is better than they feel it is, even though polls show Americans are frustrated with the way he's handled it. The high cost of living, including gas prices elevated by Trump's war on Iran, is a top issue in the Dayton area, too. And just days before Trump's rally, nearly 1,400 people were laid off from a truck factory in nearby Springfield. "Your state is booming. Every -- I hate to say it -- every state is booming," Trump said Saturday. "They're all booming." Trump's rally comes as Republicans worry that Husted's campaign has failed to adequately catch fire with voters in the state. Brown and allied groups have hammered Husted for his data-centers role, and the NRSC has pinpointed it as a political vulnerability. The GOP-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats. "You got to remember, Sherrod Brown was for data centers, and Jon Husted is for data centers being responsible," Scott told reporters this week. "If a community doesn't want them, he doesn't want them either." But Trump has become one of data centers' most vocal proponents, shrugging aside voter concerns and arguing that the U.S. cannot cede advancements in AI to China. "Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio," Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump's visit. "Now, he's making Ohioans foot the bill." Brown's campaign also has hammered Husted for donations he's received from retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Husted has donated remaining Wexner contributions to an anti-human trafficking charity. There were several Epstein-themed signs outside the Vandalia school where the rally was being held, as more than a hundred protesters lined the road with a slew of anti-Trump and anti-Husted signs. But inside the school's gymnasium, the boisterous crowd -- decked out in red "Make America Great Again" hats and "Trump 47" jerseys -- greeted each Republican candidate enthusiastically as they awaited the president's arrival. From the stage, Husted said the state had been through "hard times," noting his dad had worked at a factory that closed down. But he said Republicans in the state had turned it around. "We now have the most jobs and the lowest unemployment rate we've ever had in the history of Ohio," he said. Meanwhile, in the governor's race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former COVID-era health director. A wealthy biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate, Ramaswamy's star appeal among conservatives led to quick backing by Ohio Republicans and hopes of an easy victory in the Republican-dominated state. However, despite a massive fundraising lead and more than $12 million spent in campaign advertising, he is now locked in a close fight with Acton with weeks to go until Election Day. "I'm so grateful to this state and to this country for giving a kid like me opportunities that would not have been available to my family in any other country on planet earth," Ramaswamy said at the rally ahead of Trump's arrival, as he underscored the American dream for his Indian immigrant family.

artigo.texto: 2 min leitura Mercado Voluntário de Carbono alarga projetos florestais Duas novas metodologias juntam-se à de Novas Florestações, aumentando as oportunidades para projetos de sequestro de carbono em Portugal. Carbono azul e pradarias marinhas vão seguir-se, 06 Out 2026 - 07:45 2 min leitura O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) passa a contar com três metodologias para projetos florestais, abrindo novas oportunidades à mobilização de investimento privado para o sequestro de carbono e a gestão sustentável da floresta. Foram aprovadas duas novas metodologias de carbono dedicadas à Reflorestação e à Gestão Florestal Melhorada, que se juntam à metodologia já existente para Novas Florestações. As novas metodologias permitem abranger um conjunto mais diversificado de intervenções florestais, reforçam o potencial de geração de créditos de carbono em Portugal e incentivam práticas de gestão sustentável com benefícios climáticos, ambientais e territoriais. “Estamos a criar condições para que mais proprietários, entidades e empresas possam investir na floresta e na ação climática. Ao alargar as metodologias disponíveis, reforçamos a credibilidade e a capacidade de crescimento do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono e mobilizamos financiamento privado para projetos que contribuem simultaneamente para a neutralidade carbónica, a valorização do território e a resiliência das nossas florestas”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, numa nota enviada às redações. Atualmente, o MVC conta com dois projetos registados na tipologia de Novas Florestações e um terceiro projeto está em fase de validação inicial. Estão ainda disponíveis 977 créditos de carbono para venda, a plataforma conta com 29 utilizadores registados e existem 10 verificadores qualificados para assegurar a validação inicial e a verificação periódica dos projetos, segundo o ministério. “O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono está a ganhar escala e maturidade. Depois das metodologias florestais, estamos já a trabalhar em novas abordagens para valorizar o carbono azul e as pradarias marinhas, para colocar também os ecossistemas costeiros no centro da ação climática e da valorização do capital natural”, acrescenta a ministra.

artigo.texto: A Navitas Semiconductor (NASDAQ:NVTS) e a Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP) desenvolveram em conjunto um projeto de referência de 800V CC para 6V CC para aplicações de alimentação de racks de data centers com inteligência artificial, anunciaram as empresas em 5 de outubro de 2026. A plataforma combina os controladores de sinal digital dsPIC33AK da Microchip e o dispositivo de criptografia TA100 com os dispositivos de potência de nitreto de gálio GaNFast da Navitas. O projeto está alinhado com o padrão Open Compute Project 800V DC e combina estágios de conversão de 800V DC para 50V DC e de 50V DC para 6V DC em um único conversor. O projeto visa atingir uma eficiência máxima de 96% Segundo as empresas, a plataforma de referência visa uma eficiência máxima de até 96% em plena carga, uma frequência de comutação de 1 MHz e uma densidade de potência de 2.100 watts por polegada cúbica. O lado primário utiliza 16 FETs GaNFast Navitas NV6034 de 650V em uma topologia de meia ponte empilhada. A família de controladores dsPIC33AK256MPS306 da Microchip inclui um núcleo de 32 bits de 200 MHz, moduladores de largura de pulso de alta resolução de 78 picossegundos e conversores analógico-digitais de 12 bits operando a até 40 MSPS. Os controladores também são compatíveis com algoritmos de criptografia pós-quântica do pacote Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0. O dispositivo TA100 CryptoAuthentication da Microchip oferece funções de segurança baseadas em hardware, incluindo inicialização segura, geração de código de autenticação de mensagens, atualizações de firmware confiáveis e suporte a Transport Layer Security (TLS). “À medida que o ecossistema avança em direção a sistemas de alimentação de rack de alta tensão, os desenvolvedores precisam de componentes básicos comprovados que ajudem a reduzir o risco de projeto e acelerar a inovação”, disse Joe Thomsen, vice-presidente corporativo da unidade de negócios de controladores de sinal digital da Microchip. Plataforma de referência será apresentada em outubro As empresas planejam apresentar a solução no evento OCP da Microchip em San Jose, Califórnia, agendado para 12 a 15 de outubro de 2026. O projeto de referência será disponibilizado juntamente com uma placa de referência, software e documentação de apoio. artigo.texto: A Godawari Power unit gets EC in Maharashtra to build a plant for its 20 GWh battery energy storage project, boosting green power. Maharashtra’s State Expert Appraisal Committee-3, or SEAC-3, approved Godawari New Energy Private Limited, a fully owned subsidiary of Godawari Power & Ispat Limited. The approval came through the committee’s 299th meeting. The company received the papers on 5 October, and the parent told the stock exchanges on 6 October. The building will house the battery storage system. The site is the AURIC Bidkin Industrial Area in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar district. Put simply, a project like this needs an environmental go-ahead before construction can begin. It stores electricity and releases it when needed. That helps balance solar and wind power, which do not always match the hours when people use it. Here, the corporation has a 20 GWh capacity planned. The clearance announcement does not specify the construction timeline or project cost. The approval follows other recent moves. On 1 October, Godawari Power & Ispat set up a new wholly owned subsidiary, Godawari Energy Solutions Private Limited, in Maharashtra. It will handle engineering, procurement, construction and maintenance for battery storage and renewable energy projects. The parent subscribed to 1 lakh shares for Rs 10 lakh as starting capital. Late in September, the company also received an offer for about 31 acres of land in Maharashtra’s AURIC area for its cold rolling mill project. A cold rolling mill turns steel into thinner, finished sheets. Godawari Power & Ispat is best known for steel and power. The battery storage plan adds a clean energy business alongside them. artigo.texto: Utah Survey Uncovers Why Residents Oppose New Data Centers LOGAN — A new Utah State University statewide survey examines Utah residents’ views on data centers. The results indicate that 75.8% of respondents oppose or strongly oppose building new or additional data centers in Utah. The survey offers insights about what drives this opposition. The findings appear in the first executive summary from a broader research project led by Gina Gilson, Stacia Ryder, and Jessica Schad of USU’s Community and Natural Resources Institute (CANRI). The project will examine data centers’ water and energy demands, Utah residents’ views on data centers, and generate information that could help state and local leaders evaluate proposed development. The August 2026 survey gathered responses from nearly 900 Utah residents and is representative of the state adult population. “We are excited to share some of the initial results from our statewide survey on data centers,” said Schad, CANRI director and administrator of the survey. “One of the most important findings in my view is that public participation in decision-making processes is nearly as important as the amount of energy and water projects consume, meaning that government and business leaders may want to consider how they can engage communities throughout the planning process.” The results show that water and energy use, location, and opportunities for public participation are important considerations for residents evaluating data center projects. The survey predominantly measured reported views of hypothetical project features; it only asked about whether residents support or oppose the Stratos data center in Box Elder, which 60.7% strongly opposed. More than half of respondents (57.2%) strongly oppose data center development, and opposition rises when proposed projects are closer to where respondents live. Residents’ responses also vary with the characteristics of a proposed project. Asked how specific features would affect their views of a data center within 3 miles of home, 54.1% said usage of recycled or other non-potable water would make them more likely to support it. Renewable energy infrastructure had a similar effect for 51.2%, while 43.4% said a project that built or paid for new energy infrastructure would increase their likelihood of support. By comparison, 61.3% said using nonrenewable energy would make them more likely to oppose a local project. The use of nuclear energy increased the likelihood of opposition for 41.4%. Responses to a proposal for public reporting of annual water and energy use were more mixed. “Similar to what we have seen in the context of other energy infrastructure project siting processes, like for shale gas, residents in our survey indicate the continued importance of processes creating avenues for meaningful community participation in these decision-making processes,” said Ryder, assistant professor of sociology. "Additionally, the type of energy and water used to support data centers matters to residents, as respondents were likely to respond more positively to the use of renewable energy and recycled or non-potable water. These are important considerations for shaping planning and public reception." Gilson, assistant professor of environment and society and interim director of USU’s Center for Colorado River Studies, said: “Our survey findings underscore the concern that Utahns feel about our water resources. I think it’s important for us to better understand where the water comes from, how much water is used on-site, and how much is used to generate the electricity that powers data centers. Our research will gather information to help answer these questions." The survey is one part of an ongoing project. CANRI researchers also want to examine public documents and media coverage to assess what information is available about data centers’ water and energy use, and to interview policymakers, developers, community leaders, and residents of select Utah communities affected by data center development. A follow-up survey in 2027 is planned to assess whether residents’ views change over time. To learn more, read the executive summary: https://artsci.usu.edu/canri/projects/data-center-development-in-utah. artigo.texto: Hallam Village Board approves zoning rights for data center HALLAM, Neb. (KOLN) - The village of Hallam is now one step closer to getting a data center. The village board approved zoning rights in a vote on Monday. It was about an hour of discussion between board members, the public, and a representative from Crusoe Technologies, who signed a special permit alongside Monolith Materials back in July to get the data center plan started. People had questions about fire safety and noise, but Steve Buster, a Crusoe Technologies representative, said they have a fire plan just in case something does happen. A handful of people from Hallam were invited to a data center to help calm worries about excessive sounds. Even though there wasn’t much drama during the vote, some weren’t happy with the decision. “Well at first I thought that’s okay, you can just move somewhere but everywhere you look they are fighting data centers,” said a woman at the discussion. “So where will you move where there won’t be another data center.” While a number of people were disappointed, a reporter said about half the room applauded when the zoning rights were approved. Information on when the data center will be built has yet to be released. Stay connected to 1011now.com for updates on this story. artigo.texto: Jupiter Wagons shares hit a day high of Rs 226.99 on 5 October, up 1%, after the firm won a Rs 100 crore battery storage order in Uttarakhand. The company told exchanges about the win at around 13:30 pm. Jupiter Wagons, better known for building railway wagons, landed the job through JEM Energy, its clean energy arm. Madhav Infra Projects Limited is its partner on the project. The customer is Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL). The project is essentially a giant battery. It stores electricity when demand is low and sends it back to the grid when demand peaks. The system is rated at 41 MW and can hold 102.5 MWh of energy. Jupiter and its partner will supply and set it up, and the work is worth about Rs 100 crore. The two firms won by quoting the lowest price in a competitive bidding round run by UPCL. It is JEM Energy’s first project in Uttarakhand. This is not the only recent win. In August 2026, the company also received a formal award letter from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited. That job is a 50 MW/200 MWh battery project at the Jeerat substation in North 24 Parganas. Managing Director Vivek Lohia called both wins important steps in turning JEM Energy into a bigger business. Jupiter Wagons still aims to build a battery storage order book of about Rs 1,000 crore by FY27. Lohia also said the electric mobility arm, Jupiter Electric Mobility, should start making an operating profit in the October to December quarter of FY27. He expects it to turn profitable overall by FY28. The orders follow the Union Cabinet’s approval of Green Energy Corridor Phase-III, which includes 50 GWh of battery storage. The early rally did not hold. Jupiter Wagons closed at Rs 223.44 on the NSE, down 0.22%, after swinging between a low of Rs 218.61 and its high of Rs 226.99. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA atNorth planeja o Data Center FIN05 em Salo, Finlândia, com caminho para 230 MW Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google O operador nórdico de data centers atNorth, em 5 de outubro de 2026, anunciou planos para desenvolver o FIN05, um novo data center em Salo, Finlândia. A empresa espera investir aproximadamente €2 bilhões no site de 28,6 hectares, onde a energia para a primeira fase planejada de 75 MW está garantida, com um caminho para até 230 MW para o desenvolvimento mais amplo. Especificações do Site e Planos de Investimento A atNorth afirmou que Salo oferece uma localização forte para infraestrutura crítica que atende clientes com exigentes requisitos de conectividade e resiliência. A empresa citou a proximidade da cidade com Helsinque e o pool de talentos digitais da Finlândia como fatores adicionais que sustentam o desenvolvimento, e posicionou o FIN05 como parte de seu objetivo contínuo de atender à demanda por infraestrutura digital de alto desempenho de maneira responsável. O site será conectado por meio de uma subestação da Fingrid. O investimento esperado de €2 bilhões da empresa não inclui servidores de propriedade dos clientes ou sua instalação, o que a atNorth estima que pode representar um investimento adicional de até €10 bilhões. A empresa planeja celebrar acordos de compra de energia de longo prazo com fornecedores locais para apoiar a produção de energia na região, juntamente com soluções de flexibilidade que, segundo ela, podem apoiar a operação eficiente da rede de transmissão da Fingrid. A atNorth também trabalhará com partes interessadas locais para explorar oportunidades de uso do calor gerado pelo data center, que a empresa afirma ter como objetivo gerar valor além da própria instalação. Esse esforço baseia‑se em colaborações existentes de reutilização de calor com a Kesko Corporation na Finlândia, a Stockholm Exergi na Suécia, e a Vestforbrænding e a Selected Group na Dinamarca. Declarações da atNorth e Parceiros Locais “O FIN05 é uma oportunidade de desenvolver infraestrutura digital crítica enquanto trabalhamos com a região para criar valor local duradouro”, disse Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson, CEO da atNorth. Ele afirmou que a empresa está explorando como parcerias energéticas locais, soluções de flexibilidade e reutilização de calor podem contribuir para o sistema energético mais amplo e para a comunidade, e espera trabalhar com Salo e parceiros regionais à medida que o projeto avança. Anna‑Kristiina Korhonen, prefeita de Salo, disse estar encantada em receber o investimento na região. Ela afirmou que o novo data center criará oportunidades de emprego valiosas tanto durante a construção quanto nas operações contínuas, gerando benefícios econômicos mais amplos para os negócios locais, acrescentando que o desenvolvimento reforça a posição de Salo como um destino atraente para indústrias inovadoras e apoia o crescimento sustentável de longo prazo da comunidade. Matti‑Juho Ervasti, sócio da Regant Oy, afirmou que o projeto demonstra o potencial de Salo como local para investimentos significativos em infraestrutura digital. Ele disse que a Regant trabalhou de perto com a atNorth e a municipalidade para oferecer um site pronto para desenvolvimento, com a escala, prontidão de planejamento e roteiro energético necessários para grandes projetos de data center. Cadeia de Valor Nórdica e Histórico de Propriedade A atNorth descreveu o FIN05 como parte de seu investimento contínuo nos países nórdicos, juntamente com desenvolvimentos em Estocolmo e Sollefteå, na Suécia, Haugaland, na Noruega, Ølgod, na Dinamarca e Kouvola, na Finlândia. O projeto de Kouvola, FIN04, foi anunciado em dezembro de 2023 como um mega site em um terreno de 21 hectares, a 139 km a nordeste de Helsinque e a 52 km da cidade de Hamina, atendendo tanto clientes de colocation quanto projetos build‑to‑suit. A atNorth disse na época que o FIN04 teria um fornecimento de energia imediato de 60 MW, uma primeira fase pronta para operação no segundo semestre de 2025, e um caminho para potência de várias centenas de megawatts quando totalmente construído, descrevendo‑o como o décimo data center da empresa nos países nórdicos e seu quarto campus na Finlândia. Trabalhando com a cidade de Kouvola e o parceiro energético KSS Energia, o site foi projetado com capacidades de reutilização de calor, permitindo que o excesso de calor do data center fosse reciclado para possível reutilização na comunidade local. O projeto de Salo também segue uma mudança na propriedade da atNorth. A CPP Investments e a Equinix concluíram a aquisição de US$4 bilhões da atNorth em 2 de setembro de 2026, com a CPP Investments detendo uma participação controladora de cerca de 51 % com um compromisso de US$1,3 bilhão, a Equinix detendo cerca de 34 % com um compromisso de US$895 milhões, e a Partners Group detendo cerca de 10 % com um compromisso de US$260 milhões. O restante está nas mãos dos acionistas internos da atNorth, que mantiveram uma parte substancial de sua participação acionária. A transação envolveu um pacote de financiamento de US$4,1 bilhões (€3,6 bilhões) garantido por um grupo de credores europeus e canadenses, e a atNorth continua a operar de forma independente sob sua marca existente.

artigo.texto: The two battery energy storage facilities in East Hampton Town, jointly owned by NextEra Energy and National Grid, have been temporarily shut down. The move comes after the town board passed a resolution at Thursday’s meeting to hire Rigano L.L.C., an environmental law firm, and authorized up to $50,000 for a lawsuit against NextEra Energy that would compel it to do the same. In a statement, Supervisor Kathee Burke-Gonzalez took a victory lap. “Less than 24 hours after the town board unanimously authorized litigation to shut down the East Hampton and Montauk battery storage facilities, NextEra has temporarily shut both facilities down,” she wrote. Those facilities are on Cove Hollow Road in East Hampton and North Shore Road in Montauk. “This is the action we demanded, and I am pleased that NextEra responded swiftly to my Sept. 29 letter and the town board’s action.” Gary Morris, the vice president of the East Hampton Storage Center and the Montauk Storage Center, had, as recently as Thursday, been defiant and unmoved by a series of demands made by the supervisor in a string of letters dating back to July 31. Her most recent letter, dated Sept. 30, had asked that the facilities cease operations by Friday unless it removed Novec 1230, a chemical that the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation has blamed for contaminating nearby drinking water wells after its use in a May 2023 fire at the 3 Cove Hollow Road energy storage center. “The town’s September 29, 2026, letter identifies no basis for its request that the facilities cease operations by October 2, 2026, and we are aware of none,” wrote Mr. Morris, in an Oct. 1 response to the supervisor, adding that he intended to continue operations there. Newsday reported that Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine had also been negotiating with NextEra, apparently threatening a county lawsuit, before the energy supplier decided to change course and suspend operations while it manages the Novec 1230. East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen had also been calling for the facilities to be shut. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

artigo.texto: An ambitious ETS can strengthen European competitiveness The Commission’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) proposal maintains the pathway towards decarbonisation by 2050 but risks slowing down industrial renewal in Europe. Co-legislators should keep the supply of allowances in check to enable frontrunner investments in decarbonisation. In her State of the European Union speech, President Ursula von der Leyen correctly noted that our dependence on fossil fuels has led to over 90 billion euros in additional costs, “without a single molecule of energy added”. A large part of that amount flowed outside of Europe. She also set out the alternative: an electrified Europe that could cut the fossil fuel import bill by 260 billion euros a year. She also reiterated her support for the EU’s climate targets, which are the basis for flagship energy and climate legislation of this mandate: namely, the revision of the EU Emissions Trading System, which the Commission adopted in mid-July this year. It’s not just the destination that matters The Commission’s proposal does indeed align the ETS with the EU’s emission reduction target. But in addition to the destination, the journey there matters: the Commission’s proposal and the alternative option included in the Parliament’s draft report would increase the volume of allowances released by roughly 30–40 percent between 2030 and 2040. Furthermore, free allocation would continue for several years longer. These changes would weaken the incentives for the deployment of clean technologies in Europe. In practice, a significantly less ambitious trajectory for cutting emissions would affect European companies investing in the development of clean technologies and production of near-zero emissions materials. Manufacturers like Metso, Andritz and Valmet provide state-of-the art solutions for industrial processes such as clean steelmaking and hydrogen production. Metal producers such as SSAB, Outokumpu and Boliden offer low-carbon metals for customers globally, with plans to go even further. Furthermore, all of this is supported by a strong grid technology sector, whose ranks include companies like ABB and Prysmian. In many of these sectors, European companies remain global leaders and the EU, with ambitious policies like the ETS, has built an excellent environment for deploying their technologies. A large number of countries and regions are following Europe’s example, with the share of global emissions covered by carbon pricing on the rise. The IEA estimates the global market for clean technologies to grow rapidly from the current 1.2 trillion to 2–5 trillion USD by 2035. There is also significant untapped potential in the market for near-zero emissions materials such as clean steel, that will, according to the IEA, remain unrealised without a strong policy push. Taking a giant leap requires trust To take the next step in decarbonisation, gradual change is not enough: we need frontrunner investments in ground-breaking technologies, such as steelmaking based on clean electricity and hydrogen. Trust in the system is crucial for turning plans into reality: the ETS works not only because it encourages companies to cut emissions here and now but also in the long run. That helps companies plan long-term and make investments in innovative new technologies instead of only making their existing processes more efficient. Keeping the increase in in the volume of released allowances more modest than in the Commission’s proposal is important for securing that trust. Similarly, sticking to the previously agreed timeline for phasing out free allocation is crucial. Putting revenues to work The ETS does come with costs. But unlike the money spent on imported fossil fuels, ETS revenues stay in the coffers of the EU and the Member States. Yet only around 5 percent of them are currently channelled back to industry to speed up decarbonisation. This needs to change: smarter use of the revenues and free allocation can help kickstart the switch to clean steelmaking, fuels and feedstocks. The need to develop and tune the EU ETS has been part and parcel of the journey from the beginning. The revision of the ETS is an opportunity to prove that we can also persist, by holding the agreed course on the cap and free allocation, and by putting the system’s own revenues to work. In doing so, we can also show that climate action and competitiveness can go hand in hand. TIF recommendations for the revision of the EU ETS - Align the cap with the 90 % emissions reduction target while keeping the cumulative number of issued allowances in check: an ambitious LRF in the early 2030s is crucial for achieving this goal. - Ensure that the revenues collected are channelled back to the sectors affected by the EU ETS - Shape free allocation into an instrument for speeding up the decarbonisation in Europe, especially in energy-intensive industry - Allocate EU funding to projects based on excellence - Include a broad range of permanent carbon removal technologies in the EU ETS

US Solar Financing Three US solar and battery deals raise $1.26B CleanChoice, Maxwell and Lydian close new funding Projects target 2027 operations and 6GW build-out Stock video by K via Pexels Oct 5, 2026 US Solar and Battery Storage Financing: $1.26B Across Three Deals US solar and battery storage financing activity has produced a trio of transactions spanning the Northeast and the consumer and small commercial segment, according to a round-up published by pv-tech.org. CleanChoice Energy has secured more than US$166 million in financing for two solar photovoltaic projects in the US Northeast, the Dolan project in New York at roughly 27MW and the Kylertown project in Pennsylvania at roughly 28MW. The package included a US$105 million construction loan from Investec Bank, which acted as lead arranger, green loan structuring agent and collateral agent. BHI, the US branch of Bank Hapoalim, BM and Stifel Bank served as coordinating lead arrangers. Advantage Capital supplied a US$61 million tax equity commitment for the portfolio. Both projects are expected to reach commercial operations in 2027. Separately, distributed energy company Maxwell Power has closed an US$800 million investment from private equity firm Fairtide Partners to acquire battery storage and solar PV power projects. The deal follows investments of US$250 million and US$750 million in 2024 and June 2026, lifting Fairtide's total commitment to US$1.8 billion for projects developed by Maxwell. Maxwell said it has helped its consumer and small commercial customers achieve US$100 million in future energy savings so far this year. The company also relocated its headquarters from San Diego, California, to Salt Lake City, Utah, a move it described as fulfilling a promise to Utah Senator John Curtis. In a third transaction, independent power producer Lydian Energy and infrastructure asset manager Infranity agreed on a US$300 million holding company credit facility intended to support expansion of Lydian's 6GW portfolio of solar PV and utility-scale battery energy storage systems. The bespoke facility is based on Lydian Energy's existing operating and construction-ready assets and is designed to give the company added flexibility to accelerate build-out of its business pipeline. Lydian said the financing will help it advance projects from development through construction and retain ownership of operating assets. Lydian Energy is backed by Exelsior Energy Capital. Sacha Kamp, global head of debt investment at Infranity, characterized the transaction as resting on a portfolio of high-quality contracted projects and a strong pipeline of energy infrastructure assets developed and owned by Lydian, adding that the support of an experienced and committed sponsor provides a foundation for long-term growth. artigo.texto: Amazon Commits $1 Billion to US Data Center Communities Amid AI Backlash - Amazon will invest more than $1 billion over five years in US communities hosting its data centers, targeting education, workforce training, energy affordability and water preservation. - AWS says it is 75% of the way toward its 2030 water-positive goal, as scrutiny grows over the electricity and water demands of AI infrastructure. - More than 100 data center moratoriums are under consideration across the US, raising political and investment risks as technology companies accelerate AI infrastructure spending. Amazon is committing more than $1 billion over five years to communities hosting its US data centers. The investment comes as the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure faces growing resistance over energy costs, water consumption and local impacts. Amazon Web Services will direct the funding through its new Built Together framework. It will support education, job training, energy affordability, water preservation and other community priorities. The initiative adds a community investment component to one of the largest private infrastructure expansions underway in the United States. Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers between 2011 and 2025. Large projects or expansions are now underway across several states, including Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia and Mississippi. AI growth collides with local infrastructure concerns Data centers provide the computing capacity required to train and operate AI models. Their rapid expansion has also intensified questions about who bears the infrastructure costs. Communities across the US have raised concerns about electricity demand, utility bills, water use and pressure on local infrastructure. More than 100 data center moratoriums are currently being considered nationwide, according to Amazon. That opposition creates a growing governance challenge for technology companies and policymakers. It also adds a political dimension ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. AWS CEO Matt Garman framed continued construction as an economic and national security priority. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it,” Garman said. Amazon compared the current expansion of digital infrastructure with the construction of the US interstate highway system. However, the company stressed one major difference. Private companies, rather than taxpayers, are financing much of today’s infrastructure buildout. AI infrastructure is increasingly tied to healthcare, education, financial services, cybersecurity, defense and scientific research. That broadening role has strengthened the case for investment while increasing scrutiny of its environmental footprint. RELATED ARTICLE: Amazon Adds 50+ Mercedes Electric Trucks in Germany Water and energy move higher on the agenda Amazon’s investment framework seeks to address some of the most contentious environmental issues surrounding data centers. AWS has committed to becoming water positive across its data center operations by 2030. The company said it is now 75% of the way toward that goal. Water positive means returning more water to communities than its operations consume. The commitment has become increasingly relevant as new data centers expand into regions facing competing demands for water and electricity. Energy affordability is another focus of the $1 billion program. Rising data center demand has prompted questions about grid investment and whether households could face higher costs as utilities build infrastructure to serve large technology customers. For Amazon, addressing those concerns has become part of maintaining community support for continued expansion. Community acceptance becomes an investment risk The scale of proposed data center development means community relations are moving from corporate philanthropy into core infrastructure strategy. Moratoriums, permitting disputes and public opposition can delay projects and raise development costs. They can also complicate the long-term power procurement and grid planning needed to support AI investment. Amazon’s Built Together framework gives communities a role in determining how funds are allocated. That approach could help companies align investments with local concerns rather than applying a uniform national model. For executives and investors, the broader issue extends beyond Amazon. AI growth depends on physical infrastructure that requires land, power, water and political approval. The next phase of the AI investment cycle will therefore depend on more than access to capital and computing technology. Developers will need credible plans for resource use, community benefits and energy affordability. As governments compete for leadership in AI, those local constraints are becoming part of the global race for digital infrastructure. The companies that manage them effectively may gain an advantage in securing the permits, power and public support required for continued expansion.
