artigo.texto: MONTEZUMA COUNTY, Colo., Oct. 5, 2026 (SEND2PRESS NEWSWIRE) — NoValleyRange, a neighborhood group located near Mesa Verde (a UNESCO World Heritage site and National Park), are fighting a Texas developer proposing a $240 million dollar solar and lithium battery development. The proposed project consists of 900 acres of solar panels and 8 acres of lithium battery storage at the base of Colorado’s only UNESCO world heritage site. This project is comparable in size to the 500,000-panel Cleve Hill Solar Park, the largest solar field in the UK. The neighbors are fighting the project for the same reasons that many other rural communities across the US are fighting similar projects. Namely, that the solar field and BESS facility will degrade property values, harm tourism, and put small businesses out of business. However, the Valley Range Energy Park presents unique problems. It will dominate the views from the northside overlooks from Mesa Verde National Park and degrade the park visitor experience. Mesa Verde is not only a cultural treasure, but also the economic tourism engine that supports the entire community. Even more alarming is the potential for a catastrophic battery fire. According to Lillian Wakeley, Board Director at Mesa Verde Association, in a recent social media comment, “The solar array will overwhelm the views from every overlook on the north escarpment in Mesa Verde National Park. Large battery storage means fire risk and also huge security lights. One of Mesa Verde’s major drawing points is the dark night sky, and ranger programs with new night-scopes are hugely popular. Please think about the impact on our tourist industry if we encroach on our national park with overwhelming lights, noise, and nearly a thousand acres of solar panels.” Mesa Verde National Park is also a huge driver of the local economy. According to a National Park Service report, in 2023 505,000 visitors came to Mesa Verde National Park and spent $59.5 million in communities near the park. That spending in the local area had a cumulative benefit to the local economy of $75.6 million (*see note 1). Park visitation was directly responsible for approximately 8% of total employment in Montezuma County (*2). The Valley Range solar project also includes 8 acres of lithium battery storage commonly referred to as a BESS. BESS facilities are new technology with a dismal safety record. Most of the BESS systems in the US have been installed since 2020 (*3) Unlike conventional fires, BESS fires produce their own oxygen and are nearly impossible to extinguish (*4). BESS fires also produce poisonous gasses including hydrogen cyanide and hydrogen fluoride. Most troubling, is the ability of a BESS fire to produce carcinogenic fallout in the form of aerosolized exotic metals (*5). In the 2025 Moss Landing battery fire, 55,000 pounds of carcinogenic metals were aerosolized into the neighboring tourist town and surrounding marshes (*6). BESS installations present unique economic problems when located near a major tourist attraction, such as Mesa Verde National Park. According to KAZU News, the 2025 lithium-ion battery fire in the popular tourist town of Moss Landing California (and the accompanying repeated evacuation orders and national news coverage) devastated the local tourism industry (*7). According to neighboring business owner, Bryan Davis, “Anything negatively effecting Mesa Verde National Park is a critical economic issue here. This community relies on the National Park for a huge percentage of the local economy.” In recent weeks the Valley Range project has become a local political issue in Montezuma County with Republican commissioner candidate Rodney Cox saying “There is a solar farm being proposed now, and I’m against everything about that.” Rodney Cox’s opponent Democrat Rebecca Busic has said she supports the solar project and lithium battery installation (*8). artigo.texto: Investimento da Amazon em Data Centers em Ohio Enfrenta um Novo Teste para os Consumidores de Energia A Amazon comprometeu bilhões de dólares com data centers em Ohio, mas sua expansão em IA agora enfrenta contratos de energia mais rigorosos, escrutínio tributário e oposição local organizada. O investimento da Amazon em data centers em Ohio deixou de ser uma história simples de capacidade de nuvem. Tornou-se um teste sobre quem paga pela infraestrutura por trás da inteligência artificial. Um resumo recente do TradingView descreveu uma expansão plurianual em Ohio até 2030, sem identificar novos locais, número de projetos ou um novo compromisso de investimento. Esse resumo trazia um importante aviso: foi gerado por IA e poderia conter imprecisões. O registro verificado é mais específico, mas aponta principalmente para investimentos já anunciados, e não para um novo projeto divulgado em Ohio. A AWS opera sua região de nuvem em Ohio desde 2016. A Amazon anunciou outra grande expansão em dezembro de 2024, com base em compromissos assumidos em 2023 e em construções anteriores. Desde então, o ambiente político mudou. Ohio impôs compromissos mais fortes de eletricidade aos data centers e suspendeu novas concessões sob um valioso incentivo tributário. A Amazon ainda tem capital e demanda para construir. A questão mais difícil é se as comunidades de Ohio, os reguladores e os clientes das concessionárias aceitarão os termos. Esse conflito agora importa tanto quanto o número de servidores que a AWS pode instalar. O Que o Investimento da Amazon em Data Centers em Ohio Realmente Abrange A história verificada é um programa contínuo de infraestrutura, não uma coleção recém-detalhada de campi de IA. A AWS anunciou em dezembro de 2024 que planejava outro grande investimento em infraestrutura de nuvem em Ohio. A empresa afirmou que a expansão poderia incluir até oito novos locais de data centers até 2030. Ela não identificou todos os locais. O anúncio seguiu um compromisso anterior, feito em junho de 2023. Na época, a AWS disse que pretendia expandir suas operações no centro de Ohio até 2029. A empresa já havia investido em instalações que atendem sua região de nuvem US East Ohio. Os compromissos combinados colocaram a Amazon entre os maiores investidores em data centers de Ohio. Uma ficha informativa atualizada da Amazon afirmou que a empresa investiu US$ 19,7 bilhões em infraestrutura de IA e nuvem em Ohio desde 2011. Essa categoria incluía data centers e redes de fibra. O plano de investimento em Ohio mais amplo da Amazon descreve instalações com servidores, sistemas de armazenamento, hardware de rede e equipamentos de suporte. Esses ativos atendem clientes convencionais de nuvem, além de cargas de trabalho mais recentes de inteligência artificial. A distinção importa. Nem todo data center da AWS é exclusivamente uma instalação de IA, mesmo quando a demanda por IA ajuda a justificar sua construção. A mesma região de nuvem pode oferecer suporte a bancos de dados, sites, aplicações empresariais, treinamento de modelos e inferência. Inferência é o processo de executar um modelo de IA treinado para gerar uma resposta ou previsão. O treinamento cria o modelo, enquanto a inferência entrega suas capacidades aos usuários. Ambas as atividades exigem capacidade computacional, embora seus perfis de hardware e energia possam ser diferentes. A AWS lançou a região de Ohio em outubro de 2016 com três zonas de disponibilidade. Uma zona de disponibilidade é um grupo de instalações fisicamente separadas, projetadas para isolar falhas. Os clientes usam várias zonas quando precisam que aplicações permaneçam disponíveis durante uma interrupção de equipamento ou instalação. A expansão da Amazon, portanto, faz mais do que adicionar espaço físico. Ela aumenta a oferta regional de capacidade de computação, armazenamento e rede disponível aos clientes da AWS. Também pode oferecer às empresas mais opções para manter cargas de trabalho geograficamente próximas aos usuários. O anúncio da empresa em 2024 afirmou que as futuras construções dependiam de acordos de serviço de energia de longo prazo. Essa condição tornou-se central para a história. Terrenos e edifícios têm pouco valor como infraestrutura de IA sem eletricidade confiável na escala necessária. A Associated Press informou que o investimento adicional elevaria o compromisso total da Amazon em Ohio até 2029 acima do patamar anterior. Sua cobertura do investimento também observou que os locais futuros ainda não haviam sido definidos quando o plano foi anunciado. Isso deixa uma lacuna entre um compromisso de capital em nível estadual e um cronograma de construção por projeto. A Amazon pode descrever a escala pretendida sem prometer que todos os campi potenciais serão concretizados. Contratos com concessionárias, licenças, aprovações de terrenos e resistência local ainda podem alterar a sequência. A manchete recente não elimina essa lacuna. Ela reembala a expansão já estabelecida da Amazon enquanto investidores reavaliam a exposição da empresa a data centers. Os leitores devem tratá-la como um resumo conciso de investimentos, e não como prova de uma expansão adicional em Ohio. Essa interpretação também explica por que as contagens exatas de projetos parecem inconsistentes entre diferentes resumos. A Amazon discutiu locais potenciais, investimentos históricos e compromissos futuros em documentos distintos. Essas medidas descrevem atividades relacionadas, mas não são intercambiáveis. A conclusão confiável é mais restrita. A Amazon continua expandindo sua presença de nuvem em Ohio por meio de um programa que avança em direção a 2030. O tamanho final e a localização de cada componente continuam sujeitos a decisões de infraestrutura e regulação. Por Que a Expansão de IA em Ohio Agora É uma História de Energia A demanda por computação criou o argumento para a expansão, mas a disponibilidade de eletricidade agora determina quais projetos se tornam reais. artigo.texto: As AI moves from experimentation into production, data centers face growing demands for power, cooling, and space. Real-time inference and other AI workloads require infrastructure that can scale without adding unnecessary complexity. Conventional rack designs may not provide the density, or flexibility operators need, while proprietary designs can limit hardware choices and make expansion more complex. Cisco helps operators integrate and scale networking into ORv3 environments while maintaining a consistent operating model. What ORv3 changes for high-density AI data centers Open Rack Version 3 (ORv3) is designed for high-density environments. Developed through the Open Compute Project (OCP), it defines an open rack architecture with mechanical and serviceability specifications and supports power designs suited to modern AI, machine learning, and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. ORv3 racks use a 21-inch equipment bay and Open Units (OU); traditional enterprise equipment commonly uses 19-inch racks and Rack Units (RU). One OU measures 48 mm, while one RU measures 44.45 mm. Some ORv3 designs accommodate 19-inch equipment with mounting adapters, but rack dimensions and usable space vary. That flexibility can help organizations introduce high-density infrastructure while continuing to support compatible equipment and existing deployment strategies. The value of ORv3 comes down to efficiency and scale. ORv3 delivers several important advantages: - Standardized interoperability: Components from different manufacturers can work together more seamlessly, enabling a more open, plug-and-play approach and reducing concerns about hardware compatibility. - Higher power and cooling: A 48V DC busbar power distribution system can reduce power loss and support higher power densities compared to traditional designs. It also offers built-in support for direct liquid cooling (DLC) manifolds and blind-mate connections to manage the intense heat of AI servers. - Sustainability benefits: Reusable components and standardized hardware help reduce waste, lower carbon footprints, and minimize operational inefficiencies. - Operational Efficiency: Features tool-free, “click-in” assembly for IT gear and power rails, allowing for faster maintenance and reduced cabling complexity. It also supports hybrid mounting for both 21-inch OCP (OU) and traditional 19-inch (RU) equipment within the same frame. These features make ORv3 more than a rack specification. They offer a practical foundation for aligning infrastructure density, operational needs, and future growth. How Cisco is supporting the transition Cisco is preparing its data center networking portfolio for evolving rack designs. Cisco offers ORv3- compatible trays for Cisco N9000 Series switches. The trays align networking hardware with open-rack mechanical and power designs, giving operators more flexibility as they build or expand high-density data centers. Customers can choose a bundle with the switch preinstalled on the tray or purchase a spare tray for self-installation, depending on their deployment needs. Cisco N9000 ORv3 compliant trays for operational choice Key capabilities include: - Compatibility with ORv3 rack environments for Cisco N9000 Series switches. - Support for 48V DC power architectures aligned to modern high-density requirements. - Mounting kits for existing 19-inch equipment, enabling traditional gear to fit into the 21-inch ORv3 environment. Cisco power trays are designed to connect at different busbar positions, helping ensure the hardware receives the power it needs in supported rack configurations. This design readiness is essential in high-density environments, where small physical differences can have a significant operational impact. Together, these options give organizations a path to adopt ORv3-based infrastructure while maintaining continuity in network operations, accommodating compatible existing equipment, and aligning the rack with AI’s power, cooling, and density demands. Cisco accelerates AI infrastructure with new liquid-cooled switches: the ORv3-native N9364F-SG3-RL and the purpose-built N9164F-NS6-ML for NVIDIA MGX accelerated-computing rack deployments. These platforms deliver the critical thermal and connectivity efficiency required for modern, high-density AI fabrics. Cisco Nexus switches are part of Cisco Nexus One, a data center networking architecture for AI and modern workloads. With Cisco Cloud Control, Nexus One supports a unified AgenticOps experience for managing infrastructure from silicon to workloads. Who benefits most from an ORv3-ready approach ORv3 is especially relevant for hyperscale and enterprise data centers with roadmaps that include large-scale AI or machine learning workloads. For these organizations, the move to ORv3 is not simply about following the latest hardware standards. It is about creating a data center foundation that can scale with the performance, density, and efficiency requirements of modern workloads. - Simplify the deployment of a high-density fabric. - Maintain environmental goals as infrastructure grows. - Future proof existing investments and extend their longevity. - Reduce total cost of ownership. Building the foundation for what comes next As AI shifts into production and real-time inference, the physical design of the data center becomes a strategic consideration. ORv3 introduces an open, high-density architecture built for the power and thermal realities of AI, machine learning, and HPC. Cisco N9000 support for ORv3 helps organizations adopt that architecture with greater confidence, while preserving proven networking performance and management consistency. Data centers need a smarter, more scalable infrastructure foundation to support continued compute growth. artigo.texto: Since the Iran-US military conflict began earlier this year, disrupting global oil markets, Australia’s electric vehicle (EV) market has experienced an unprecedented boost. With motorists facing sharp increases at the bowser and continuing uncertainty about fuel prices, many drivers have decided to go electric. EVs accounted for 25.8% of total car sales in the first half of 2026. One brand in particular is capitalising on this trend, and that’s the Chinese carmaker BYD, whose name was previously spelled out as “Build Your Dreams”. It is now outselling many far older and more established competitors in Australia. Fifteen years ago, Elon Musk poked fun at BYD, saying it was not a serious competitor in the electric vehicle business. And until just a few years ago, hardly anyone in Australia had even heard of the brand. So how did BYD become such a formidable competitor in the EV market so quickly? BYD’s origin story BYD’s story began not with cars, but batteries. In 1995, 29-year-old battery specialist Wang Chuanfu founded the company in Shenzhen with a small team. BYD initially manufactured rechargeable nickel-cadmium batteries, before moving into lithium-ion batteries. The company grew quickly, and by 2000, BYD had become Motorola’s first Chinese supplier of lithium-ion batteries. Nokia followed in 2002, and the same year BYD listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. In 2003, BYD entered the automotive industry by acquiring a struggling Chinese manufacturer. Its first model, the petrol-powered F3, arrived in 2005. By then, BYD was already looking towards electrification. In 2008, it launched the F3DM plug-in hybrid. That same year, legendary US investor Warren Buffett backed the company with an investment of about US$230 million for a 9.9% stake, which he later sold. When Bloomberg asked Tesla chief executive Elon Musk in 2011 about BYD as a potential competitor, he laughed. “Have you seen their car?” he asked, before saying he did not see BYD as a competitor. But, by 2023, his assessment had completely changed: “Their cars are highly competitive these days.” What do the sales numbers say these days? Sales figures both in Australia and overseas show just how rapidly BYD has become a formidable name in the automotive industry. Globally, BYD went from selling about 190,000 battery or hybrid vehicles in 2020 to 4.6 million in 2025 – a roughly 24-fold increase in just five years. Of the 2025 sales, 2.26 million were fully electric, enough to overtake Tesla’s 1.64 million deliveries. Its rise in Australia has been similarly striking. In the first eight months of 2026, BYD sold more than 68,000 vehicles, making it Australia’s second-highest-selling car brand behind Toyota. In the month of June, just 243 sales separated the two. Among electric vehicles, over the same period, BYD sold more than 39,000 cars, overtaking Tesla to become Australia’s highest-selling electric vehicle brand. What is BYD’s secret sauce? BYD’s rise from a relatively unknown battery maker to a global automotive giant cannot be attributed to any single factor. But four factors have likely been instrumental to its success. First, BYD makes an unusually large proportion of its cars itself. This includes batteries, electric motors, power electronics and even some of the semiconductors its vehicles need. This high degree of “vertical integration” reduces its reliance on outside suppliers and gives BYD greater control over both its supply chain and production costs. The company even owns and operates its own ships to transport the vehicles to Australia and other markets. Second, BYD did not bet everything on fully electric vehicles. It also sells a large range of plug-in hybrids. This gave buyers who are not yet ready to rely entirely on battery power another route into electrification. Third, BYD took a different approach to battery technology. Its Blade Battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry, which is generally cheaper than nickel-based alternatives and requires neither nickel nor cobalt. Fourth, BYD has benefited substantially from China’s long-running support for its electric vehicle industry. This has included direct subsidies to manufacturers as well as subsidies and tax incentives for consumers buying electric vehicles. A history of controversy BYD’s rapid expansion has not been without controversy. Despite its global success, BYD has never established passenger-car sales in the United States. More recently, high tariffs and national-security concerns about Chinese vehicles have created prohibitive barriers to entry to the US market. Cybersecurity concerns have also attracted scrutiny in Australia. This was highlighted in a recent ABC Four Corners investigation showing a cybersecurity expert remotely accessing functions in a BYD Shark 6. Safety concerns have emerged too. While safety regulator ANCAP awarded the Shark 6 five stars, it also applied a penalty score for posing a greater risk to oncoming vehicles due to its size, weight and front-end design. The Shark 6 is larger than many of Australia’s largest utes, including some variants of the Ford Ranger. A new global order for autos For decades, Australia’s car market has been dominated by Japanese brands, with US, Korean and European manufacturers also prominent. Chinese brands are now challenging that order remarkably quickly. China made becoming a global leader in electric vehicles an industrial priority. It has largely achieved that ambition. If current momentum continues, the badges Australians see on their roads over the coming decade could look very different from those they grew up with. BYD is one name they are likely to see much more often.

artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Sets November 12 as Investor Day to Discuss Michigan AI Expansion and Strategic Alternatives Across Its Portfolio Company reiterates 2027 guidance of $300–$350 million in revenue and $60–$80 million in consolidated Adjusted EBITDA LAS VEGAS , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it will virtually host an investor day (the "Investor Day") on November 12, 2026, from 1:15 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. Pacific Time, to discuss the Michigan AI data center campus (the "Michigan Campus"), the status of its other portfolio businesses and strategic alternatives intended to enhance stockholder value. Participation details for Investor Day will be provided at a later date. During the Investor Day, management will provide an update as to the progress on, and expansion of, the Michigan Campus and the executed master services agreement (the "MSA") with a California-based neocloud provider (the "Customer"). As previously disclosed, the MSA contemplates the deployment of an initial 20 megawatts ("MW") of critical AI compute capacity and, if the Customer exercises all of its options to extend the term, and rights to an additional 32 MW of critical AI compute capacity, the MSA could generate more than $3.0 billion in total contract revenue from the potential 52 MW deployment over a 20-year period. The Company has previously announced that it believes the Michigan Campus could ultimately support more than 300 MW of total power capacity. The development of any capacity beyond the initial 20 MW covered by the MSA is subject to financing, regulatory approvals, engineering, utility agreements, infrastructure availability, customer demand and other conditions. There can be no assurance that additional capacity will be developed, financed, contracted or placed into service. Additionally, management is expected to provide a review of the Company's various portfolio businesses within its various sectors, including: defense; energy and infrastructure; hotel operations and commercial real estate holdings; technology and finance; and commercial lending and trading and activist investing. In addition, the Company will be discussing ongoing initiatives, including, without limitation, the AI software platform by the Company's subsidiary askROI, Inc. ("askROI") and blockchain and digital technology initiatives by Ault Markets, Inc., another subsidiary. Management anticipates discussing the Company's evaluation of strategic alternatives, including potentially selling the Michigan Campus, taking public the Company's wholly owned subsidiary, Sentinum, Inc. ("Sentinum") through an initial public offering or the Company's continued ownership and development of the Michigan Campus. The discussion will also address options involving askROI, including a potential sale, strategic partnership or divestiture, and the possibility of combining askROI with a broader technology business. Transactions under evaluation could include equity consideration, which would allow Hyperscale Data to retain an ownership interest in the combined business and participate in its potential upside. "We are focused on delivering the contracted capacity in our Michigan Campus and turning that investment into cash flow," said Milton "Todd" Ault III, Executive Chairman. "Investor Day will also provide an update on the strategic alternatives we are evaluating for the Michigan Campus and our other portfolio businesses. Our objective is to place these businesses in structures that support their development and make their value more identifiable to our stockholders." artigo.texto: EcoPro BM (247540) is strengthening its strategic partnership with Samsung SDI (006400) with the aim of commercializing sulfide-based solid-state batteries in 2027. EcoPro BM said on the 6th that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Samsung SDI to cooperate on materials development for solid-state batteries. The two companies will pursue joint research and development in solid-state batteries, a core next-generation battery technology. EcoPro BM and Samsung SDI plan to strengthen their cooperation framework from the early development stage through quality evaluation and the establishment of mass-production systems, raising both technological maturity and business competitiveness. They will also widen the scope of cooperation across core materials, including cathode materials for solid-state batteries as well as electrolytes for cathodes and for separators. Samsung SDI will work on solid-state battery cell development and the advancement of mass-production technology, while EcoPro BM will handle the development of core materials for solid-state batteries. Solid-state batteries can improve safety and performance at the same time, making them a key technology for future industries such as electric vehicles and humanoid robots. EcoPro BM has secured proprietary process technology in sulfide-based solid electrolytes, a core material for solid-state batteries, and operates a pilot plant with annual capacity of 40 tons. In August, the company was selected for the "Super Eul Project," a government program supporting materials, parts and equipment companies run by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, in recognition of those research and development results. Through the program, it will receive 20 billion won in research and development support over more than seven years. In July, EcoPro BM unveiled a full value chain roadmap for solid-state batteries at an investor briefing for retail investors. "We are currently reviewing trial production with leading customers, and we expect the earliest mass-production timing to be 2027," said Kong Bo-hyun, an executive director in charge of research and development at EcoPro BM. "We have completed the design of the mass-production line and are preparing so that construction can begin immediately in line with customer demand."

artigo.texto: Key Stats for Amazon Stock - Price change for Amazon stock in last 6 months: 18% - $AMZN Stock Price as of Oct. 2: $252 - 52-Week High: $287 - $AMZN Stock Price Target: $331 What Happened? Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) said its cloud unit will invest more than $1 billion over the next five years. The money will go to US communities that host its data centers. Amazon Web Services made the announcement on Friday. The plan covers education, job training, and energy affordability. It also covers water and energy preservation. AWS also promised to tackle the impact of its data centers on electricity and water use. The move makes sense. Data centers power and run AI models. But communities across the US have pushed back. They worry about electricity demand and utility costs. AWS noted that more than 100 data center moratoriums are being considered nationwide. The backlash is also a political issue ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers between 2011 and 2025. It has large projects or expansions planned in Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia, and Mississippi. AWS CEO Matt Garman said the buildout is urgent. He said other countries also see the benefits of AI. He added that the countries leading in AI will shape it. AWS also said it will be water positive by 2030. That means it will return more water to communities than it uses. It says it is 75% of the way there. What the Market Is Telling Us About Amazon Stock $1 billion is small compared with what Amazon spends. On the Q2 call, management said it expects about $220 billion in cash capex this year. Most of that supports AI and AWS. So this pledge is more about public trust than cost. That trust matters for Amazon stock. AWS is the growth engine. Revenue rose 36.7% last quarter, its fastest pace in 18 quarters. Backlog reached $496 billion. AWS also posted $16.6 billion in operating income. Management says demand is higher than capacity. It expects that to stay true in 2027. New data centers are how Amazon meets that demand. If local opposition slows approvals, that could hold back growth. That is the real risk for Amazon stock. Amazon also said it plans to double its power capacity by the end of 2027 from 2025 levels. Community support will help make that possible. For now, the market will likely stay focused on AWS growth and capex returns. Still, rising local pushback is worth watching. Any new moratoriums could affect how investors view Amazon stock. A clear community plan may ease some of that worry for Amazon stockholders.

artigo.texto: Amazon warns $68 billion in blocked data centers threatens US AI lead — AWS CEO decries 100 proposed bans, pledges $1B community fund Various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the U.S. about data centers to trick us into slowing down - AWS CEO Amazon has issued grave warnings to communities opposing data centers, stating that their actions could cause irreversible damage to the U.S. economy and national security. In a lengthy 3000-word post earlier today, October 2, CEO of Amazon Web Services (AWS), Matt Garman detailed the many benefits of Artificial Intelligence, comparing the technology’s impact on the economy to those of modern transportation systems and the Internet, before attempting to debunk “myths” around data centers and calling on local communities to be more receptive to build-outs as a matter of national urgency. The post also details Amazon's plans to do more for data center host communities through its “Built Together” community investment frameworks. After outlining AI’s impact and the need for data center buildouts, Garman explained why it was imperative for the U.S. to lead the AI race. “The countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run. The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so,” he wrote, presenting urgent buildouts as a key factor in leading that race. Next, Garman addressed growing anti-data center movements that have reportedly blocked data center projects worth $68 billion in the second quarter of 2026 alone, warning that if the 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country should go through, “the US could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations.” He also pointed out that unlike transportation infrastructure, the comparably critical data center buildout is not funded by taxpayer money, but by private firms. The post dismissed many of the concerns about the buildouts as myths, then proceeded to attempt to debunk them. Garman said that, contrary to popular belief, “Data centers actually use very little water relative to other industries,” a position many hyperscalers have repeated. Amazon earlier claimed that its data centers consume only 0.075% of the water Americans use to water their lawns and gardens. Garman also claims the narrative that data centers are driving up energy bills is “misleading and convenient scapegoating.” He argues that AI is simply precipitating an expansion of power infrastructure that was always bound to happen. “Once we collectively build out this new capacity, again funded by the private sector, it should lead to flat or lower rates in the future for residents living in communities with these expanded grids,” he said. On the other hand, contradictory reports claim that AI data centers trigger a "massive irreversible" 76% electricity price spike. The U.S. House also recently passed a bill that directed regulators to consider making AI data centers pay for grid upgrades to minimize the impact on residents. The bill was eventually rejected in the Senate, with opponents saying it was "toothless" and didn't do enough to protect residents. Speaking on pollution, Garman says that data centers emitting huge amounts of pollution with their large backup diesel generators is a myth. He claims that while data centers have rarely used backup power in case of a power outage, this is only necessary because many industries depend on the facilities. This claim doesn’t exactly address growing concerns of pollution from gas turbines powering off-grid data centers. Elon Musk recently came under fire for using unlicensed gas turbines at the Colossus data center. Lastly, Garman said claims that communities do not benefit from data centers are false, citing “considerable tax revenue, positive economic impact, large numbers of good jobs, and education programs” as some of the benefits to the communities where data centers are built. Microsoft pledged to invest $1 billion in local infrastructure improvements in its Hyperion data center community and had reportedly awarded $1.6 billion in contracts to local businesses since construction began, in addition to paying teacher bonuses. As benefits specifically on Amazon’s part, Garman listed an estimated $3 billion in taxes to St. Joseph County, Indiana, over time; more than $1 billion already contributed to communities across the U.S.; thousands of jobs created in building and running the data centers; and education programs with over 10,000 educators and learners enrolled. artigo.texto: India’s emerging carbon economy is beginning to connect sectors that have traditionally been treated separately: sugar, ethanol, renewable gas, agriculture, waste management, carbon removal and climate finance. Sugar mills are no longer only food-processing enterprises. They are increasingly becoming integrated biorefineries with access to bagasse, molasses, press mud, spent wash, sugarcane trash, biogas and other biomass streams. These resources can support electricity generation, ethanol, compressed biogas, biochar, soil amendments and potentially carbon-removal projects. The central question is no longer whether these activities can produce environmental benefits. The more important question is whether those benefits can be measured, verified, monetised and converted into dependable project revenues. Sugarcane as a carbon sink Dr. Sanjay Kolte, IAS, Commissioner of Sugar, Government of Maharashtra, highlighted the opportunity for sugar mills to participate in the offset side of India’s emerging carbon market. That opportunity follows from the biological and industrial characteristics of sugarcane. Sugarcane is a C4 crop with a highly efficient photosynthetic pathway suited to warm, high-light environments. It can produce substantial biomass and absorb significant quantities of atmospheric carbon dioxide during growth. Carbon is temporarily stored in the stalks, leaves and roots, while some carbon can enter the soil through roots, residues and organic matter. Research has identified sugarcane and agricultural soils as having meaningful carbon-sequestration potential. However, sugarcane should not be described as a permanently storing carbon sink merely because it absorbs carbon dioxide during growth. Much of the carbon fixed in the plant is released when the cane is harvested, processed, combusted or decomposed. The relevant climate benefit depends on the complete carbon balance, including fertiliser use, irrigation, diesel consumption, transport, processing, residue management and the end use of sugar, ethanol, electricity or other products. A sugarcane-based carbon project must therefore calculate net mitigation rather than gross photosynthetic uptake. It must establish a credible baseline and account for emissions throughout the relevant project boundary. It must also distinguish temporary biological carbon storage from durable removal. A sugar mill can strengthen its carbon position by reducing fossil-fuel consumption through bagasse-based energy, avoiding open burning or unmanaged decomposition of residues, converting organic waste into biogas or compressed biogas, improving soil organic carbon, producing and applying biochar, reducing methane emissions from effluent or manure, displacing fossil fuels with ethanol or renewable electricity, and measuring emissions across the farm-to-factory value chain. This creates an opportunity for sugar mills to participate in the offset mechanism of the Indian Carbon Market. But the opportunity will depend on approved methodologies, monitoring, reporting and verification, as well as proof that the credited activity is additional and not simply the result of an existing legal obligation or commercially attractive investment. The sugar mill as a biorefinery The modern sugar mill can be understood as a biorefinery rather than a single-product factory. Bagasse can generate renewable electricity and process heat. Molasses can be converted into ethanol. Press mud and spent wash can be treated and used in soil applications or anaerobic digestion. Sugarcane trash can become feedstock for biomass energy, compressed biogas or biochar, provided its removal does not damage soil health. This integrated model creates several possible economic streams: sugar, ethanol, renewable electricity, compressed biogas, renewable-gas attributes, renewable-energy certificates, carbon credits, biochar and avoided waste-treatment costs. The central challenge is the separation of environmental attributes. If the same tonne of biogas is used to issue a renewable-gas certificate and also claimed as a carbon credit, the accounting system must determine whether both claims are permissible and how they should be adjusted. Similarly, renewable electricity may generate a Renewable Energy Certificate, but its associated emissions reduction cannot automatically be counted again as a separate carbon credit. Environmental attributes must therefore be defined, tracked, transferred and retired through a transparent registry. This is the difference between a credible environmental market and a collection of overlapping claims. Ethanol and the policy signal India’s ethanol programme has created one of the country’s strongest policy signals for bio-based energy. Under the Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme, blending increased from less than 1.5 per cent in 2013–14 to 20 per cent in the 2025–26 ethanol supply year. The National Policy on Biofuels, as amended in 2022, advanced the 20 per cent blending target from 2030 to the 2025–26 supply year. The increase in blending has been driven by several objectives, including reducing crude-oil imports, improving energy security, creating demand for agricultural feedstocks and supporting the sugar industry during periods of surplus production. It has also strengthened the commercial case for distilleries and sugar mills investing in ethanol capacity. artigo.texto: LG Electronics expands chiller production for AI data centers The company plans to invest a total of USD 110 million in a new air-cooled chiller production facility in the US and in expanding two air-cooled chiller production lines in South Korea. LG Electronics (LG) is expanding its chiller manufacturing capabilities with a new production facility in the United States and increased production capacity in South Korea, further strengthening its ability to deliver end-to-end cooling solutions for AI data centers (AIDCs). The company’s new air-cooled chiller production facility in Windsor, Virginia will produce air-cooled chillers for AIDCs, with production scheduled to begin in the first half of 2027. The facility’s chiller production will support a stable, responsive supply system for rising demand across North America, while serving as a strategic base for LG’s regional expansion, the company said. LG is also expanding its air-cooled chiller production lines in Pyeongtaek and Changwon, South Korea. The company is improving operational efficiency by adopting a conveyor-based production system designed for mass production. The company plans to invest a total of KRW 150 billion (about USD 110 million) in its new US facility and its factories in Pyeongtaek and Changwon. LG is also broadening its AIDC thermal management business through its Chip-to-Chiller solution strategy. The portfolio includes chillers, Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) and cold plates that absorb heat directly from chips. LG is pursuing additional AIDC projects in North America through its relationships with leading hyperscalers and big tech companies. In Asia, LG is applying its “One LG” strategy by combining heating, ventilation and air conditioning technologies with battery solutions and data center design, build and operation capabilities from other LG affiliates. LG is also applying this integrated approach to Sinar Mas Group’s hyperscale AIDC project in Jakarta, Indonesia, the company said. “We will continue to strengthen our core capabilities in AI data center cooling solutions, from differentiated product technologies to production capacity,” said James Lee, president of the LG Eco Solution Company. “With these capabilities, we will ensure a stable supply and actively address rapidly growing market demand.”

artigo.texto: Desperdício de comida agora pode gerar créditos de carbono Nova modalidade de crédito de carbono busca unir redução de emissões, combate ao desperdício de alimentos e segurança alimentar Se uma empresa quiser reduzir sua pegada de carbono, pode comprar créditos de carbono emitidos pela Verra, o maior programa de certificação de créditos de carbono do mundo. Esses créditos podem ser destinados a projetos como energia renovável ou restauração de florestas, permitindo que uma empresa reivindique os benefícios ambientais de um novo parque eólico ou de árvores plantadas em uma área que havia sido desmatada. Agora existe uma nova opção: créditos de carbono para alimentos resgatados, que ajudam a financiar organizações que coletam alimentos que seriam desperdiçados e os distribuem para pessoas necessitadas. Esses créditos emitidos pela Verra agora estão disponíveis graças à Brightly, uma startup de Boston fundada em 2023 por Andy Levitt, que anteriormente fundou e comandou a Purple Carrot, uma empresa de kits de refeições à base de plantas. A Brightly já tem contratos com mais de 25 organizações de resgate de alimentos. Agora, porém, seus créditos de carbono relacionados ao desperdício de alimentos estão sendo emitidos pela Verra, tornando-os os primeiros do tipo dentro da metodologia do padrão de certificação para reduzir a perda e o desperdício de alimentos. Os créditos de carbono são cercados de controvérsias. Pesquisas descobriram que alguns projetos não entregaram benefícios climáticos reais; especialistas afirmam que a possibilidade de usar créditos pode permitir o greenwashing. Levitt sabe que existe desconfiança em relação ao mercado de carbono, mas afirma que a solução da Brightly cria um “ciclo virtuoso de atividade” que financia ainda mais o resgate de alimentos, permitindo que organizações sem fins lucrativos alimentem mais pessoas. “Agora somos capazes de oferecer uma solução inovadora para empresas que querem se concentrar em enfrentar tanto os desafios ambientais quanto a fome”, diz Levitt. “É uma categoria e uma classe completamente novas de créditos de carbono que existem no mercado.” Reduzir o desperdício de alimentos é uma maneira clara de enfrentar as mudanças climáticas. Globalmente, o desperdício de alimentos responde por entre 6% e 10% das emissões mundiais. A aviação, para comparação, responde por cerca de 3%. Ao mesmo tempo, dezenas de milhões de americanos têm acesso limitado ou incerto a alimentos e dependem de bancos de alimentos ou despensas comunitárias para complementar suas compras. A Feeding America estima que cerca de 50 milhões de americanos receberam assistência alimentar de organizações beneficentes em 2023. Muitas dessas organizações, porém, enfrentam dificuldades de financiamento, especialmente diante do aumento da demanda provocado pela alta dos preços dos alimentos e pelo estresse econômico generalizado. ENFRENTANDO O DESAFIO AMBIENTAL E A FOME A Brightly afirma que sua solução enfrenta os dois lados dessa questão. “Nosso objetivo é criar financiamento sustentável para organizações sem fins lucrativos de resgate de alimentos, permitindo que elas mantenham os alimentos fora dos aterros sanitários e alimentem pessoas que passam fome”, diz Levitt. Ao financiar o resgate de alimentos, a Brightly afirma evitar que o metano emitido pelo desperdício de alimentos chegue à atmosfera. Uma parte fundamental de um crédito de carbono eficaz é a adicionalidade, o que significa que a redução das emissões não teria acontecido de qualquer maneira sem a receita gerada pelo crédito de carbono. A Brightly afirma quantificar os benefícios de seus créditos de carbono coletando um histórico de três anos da atividade de uma organização de resgate de alimentos, estabelecendo uma linha de base para o benefício ambiental gerado por aquela organização. A empresa contabiliza apenas o impacto ambiental que excede essa linha de base. Essas organizações sem fins lucrativos coletam todos os tipos de alimentos; algumas podem se concentrar em frutas, legumes e verduras, enquanto outras trabalham com produtos não perecíveis. Cada um desses alimentos tem seu próprio impacto ambiental. A Brightly analisa todos os dados fornecidos pelas organizações sobre o que foi resgatado e em que quantidade, atribuindo um impacto climático a cada tipo de alimento, do pão à carne. “Isso é tratado em um nível hiper específico, linha por linha, alimento por alimento, para alcançar esse grau de precisão e conservadorismo necessário para obter uma classificação de crédito de carbono de alta qualidade”, diz Levitt. Empresas que vão de fabricantes de alimentos a supermercados, e até mesmo companhias de fora do setor alimentício, como empresas de vestuário, poderiam comprar os créditos da Brightly relacionados ao desperdício de alimentos. A Brightly repassa até 80% da receita obtida com a venda dos créditos para as organizações de resgate de alimentos, financiando seus esforços e permitindo que elas ampliem suas operações. É difícil especificar quanto, em dólares, uma organização média de resgate de alimentos poderia receber, diz Levitt, porque os créditos de carbono não são criados individualmente para cada organização; em vez disso, as ações daquela organização representam uma parte de um conjunto maior de créditos. UM IMPACTO HIPERLOCAL A Brightly já analisou mais de 5 bilhões de libras de dados sobre alimentos resgatados, o equivalente a mais de 1 milhão de toneladas métricas de emissões de gases de efeito estufa evitadas. A empresa também já contratou vendas futuras de mais de 80 mil créditos. Com a notícia de que a Verra está emitindo os créditos da Brightly, Levitt espera que esse impacto cresça. A Brightly espera emitir 300 mil créditos por ano, com base em projetos de resgate de alimentos nos Estados Unidos. A empresa também está trabalhando em projetos no exterior. artigo.texto: Jupiter Wagons Secures 41 MW/102.5 MWh BESS Project from UPCL JEM Energy, in partnership with Madhav Infra Projects, emerged as the L1 bidder for UPCL’s Cluster C tender under the TBCB mechanism. October 06, 2026. By News Bureau Jupiter Wagons (JWL), through its energy business JEM Energy, has won a 41 MW/102.5 MWh standalone Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project from Uttarakhand Power Corporation (UPCL), in partnership with Madhav Infra Projects. The partnership emerged as the L1 bidder for Cluster C of UPCL's tender, which was conducted under the Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) mechanism. The projects envisage supply and commissioning of approximately INR 100 crore of BESS system. JWL has also received the formal Letter of Award (LoA) from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company (WBSEDCL) for the 50 MW/200 MWh standalone BESS project at the Jeerat 132 kV substation in North 24 Parganas, West Bengal. The project was secured in August 2026. These developments follow the Union Cabinet's approval of Green Energy Corridor Phase-3, which was welcomed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The scheme provides for 50 GWh of battery energy storage alongside stronger intra-state transmission networks. Substation-level storage of the kind being deployed in Uttarakhand and West Bengal is central to this framework, and JEM Energy is building its utility-scale portfolio in line with it. Speaking on the development, Vivek Lohia, Managing Director, Jupiter Wagons, said, "Winning the Uttarakhand project and receiving the formal award for Jeerat are important steps in building JEM Energy into a scalable energy storage business. With the approval of Green Energy Corridor Phase-3, battery storage is now firmly part of how India will plan and strengthen its grid, and substation-level projects such as these are where that work begins. We reiterate our target of building a BESS order book of approximately INR 1,000 crore by FY27. As the business scales, we expect Jupiter Electric Mobility (JEM) to turn EBITDA positive in Q3 FY27 and to turn profitable by FY28. We will continue to bid with discipline for utility-scale and Commercial and Industrial (C&I) opportunities across India." The Uttarakhand win takes JEM Energy's presence into a new state. It also strengthens JWL's position in the energy transition ecosystem, in line with the Company's strategy of expanding into high-growth businesses beyond its traditional railway and mobility operations. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Raleigh leaders could decide Tuesday night whether to pause future data center development in the city. A public hearing will be held Tuesday at 7 p.m. during the Raleigh City Council meeting. Citizens will have a chance to share their opinions on whether the city should approve a six-month pause on data centers before a possible vote. Other WRAL Top Stories A moratorium is a pause, not a ban, on data centers. The conversation started months ago when the city of Raleigh received an application for a large data center on Jones Sausage Road. Raleigh is currently the largest city in North Carolina without a moratorium on data centers. Several cities and counties, including Apex, Durham, Greensboro and Charlotte, have approved similar pauses on data center development. Raleigh already has smaller data centers, but the proposed moratorium would be for large-scale data centers that raise concerns about noise, energy and water use. Raleigh Mayor Janet Cowell previously said the city has to protect its residents while maintaining its status as an innovative city. "We definitely want to protect those that are already operating and not disrupt existing research and development or companies that have located here," Cowell said. "Then we want to have a very rational and careful approach that protects individuals who live in Raleigh and still be known as a tech, innovative city." At last month's Raleigh City Council meeting, some people expressed their support for a moratorium. “When new technology develops, policy usually lags behind, and a moratorium gives you a chance to put a pause on that [and] figure out how to handle this thing," said Laura Harris, a Raleigh resident. Data centers, which support AI computing, are packed with graphics processing units, or GPUs, that generate significantly more heat than traditional computing equipment and often require large amounts of water to cool.

artigo.texto: Solid-state batteries have long been heralded as the next great leap in energy storage, promising to replace the flammable liquid electrolytes inside today’s lithium-ion cells with solid materials that could make devices safer and more energy dense. Yet a persistent engineering problem has slowed their progress: the solid materials that shuttle lithium ions between electrodes are often stiff and unforgiving, struggling to maintain the intimate contact with electrode surfaces that a working battery demands. Now, researchers at Rice University have taken an unusually elegant approach to that problem by asking a question that most electrolyte designers have overlooked — what if the material that carries the ions could also bend, flex, and adapt mechanically to the environment inside a cell? The Rice team, drawn from the departments of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Chemistry, and Materials Science and Nanoengineering, along with the Rice Advanced Materials Institute, has developed a relatively soft and flexible porous material that selectively transports lithium ions. The work, published in the peer-reviewed journal Chemical Science, introduces a new design philosophy for porous solid electrolytes, one that treats mechanical adaptability not as an afterthought but as a core performance criterion, sitting alongside ionic conductivity and chemical stability in the designer’s toolkit. The material at the heart of the study is called ZnBTCA, and it belongs to a family of compounds known as metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs. These are porous crystalline materials built from metal atoms connected by organic molecules into repeating, lattice-like structures. What makes MOFs so compelling for battery applications is their architecture: they contain tiny, ordered channels whose size and chemistry can be tailored to move or hold specific molecules and ions. In principle, a MOF can act as a molecular sieve for charge, allowing lithium ions to stream through its pores while blocking everything else. Many MOFs previously explored as battery electrolytes, however, have been constructed from relatively rigid aromatic linkers — the organic struts that connect the metal nodes — which produce frameworks that are stiff and mechanically unyielding. ZnBTCA takes a fundamentally different route. Instead of an aromatic linker, it employs a flexible aliphatic linker, an organic molecule with a pliable carbon-chain backbone. That single design choice ripples through the entire material: the framework itself becomes softer and more mechanically adaptable, capable of deforming and conforming rather than resisting. The researchers also emphasized practicality in their selection of building blocks. The material is assembled from relatively abundant, low-cost components, including zinc — one of the most accessible metals in the battery chemist’s repertoire — and an inexpensive aliphatic linker, an important consideration if such materials are ever to move from the laboratory bench toward real-world manufacturing. First author Zina Deriche, a graduate student in chemical and biomolecular engineering at Rice, framed the shift in thinking that underpins the work. MOF electrolytes, she noted, are often designed primarily around how effectively they transport ions. The Rice study demonstrates that the mechanical properties of the framework can also be an important part of the design equation. It is a deceptively simple reframing, but one with significant consequences: a material that can flex with the battery as it charges and discharges may hold up better over thousands of cycles than one that cracks or delaminates under mechanical stress. The dual functionality of ZnBTCA is what excites the team most. The material’s flexible molecular building blocks make it relatively soft, while its negatively charged framework structure favors the movement of positively charged lithium ions through its channels. Stavroula Alina Kampouri, a corresponding author of the study and assistant professor across chemical and biomolecular engineering, chemistry, and materials science and nanoengineering, described the convergence of these properties as the most thrilling aspect of the result. The same material, she explained, brings together flexible building blocks that make the framework softer and more adaptable with a negatively charged structure that promotes selective lithium-ion transport. Bringing those properties together, she said, offers a new way to design MOF electrolytes by considering how ions move and how the material behaves mechanically at the same time. The experimental results lend strong support to the design concept. The researchers first exchanged the sodium ions residing within the framework for lithium ions, a process known as ion exchange that is common in MOF chemistry. After the exchange, they found that roughly 95 percent of the mobile charge-balancing ions in the material were lithium, while the framework itself remained structurally intact — a critical demonstration that the delicate crystalline lattice could survive the swapping of its guest ions without collapsing. Selectivity matters enormously in an electrolyte: a material that carries only lithium ions, rather than a mixed crowd of mobile species, delivers cleaner, more efficient battery operation and helps prevent parasitic reactions that degrade performance over time. During the 2026-2027 period, Vietnam will focus on building a foundation in terms of institutions, data, technical standards, and a blue classification system; promoting investment opportunities and developing an efficient carbon market. Vietnam is gradually laying the groundwork for a truly functioning carbon market, while simultaneously transforming climate change response goals into drivers for green transition and sustainable development. Notably, to lay the groundwork for the carbon market to "take off," the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment recently issued Decision No. 3696/QD-BNNMT implementing Decision No. 505/QD-TTg of the Prime Minister on the National Digital Transformation Day 2026; which stipulates the completion of the construction and operation of the National Registration System for Greenhouse Gas Emission Quotas and Carbon Credits before October 10, 2026. Building a solidlegal foundation According to Mr. Nguyen Hung Minh, Deputy Head of the Carbon Market Department, Climate Change Agency, greenhouse gases and the greenhouse effect are the core causes of global warming and lead to many consequences of climate change such as rising sea levels and extreme weather events. In Vietnam, the average annual temperature across the country between 1961 and 2023 has been recorded as increasing by approximately 0.2 degrees Celsius per decade. Notably, Vietnam ranks 10th in the world in terms of climate change risk in 2024. Faced with these challenges, Vietnam's system of policies and laws on climate change response has been gradually improved over time, from guidelines, laws, decrees, decisions, and circulars to international agreements and treaties. Among these, Resolution 24-NQ/TW dated June 3, 2013, on proactively responding to climate change, strengthening resource management and environmental protection; Resolution 120/NQ-CP of 2017 on sustainable development of the Mekong Delta adapting to climate change; and Government Resolution 06/NQ-CP promulgating the Action Program to continue implementing Resolution 24-NQ/TW, are fundamental policy decisions. By 2026, the focus will continue to be on building databases, early warning systems for natural disasters, developing a circular economy , efficient resource utilization, and a carbon market. However, climate change provisions are currently regulated in different laws. In particular, the 2020 Environmental Protection Law is a crucial legal foundation for responding to climate change. Specifically, Article 139 of the 2020 Environmental Protection Law provides the legal basis for organizing and developing a carbon market. This forms the fundamental basis for building a carbon market in Vietnam. Looking ahead, Mr. Minh stated that Vietnam will continue to improve its climate change legislation, including researching and proposing the development of a Climate Change Law; reviewing relevant regulations in the 2020 Environmental Protection Law; perfecting technical standards and regulations; promoting the circular economy and green transition; and strengthening the dissemination and popularization of the law. The Climate Change Department has also coordinated with the Environment Department to finalize the draft Law amending and supplementing a number of articles of the Law on Environmental Protection for the Government to report to the Standing Committee of the National Assembly . It is currently undergoing further technical review to be ready for submission to the National Assembly for consideration and approval at the October session. Furthermore, the Climate Change Department has advised the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment to submit to the Government a Resolution approving the Agreement on implementation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement between Vietnam and the Government of Singapore. Currently, the Government has approved bilateral carbon credit exchange agreements with Singapore and Japan; regarding South Korea and Switzerland , the department is promoting technical negotiations, with the signing expected to be completed by the end of 2026. artigo.texto: HDOT, Sustainability Partners and Hensel Phelps Mark the Start of Construction on Oʻahu and Kauaʻi Microgrids with PV, BESS and Charging Infrastructure The State of Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation (HDOT), Sustainability Partners (SP), and Hensel Phelps have marked the start of construction on new microgrid projects on Oʻahu and Kauaʻi that include solar PV canopies, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and electric vehicle charging stations. Construction Hawaiian Blessing ceremonies commemorating the start of construction were held in August. The projects are designed to strengthen energy resilience at critical HDOT facilities by integrating solar generation with battery energy storage and intelligent microgrid controls to manage energy generation, storage, and use. Together, the projects are expected to generate 2.2 MWh of renewable energy each day and will include two 1 MW battery energy storage systems. The microgrids are part of HDOT’s broader work to modernize HDOT’s infrastructure and advance the state’s clean energy and resilience goals. “These projects represent another important step in strengthening the resiliency of Hawaiʻi’s infrastructure,” said Ed Sniffen, Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation Director. “These PV and battery storage systems provide critical energy security for our teams during severe weather and multi-day blackouts.” Oʻahu The Oʻahu microgrid will serve HDOT Highways’ Oʻahu District Main Office Facility on Kakoi Street. The project includes a 1 MW battery energy storage system and solar PV canopies expected to generate 1.5 MWh of renewable energy per day. This site will include over 40 Level 2 Chargers and 1 Dual-Port 200 kW DC Fast Charger. Schneider Electric’s EcoStruxure microgrid technology will provide the intelligent control layer that coordinates solar generation, battery storage, EV charging, and interaction with the utility grid to optimize how energy is generated, stored, and used. SP is also working with Hawaiian Electric toward enrollment in its Energy Export program, which would allow the site to export surplus power back to the electric grid. Kauaʻi The Kauaʻi microgrid will serve HDOT Highways’ Kauaʻi District Main Office Facility on Haleukana Street. The project includes a 1 MW battery energy storage system and solar PV canopies expected to generate 700 kWh of renewable energy per day. This site will include over 12 Level 2 Chargers and 1 Dual-Port 200 kW DC Fast Charger. As on Oʻahu, Schneider Electric’s EcoStruxure microgrid technology will provide centralized visibility and intelligent control of the site’s distributed energy resources, helping coordinate generation, storage, and electrical loads. Hensel Phelps is leading construction of both projects and has worked alongside HDOT and Sustainability Partners on transportation and energy infrastructure throughout Hawaiʻi.

The quarterly figures show that Tesla delivered about 22,000 more vehicles than it produced, indicating that deliveries came partly from vehicles manufactured in previous quarters, in addition to third-quarter production. Model 3 and Model Y continued to account for the overwhelming majority of Tesla’s automotive activity. Tesla produced 457,387 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles during the quarter and delivered 478,237 of the two models. That means Model 3 and Model Y represented approximately 98% of Tesla’s total vehicle deliveries during the period. Deliveries of Model 3 and Model Y exceeded production by 20,850 vehicles, contributing most of the difference between companywide production and deliveries. Approximately 1% of Model 3 and Model Y deliveries were subject to operating lease accounting. Tesla does not break out Model 3 and Model Y results separately in its quarterly production and delivery announcement, instead reporting the vehicles as a combined category. The company’s Other Models category accounted for a much smaller portion of automotive volumes. Tesla produced 7,004 Other Models vehicles during the third quarter and delivered 8,295. Approximately 4% of Other Models deliveries were subject to operating lease accounting. The category includes Tesla vehicles outside the Model 3 and Model Y group, although the company’s production and delivery announcement did not provide individual results for each vehicle within the category. Across the company’s complete vehicle portfolio, deliveries exceeded production by 22,141 vehicles. The difference is notable because production and deliveries do not necessarily move in parallel from quarter to quarter. Vehicles produced near the end of a reporting period may not be delivered until the following quarter, while vehicles produced during earlier periods can contribute to current-quarter deliveries. Transportation timing, geographic distribution and customer handoffs can also create differences between the two figures. Tesla’s third-quarter release provides an early indication of operating activity but does not include enough information to determine the profitability of those deliveries. The company did not disclose quarterly automotive revenue, average selling prices, gross profit, operating income, net income or free cash flow in the production and delivery announcement. Tesla will report those figures as part of its complete third-quarter financial results. Tesla specifically cautioned investors that vehicle deliveries and energy storage deployments represent only two measures of company performance and should not be relied upon independently to estimate quarterly financial results. Several factors can significantly affect the financial contribution associated with any given level of vehicle deliveries. Average selling prices are one major variable. Changes in vehicle pricing, product mix, geographic mix and incentives can cause automotive revenue to rise or fall even when the number of vehicles delivered remains relatively stable. The mix between Model 3 and Model Y and Tesla’s higher-priced vehicles can also affect revenue and margins. Cost of sales is another important factor. Vehicle profitability depends on manufacturing costs, raw materials, factory utilization, logistics expenses and other costs associated with producing and delivering vehicles. As a result, higher delivery volumes do not necessarily translate directly into higher earnings. Foreign exchange movements can also influence Tesla’s reported results because the company sells vehicles and other products across multiple international markets. Currency changes can affect the dollar value of international revenue and expenses when Tesla translates them into its reporting currency. Investors will therefore need to wait for the company’s full earnings report to assess how the third-quarter operating volumes translated into revenue, margins, and cash generation. Tesla’s energy business also accounted for a significant share of the quarter’s operating activity. The company deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage products during the third quarter. Tesla’s energy storage business includes systems that store electricity for later use, helping customers manage energy supply and demand and integrate power from different generation sources. Energy storage has become an increasingly important part of Tesla’s business alongside electric vehicles. Utilities, power producers, and other customers can use large-scale battery storage to store electricity and release it when grid demand is higher or when generation from other sources is lower. The third-quarter deployment figure measures the storage capacity Tesla delivered during the period, but as with vehicle deliveries, it does not reveal the financial contribution from those deployments. Revenue and profitability from energy storage can vary depending on product mix, pricing, project timing and associated costs. Tesla will provide greater visibility into those factors when it reports complete quarterly results. artigo.texto: Data centers are preventing a US recession, NMSU economist says Despite a weak housing market, data center growth has buoyed the US economy, New Mexico State University economics professor Chris Erickson tells KOAT. Data centers are preventing the U.S. from falling into a recession, a New Mexico State University economic expert told KOAT on Saturday. "Data centers are keeping the economy growing at this point; they are the main drivers of the economy," said Chris Erickson, a professor of economics at NMSU. RELATED: Data centers become key issue in New Mexico governor’s race "Its investment in data centers has kept the economy buoyed up. The housing sector has been quite weak for a while. Usually when the housing sector is that weak, you can expect either slowdown or even a recession to follow that because construction is such an important source of jobs. But because the data centers have taken up all the slack in construction, that hasn't happened," Erickson explained. Data center growth in New Mexico is not uncontroversial, and Erickson said he believes there could be a slowdown in new data center development. The controversy surrounding them might make it difficult for companies to secure funding for new projects, he said. Three New Mexico counties have placed moratoriums on data center development, and a fourth is currently considering one. Democratic lawmakers in Santa Fe are proposing a statewide moratorium for the 2027 legislative session. Opponents are wary of the environmental impacts and financial costs of data centers. Still, there are major data centers currently operating or in development across the state, including an operational Meta data center in Valencia County and a major Oracle data center under construction in Doña Ana County. Google is also exploring a potential site in Lea County.

artigo.texto: Wisconsin Policy Forum Data centers can deliver multi-billion-dollar investments and large numbers of jobs to Wisconsin communities. But key issues around their development remain unresolved, including how to ensure residents are spared from increases to transmission rates or property taxes. Far from being a hub of data center construction, a new Wisconsin Policy Forum report finds Wisconsin lags states such as Virginia and Ohio in both the number and size of its data centers. Still, three major hyperscale data centers are being built in Wisconsin in recent years, with more being proposed and often facing significant opposition. A Microsoft data center is up and running in Mount Pleasant, while centers are under construction in Port Washington and Beaver Dam. Recent technological advancements in artificial intelligence are driving a national data center boom. A broader examination of the impacts of this technology — an understandably salient issue for many — is beyond the scope of this report. Instead, our report seeks to ground discussions in facts about how they affect local government finances, the regional economy, the energy grid, and more. For example, due in large part to these centers, the latest state projections show peak power demand in Wisconsin is expected to increase by more than 5 gigawatts between 2024 and 2030. This raises the question of who will pay for the added capacity to serve these centers. Electricity arguably represents the single biggest challenge for large data centers– and the single biggest issue for policymakers, our report finds. In considering data center proposals, elected officials have a difficult balance to strike. An August Marquette University Law School poll found 78% of registered voters in Wisconsin felt the costs of large data centers outweigh their benefits, while only 21% felt their benefits outweighed their costs. Some Wisconsin communities have recently blocked construction of large data centers, either by rejecting a specific proposal or approving a blanket moratorium. One of the implications of this is that local officials may have leverage in negotiating data center deals with developers, since there is a credible risk that these proposals will be rejected. The Forum reviewed deals between data center developers and the communities of Mount Pleasant, Port Washington, and Beaver Dam, as well as in two communities where centers were proposed but later canceled: Janesville and DeForest. In general, we found communities were striking reasonable deals that included fiscal safeguards. However, state law makes it challenging for local officials to protect existing taxpayers in the case of data center developments that require significant tax increment finance (TIF) spending on infrastructure or developer incentives. Under current law, there could be initial tax increases on existing property owners — despite the possibility that once the TIF district closes, residents’ taxes could decline to what they were prior to the data center or even less. In addition, most states offer a state sales tax exemption to data centers, as Wisconsin does. While other industries such as manufacturing receive similar treatment here, the cost of these forgone tax revenues is significant. Our report concludes by offering a menu of options for state and local policymakers to consider in response to issues highlighted in our report. Click here to read the full report and learn more. This information is a service of the Wisconsin Policy Forum, the state’s leading resource for nonpartisan state and local government research and civic education. Learn more at wispolicyforum.org
