artigo.texto: BYD puts battery cells directly in cooling liquid in new patent BYD has filed an invention patent application describing a battery cabinet that separates its electrical equipment from a lower compartment where cell modules are submerged in dielectric fluid. The design centres on a relatively simple question with significant consequences for an immersion-cooled battery system: how do electrical connections cross the boundary between a dry compartment and a liquid-filled one? Published by the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA) on October 5, 2026, as CN 122868832 A, the application covers battery cabinets and energy storage equipment. Filed in March 2025, it describes a two-chamber enclosure in which the cooling medium surrounds the cell modules while electrical equipment remains outside the liquid volume. Why immersion cooling changes the battery enclosure Many contemporary battery systems use indirect liquid cooling. Coolant circulates through aluminium cold plates positioned against the battery modules, with heat passing through the cell casing and intervening materials before reaching the coolant. Immersion cooling changes that arrangement. Instead of bringing coolant to a separate cooling plate, the battery modules sit directly in a non-conductive dielectric fluid. Heat can therefore transfer from the wetted surfaces of the modules directly into the surrounding fluid. The arrangement shortens the thermal path between the battery and the cooling medium, but it also changes the enclosure problem. The liquid must be contained, while electrical components and connection points that are not intended to operate in the fluid must remain isolated from it. That boundary is where BYD’s patent application focuses. Production battery systems still rely on indirect cooling. The distinction is easier to see against BYD and CATL’s existing production architectures. BYD’s MC Cube energy storage system integrates Blade batteries using its cell-to-system architecture, while the MC Cube-T specifies liquid cooling. CATL’s EnerOne and EnerC storage systems likewise use liquid cooling, with cooling plates positioned outside the battery modules. CATL’s Qilin passenger-vehicle battery uses a different packaging arrangement, integrating a liquid-cooling plate into a multifunctional interlayer positioned between adjacent cells. These systems keep the cooling medium in a defined thermal path rather than surrounding the battery modules directly. BYD’s new filing describes another arrangement: the cell modules occupy the liquid-filled chamber itself, while electrical equipment is kept in a separate dry chamber. The resulting engineering problem is not simply how to transfer heat. It is how to maintain an electrical connection across a liquid-tight boundary. BYD routes the connections through the top CN 122868832 A divides the cabinet into two isolated chambers: - Chamber 1: An upper dry compartment containing electrical equipment components. - Chamber 2: A lower liquid compartment containing cell modules submerged in dielectric fluid. The connection between the two chambers is routed through the upper portion of the liquid compartment. Rather than bringing the electrical and signal leads through the floor or side walls of the wet chamber, the design directs them upward before they enter the dry compartment. Location matters because hydrostatic pressure increases with liquid depth. A sealing interface positioned higher in the chamber therefore experiences less hydrostatic pressure than an equivalent interface positioned deeper in the liquid. The electrical equipment remains outside the liquid volume while maintaining the connection to the submerged battery modules. In other words, the filing does not rely solely on the fluid’s cooling dielectric properties to separate the battery’s thermal and electrical environments. It also uses the cabinet’s physical layout to keep the electrical connection points above the main liquid volume. The filing is about a cabinet, not a new vehicle battery The application covers battery cabinets and energy storage equipment and does not identify a passenger vehicle application. It specifies dielectric fluid, including hydrocarbon- or ester-based formulations, rather than standard liquid coolant. The filing therefore describes an immersion-cooled stationary battery enclosure with a dry electrical compartment and a wet battery compartment. That distinction matters because a patent application is not evidence that the architecture has entered production. The application remains under substantive examination, and BYD has not announced commercial production plans for the design. For now, CN 122868832 A documents an enclosure architecture and a specific way of routing electrical connections through the boundary between its dry and liquid-filled sections.

artigo.texto: Old Town became the second Greater Bangor community to pass a short-term ban on data centers Monday. The six-month ban, which outlaws the development of data centers in the city’s industrial zones, is retroactive to Sept. 8, when the Old Town City Council first discussed the possibility of a ban. Data center developments are already not allowed in other zones, according to the city’s land use ordinance. Communities across Maine have passed moratoriums, or temporary bans, on data center developments this year due to the limited knowledge of how they will affect municipalities. The bans, which are generally set to last six months, give towns time to learn about the technology and draft laws to regulate its development. The Old Town City Council passed the ban unanimously at its Monday meeting. Due to extensive conversation about a possible ban during a September meeting, discussion on the ban Monday lasted for about one minute. “I think that our conversation last time was pretty substantial and overarching, and as previously stated, it gives us plenty of time to adequately assess the risks and benefits and pros and cons of all that this super complex, super new thing entails,” Councilor Zachary Wyles said. Residents reached out to councilors before the ban was proposed to say they didn’t want a data center to come to Old Town. Old Town could be a desirable location for a data center because of its history with businesses like Nine Dragons Paper and Old Town Canoe, and its industrial zones, Council President Christian Pushor said at the Sept. 8 meeting. Councilors previously said a long-term ban in the form of zoning changes would be sent to a public referendum to allow voters to decide. The next possible election date would be June 2027. The six-month ban is set to expire in March, but an extension to June could be approved. “I feel like this is such a hot topic that I would like it to go to the public instead of relying on people who have the time and energy to contact us,” Councilor Katrina Wynn said on Sept. 8.

artigo.texto: 43 proposed power plants needed to fuel data centers listed across NEPA PHILADELPHIA (WOLF) — A new environmental report warning about Pennsylvania’s expected growth in natural-gas power generation comes as proposed power plants are already listed across much of northeastern and central Pennsylvania. PennEnvironment Research & Policy Center and Frontier Group project Pennsylvania could add 4.4 gigawatts of natural-gas capacity by the end of 2030, an increase of nearly 15% over the state’s existing gas footprint. The groups say growing demand from data centers is a major driver behind the proposed expansion. A separate Track Data Centers listing provided to FOX56 identifies 43 proposed power plants across the station’s coverage area. Lackawanna County has the largest number, with 15 proposals and 4.8 gigawatts of listed capacity. Luzerne County has nine proposals and 4.3 gigawatts of listed capacity. Three plants are listed in each of Carbon, Northampton and Schuylkill counties. Carbon County’s listed capacity is 350 megawatts, while Northampton and Schuylkill counties each have 1.2 gigawatts listed. Bradford, Monroe and Union counties each have two proposed plants. Listed capacity is 248 megawatts in Bradford County and 300 megawatts in Union County; no capacity figure was listed for Monroe County. One proposed plant is listed in each of Columbia, Lycoming, Montour and Wayne counties. The listed capacity figures total nearly 12.4 gigawatts in the counties where capacity was provided. The database listings may cover projects with different timelines and scopes than the statewide projections cited in PennEnvironment’s report. PennEnvironment says new gas plants can operate for 25 to 30 years and has called for a moratorium on new data centers, arguing that the projects could increase air pollution and long-term greenhouse-gas emissions. The organization’s conclusions and policy recommendations reflect its environmental advocacy position.

artigo.texto: Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) delivered more vehicles than Wall Street expected in the third quarter of 2026, giving investors a reason to turn more positive on the electric vehicle maker’s near-term outlook. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, beating the company-compiled analyst consensus of 461,974. Deliveries also rose 1.3% from 480,126 vehicles in Q2. However, they remained 2.1% below the 497,099 vehicles delivered in Q3 2025. The stronger-than-expected result helped Tesla stock rebound. Shares closed at $370.59 on October 2, up 4.7% in the session. Reuters reported that the stock gained more than 5% earlier in trading after the delivery figures were released. Still, Tesla faces a growing challenge from Chinese EV giant BYD. BYD’s battery-electric vehicle sales continued to pull further ahead of Tesla during the quarter. Tesla Q3 Deliveries Beat Estimates Tesla’s Q3 delivery result came in well above the latest company-compiled consensus. Analysts surveyed by Tesla had expected 461,974 deliveries, with a median estimate of 463,406. Tesla ultimately delivered 486,532 vehicles, exceeding the consensus by about 24,600 vehicles. The Model 3 and Model Y remained the company’s main volume drivers. Tesla delivered 478,237 Model 3/Y vehicles during the quarter, compared with just 8,295 deliveries across its other models. Production, meanwhile, reached 464,391 vehicles. Tesla also deployed 13.7 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage products during Q3. That figure was below the 15.9 GWh analyst consensus, highlighting that Tesla’s energy business remains an important part of the company’s broader growth story. The delivery beat is significant because analysts had entered the quarter expecting a decline. FactSet estimates cited by MarketWatch had pointed to roughly 461,000 vehicles, or a 7% year-over-year decline. Instead, Tesla limited the decline to about 2%. Tesla vs. BYD: The EV Gap Is Growing Despite Tesla’s better-than-expected quarter, its competition with BYD is becoming more intense. BYD sold 762,478 battery-electric passenger vehicles during Q3, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. That was up nearly 31% from a year earlier and 37% from Q2. As a result, BYD sold about 275,946 more battery-electric vehicles than Tesla during the quarter. The comparison needs some context. Tesla reports deliveries of its vehicles, while BYD sells both battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids under its broader new-energy vehicle category. BYD sold 1.32 million new-energy vehicles in Q3, including both types. Total NEV sales rose 18.8% year over year. BYD also recorded 463,561 new-energy vehicle sales in September alone, its strongest monthly result of 2026. Overseas passenger vehicle and pickup shipments jumped 153.9% year over year to 179,877 in September, Reuters reported. This international expansion could become increasingly important for the global EV market. It also shows how competition is moving beyond traditional EV strongholds as Chinese manufacturers expand into overseas markets. Sustainability Remains a Key Part of Tesla’s Story Tesla’s delivery numbers also matter from a sustainability perspective because more EV sales can accelerate the shift away from gasoline-powered vehicles. The International Energy Agency said global electric car sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, with EVs accounting for one in four new cars sold worldwide. China remained the largest EV market, accounting for six out of 10 electric cars sold globally. - Tesla says its products helped avoid 37 million metric tons of CO₂e emissions in its 2025 Impact Report. The company’s sustainability strategy also extends beyond vehicles to battery storage, solar energy, and its supply chain. The company also highlighted the emissions benefit of its electric vehicles over their operating lives. It estimates that one Tesla vehicle can avoid about 32 metric tons of CO₂ emissions over its lifetime compared with a comparable gasoline-powered vehicle. However, the actual benefit varies by factors such as electricity generation, vehicle efficiency, and driving patterns. However, EV growth does not eliminate the environmental impact of manufacturing. Batteries require minerals such as lithium, nickel, graphite, and other materials, while vehicle production and electricity generation also create emissions. That makes the growth of energy storage particularly relevant. Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of storage products in Q3, while the company-compiled analyst consensus had expected 15.9 GWh. Large-scale batteries can help integrate renewable power into electricity systems by storing electricity when supply is high and releasing it when demand rises. Can Tesla’s Q3 Delivery Beat Support Its Stock? Tesla stock entered October under pressure after a volatile year. Shares closed at $370.59 on October 2, although the latest delivery beat provided some relief. Investors are now looking beyond vehicle sales. Tesla’s valuation increasingly depends on its plans for robotaxis, AI, robotics and energy storage, while its automotive business remains critical to funding those investments. Tesla will report its full Q3 financial results on October 21. The earnings report should give investors a clearer view of vehicle margins, revenue, cash flow, and spending on its next-generation businesses. For now, the delivery beat strengthens Tesla’s near-term position. However, BYD’s growing lead in battery-electric vehicle sales highlights the competitive pressure facing Tesla as global EV adoption accelerates. The longer-term sustainability opportunity remains significant, but Tesla must balance EV growth with improving manufacturing efficiency, battery supply chains and the emissions impact of its operations.

artigo.texto: Springfield, IL-(Effingham Radio)- As more Illinois municipalities weigh moratoriums on data center construction, Gov. J.B. Pritzker is pressing state lawmakers to pass uniform regulations – despite light pushback from some who view the proposed rules as potentially misguided. The Illinois General Assembly failed to pass legislation to further regulate data centers statewide through the POWER Act before the end of the spring session on June 1. Pritzker said recently he’s not concerned about getting short-term solutions passed sooner than when state lawmakers return to Springfield. Pritzker noted there isn’t always transparency for communities when a data center project is being pitched in a locality. State Rep. Jeff Keicher, R-Sycamore, said data center non-disclosure agreements aren’t much different from privacy measures put in place when others buy a property, but there should be transparency after that. He also said there’s been benefits in his district including significant decreases to the property tax levy – though he acknowledged there are bad actors in the space. Lawmakers are set to return to Springfield for a six-day veto session from Nov. 17-19, and Dec. 1-3. The legislature is expected to return to bills that didn’t pass in May, such as the Power Act. artigo.texto: Demand for artificial intelligence data centers will continue to push shares of Vertiv higher, according to BMO Capital Markets. The firm initiated coverage of the stock on Sunday with an outperform rating and $329 price target, which implies roughly 30% upside from Friday's close. The company provinces digital infrastructure and hardware for data centers and other facilities, with data centers making up about 85% of its revenue, said analyst Daniel DiCicco. He called Vertiv a "premium data center play" that has already run up more than 900% in the last five years. Shares have pulled back from their peak in May and now offer an attractive entry point, he said. "Vertiv is well positioned as data centers are increasing in scale and intensity (more power to the rack) and demand for resilience and speed to deployment continues to increase," DiCicco wrote in a note to clients. VRT YTD mountain Vertiv year to date There are more than 4,700 data centers in the United States — and the number is growing . Some $6 billion was spent on land purchases in the U.S. for future data centers in the first half of 2026, according to commercial real estate firm Avison Young. That's a 79% increase from last year, the firm found. Vertiv's management has estimated that its $75 billion total addressable market is increasing 16% to 18% a year, with data centers growing 18% to 20% annually, DiCicco said. However, the company's long-term growth forecasts could be conservative, he noted. Plus, Vertiv has a full suite of offerings. The current rate for data center content is $3.25 to $3.75 per megawatt, but innovation, standardization, service growth and integrated systems can all push that higher, DiCicco pointed out. "VRT has positioned itself as one of the few providers capable of delivering a fully integrated power and thermal management solution across the entire data center," he said. Shares of Vertiv are up nearly 56% year to date. — CNBC's Tobias Burns contributed reporting.

artigo.texto: Silicon has long been the tantalizing prize of lithium-ion battery research. Theoretically, it can hold roughly ten times more lithium than the graphite that dominates today’s anodes, promising batteries that last dramatically longer on a single charge. Yet silicon has a fatal flaw that has kept it out of most commercial cells: when lithium floods into the material during charging, it swells by hundreds of percent, cracking particles, fracturing electrodes, and destroying the delicate interfaces that make a battery work. A team of researchers in Qinghai, China, now reports a practical route around this problem, combining a metal-processing technique borrowed from metallurgy with a carefully tuned dose of ordinary graphite. The study, published in the journal Ionics by Zhanshou Yang, Fa-Feng Xu, and colleagues at the Qinghai Institute of Salt Lakes of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, centers on a process called dealloying. In dealloying, one element is selectively dissolved out of an alloy, leaving behind a sponge-like scaffold of the remaining element riddled with pores at the nanometer scale. The technique has a pedigree in materials science, having been used to create nanoporous gold and other architectures, and it has increasingly attracted attention as a scalable way to fabricate porous electrode materials for rechargeable batteries. Applied to silicon-bearing alloys, it produces porous silicon structures whose internal voids act as built-in expansion chambers. That architectural trick addresses the core failure mode of silicon anodes. In a dense silicon particle, the volume change that accompanies lithiation generates enormous mechanical stress. Particles pulverize, fresh surfaces are repeatedly exposed to the electrolyte, and a thick, unstable solid electrolyte interphase layer grows and rebuilds with every cycle, consuming lithium and raising the cell’s internal resistance. A porous particle, by contrast, can expand into its own empty space. The pores absorb much of the strain, the particle’s outer dimensions stay comparatively stable, and the electrode’s conductive network and binder matrix survive far longer. Porosity alone, however, does not solve every problem. Silicon is a semiconductor with modest intrinsic conductivity, and the tortuous pathways through a porous structure can slow both electrons and lithium ions. The Qinghai team therefore wrapped the porous silicon in a carbon coating, producing a composite they designate Si@C. The carbon shell serves a dual role: it provides an electron-conducting highway that connects the silicon to the current collector, and it acts as a mechanical and chemical skin that stabilizes the electrode structure and limits parasitic reactions with the electrolyte. Carbon coatings of this kind have become a standard strategy in silicon anode research, but their effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of the underlying silicon architecture and on how the composite is formulated. The second half of the team’s strategy is arguably the more pragmatic one: blending the carbon-coated porous silicon with graphite. Graphite remains the workhorse anode of the lithium-ion industry, prized for its low cost, flat voltage profile, and remarkable structural stability over thousands of cycles. By mixing silicon with graphite, researchers can trade some of silicon’s enormous capacity for graphite’s reliability, while the graphite matrix helps buffer swelling and maintains electronic contact throughout the electrode. The ratio matters enormously. Too little silicon and the energy-density gain is marginal; too much and the electrode’s mechanical integrity collapses within a few hundred cycles. Yang and colleagues systematically optimized this ratio, testing different proportions of porous silicon to graphite before settling on a mass ratio of 1:2. At that composition, the composite delivered the best combination of capacity, stability, and rate performance in their experiments. The finding underscores a broader lesson in battery engineering: the performance of a composite electrode is not simply the weighted average of its components, but emerges from how those components interact mechanically and electrochemically during cycling. The graphite appears to function not merely as a diluent but as an active structural partner for the swelling silicon. The electrochemical results reported in the paper are striking. After 500 charge-discharge cycles, the optimized Si@C anode retained a reversible capacity of 688.5 milliampere-hours per gram, corresponding to a capacity retention of 63.6 percent. For context, conventional graphite anodes typically deliver around 350 to 370 milliampere-hours per gram, so even after substantial degradation the composite still stores nearly twice as much charge per unit mass. Equally important is the coulombic efficiency, which the team reports at 99.9 percent. This figure measures how many lithium ions that enter the anode during charging come back out during discharge, and values approaching 100 percent indicate that parasitic side reactions, which slowly poison a cell, have been largely suppressed. The authors state that these results surpass previously reported data for comparable silicon-based anodes in both cycling stability and rate performance, the latter describing the electrode’s ability to deliver capacity at high charging speeds. Rate capability is often the quiet casualty of silicon anode designs, because the same structural features that buffer swelling can impede ion transport. The combination of porous silicon, a conductive carbon coating, and a graphite matrix appears to keep those transport pathways open even as the electrode ages, allowing the material to sustain fast charging without catastrophic capacity loss. The work also carries a regional and industrial dimension. artigo.texto: A Posição de Byron Donalds sobre Data Centers Entra em Choque com a Reação dos Eleitores da Flórida Byron Donalds transformou os data centers em uma prioridade econômica, apesar de uma pesquisa na Flórida apontar 79% de oposição à construção de instalações de IA no estado. Esse conflito tornou a posição de Byron Donalds sobre data centers um teste decisivo para sua campanha ao governo. Donalds argumenta que a Flórida pode receber grandes campi de computação sem transferir seus custos de eletricidade e água para os moradores. Ele apoia o controle local e proteções ao consumidor, mas rejeita uma paralisação estadual de novos empreendimentos. Seu adversário democrata, David Jolly, escolheu uma linha divisória mais clara. Jolly apoia uma moratória, enquanto Donalds afirma que construções cuidadosamente reguladas devem continuar. Essa diferença oferece aos eleitores uma escolha incomumente direta sobre quem deve arcar com os custos da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. A disputa deixou de ser um debate abstrato sobre a tecnologia do futuro. Condados e cidades da Flórida já estão suspendendo projetos enquanto estudam a demanda por eletricidade, o consumo de água, o ruído, o uso do solo e o financiamento dos serviços públicos. Para Donalds, o problema político é maior do que defender uma única política. Ele precisa convencer moradores céticos de que as proteções funcionarão, enquanto interesses ligados a data centers investem pesadamente nas eleições do estado. A Posição de Byron Donalds sobre Data Centers Enfrenta uma Revolta Local Donalds avançou em direção a salvaguardas mais fortes, mas não se juntou à campanha crescente para interromper a construção em escala hyperscale. Em um evento de campanha em julho, em Clearwater, Donalds disse que era favorável a desacelerar o desenvolvimento quando as comunidades precisassem de proteções mais robustas. No entanto, ele se opôs a uma moratória estadual que suspenderia todos os projetos qualificados. Ele também prometeu respeitar as decisões dos governos locais. Se um condado ou cidade rejeitar um data center, disse Donalds, o estado não deveria forçar essa comunidade a aceitá-lo. Essa posição o coloca entre defensores da indústria e eleitores que exigem uma pausa abrangente. Ela reconhece a oposição local sem aceitar a política central proposta por Jolly e por vários governos de condados. A distinção importa porque os projetos em debate não são simples salas de servidores. Instalações hyperscale são campi de computação concebidos para operar enormes frotas de servidores para serviços em nuvem e inteligência artificial. Suas necessidades contínuas de eletricidade podem se equiparar às de grandes operações industriais. Os equipamentos de refrigeração também podem aumentar a pressão sobre os sistemas de água, dependendo do projeto e das condições operacionais da instalação. A Flórida já tem mais de 100 data centers em operação, segundo reportagens citadas por organizações de notícias estaduais. As disputas mais intensas envolvem locais hyperscale propostos, e não todos os prédios existentes que armazenam ou processam dados. Condados em todo o estado adotaram ou consideraram moratórias temporárias. Leon, Nassau, Pasco, Sarasota e outros governos locais avaliaram pausas enquanto autoridades desenvolvem regras de zoneamento e infraestrutura. O Condado de Nassau, por exemplo, publicou uma moratória temporária que abrange o recebimento, a análise e a aprovação de pedidos para data centers. Autoridades de Pasco também consideraram uma pausa de um ano devido a preocupações com infraestrutura e recursos naturais. Essas ações revelam um movimento político de baixo para cima. Autoridades locais estão respondendo a moradores que temem custos mais altos de serviços públicos, esgotamento dos recursos hídricos, ruído persistente de geradores e construções industriais perto de suas casas. As objeções também refletem incerteza. As comunidades muitas vezes não dispõem de informações públicas suficientes sobre a demanda final de energia de uma instalação proposta, seu método de refrigeração, geração de reserva, incentivos fiscais ou empregos de longo prazo. Essa lacuna de informação oferece aos defensores da moratória uma mensagem direta. Eles argumentam que os governos devem estabelecer as regras antes de aprovar empreendimentos que podem remodelar o planejamento dos serviços públicos por décadas. Donalds propõe uma sequência diferente. Ele quer proteções aplicáveis, tomada de decisão local e continuidade das construções onde as comunidades concederem aprovação. Sua posição pressupõe que a Flórida consegue avaliar os projetos individualmente. A oposição argumenta que decisões fragmentadas deixam os moradores expostos a riscos que ultrapassam as fronteiras dos condados e das concessionárias. Esse desacordo criou a tensão central da campanha. Donalds apresenta o desenvolvimento regulado como um caminho para o crescimento econômico, enquanto críticos veem a mesma política como um subsídio público evitável. A disputa se intensificou à medida que desenvolvedores de data centers e organizações aliadas ampliaram sua atividade política. Reportagens compiladas a partir de registros estaduais de campanha estimaram seus gastos na Flórida em mais de US$ 22 milhões durante o ciclo eleitoral. Mais de US$ 5 milhões teriam apoiado Donalds ou iniciativas alinhadas à sua candidatura. Esses gastos não comprovam que doadores controlem sua política, mas intensificam o escrutínio público sobre cada promessa que ele faz. Para os eleitores, portanto, a questão central não é se Donalds reconhece as preocupações locais. É se suas salvaguardas propostas conseguem superar as pressões financeiras e técnicas criadas por projetos de dimensão sem precedentes. As Contas de Energia se Tornaram a Promessa Mais Difícil da Campanha Donalds afirma que os data centers devem pagar seus próprios custos, mas a lei da Flórida não garante que as contas das famílias permanecerão inalteradas. artigo.texto: Large-scale battery storage, life extension for Lepreau and new nuclear feature in N.B. Power’s latest plan Ramp-up of wind, solar and gas combustion turbines also figure in utility's future N.B. Power’s latest plan is calling for large-scale battery storage in the province by 2035. The utility released a new integrated resource plan on Monday, replacing a 2023 version of the plan that was criticized as out-of-date during hearings on the proposed 500-megawatt Tantramar gas plant earlier this year. The plan is N.B. Power’s roadmap for making sure it can meet energy demand over the coming decades. It calls for 500 megawatts of battery storage in the province in the next decade and also for an extension of life for the Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station that would take it beyond its estimated expiry date in 2045. The plan also calls for big build-outs of wind and solar generation, an expansion of gas turbine generation, and the possible addition of new nuclear generation on the Point Lepreau site. 'Final throes' of analysis on battery proposals Brad Coady, the utility's chief commercial officer, said he’s “hopeful that we can get to a battery here in the short run.” N.B. Power issued requests for proposals for 50-megawatt battery storage projects in 2023 and in 2025, but the utility has yet to build a large-scale project. The batteries allow energy to be saved up and used during peak times. Coady said the utility is “in the final throes of doing the analysis at our latest call for proposals.” According to the new resource plan, the first 500 megawatts of battery storage development is cost-competitive with combustion turbine technology, such as the Tantramar gas and diesel plant. But Coady said the proposals he has seen in response to N.B. Power’s December 2025 request for proposals would require government subsidies. “Based on the bids and offers that were submitted, they're not great without government help,” said Coady. “So we're working very closely with our federal government to say, 'Can we make these cost effective solutions for New Brunswickers?'” Nuclear decision has public policy angle The 2023 version of the plan named small modular nuclear reactors as a critical part of N.B. Power’s future. The 2026 plan takes a more technology-agnostic approach, which “could include large nuclear or could include small modular nuclear,” said Coady. The plan explores the possibility of adding 750 megawatts of new nuclear capacity at the Point Lepreau site by 2039 or 2040. It also calls for either another new nuclear project or the refurbishment of Point Lepreau in 2045. Coady acknowledged the conversation over nuclear power would go beyond the scope of N.B. Power’s plan. “The decision for a future nuclear plant in New Brunswick is also going to have to be a pretty strong public policy angle,” said Coady. While the utility does not include a new nuclear plant in its “base case," said Coady, it does identify “the amount of utility it brings the power system.” Lepreau costs, especially when it's down Coady acknowledged that repairs to Lepreau have been driving increased debt with N.B. Power in recent years. But he noted those investments are expected to pay off for the next 20 years. “I'd argue the larger driver to our debt is actually when [Lepreau] doesn't produce the electricity that we depend on it for,” said Coady, “and we have to turn to more expensive sources.” In addition to proposed nuclear and battery capacity, the plans also calls for big increases to wind and solar generation and more gas turbine projects. “I often describe the power system much like an orchestra,” said Coady, “and we need all parts of that orchestra performing the tune or we're not going to sound very good at the end of the day.”

Commissioners meeting, where a proposed 15-data-center campus is expected to be the main topic of discussion. After it was announced at last month’s meeting that 15 permits were issued for the data center campus, the commissioner moved the meeting to the high school to accommodate the large crowd. artigo.texto: On Monday, 5 October, the European Commission published the price for the third quarter of 2026, which will be used to calculate the charges for importers whose products are subject to the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The cost of 1 metric tonne of CO₂-equivalent emissions stood at €82.32. This information was revealed in updates on the European Commission’s website. By way of comparison, the price in the first quarter was €75.36, and in the second quarter €75.28 per metric tonne of embedded emissions. In other words, over the course of three months, the cost of atmospheric pollution on the European market rose by almost 10 per cent. Link to the EU ETS To determine the average quarterly price for the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), the EU uses the average price of emission allowances within the EU ETS. In this way, the EU seeks to maintain a balance between what European producers and importers pay for emissions, in order to achieve what the EU considers to be a fair environmental burden on businesses. For 2026 — the first year in which the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) will be fully operational — prices will be set on a quarterly basis. From 2027 onwards, the European Commission will publish the price of these allowances on a weekly basis. The sale of certificates under the CBAM scheme will begin on the central platform in February 2027. As a reminder, emissions calculations under the CBAM are carried out either using standardised values or actual figures. The former are usually higher than the latter, but the latter must be verified by accredited verifiers. Ukraine, which is not yet a member of the EU, is entitled to apply to the national accreditation body of any EU country. The Ministry of Economy has agreed on such cooperation with the Swedish body SWEDAC. A company from Greece was the first in the world to receive accreditation for verifying CBAM emissions. Experts noted a curious approach — granting the accrediting body the authority to assess emissions across all industrial sectors covered by CBAM. Also in September, the European Parliament extended the scope of the emissions trading scheme to include derivatives. Due to the CBAM, Ukraine has already lost more than half of its exports of certain types of products, as industry, which is trying to operate under wartime conditions, is unable to cope with the additional financial pressure.

artigo.texto: Physical AI’s bottleneck shifts from what robots can do to whether factories trust them AI is moving beyond the data centers where models are trained and onto factory floors where machines must handle constant change. But traditional industrial robots work behind a cage, repeat a single task and were never designed for the complexities of today’s market. Manufacturers now want general-purpose machines that can switch tasks and improve as processes evolve. The hard part is deploying it, according to Adrien Gaidon (pictured, right), co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics Inc. “If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon said. “What we do is we do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.” Gaidon and John Mancuso (left), vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc., spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante at Fully Connected, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how cloud infrastructure, simulation and human assistance help robots learn and adapt on factory floors. (* Disclosure below.) Physical AI moves from data centers to the factory floor Walden spun out of Toyota Research Institute in January 2026 and launched with $300 million in July to put general-purpose robots to work in manufacturing. Its robots have worked full production shifts alongside people since May. They handle machine tending, parts kitting, and subassembly, tasks manufacturers had either failed to automate or never tried, Gaidon explained. “There’s half a million open positions for machinists in the U.S. because it’s a hard job and it requires skills,” Gaidon said. “But part of that job does not require the craft or the human creativity.” Getting a robot to that point takes serious compute long before it reaches a production line. CoreWeave, which has been betting on physical AI, also brings mechanical engineers and robotics experts into customer engagements alongside its infrastructure, Mancuso explained. “In the end, before a model is ever going to do something in the physical world, it’s going to have a tremendous amount of simulation that happens in the virtual world,” Mancuso said. “We’re providing the infrastructure.” But while simulation in data centers can make a robot useful, but it can’t make it perfect. Walden pairs autonomous robots with remote human assistants. The setup is comparable to automated looms of 120 years ago, when one person oversaw 40 machines, Gaidon noted. “Our robots are autonomous, but they know how to call for help,” Gaidon said. “They know when they need some assistance – and that assistance feeds the most valuable data to improve over time.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of Fully Connected: (* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Fully Connected 2026 event. artigo.texto: The electric vehicle revolution has a hidden Achilles’ heel, and it is not the batteries themselves but the fragile web of companies that mine, refine, and ship the minerals inside them. A new study published in iScience has mapped the entire firm-level supply network of the lithium-ion battery industry and stress-tested it against shortages of lithium, cobalt, and nickel. The results reveal a system that is far more vulnerable than its headline market size suggests, with losses cascading through unexpected pathways and recovery depending less on direct suppliers than on a handful of shared corporate hubs. The research team, led by Xuena Liu and Haibin Liu, constructed a multilayer supply chain network centered on nine of the world’s dominant battery manufacturers, including CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, SK Innovation, CALB, Samsung SDI, Gotion, and EVE Energy. Using the FactSet Revere database of interfirm supply relationships, supplemented by corporate disclosures and stock-market volatility data, they built a directed, weighted network spanning mineral extraction, intermediate materials, battery assembly, electric vehicle manufacturing, and recycling. The timing could hardly be more pressing: global electric vehicle battery demand reached 950 gigawatt-hours in 2024 and is projected to exceed 3 terawatt-hours by 2030, while the International Energy Agency expects electric vehicles and energy storage to account for more than 90 percent of future lithium demand. The network’s anatomy alone tells a striking story. All nine manufacturer-centered networks follow power-law degree distributions, meaning a few hub firms dominate connectivity while most firms maintain only a handful of relationships. The commodity trader Glencore, the Australian lithium producer Pilbara Minerals, and the Chinese materials firm CNGR each maintain business relationships with seven to nine core battery makers, forming what the authors call cross-layer super-hubs. Meanwhile, most shared nodes connect to only two manufacturers. The networks led by Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution are strongly correlated with each other and with Panasonic’s, implying that a shock at a shared supplier could transmit simultaneous damage across multiple corporate ecosystems. By contrast, the SK Innovation- and Gotion-led networks show slightly negative correlations, hinting at potential substitutability at certain supply nodes. When the researchers simulated shortages of increasing intensity, from 10 percent to a complete cutoff of supply, lithium emerged as the most damaging mineral by a clear margin, with network losses ranking lithium above cobalt above nickel under every scenario. This asymmetry reflects chemistry as much as geology. Lithium is an indispensable element in every lithium-ion battery, whereas cobalt is progressively being engineered out of newer cathode designs, and nickel benefits from abundant resources and diversified supply. At a shortage intensity of 0.9, the CATL-dominated network suffered losses of 1171.42 under lithium scarcity, compared with 909.05 for cobalt and 918.45 for nickel. The BYD-led network fared worst of all under lithium stress, reaching 2587.49, a consequence of its enormous lithium iron phosphate production volumes and vertically integrated business model. Manufacturer-level losses varied dramatically, defying any simple ranking of corporate might. CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, recorded the highest losses across all three minerals, ranging from roughly 130 to 160 under lithium shortages, a pattern the authors attribute to its simultaneous operation of both LFP and high-nickel NMC pathways, which broadens its mineral exposure and concentrates its supplier base. SK Innovation’s network proved exceptionally vulnerable to nickel because its product portfolio is dominated by high-nickel NCM811 cells, while EVE Energy’s cobalt-containing cathode materials and stringent certification requirements concentrated its dependence on upstream refining hubs. Panasonic, by contrast, recorded the lowest losses and responded only weakly to changes in shortage intensity, reflecting its comparatively low structural exposure. Tracing exactly where the damage came from produced some of the study’s most actionable findings. Under cobalt shortages, a single firm, Glencore, accounted for between 73.43 and 92.75 percent of CATL’s attributed losses, a near-single-source structure in which one disruption could rapidly amplify risk downstream. Nickel losses for CATL were dominated by Glencore and the Indonesian producer Trimegah Bangun Persada, the latter reflecting the localized supply concentration fostered by Indonesia’s nickel ore export ban. Lithium losses were far more dispersed, spread across Tianqi Lithium, Ganfeng Lithium, Yahua, and Albemarle. Path analysis of a total Tianqi Lithium shortage showed that two pathways, a direct cross-chain link to BYD and a long cascade through the midstream materials firm BTR, together accounted for roughly 70 percent of BYD’s total impact, with the cathode makers Hunan Yuneng and Ronbay emerging as the most frequently traversed intermediary nodes. Perhaps the most surprising result concerns how the industry recovers. The researchers decomposed recovery into three mechanisms: direct restoration through existing supply relationships, indirect recovery through shared nodes that connect multiple manufacturer networks, and recovery through newly established supply links. Indirect recovery dominated overwhelmingly, contributing 70 to 74 percent of total recovery, followed by new links at 15 to 18 percent, with direct recovery contributing a mere 10 to 12 percent. In other words, when a mineral shortage strikes, battery makers do not primarily heal through their own contracted suppliers; they heal through the network’s hidden cross-connections, as shared suppliers reallocate resources across tiers. artigo.texto: Hawaii County considers curbing AI data centers HILO — Two Hawaii County commissions are considering a bill aimed at prohibiting artificial intelligence data centers on the Big Island through the creation of a new definition in the county code. The Windward Planning Commission discussed the bill at its meeting on Thursday after previously deferring on Sept. 3. Introduced by Hamakua Councilperson Heather Kimball, Bill 170 distinguishes between “data processing facilities” and “data centers.” Data processing facilities are defined as places where records and other digital information are stored and are currently a permitted use under the county code in certain zoning districts, while data centers refer to the large-scale facilities being built to house the infrastructure needed to power AI. These data centers, which use significant amounts of energy, water and other resources, have drawn concern and pushback from communities across the country where they have been built or proposed. The Leeward Planning Commission will also evaluate the bill and make a recommendation to the Council. The Leeward commission’s next meeting is scheduled for Oct. 15. Kimball told the Hawaii Tribune-Herald that her goal in introducing the bill was to close a potential loophole that could allow such centers to be constructed on the island. “I think we have to preemptively prepare for an interest in developing data centers in Hawaii,” she said. “The purpose of this bill is very simple, very straightforward, from the standpoint that it defines what data centers are, and therefore, because it defines them and then does not put them anywhere in Chapter 25 (of the county code) as a permitted use, they become prohibited through that absence.” The bill defines a data center as “a facility used for the industrial-scale operation of computer systems and associated equipment for the processing, computing, transmission, or dissemination of digital data, and that requires supporting infrastructure beyond that typically accessory or incidental to office, commercial, or public institutional uses.” Kimball said this definition came from the National Association of Counties. While commissioners expressed support for the intent of the bill at the Thursday’s meeting, they voted 5-1 to send an unfavorable recommendation to the County Council, due primarily to concerns that the definition was not specific enough. “They need to come up with something better that involves expertise, opinions, and it needs to be done in a way that’s separated and in a clean way so that there’s no loopholes left,” said Commissioner JoNelle Fukushima. “That’s the biggest issue here, is that if we do this too quickly, and we don’t take our time in understanding what the definition is, we may leave with unintended consequences, pathways to them being able to come in and do the data centers.” Windward Planning Commission Vice Chair Chantel Perrin, who was the sole vote in favor of the bill, said there would be future opportunities for additions and clarifications to be made to the bill once it returns to Council. She suggested that instead of submitting an unfavorable recommendation for Bill 170, the commission instead indicate support for the intent of the bill and submit a list of the changes they would like to see made to the definition. “Bill 170 needs to happen. It needs a definition,” she said. “Nonetheless, we may not agree with what’s being written, but it doesn’t mean it’s done there. We can tell them, that’s why we can suggest recommendations as to how we want it worded.” Several members of the public who provided testimony during the meeting, expressed strong opposition to data centers and support for the bill’s goal, but also asked for additional, more specific language to be included. “Bill 170’s intent is what our hopes and dreams are as a community,” said Hilo resident Cristina Holt. “However, the only thing that we are doing with Bill 170 is creating a definition. As I’m sure you guys have seen in your own research and the testimony that has come your way, there’s a lot of confusion about what we’re even talking about, so, setting a clear definition for what we are talking about is literally the very first step.” There was also confusion surrounding recommendations submitted by the county Planning Department in response to the bill which included potential permitting regulations, which Kimball and Deputy County Corporation Counsel Jean Campbell noted are beyond the scope of this bill and would acquire additional legislation. “(The Council) would not be able to amend this particular bill in the ways that are being recommended,” Campbell said. “However, they have other options. They could withdraw this bill and introduce one that’s broader. They could pass this bill and then introduce something else that would address your recommendations.”

artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil: quem vai construir, operar e crescer com eles? Em artigo à CNN Infra, Léo Oliveira explica como infraestrutura de data centers deve transformar o investimento em capacidade local no país A chegada de um data center deve levar quem lidera empresas e políticas de desenvolvimento a pensar em como transformar esse investimento em oportunidades para as pessoas e os negócios da região. Com a sanção do Redata, o Brasil reforça sua aposta na atração de data centers. Energia, conectividade e equipamentos estão no centro dessa agenda, mas a preparação das regiões para construir, operar e prestar serviços a esses empreendimentos também precisa fazer parte do planejamento. Quem vai transformar o investimento em capacidade local? Como CEO de uma plataforma de IA, Executivo de RH e Líder, vejo três prioridades. A primeira é preparar pessoas antes da inauguração, considerando que construção, operação e manutenção exigem competências diferentes. O plano de formação deve acompanhar o cronograma e prever os profissionais necessários na obra, na entrada em operação e nos anos seguintes. É preciso um planejamento rigoroso para estabelecer vagas temporárias, permanentes e explicar quais caminhos de qualificação permitem transitar entre essas etapas. Empresas, escolas técnicas e universidades devem organizar essa preparação a partir das demandas concretas. As empresas devem sinalizar as competências e os prazos para que as instituições de ensino avaliem como preparar os profissionais com antecedência. Quem já trabalha também precisa encontrar caminhos para ampliar sua qualificação através de cursos, formações e trocas para se manter relevante. Que oportunidade terá o jovem que mora perto desse investimento? Ele precisa saber quais profissões serão necessárias e encontrar condições para conciliar formação, deslocamento e renda. Os programas devem considerar essas questões para que as pessoas consigam frequentar o curso, concluir os estudos e disputar uma vaga. A segunda prioridade é criar condições para que empresas brasileiras participem da cadeia de fornecedores desses projetos. Os empreendedores precisam informar quais serviços pretendem contratar na região e os requisitos técnicos e de segurança que serão exigidos, permitindo que empresas locais se preparem para disputar contratos. Pense em uma empresa regional de manutenção elétrica interessada em atender um data center. Ela precisará conhecer as exigências da operação, qualificar profissionais e demonstrar que consegue cumprir os padrões do contratante. Um programa de desenvolvimento de fornecedores pode apoiar essa preparação, com critérios claros e sem garantia de contratação. Essa conexão pode ampliar a competência de empresas locais e abrir mercados para seus serviços. Cabe aproximar universidades e empreendimentos para pesquisar soluções para a operação. O desenvolvimento que buscamos inclui conhecimento que permaneça na região e possa ser utilizado em outros negócios. A terceira prioridade é trazer o RH e a liderança para o planejamento desde o início. Se a formação necessária leva mais tempo que o previsto para contratar, o projeto precisa reconhecer esse descompasso. Quem vai formar os gestores, organizar o trabalho e acompanhar os resultados? Essas decisões precisam estar presentes quando os investimentos e os prazos são definidos. O RH pode contribuir com o diagnóstico de competências, a formação, os caminhos de carreira e se antecipar conhecendo o negócio. As lideranças precisam traduzir a estratégia em responsabilidades, recursos e condições de execução. Essa construção exige muita articulação entre operação, finanças e compras, instituições de ensino técnico e superior, governos, lideranças locais e movimentos sociais. A articulação precisa ter responsáveis, prazos e compromissos claros. Governos podem coordenar ações de qualificação e acesso em parceria com instituições de ensino técnico e superior. Lideranças locais e movimentos sociais ajudam a identificar barreiras de transporte, renda e informação, enquanto as empresas devem explicitar suas demandas e os critérios de seleção. Essa pode ser uma chance de ampliar o emprego e desenvolver essas regiões, abrindo caminhos para as profissões do futuro. O legado que devemos buscar inclui profissionais mais preparados e empresas locais mais capazes de inovar. Quando os data centers estiverem operando, o que os brasileiros estarão mais preparados para fazer, criar e liderar? Léo Oliveira é fundador e CEO da Humanos & Inteligência Artificial*

artigo.texto: Memphis mayor defends data center benefits ahead of moratorium vote Leaders speak ahead of highly anticipated vote MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Memphis Mayor Paul Young said his goal is to make the city better by accommodating everyone as data centers continue to be an issue for some Memphians and surrounding cities. The comment comes a day before a critical vote on a data center moratorium. “We must do it in a way where our people are protected; I think that’s really important. They need to have confidence they’re protected,” Young said. Addressing community concerns “That’s part of governance; governance is finding a way to address the potential negatives and harms that could be brought to the community and find a way to maximize the potential benefit to the community,” Young said. Groups like Memphis Community Against Pollution (MCAP) have laid out what the negatives are: - Air pollution - Nearby residents dealing with noise complaints - Effects on the water supply - Rising energy prices Tax revenue from data centers Young said significant tax dollars are generated by projects like data centers. He said Memphis is the only city with an ordinance requiring data centers to pay full taxes, with 25% of those taxes going back to the community most adjacent to them. Young said SpaceXAI alone generated $54 million between the city and county this year. He gave a comparison to help people understand the scale: “That’s the equivalent of 12,400 units of housing built in our city at $300,000 each,” Young said. The initial vote was supposed to happen September 15, but Councilman JB Smiley Jr., the ordinance’s leading sponsor, says the council wanted to factor in more community concerns. “One of the things that I heard consistently from the community is, ‘What about us? You can create laws, but you’re not talking to us,’” Councilman Smiley told Action News 5. While the council is speaking to various experts, Sarah Houston, executive director of Protect Our Aquifer, says they should also prioritize lifting up the voices of local organizations on concerns about the data centers, since they’re the ones on the ground. “There’s been a lot of confusion and a lot of listening to people with fancy titles,” says Houson. “The reality is there’s a lot of expertise in the Memphis community that city council members really need to lean on and really need to listen to.” Smiley says he believes the council likely has six votes for the moratorium and four against it, leaving the remaining three councilmembers to decide its fate. He says the point of a temporary moratorium is not necessarily to shut the door on the industry, but to make sure the city understands what it’s getting into before moving forward. “What I don’t want to happen is we allow 20, 30 more data centers to come in and in a year’s time, data centers stop being the hot thing and we have 30 empty buildings,” says Smiley. The final, amended ordinance that will be presented before Memphis City Council on Tuesday can be viewed within the regular meeting agenda documents here, beginning on page 73. artigo.texto: Escobar: Fort Bliss data center to shrink, shift site and use brackish water EL PASO, Texas (KFOX14/CBS4) — Changes to a planned data center at Fort Bliss are being touted as progress by U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, who said the Army and the Carlyle Group appear to be responding to community concerns even as key issues remain unresolved. On Monday, Escobar released a statement describing what she called “positive developments” about the project, including a smaller footprint, the use of brackish water and a move away from residential areas. She said the facility will still be located close to neighborhoods and that she will continue pushing for a different location. Escobar also said she remains concerned the data center will rely on gas-generated power. RECOMMENDED: Proposed Fort Bliss data center could use more power than all of El Paso Below is Escobar's full statement: "Today, the Army and Carlyle Group held a meeting of El Paso community stakeholders to discuss the latest updates on the Fort Bliss data center. "Since March, when my team and I first learned of this project, we have asked that the public and local representatives be kept in the loop and be allowed to voice their concerns and ask questions. I’m grateful to the Army and Carlyle for their continued engagement. "I’ve consistently had a number of requests, including that they: - Move the data center far away from any neighborhood; - Preserve our water; - Use renewable energy for the electrical generation; - Be transparent and accountable. "Today we learned that the location of the data center has indeed been moved, but it is still too close to residential areas. Close proximity to homes is not acceptable, and I will continue to advocate for a different location. "We also learned that their water use will likely be of brackish water that will be sent to the Kay Bailey Hutchison Plant for desalination, which I see as a positive development. And while the scale of the data center has also been reduced, they are still on track to utilize gas generation for their power needs. The gas generation for power remains an additional serious concern. We must protect our community’s air quality, and I will continue to push for the use of renewable energy. "As more information becomes available, my team and I will continue to keep the community updated." artigo.texto: Wartsila Launches Valo Joint Venture with RCT Solutions for Energy Storage According to ESS News, Finnish technology group Wartsila has shifted its worldwide energy storage operations into Valo, a joint venture it co-owns on an equal basis with German engineering firm RCT Solutions. The company anticipates that the new entity will post losses during 2026 before returning to profitability near the close of 2027. Valo, characterized as a utility-scale battery energy storage system integrator encompassing Wartsila's Energy Storage operations, commenced on Oct. 1 following the completion of the joint venture between the two owners. Valo starts with over 20 GWh spanning more than 130 projects globally. Peter Fath, who formerly served as chief executive of RCT Solutions, heads the new venture as chief executive, while Luke Witmer holds the position of chief technology officer. Wartsila disclosed the transaction on June 15, stating it would hand over net assets amounting to under 5% of its total net assets. Finalization hinged on regulatory clearances and securing a financing package. Additional investors could enter at a later stage, possibly reducing the stakes of the two founding shareholders, and the joint venture will gain from project guarantees Wartsila has already provided on ongoing projects, according to the Helsinki-based group. Wartsila further indicated that the joint venture would operate at a loss in 2026 owing to weak recent order intake and transformation expenses, primarily a write-down of capitalized research and development. It projected the effect on its full-year 2026 operating result at EUR40 million to EUR50 million, or $45.2 million, contingent on when closing occurs. The company expressed expectations that the joint venture would deliver positive results near the end of 2027, and its Oct. 1 closing release restated the anticipated 2026 loss. Wartsila noted that the energy storage business represented its smallest segment, employing roughly 480 people. It recorded net sales of EUR694 million in 2025 with an operating margin of 3.3%, finishing the year with an order book valued at EUR719 million. Wartsila stated that RCT Solutions, established in 2012, has overseen the engineering and creation of multiple battery and solar manufacturing plants across the globe, and that one RCT entity has served as a crucial supplier to Wartsila Energy Storage for several years. It added that RCT also offers a chance for vertical integration via an existing integrated battery energy storage system manufacturing effort in the United States in the near term. Neither company has disclosed the project's name. Wartsila initiated a strategic review of the business in October 2023 and concluded it in March 2025 by separating storage into a distinct reporting segment with its own financial objectives. Following the joint venture agreement, it reclassified the unit as discontinued operations, and it will now report its stake as a share of result in associated companies. At the time it began the review, Wartsila reported net sales of EUR983 million for the business on a 12-month rolling basis through the end of the third quarter of 2023. artigo.texto: One third of the way there: is the CATL dream lost in translation? The Orbán government had expected the transition to electric mobility to happen more quickly, but the revolution in the automotive industry was delayed. The Hungarian economy was intended to serve as a link between German premium manufacturers and Asian suppliers of key components. To that end, an extremely large amount of funding was made available — at CATL in Debrecen, roughly one in every seven forints of the investment was subsidised — in the hope of achieving economic growth, technology transfer, and job creation. CATL, the global market leader in battery technology, began producing modules at the Debrecen site in 2024, while the battery plant in the immediate vicinity of the BMW New Class factory was still under construction. Since then, BMW has been assembling the cells delivered by its partner into battery packs at its own plant, as has Mercedes at its separate battery final assembly facility in Kecskemét. CATL plant director Qin Lang, speaking during a factory tour ahead of the weekend, said that more than 500,000 modules had been built in just under two years across three production lines in the temporary facility. According to him, the company’s revenues have since totalled 100 billion forints. Both NCM and LFP batteries are manufactured in Debrecen. Nickel technology delivers greater range thanks to its higher energy density, while batteries made from lithium iron phosphate are extremely long-lasting and free of expensive raw materials such as cobalt. On 22 September, a trial run for battery cell production began at the new plant, initially on two production lines. Two further production lines are still being prepared technically for the start of operations. The battery cell plant’s capacity of 40 GWh has long been fully committed by its clients. The original site plan envisaged a total capacity of 100 GWh across three construction phases, for which CATL intended to invest a total of 7.5 billion euros. With the Tisza government taking office, however, the plant expansion appears to be under threat, as the environmental lobby is said to have strong backing within the new political movement. This would freeze the large Chinese investment at one third of its originally planned volume, amounting to a maximum of 4,000 jobs. CATL has not yet abandoned all hope of reaching an agreement with the government on the terms for the plant expansion — an expansion that involves a total of 9,000 jobs, which by 2030 would be filled to around 90% by domestic workers. Artificial intelligence was used for the translation of parts of the original German text.

artigo.texto: Supercapacitors charge in seconds and batteries store vast amounts of energy, but no single device has ever managed to do both at once. A team of researchers from India, China, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Thailand now reports a promising step toward closing that gap. In a study published in the Journal of Materials Science, the group synthesized petal-like nanostructures of bismuth sulfide (Bi2S3) and demonstrated that these flower-shaped particles can serve as the workhorse positive electrode in a supercapattery, an emerging hybrid device that combines the battery-like ability to store large amounts of charge with the supercapacitor-like ability to deliver it rapidly. The work stands out not only for its impressive performance numbers but also for the depth of its explanation: the team paired meticulous electrochemical experiments with density functional theory (DFT) simulations to reveal, atom by atom, why the device works best in one particular electrolyte. The choice of material is deliberate. Bismuth sulfide is an earth-abundant, environmentally benign semiconductor that has attracted growing attention as an electrode material for energy storage. Its layered orthorhombic crystal structure, built from covalently bonded Bi2S3 ribbons held together by weaker van der Waals forces, offers open channels along which ions can migrate, making it naturally suited to intercalation-based charge storage. Previous studies have produced Bi2S3 in the form of nanorods, nanowires, nanoflowers and nanoflakes using solvothermal, chemical bath and spray methods, and several groups have reported respectable supercapacitor performance from composites that pair the sulfide with graphene, carbon nitride or nickel foam. What has been missing, the authors argue, is a systematic understanding of how the electrolyte itself, not just the material, controls the charge storage process. To build their electrode material, the researchers turned to hydrothermal synthesis, a technique that grows crystals from aqueous precursors inside a sealed, heated vessel. Under the right combination of temperature, time and precursor chemistry, the reaction self-assembles Bi2S3 into petal-like nanopetals, which the team abbreviates BSNP. This flower-like architecture is more than aesthetic. The petals create a high surface-area scaffold with abundant exposed active sites, short diffusion pathways for ions and open voids that accommodate the volume changes that occur as charge is stored and released. Such morphological engineering is a central strategy in modern electrode design, because electrochemical reactions happen only at surfaces and interfaces; the more accessible surface a material presents to the electrolyte, the more charge it can store and the faster it can deliver it. The heart of the experiment is a comparison across three alkaline electrolytes: 2 M solutions of lithium hydroxide (LiOH), sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and potassium hydroxide (KOH). All three contain the same charge-carrying hydroxide ion, but they differ in the size and hydration behavior of their cations, and those differences ripple through every aspect of electrode kinetics. When the team tested BSNP as the positive electrode in each solution, the results were striking. In 2 M KOH, the nanopetals delivered a gravimetric capacity of 797.9 coulombs per gram at a scan rate of 1 millivolt per second, outperforming the same material in LiOH and NaOH. In other words, simply swapping the electrolyte cation from lithium or sodium to potassium unlocked a substantially larger fraction of the material’s theoretical storage capability. Why would potassium ions give bismuth sulfide an edge? The answer, the researchers show, lies in the electronic and ionic interplay at the material’s surface. Using DFT calculations, they probed how hydroxide species interact with the Bi2S3 lattice under each electrolyte condition. Orbital hybridization analysis revealed favorable overlap between the electronic states of the surface and the adsorbed species in the KOH case, while Bader charge analysis quantified the electron transfer between them. Charge density difference maps and electron localization function analysis visualized where electrons accumulate and deplete during adsorption, painting a consistent picture: the potassium-containing environment promotes stronger, more favorable electronic coupling at the Bi2S3 surface, which lowers the energetic barriers for the redox reactions that store charge. This computational evidence aligns neatly with the electrochemical data, giving the performance claims a mechanistic foundation rather than leaving them as empirical observations. Kinetic analysis added another layer of insight. Applying Dunn’s method, a widely used technique that separates the capacitive (surface-controlled) and diffusion-controlled contributions to charge storage from cyclic voltammetry data measured at different scan rates, the team confirmed that diffusion-dominated processes govern the behavior of the BSNP electrode. That finding matters because it places the material firmly in the battery-type category rather than the purely capacitive one. Battery-type electrodes store charge through faradaic reactions, in which ions insert into the crystal lattice and electrons transfer to or from the metal centers, allowing much more charge to be packed per gram than in the electrostatic double-layer storage that characterizes carbon-based supercapacitor electrodes. It is precisely this battery-like positive electrode, paired with a capacitive negative electrode, that defines the supercapattery architecture. To prove the concept at the device level, the researchers assembled an asymmetric supercapacitor (ASC) in which the BSNP nanopetals served as the positive electrode and activated carbon, a classic high-surface-area capacitive material, served as the negative electrode. artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – Indonesia is pushing ASEAN to make its emerging carbon pricing systems more compatible as countries across the region develop different national approaches amid growing pressure from carbon-related trade measures and international markets. Mari Elka Pangestu, Indonesia’s Special Envoy for International Trade and Multilateral Cooperation and Co-Chair of the Green Investment Principles (GIP) ASEAN, said ASEAN countries were no longer debating whether carbon pricing was needed, but how their systems could work together. “We are no longer now talking about whether we need carbon pricing. We know we do need it, but we need to figure out how we should be doing it, whether as each country or as ASEAN as a region,” Mari said at the GIP ASEAN research dissemination of The Emerging Carbon Pricing Landscape in Southeast Asia in Jakarta on Monday (Oct. 5, 2026). She said ASEAN countries had made progress in developing carbon pricing systems over the past decade, with each country pursuing a different model based on its own circumstances. Singapore has established a carbon tax and recently raised the price to US$45, while Indonesia and Vietnam are developing emissions trading systems. Thailand has focused on international cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, while Malaysia is moving from voluntary toward compliance carbon markets. Indonesia is also moving to implement sectoral regulations under Presidential Regulation No. 110/2025 on carbon economic value. Mari said the country had made progress on its carbon registry and forestry regulations, while energy-sector regulations were also being prepared. She identified forestry and energy as two key sectors for Indonesia’s carbon market, with further sectoral regulations expected for agriculture, marine and fisheries, and industry. Market Access Mari said differences in national systems were natural given the varying economic conditions of ASEAN countries. However, developing carbon markets in isolation could create risks if rules become disconnected, data are misaligned and carbon prices differ significantly. “This learning by doing, of course, comes with risks if we are developing our systems in isolation with disconnected rules, misaligned data, and very different price levels,” she said. Such fragmentation could make it harder for countries to trade carbon assets, attract investment and gain recognition from international partners, she added. The pressure to improve compatibility is also coming from international trade measures, including the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), as well as green standards and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Mari said businesses, particularly exporters, were increasingly aware of the need for carbon pricing as they face growing climate-related requirements in international trade. “Being competitive today means sustainability. You have to be part of a sustainable supply chain,” she said. She said the EU CBAM and similar measures being developed elsewhere could increasingly affect how carbon pricing is linked to international trade. “If we do not price our own carbon, others will price it for us, and the revenue will go to their budgets, not ours,” Mari said. GIP ASEAN Study The research dissemination was organized by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), which has served as the secretariat of GIP ASEAN since its inception in 2023. The GIP ASEAN chapter seeks to connect research and policy recommendations with financial institutions, governments, investors and other stakeholders to support Southeast Asia’s green transition. Yose Rizal Damuri, Executive Director of CSIS, said the research presented at the event examined carbon pricing in Southeast Asia and its implications for the region. Carbon pricing, he said, should not be viewed solely as a mechanism for carbon markets, but also as a way to translate sustainability principles into economic activities, including investment and emissions reductions. “When we’re talking about carbon pricing, we have to look at also on how to translate this carbon pricing into real investment and also to emission reductions, to internalize the carbon price into our economic activities,” he said. The study also highlighted the importance of ASEAN cooperation while recognizing differences in economic structures and levels of readiness among member states. Yose said regional cooperation should focus not on creating a uniform carbon pricing mechanism, but on reducing uncertainty and improving interoperability among national systems. “It will reduce uncertainty for business and investors while also strengthening their confidence in carbon market and also in internalizing the carbon price into their decision,” he said. ***
