artigo.texto: How much are AI data centers adding to your electricity bill? Americans are worried AI data centers will raise their electricity bills. Congress has come up with a plan to protect ratepayers, but there's no easy way to find out what AI is costing them. ELISSA NADWORNY, HOST: The construction of huge, new AI data centers has become a political lightning rod. Communities near proposed projects are raising questions about their impact, including on electricity costs. One big question is who will end up paying for expensive new infrastructure needed to power these massive facilities. NPR's Scott Neuman has been looking into that question, and he joins me now. Hi, Scott. SCOTT NEUMAN, BYLINE: Hi, Elissa. NADWORNY: So, Scott, most of us know by now that these hyperscale AI centers require a lot of power and upgrades to the electrical grid. Who is paying for all that? NEUMAN: Well, the simple answer is everybody who buys electricity. That means people who are building and using these data centers for sure, but also local businesses and homeowners and renters, even if they don't think they're using AI. During my reporting this past week, I spoke with Ari Peskoe. He's the director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative. He says that, ultimately, everyone is shouldering the burden for the billions of dollars in new upgrades to the electrical grid. ARI PESKOE: Everyone pays those costs. They're spread across the region to every business and resident that has an electricity meter. NEUMAN: Now, in many cases, the pace and scale of the demand is coming at - it's really breakneck speed, and that makes all of this unpredictable. The demand for new transmission lines, substations and other infrastructure is ramping up faster than the utilities can keep up in many cases. And that creates an enormous planning challenge. But, you know, Peskoe brings up another interesting point. He says that the speed that all of this is happening can actually drive up the cost of these improvements. Components, things like transformers, are in short supply, and everybody wants them and wants them now. So there's a scarcity, and that makes everything more expensive. NADWORNY: OK, so we're all paying for the AI upgrades, but how are those costs divided up? NEUMAN: That's a really tough question to answer. Even if an AI data center is - in your area is the reason for these improvements, everyone is going to be getting the use of them. But Peskoe says no one has really figured out how to divvy up the costs in an equitable way. PESKOE: There's no agreement as to what infrastructure is for a data center versus for the public. That itself is a disputed point. NEUMAN: So in 2024, Maryland's Office of People's Counsel, an independent state consumer agency, forecast that new costs due to data centers would run residents as much as $216 a year. But the rapid buildout of these data centers means there's a lot of uncertainty. NADWORNY: Do individual customers get any benefit from all this new grid infrastructure? NEUMAN: Yeah, so the fact that everyone gets the use of these improvements to the grid means everyone gets the benefits too. Lucy Qiu is a professor at the University of Maryland who is looking into all of this. She says that in many places, the upgrades are long overdue. They'll be needed for AI data centers, but they'll also be needed for things like meeting the charging capacity for electric vehicles. LUCY QIU: On the positive side, you can accelerate the upgrade of the grid infrastructure. NEUMAN: Qiu says studies show that people who live near data centers where the grid has been more - made more robust to accommodate them, those residential rate payers have fewer power outages during extreme weather events. NADWORNY: All right, so some positive side too, thank you. That was NPR's Scott Neuman. NEUMAN: Thank you. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. artigo.texto: O Histórico de Jon Husted com Data Centers Transforma um Ativo de IA em um Passivo para as Eleições de Meio de Mandato O histórico de Jon Husted com data centers tornou-se um passivo, apesar de sua tentativa de proteger as famílias de Ohio dos custos de infraestrutura antes das eleições de meio de mandato de novembro. O senador republicano já promoveu os data centers como motores de investimento, emprego e força tecnológica americana. Sua campanha atual agora enfatiza responsabilização, controle local e proteção contra contas de eletricidade mais altas. Essa mudança reflete uma reversão política mais ampla. A Newsweek identificou 16 candidatos em disputas acirradas cujos históricos favoráveis a data centers agora colidem com a crescente resistência dos eleitores. A discussão já não se limita a saber se os Estados Unidos precisam de mais capacidade computacional. Agora, ela se concentra em quem paga pela eletricidade, pelos equipamentos de transmissão, pela água, pelos terrenos e pelos incentivos fiscais que sustentam essa capacidade. Husted enfrenta o ex-senador democrata Sherrod Brown em uma disputa que pode influenciar o controle do Senado. Brown usou o histórico anterior de Husted em desenvolvimento econômico para retratá-lo como excessivamente próximo dos interesses dos data centers. Outros candidatos enfrentam versões do mesmo problema. Instalações antes apresentadas como vitórias econômicas quase automáticas tornaram-se símbolos visíveis dos custos locais da IA. O Histórico de Jon Husted com Data Centers Encontra um Eleitorado Transformado O valor político de apoiar data centers se inverteu mais rápido do que muitos candidatos conseguiram reescrever seus históricos. Husted passou seis anos como vice-governador de Ohio antes de ingressar no Senado em 2025. Nesse período, Ohio buscou ativamente grandes instalações de tecnologia com incentivos fiscais e apoio ao desenvolvimento. Essas políticas antes se encaixavam em uma mensagem econômica familiar. Os data centers representavam investimento privado, empregos na construção, ampliação da base tributária e uma posição mais forte na economia da tecnologia. Essa mensagem perdeu força à medida que os projetos se multiplicaram. Os moradores associam cada vez mais as novas instalações à demanda por eletricidade, à construção de infraestrutura de serviços públicos, ao uso de água, ao desenvolvimento de terrenos industriais, ao ruído e ao número limitado de empregos permanentes. A análise da Newsweek de 4 de outubro identificou 16 candidatos em disputas competitivas com históricos favoráveis ao desenvolvimento de data centers. A conclusão insere Husted em um grupo mais amplo, em vez de tratar Ohio como uma disputa de campanha isolada. O risco exato varia conforme o distrito. Alguns candidatos apoiaram isenções fiscais, enquanto outros promoveram projetos específicos ou se opuseram a restrições ao desenvolvimento. Ainda assim, a vulnerabilidade política segue um padrão comum. A promessa anterior de um candidato de benefícios públicos amplos agora enfrenta questionamentos sobre ganhos privados concentrados e custos distribuídos entre as famílias. O histórico de Husted torna essa tensão particularmente direta. Ohio se tornou um mercado relevante de data centers enquanto ele desempenhava um papel central na estratégia de desenvolvimento econômico do estado. A Newsweek informou que a isenção de imposto sobre vendas para data centers em Ohio custou ao estado quase US$ 1,6 bilhão em receita não arrecadada durante 2025. Esse número deu aos adversários uma medida concreta para contestar os incentivos anteriores. Brown argumentou que os moradores de Ohio não deveriam subsidiar as necessidades energéticas e de infraestrutura do setor. Ele também chamou Husted de “o rosto dos data centers” no estado. Husted rejeita a sugestão de que abandonou os interesses locais. Sua campanha afirma que ele tem defendido de forma consistente o controle das comunidades sobre a decisão de os projetos avançarem ou não. No entanto, a consistência quanto à autoridade local não elimina a mudança mais ampla de ênfase. As mensagens anteriores celebravam a expansão, enquanto as atuais se concentram em impedir que os custos cheguem aos consumidores comuns. A transição é relevante porque os eleitores podem comparar a linguagem da campanha com registros criados antes da reação negativa. O reposicionamento político se torna mais difícil quando políticas fiscais, anúncios de projetos e declarações públicas continuam disponíveis. O debate mais amplo sobre data centers nas eleições de meio de mandato, portanto, envolve mais do que instalações individuais. Ele testa se os candidatos conseguem separar o apoio à infraestrutura de IA da responsabilidade por suas consequências locais. Essa distinção era mais fácil quando a maior parte dos custos parecia distante ou técnica. É mais difícil quando as famílias conectam novos empreendimentos às contas mensais de serviços públicos. A Lei de Proteção aos Pagadores de Tarifas Não Resolveu a Questão dos Custos A resposta federal de Husted colocou a proteção aos pagadores de tarifas na agenda, mas não decidiu se os data centers devem arcar com todos os seus custos de infraestrutura. Husted patrocinou a Lei de Proteção aos Pagadores de Tarifas à medida que a oposição a grandes instalações de computação se intensificava. A legislação abordava clientes de grande carga, ou seja, instalações que consomem quantidades excepcionais de eletricidade. A proposta orientava os reguladores estaduais de serviços públicos a considerar padrões que abrangessem as melhorias de geração, transmissão e distribuição exigidas por esses clientes. Seu objetivo era evitar que essas despesas fossem transferidas para famílias e pequenas empresas. A Câmara aprovou a legislação por 417 votos a 3 em 16 de setembro. artigo.texto: Power U.S. Battery-Power Kickoffs Hit $3.2 Billion in September Industrial Info Resources is tracking 11 standalone U.S. BESS projects that were scheduled to kick off in September, totaling US$3.28 billion of investment Released Monday, October 05, 2026 Written by Jesse Broehl, Editor-in-Chief, Breaking Energy News (BEN), IIR Intelligence, (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Eleven standalone BESS projects were scheduled to break ground across the U.S. in September, representing $3.28 billion in combined investment and 2,236 MW of capacity. BESS Ranks Third Among Power Plant Types for September Sixty power generation projects in the U.S. are scheduled to break ground this September, representing a total investment value (TIV) of $16.8 billion and roughly 18,083 megawatts (MW) of capacity across 10 fuel categories. Standalone battery energy-storage systems (BESS) rank third among power plant types this month for total investment, and it trails only solar in project count. Rarely built a decade ago, BESS plants are a rapidly growing market. According to Industrial Info Resources data, 11 standalone BESS projects are scheduled to break ground across the U.S. in September, representing $3.28 billion in combined investment and 2,236 MW of capacity. This story focuses on project starts in the BESS sector for September. For a look at all generation types of plants kicking off, see this accompanying overview news story by IIR Energy. Solar focus is here and natural gas here. See this data compilation for the full list of projects, all generation sources for September. Multiple Enabling Factors Drive Fast-Growing BESS Market BESS's success is driven by multiple factors: battery costs have drastically fallen, making the plants more cost-effective to build. According to BloombergNEF's annual Lithium-Ion Battery Price Survey, overall, battery pack prices have fallen 93% since 2010 -- from roughly $1,436 to $1,474 per kWh (in real 2025 dollars, per BNEF's own inflation-adjusted figures) down to $108 per kWh in 2025. Policy also has been a key factor. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) provided for the first time tax credits for standalone BESS, which before had been limited to co-located with solar. After U.S. elections in the fall of 2024 ushered in a second Trump Administration and full Republican control of Congress, wind and solar tax credits were phased out while the credits for BESS were left intact. Eleven Battery Storage Projects, 2,236 MW of Capacity Texas hosts the largest project (the 1,043-MW Zeus Armstrong BESS), while California and New Mexico each host multiple smaller projects. Minnesota, Indiana and Michigan each have one project. Every one of the 11 projects is new construction; as with solar, there is no refurbishment or life-extension activity in this category, consistent with battery storage being a fundamentally newer technology at utility scale. Ownership skews heavily nonutility, similar to solar: Nine of the 11 projects, representing $2.91 billion, are developed by nonutility/IPP entities. Only two projects are utility-owned--and, notably, both belong to the same company, Xcel Energy. Some notable projects and ownership or offtake structure include: Zeus Armstrong BESS Unit Addition (Claude, TX): At 1,043 MW and $1.57 billion, this is the largest battery-storage project in the September pipeline, and the largest planned standalone battery project in Texas overall, according to third-party interconnection-queue tracking. The project, developed by Zeus Renewable Energy Development, sits in Armstrong County, Texas -- the same county as this month's Claude Armstrong Phase I solar project profiled in IIR Energy's accompanying solar coverage for September planned starts. Armstrong County is also home to a major Crusoe Energy AI data center campus with Google as an anchor tenant, part of Google's broader $40 billion Texas AI infrastructure buildout. Becker Sherco BESS (Clear Lake Township, MN) and Shakopee Blue Lake BESS (Shakopee, MN): These two projects, together worth $549 million, are both pieces of a single, coordinated Xcel Energy clean-energy transition plan. Xcel filed a proposal with Minnesota regulators in October 2025 to double battery storage capacity at its retiring Sherco coal plant in Becker to 600 MW -- Minnesota's largest power plant, scheduled for full coal retirement by the end of 2030 -- while separately adding 135.5 MW of storage at its Blue Lake facility in Shakopee. Both projects reuse existing grid interconnections from the coal and gas infrastructure already on site. The following charts show all 11 projects in two charts, ranked by TIV value and by MW installed capacity. See this data compilation for the full list of all projects, all generation sources for September. Tax credits for BESS were added in 2022. When wind and solar tax credits were phased out by Congress in 2025, the credits for BESS were left intact. - Texas hosts the single-largest project (the 1,043-MW Zeus Armstrong BESS), while California and New Mexico each host multiple smaller projects. artigo.texto: Rethinking WUE: Data Center Water Strategy Beyond The Facitily As AI reshapes data center cooling, improving water usage effectiveness requires a system-level view. October 5, 2026 Water has always served a strategic role in hydronic applications. It carries thermal energy more efficiently than air, making it well-suited for applications where precise thermal management is critical. Today, that includes AI data centers, where rising computing densities are creating unprecedented cooling demands. But as data center development accelerates, the conversation around water is changing. Water is no longer merely a cooling input – its availability, quality and infrastructure capacity have become important considerations for siting, permitting, resilience and community alignment. That makes water usage effectiveness (WUE) an increasingly important metric, but also one that needs to be considered in context. Water as a strategic resource Liquid-based cooling isn't new. Data centers have used water for decades to absorb and remove heat generated by IT equipment. What is changing is the scale and concentration of that heat. AI and high-performance computing are driving higher rack densities that challenge traditional air-cooling approaches. As a result, direct-to-chip liquid cooling and other liquid-based architectures are moving closer to the heat source, where they can efficiently capture heat from CPUs and GPUs. Closed-loop hydronic systems can also recirculate fluid rather than continuously consuming makeup water. Together, these approaches create opportunities to reduce reliance on evaporation and improve facility-level WUE. But there's an important distinction: Using water more efficiently inside a data center doesn't necessarily tell the whole story. Look beyond WUE alone Every cooling architecture involves trade-offs. A closed-loop system, for example, may significantly reduce on-site water consumption, but the heat still has to go somewhere. Depending on the heat rejection strategy, reducing water use can increase electrical demand. Conversely, evaporative cooling can reduce cooling energy under the right conditions while consuming more water. That’s why WUE shouldn't be considered separately from power usage effectiveness (PUE). Water and energy use are closely connected, and the electricity powering a data center can carry its own water footprint depending on the regional generation mix. A cooling strategy that reduces water consumption on-site but requires more electricity may simply shift some of that water demand upstream rather than eliminate it. Liquid cooling adds another factor. Moving liquid closer to high-density computing equipment provides an effective way to manage concentrated heat loads, but liquid cooling alone doesn't determine overall water consumption. Operators and designers still need to consider the complete thermal chain, including pumping, heat exchange, heat rejection and the energy required to operate the system. The objective isn't simply to drive one metric lower. It's to find the appropriate water-energy balance for the site. That balance will look different from one data center to another. Climate, water availability and quality, workload, rack density, grid characteristics, utility capacity and local infrastructure can all influence the appropriate cooling strategy. A data center in a water-stressed region with available electrical capacity may require a different approach than a facility where water is abundant but the grid is constrained. That's where system-level thinking comes in. Instead of starting with a specific cooling technology, project teams should consider the outcomes the facility needs to achieve and consider the complete water cycle: - Where will water come from? - What quality is required? - How will it be treated and moved? - How efficiently can it be reused? - How will heat be rejected? - What happens to the water before it leaves the facility? Advanced treatment technologies can expand opportunities to use reclaimed or alternative water sources while maintaining the quality required for reliable cooling, while digital monitoring can provide visibility into water quality, flow, equipment condition and changing system performance. Meanwhile, heat recovery may create opportunities to put captured thermal energy to beneficial use rather than simply rejecting it. Collaboration outside the facility matters, too. Early coordination with water and wastewater utilities can help data center developers understand local constraints, evaluate reuse opportunities and identify infrastructure investments that strengthen long-term water resilience. Design WUE into the system As AI infrastructure scales, water strategy can no longer be something addressed after the cooling architecture is already established. While WUE provides an important measure of progress, the bigger opportunity is understanding what sits behind the metric. Water source, treatment, hydronics, cooling, monitoring, reuse, discharge and even community infrastructure are all interconnected. The goal isn't simply to use less water. It's to manage water and energy together in a way that supports thermal performance, uptime and responsible growth. For the next generation of data centers, that broader view may be the most effective way to make every drop – and every watt – count. About the Author: Steven Lucente is a business development manager for Xylem’s Applied Water business, where he leads data center business development and turns customer infrastructure challenges into scalable growth strategies and win-ready solutions.

artigo.texto: Politics & Government Operations Suspended At 2 East End Battery Storage Facilities: Romaine "Operations must cease until changes are made that will protect our drinking water." EAST HAMPTON, NY — Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine announced Monday that NextEra Energy had agreed to suspend operations at two battery energy storage facilities on the East End: the facility at Cove Hollow Road in East Hampton and the facility in Montauk near Fort Pond. Both facilities are jointly owned by NextEra Energy and National Grid. "Less than 24 hours after the town board unanimously authorized litigation to shut down the East Hampton and Montauk battery storage facilities, NextEra has temporarily shut both facilities down," East Hampton Town Supervisor Kathee Burke-Gonzalez said. "This is the action we demanded, and I am pleased that NextEra responded swiftly to my September 29 letter and the town board’s action. The board had authorized litigation, retained counsel and taken the steps necessary to go to court to secure this shutdown. I am pleased that NextEra acted before litigation had to be commenced." Find out what's happening in East Hamptonfor free with the latest updates from Patch. She added: "The town will hold off on commencing litigation while counsel reviews the agreement. The town retains all of its legal rights should NextEra fail to follow through on removing all NOVEC 1230 from both facilities and ensuring appropriate fire safety and environmental measures are in place." The suspension, Romaine said, follows weeks of discussions between Suffolk County and NextEra. Find out what's happening in East Hamptonfor free with the latest updates from Patch. NextEra did not immediately respond to a request for comment by Patch. Under the arrangement, NextEra will suspend operations at both sites and remove the Novec 1230 fire suppression agent from both facilities by about October 9, Romaine said. "We are very grateful that this agreement has been reached," said Romaine. "The 2023 fire at the East Hampton BESS location, and the consequent contamination of the site and surrounding areas, prove that the operations must cease until changes are made that will protect our drinking water." The State Department of Environmental Conservation has determined that when water was applied to the East Hampton facility during a May 2023 fire, it mixed with Novec 1230 and broke down into PFPrA, a short-chain "forever chemical," which has since been detected in drinking water in the surrounding area, Romaine said. Two Suffolk County Water Authority wells have been taken offline, he added. The county has drilled monitoring wells to investigate the contamination and supports the Water Authority's litigation against NextEra, he said. In July, Romaine and East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen sent letters to the chief executives of NextEra Energy and National Grid urging them to suspend operations at the East Hampton facility until the investigation is completed, he said. "We need a remediation plan immediately, one approved by the DEC, so the hard work of cleaning the site can begin," said Romaine. "The community did not know for years that the 2023 fire had left behind PFPrA. They should not wait any longer for the situation to be addressed." In August, the Town of East Hampton formally directed East Hampton Energy Storage Center, NextEra Energy and National Grid to take six specific actions, at their sole expense, to address fire-water containment and other safety concerns at the battery energy storage facility on Cove Hollow Road. The demands include new engineering controls capable of containing all fire water and runoff, a revised emergency and safety plan, complete and certified technical information, a hazardous-waste management plan and an independent study of whether the facility remained necessary for the East End electric grid. The action followed questions raised by the May 2023 battery fire and came as state and county agencies continued an investigation into PFPrA and other PFAS contamination near the Suffolk County Water Authority’s Bridgehampton Road Wellfield. No source had been determined, town officials said. Earlier this year, the Water Authority detected PFPrA at the wellfield, removing three wells from service and limiting a fourth to emergency use, town officials said. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation is currently sampling the battery storage property, town officials said. The Suffolk County Department of Health Services is also conducting groundwater sampling and testing private drinking-water wells in the area. The county has identified 26 homes in the area that are not connected to public water; results are not yet available for all of those wells, and several have not yet been sampled, town officials said. When the facility was reviewed in 2017 by the town’s planning board, the town relied on technical information provided by the applicant stating that no liquid within the battery cells could spill and that the only hazardous spillable liquid at the site was oil contained in the transformers and inverters, town officials said. The approved plans therefore included containment for that oil, but not a permanent system capable of capturing the fire-suppression water generated during the May 2023 battery fire, which the Water Authority alleges exceeded 2.2 million gallons, officials added. The town required the companies to: - Submit a revised emergency and safety plan for town approval explaining how the facility would respond to a worst-case battery fire, contain all fire-suppression water and promptly notify the town and emergency agencies. artigo.texto: Delphos City Council approves 18-month data center moratorium DELPHOS, Ohio (WLIO) — Delphos is joining other cities in the area that are putting a hold on new data centers. Delphos City Council voted Monday night to impose an 18-month moratorium on data centers and renewable energy projects. Each of the Ohio gubernatorial candidates has plans for data centers moving forward in the state. Delphos officials want to wait and see what Ohio lawmakers do to shape how new data center projects are addressed in the state. Council also appointed Doug Mullenhour as mayor to replace Andre McConnahea, who resigned in August. Mullenhour previously served as Delphos mayor from 2020 to 2024 and said he is glad to be back in the mayor’s seat. “Delphos is a great place to live and raise a family. I’ve done that here and we’ve made a lot of progress in the last past years and I just wanted to come back and make sure we get that progress momentum keep it keep it going. We got a safety service building to get built and we got a canal to keep pushing through to try to get it cleaned up and some development going down there. So, there’s a lot of things in the fire” says Doug Mullenhour, Delphos Mayor. During its next meeting, council will vote on a tax abatement agreement that would help establish a pharmacy in the city. artigo.texto: The Lansing Town Board decided to draft a ban on the construction of new data centers in the town at a special meeting on Tuesday night. The meeting was packed with over 200 concerned citizens, who voiced opposition to data center development during a public comment period. The approval process for a proposed data center on Cayuga Lake was paused in July when Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-N.Y.) signed Executive Order 62, enacting a one year moratorium on state permitting for data centers exceeding a 50 megawatt capacity. The board met to navigate uncertainty with how the state moratorium applies to the town — they were met with a crowd of frustrated residents who expressed concern for the future of their hometown in the event of data center construction. The event was lively, with loud reactions from the crowd throughout the evening, met with multiple requests for quiet from the town board. Many of the speakers and audience members wore red, signifying a “stop” to data center development and support of a data center ban. Of the over 30 people who spoke, all but one called for a data center ban in Lansing — the one dissenter being a TeraWulf employee. The draft of the ban will be presented to the public by the town’s attorney at a future meeting. If developed and passed, Lansing will join Dryden and Danby in being some of the first New York towns to ban data centers of any size. Background In August 2025, data center developer TeraWulf secured an 80 year lease to the former Milliken Station powerplant, located in Lansing, and approval for the construction of a data center with up to 400 megawatts of industrial capacity. The project, known as Lake Hawkeye Data, has been met with protest from groups such as No Data Center FLX and Cayuga Lake Environmental Action Now!. The groups sued Lansing’s Zoning Board of Appeals and TeraWulf in January 2026, challenging the zoning board’s classification of the center as a “general processing facility” — an undefined term in the code which makes it easier for development to proceed. The lawsuit is ongoing in spite of the moratorium, the lead attorney for the environmental groups told The Sun in July, because the zoning board’s decision remains in effect. No Data Center FLX has collected almost 23,000 signatures for their petition rejecting the project and has organized protests throughout the approval process. During the moratorium, the Department of Environmental Conservation is prohibited from issuing discretionary permits, which are a necessary step in the data center approval process. The moratorium, however, “does not directly impact local reviews and approval,” according to the board’s statement to open the public comment period. Therefore, it is unclear the exact impact of the moratorium on TeraWulf’s plans for the data center. Public Comments Over 200 people filled the Lansing Middle School auditorium to voice their concerns at the special meeting. This showing came after previous board meetings about the data center did not allow an open public comment period. Commenters were widely in agreement, raising concerns around noise from the proposed data center and stress on the electrical grid, along with potential costly litigation in the event TeraWulf breaches any agreements. However, most did not directly address the state’s moratorium, instead raising concerns about the data center itself. At the midpoint, the agenda called to shift from hearing comments from Lansing residents to non-Lansing residents, which was met with boos from the crowd. The board decided to allow a mix of Lansing and non-Lansing speakers to come forward, and many of the latter abdicated their allotted two minutes of speaking time to Lansing residents. The single voice in favor of the development was Pace Ralli, TeraWulf’s vice president of project development. He said he has worked in clean energy for over 20 years and “care[s] deeply about our environment and natural resources.” Ralli sees the Lake Hawkeye project as an opportunity for economic development and repurposing old industrial land. He described TeraWulf’s work with the town as “constructive and collaborative” and said TeraWulf has made “meaningful changes to the site plan in response” to local concerns. Ralli asked Lansing residents to keep an open mind and “evaluate the project on the facts.” Board Discussion After hearing public comments, some board members were split between a desire for economic development and opposition from the community. Council member Judy Drake, who expressed concern for Lansing’s economic development, said the town has a reputation as “not interested in business.” She said she wanted to explore the option of a “highly regulated data center” as a means to promote the economy. Regulations on project size “make an ugly project seem not quite as ugly,” Wetmore said. He added that supporting the data center as a means of economic development may push away other businesses. Town Supervisor Ruth Groff described the prospective data center as a “fiscal nightmare” that is “open[ing] the door for more problems,” noting that allowing data centers of any size into Lansing could be risky as the only way to hold these companies accountable in the event they breach contract is expensive litigation. The board discussed a town level moratorium due to uncertainty in how Hochul’s executive order would affect local governments, and expressed hope that the state would provide further frameworks or regulation to guide the local government through the evaluation and approval process. Drake said he does not “trust the state when it comes to deciding what happens in our town.” Within the final minutes of the meeting, board members decided to draft an all-out ban. Despite the complexity of regulations and the details to weigh, the sentiment in the room was voiced by Lansing resident Lisa Peter: “This is my happy place, don’t eff it up.” Lila Davis is a member of the Class of 2029 in the College of Agriculture and Life

artigo.texto: On Oct. 1, SB 484 required each of Florida’s investor-owned utilities to file a tariff for its largest customers. The law’s core is two sentences. The rules must reasonably ensure that each large-load customer, defined as one drawing 50 megawatts or more, bears its own full cost of service. And the risk that such a customer doesn’t pay may not be borne by everyone else. I published a rubric for reading those filings on Sept. 15, before any existed, and finished amending it before the first one arrived. Each filing gets one of three results: it clears, it has a shortfall to defend, or it misses a required test. Three utilities made Oct. 1 filings. Two filed new large-load tariffs, and FPL asked the Commission to deem its existing one compliant. Duke filed nothing new and relies on a petition pending since April. The scorecards are below. Tampa Electric put real numbers on the page: stated charges, a 20-year minimum term, and, in its customer contract, a termination fee covering the remaining generation, transmission, fuel transportation, and purchased-power charges for the rest of the term. Only two required tests are partly met. The tariff reaches only new or incremental load, and security for an investment-grade customer is 50% of $2.0 million multiplied by its contracted megawatts, against roughly $2.7 million per megawatt of committed plant and transmission, by my arithmetic from the company’s exhibits. The open question is year 20: a customer giving notice can leave owing nothing more, while the company’s own exhibits show about $1.07 billion of generation net plant still on the books in 2047. TECO says that plant would then serve its other customers. That may prove true; no one has agreed to pay for it if it does not. Florida Power & Light filed no new large-load tariff. It asked the Commission to find that the tariffs approved in January as part of its rate settlement, before SB 484 took effect, already comply. Those tariffs carry a 20-year term, two years’ notice, and an exit fee covering the remaining generation charges. The miss is coverage: they apply only to a customer with a projected new or incremental load of 50 megawatts or more and a projected load factor of 85% or more. A load factor can lawfully set a price; here it decides who is covered. The statute defines the customer by peak demand alone. That may describe few customers today. The rubric reads the text, not the current queue. Florida Public Utilities says it has no qualifying customers and no inquiries, and leaves every rate to customer-specific agreements the Commission must approve before service starts. That is reasonable for a small utility. But the filing states no rate, and under the rubric’s first test, a filing with no stated rate misses. Duke Energy Florida filed nothing new by Oct. 1. It relies on a petition filed in April, heard in August and briefed in September. Its president, Melissa Seixas, made the case in these pages on Oct. 2: “Floridians should never be asked to finance someone else’s business decision.” That is the right standard. The filing falls short on one required test. Duke’s policy measures the 50-megawatt threshold over 30 minutes; the statute says 15. And it reaches only firm load, so a new customer that takes interruptible service falls outside it. Duke says such customers need less capacity built for them; the statute’s definition makes no such exception. Until a large-load rate arrives in 2028, which Duke committed to in its brief, qualifying customers pay existing general-service rates, backed by a 20-year term and an exit fee. Two points for anyone following these cases. First, the statute requires the outcome and only permits the tools. The Commission may approve exit fees and minimum terms, but the full-cost result is mandatory either way. Second, FPL asked for proposed agency action, so the Commission can rule without a hearing unless an affected party asks for one. And one number belongs in every conversation about this law. SB 484 does not reach municipal utilities or rural electric cooperatives. By the Commission’s own statistics, that is about 25% of the state’s customer accounts. These are readings of the filed words, not Commission findings. Every citation is collected with the rubric. They show a promise written in mandatory terms, met unevenly. ___ Dr. Mark McNees is director of the MS in Social and Sustainable Enterprises at Florida State University’s Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship. He writes on energy cost policy.

artigo.texto: Independence council restricts future data centers after Nebius backlash INDEPENDENCE, Mo. (KCTV) - The Independence City Council voted 6-0 Monday to approve restrictions on future data center development, following a push by opponents of the Nebius AI data center project. The new rules will not affect the Nebius facility, a hyperscale data center on 400 acres at Highway 79 and Little Blue Parkway that broke ground in May. The project drew opposition earlier this year after the previous council approved tax breaks for the company. Voters later removed two city councilors who supported the project and recalled another. Under the new rules, the city council must approve “major” data centers before they can be built. Major data centers are defined as those with electrical loads greater than five megawatts. The city’s amendment to its development ordinance also sets specific requirements, including how far such facilities must be from homes. Councilman Brice Stewart, the only remaining council member who voted against the Nebius incentives, said large-scale data centers were not anticipated when the city’s code of ordinances was last updated in 2022. “The Nebius data center, everything was zoned. They could just come in, buy the land and open the data center,” Stewart said. A planning commission report on the proposed changes said large data centers differ from traditional industrial development, citing “substantial electrical demand, water consumption backup, power generation noise from mechanical equipment, large building, footprints, visual impacts, and potential compatibility, concerns with nearby residential neighborhoods, and community facilities.” The revisions include the following requirements for major data centers: - Generator testing is limited to normal weekday business hours, no more than 10 hours per month, with required sound attenuation and generator testing records. - Closed-loop cooling systems, or similar technologies that use less water than other systems, are required. - Architectural design standards are required that are “intended to reduce their appearance of large uninterrupted building walls.” - A 1,000-foot setback, measured property-line to property-line, is required from residential areas, schools, parks, playgrounds, daycares, nursing homes, hospitals and places of worship. The setback was amended from an initially proposed 500 feet before passage Monday. Resident Daniel Morehead told the council Monday that the city has failed to enforce its current rules on light and noise at the Nebius construction site. “Several of the residents have had to find alternative ways to even exist, most of them moving to their basements, finding other locations with lower noise emissions, just so they can get some sleep,” Morehead said. The new restrictions for major data centers are part of a broader set of changes that create a tiered framework with different rules for smaller facilities. A related set of rules was also created for battery energy storage systems. A six-month moratorium on new data centers, passed by the council in July, remains in effect through Jan. 2, 2027. artigo.texto: Um carro elétrico da BYD foi usado pelo Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Paraná (TRE-PR) para manter as urnas eletrônicas em funcionamento em Salto de Lontra, no interior do estado, depois que um temporal interrompeu o fornecimento de energia no cartório durante o primeiro turno das eleições de 2026. O veículo, cujo modelo não foi informado, foi conectado à estrutura do local por meio da função V2L (Vehicle to Load). O recurso permite que o automóvel libere parte da carga da bateria — em geral entre 30 kWh e 60 kWh — em tomadas comuns, com o auxílio de adaptadores, e sustente aparelhos de baixo consumo por horas. A tecnologia vem de série em modelos como o Dolphin Mini, da BYD, e o EX2, da Geely. Situações semelhantes ocorreram em Francisco Beltrão e Umuarama, também no Paraná, onde a queda de energia foi contornada com a lanterna de celulares ou com a carga própria das urnas. Em Goiás, um policial militar recorreu a um inversor de voltagem para ligar a urna à rede elétrica de um automóvel.

artigo.texto: Nearly a year after they received their first data center proposal, Ransom Twp. officials are poised to adopt an ordinance regulating the facilities’ development. Supervisors will vote Monday on an ordinance updating the township’s zoning laws to include requirements for data centers’ development, according to public notices and the agenda for the meeting. The vote comes as the township is involved in litigation over its rejection earlier this year of a proposal by Scranton Materials LLC to construct a data center campus on the company’s Newton Road property. The company in November filed for a curative amendment, challenging the validity of the township’s zoning ordinance, that would have allowed the construction of six data centers — each with a 156,648-square-foot footprint — at its 251-acre quarry at 819 Newton Road. The board voted in January to dismiss the proposed changes due to lack of testimony and evidence from Scranton Materials. Under state law, municipalities are required to allow every type of lawful land use within their borders, or else face legal challenges over exclusionary zoning. The law is the focus of several legal challenges related to the supervisors’ January dismissal of the zoning change. The developer appealed the decision and filed a second lawsuit seeking a declaratory judgment against the board earlier this year. The second lawsuit is ongoing. A Lackawanna County judge ruled in July that a Scranton woman can legally oppose the plans despite not living in Ransom Twp. Officials have not said how the new ordinance would affect the litigation with Scranton Materials. Efforts to reach township Solicitor William Rinaldi about whether the ordinance would render the lawsuits moot were unsuccessful Friday. The Pennsylvania Municipal Planning Code states that no zoning changes or other governing ordinance may adversely affect an existing land development application. More recently, Mudiita Land Venture LLC, a Carbon County-based firm with a parent company in New Jersey, purchased 528.6 acres south of Ransom Road and west of South Keyser Avenue in the township to build a hyperscale data center campus. There have been no other data centers proposed in the township, officials have said. At public meetings on the ordinance, people have been receptive to the proposed law but worry about future development. The ordinance says data centers would be allowed only in the township’s general commercial/manufacturing and heavy manufacturing districts — along the southeastern part of the municipality at the Taylor border and in the southwestern part along the Susquehanna River, respectively — as a conditional use. As a conditional use, the developer would need to meet specific criteria outlined in the ordinance and receive township approval. The board of supervisors would be required to render a written decision on the application within 45 days after the final hearing. Under state law, if a governing body fails to hold a public hearing within 60 days of the application being received, the decision is deemed in favor of the applicant. The ordinance stipulates that data centers have a maximum height of 40 feet and lot area of 8 acres. Other requirements address buffering, fencing, wastewater management, air quality, odor, glare and emissions, battery and fuel storage, parking, noise and vibration, and lighting.

artigo.texto: Sen. Britt rallies Mobile County GOP, talks data centers and AI accountability MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Alabama Sen. Katie Britt headlined the Mobile County Republican Party meeting at Regency Church of Christ, rallying voters with less than a month until the midterms. Senator warns against complacency Britt faced a packed house. Her message: don’t get complacent. While Republicans are used to winning big in Mobile County, some polls show Democrat Doug Jones within striking distance of Republican Tommy Tuberville in the governor’s race. In May, more Mobile County voters voted in the Democratic primary than the Republican one. That hasn’t happened since 1994. Data centers divide governor’s race candidates Data centers have emerged as a top issue dividing Republican gubernatorial candidate Tommy Tuberville from his Democratic opponent, Doug Jones. Tuberville considers them essential, while Jones has called for a one-year moratorium. At the Mobile County Republican Party event, Britt sought to strike a middle ground. She said she doesn’t want to stop the construction of data centers, and she doesn’t support a national one-size-fits-all policy. But she said she favors “guardrails” to make sure data centers don’t receive special tax breaks and pay their own way when it comes to electricity and water usage. Britt warned that the U.S. can’t fall behind China. “What we have to understand is what’s good for one community may not be good for another, and that’s why I reject that we have to have a moratorium across the country because for some communities, this is the right pathway forward. And I also don’t believe that we should put one in every corner,” Britt said. “Guys, you don’t want our greatest adversary having capabilities that we do not. So we have to do that, but I think we also have to do that in a very smart and measured way,” Britt said. Britt discusses AI accountability efforts Britt also talked about her efforts to hold artificial intelligence companies accountable. She pointed to conversations she’s had with parents whose children have committed suicide after receiving encouragement to do so from chatbots. Copyright 2026 WALA. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Across the country, data centers are driving a rise in utility prices, imposing a massive demand on our electricity grid and contributing to increased noise pollution in communities large and small. They are also projected to increase both our yearly consumption of fresh water and our carbon emissions. In short, data centers are bad news: for the environment, and for all of us. So it might shock you to learn that one is rising up in Princeton’s backyard. Right this moment, a data center is being built a mere 10-minute drive from our main campus. The South Brunswick data center on Route 1 will rely on 20 diesel generators for backup power and store an estimated 400,000 gallons of diesel fuel on site. But to term these generators as “backups” is deceptive when their operation will not really be an exception or an emergency measure. As Princeton’s mayor and Council explained in a statement to the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection, “the 20 generators, misleadingly characterized as ‘minor sources’ of emissions, will run not only during power outages but also for routine testing and during periods of peak or critical demand … operating the generators will make the site a major source of emissions.” Diesel exhaust particles and gases are linked to asthma and other respiratory health issues: When running, the generators of the South Brunswick data center will send these harmful substances across Princeton’s municipal boundaries. Fortunately, there is something that the University can do about it. Princeton University should submit a statement to the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection urging them to deny the permit for the center as it runs in its current form. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection is currently considering whether to grant an air permit to the data center, which will be located on a site that was owned by Princeton University until 2024. The University may no longer own the land, but that doesn’t mean it should stand by and remain passive to the approval of an industrial project whose generators will threaten the health of all those local to the area. Air doesn’t care about municipal boundaries or campus borders; the emitted particulates and gases will affect our University community, from the student body to faculty and staff to the foxes and squirrels that live on our campus. It is understandable that universities sometimes try to skirt political hot topics to evade unwelcome attention from the media or the government. But the demand for the regulation of data centers is a rare bipartisan issue, with seven in 10 Americans opposing constructing AI data centers in their local area. Speaking out against the construction of the data center is not a political statement: It’s about standing in opposition to a direct threat to the health and safety of our community. The Princeton Undergraduate Student Government and the Princeton Municipality have both published statements to the NJDEP opposing the air permit. It’s time for the University to follow their lead. Data center construction is certainly not unique to the Princeton area. But even if we consider them an unavoidable manifestation of a technologically developing society, that doesn’t mean we can’t push for their being held to higher environmental standards. We can hold data centers accountable for generating and using electricity without poisoning our air and water, and stand against their receiving air permits until they do so. Princeton University should echo the Princeton Council in asking the Department of Environmental Protection to “take every possible measure to ensure that this data center does not become an environmental blight on our region.” That means not granting an air permit until the plan is adapted with cleaner backup energy generation solutions. Until Oct. 7, the public also has the opportunity to submit written comments to the NJDEP expressing concerns about the data center. The agency will issue a final decision soon after the deadline about whether or not it will grant the permit, or set other environmental safeguards that will need to be met before the permit can be issued. Princeton prides itself on its policy of institutional restraint. But that doesn’t absolve the University of an obligation to speak out against a direct threat to the public health of its community. In times of trouble for higher education, the University doesn’t hesitate to turn to its community to stand up for Princeton. Now, we need Princeton to stand up for us. In his 2026 Commencement address, University President Christopher Eisgruber ’83 quoted former University President Robert Goheen ’40 GS ’48: “Courage, with temperance, is always needed to hold the university to its role and mission [...] the university as a human institution can be confident not only of its past but of its present and future, ready to stand up for its aims and basic commitments, bold to make its voice heard in the land.” As the data center rises, we’re looking towards the future not merely of the University itself, but of the land it sits on and the entire community to which it belongs. Protecting that should be its most basic commitment. Princeton, it’s time to stand up with your students and their health: Say no to the South Brunswick data center. Elif Cam ’30 is a contributing Opinion writer from Princeton, N.J. Since you read this far, she thinks you might as well take a minute to submit a comment to NJDEP opposing the South Brunswick data center air permit. She can be reached by email at elif[at]dailyprincetonian.com.

artigo.texto: Scott County candidates oppose data centers, split on Flock cameras at public forum Forum held at the Scott County Public Library on Sunday GEORGETOWN, Ky. — Debate over data centers and Flock cameras dominated a candidate forum in Scott County, where candidates hoping to represent the county after the November election weighed in on the hot-button issues at the Scott County Public Library. Many were clear: no to data centers. On Flock cameras, their answers were more nuanced. Youth voice in the debate For Scott County High School senior Nate Reeves, the stakes are high. “People like me are going to grow up with a data center in our community and be impacted by the widespread use of Flock cameras. This is why I’m here. Being young only increases my passion for this issue, it doesn’t decrease it,” Reeves said. Reeves was part of a youth-driven push for harsher restrictions in the county’s data center ordinance. On Sunday, he just listened. “We’re seeing an issue here that’s really, really powerful. And it is really, really impactful to young people,” he said. Among those hoping to earn votes like Reeves’ were candidates for Georgetown City Council, state representative and Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District. Candidates say no to data centers On data centers, most candidates offered the same message — “no” in principle — citing water consumption, driving up utility rates and use of farmland. “But it’s very clear to me that going around the Sixth District that all communities are against data centers in central Kentucky,” Peter Lynch, an independent candidate for Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, said. But some said they want to have rules on the books regulating data centers in case a full data center ban falls in front of the courts. “This is the first time the city council is passionate enough against something that they themselves brought it to the table for direction to planning and zoning. That’s how passionate we are about it,” Georgetown City Council member Karen Tingle Sames said. Nuance on Flock cameras Some candidates say they see the cameras as a useful tool for law enforcement, citing things like helping police locate missing people, but raised concerns over a private company like Flock owning the data and not enough parameters around who gets to access it. “If I had to vote today, I would not want Flock cameras,” Georgetown City Council member Willow Hambrick said. For Reeves, Sunday was about listening. He says November will be about action. Candidates who did not attend weigh in Three candidates who did not attend the forum provided statements to WKYT: U.S. Senate candidate Charles Booker said he backs a moratorium on data centers until water, utility and environmental impacts are clear, saying “while Kentucky is open for business, it’s not for sale.” He said he opposes Flock cameras as “a gross violation of Kentuckians’ privacy.” Republican candidate for Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District Ralph Alvarado, through a spokesperson, said data center decisions “belong in the hands of local fiscal courts.” Democratic candidate for Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District Zach Dembo said he opposes special tax breaks and liability protections for data center developers and backs a ban on congressional stock trading on nonpublic information. artigo.texto: O debate sobre data centers de IA no Kansas transforma a eleição para governador em um teste de controle local O Kansas transformou seu debate sobre data centers de IA em um conflito político estadual depois que comunidades questionaram projetos por causa de eletricidade, água, incentivos fiscais e controle local. A discussão agora divide os dois principais candidatos ao governo. A candidata democrata Cindy Holscher defende a suspensão de grandes empreendimentos até que o Kansas inclua proteções mais robustas na legislação. O candidato republicano Ty Masterson afirma que as regras atuais podem proteger os moradores, ao mesmo tempo que permitem aos governos locais aprovar projetos adequados. Ambos os candidatos ajudaram a criar a política que agora debatem. Os dois votaram a favor de uma lei de 2025 que oferece aos data centers qualificados uma isenção de 20 anos do imposto sobre vendas. Holscher mais tarde mudou de posição após ouvir uma oposição crescente em reuniões públicas. Masterson apresenta essa reviravolta como inconsistência política. A disputa, portanto, vai além de uma discussão já conhecida entre desenvolvimento e conservação. Ela questiona se o Kansas deve confiar nas salvaguardas regulatórias existentes ou interromper a construção enquanto os legisladores definem padrões estaduais mais firmes. Essa escolha importa além do Kansas. Empresas de inteligência artificial precisam expandir redes de instalações de computação intensivas em energia. Ainda assim, o custo político de hospedar essas instalações recai cada vez mais sobre governadores, reguladores de serviços públicos, câmaras municipais e moradores próximos. O debate sobre data centers de IA no Kansas saiu de Topeka e chegou à Main Street O Kansas já não debate data centers como uma oportunidade econômica abstrata. As comunidades estão testando quem controla suas terras, serviços públicos e processo de negociação. A base imediata da política é o Projeto de Lei do Senado 98, aprovado em 2025. A lei criou uma isenção de 20 anos dos impostos estadual e local sobre vendas para projetos qualificados de data centers. Um operador qualificado deve se comprometer com pelo menos 250 milhões em investimentos, além de cumprir exigências de emprego e operação. O programa de incentivos do Kansas também exige um plano de compra de eletricidade de longo prazo, planejamento de conservação de água e uma análise de segurança. O Kansas proibiu as concessionárias de oferecer aos data centers qualificados tarifas de eletricidade com desconto destinadas ao desenvolvimento econômico. A lei também exige uma análise pelo Kansas Intelligence Fusion Center antes que um projeto receba benefícios públicos. Essas disposições permitem que os defensores argumentem que o Kansas não ofereceu um subsídio irrestrito. Eles descrevem a lei como uma estrutura para atrair grandes infraestruturas, ao mesmo tempo que atribui obrigações identificáveis a seus operadores. A legislação ainda criou um incentivo excepcionalmente duradouro. Vinte anos vão muito além do mandato de um governador, da vida política de uma comissão municipal ou do ciclo inicial de construção. Esse horizonte temporal mudou a conversa pública. Os moradores não perguntam apenas se um projeto gerará trabalho na construção civil. Eles querem saber quem assume o risco se a demanda de energia, o consumo de água ou a propriedade mudarem ao longo de duas décadas. Disputas locais tornaram essas questões concretas. Emporia aprovou um Distrito de Sobreposição de Infraestrutura Digital em julho de 2026, criando regras de zoneamento para o possível desenvolvimento de data centers. A cidade enfatiza que não aprovou nenhuma instalação para construção. Essa distinção não encerrou o conflito. Opositores buscaram uma iniciativa para proibir data centers de alto impacto. A comissão municipal então solicitou orientação judicial sobre a situação jurídica da petição. O processo demonstra por que estruturas de zoneamento podem se tornar politicamente relevantes antes que um operador identificado apresente um plano final de construção. Depois que terrenos são designados e as discussões sobre serviços públicos avançam, os moradores podem acreditar que as decisões decisivas já foram tomadas. Lawrence adotou uma abordagem mais cautelosa. Líderes municipais aprovaram uma suspensão temporária enquanto autoridades estudavam possíveis regras para grandes instalações. Outras comunidades debateram campi propostos, compromissos com serviços públicos e a abrangência das divulgações públicas. Independence forneceu um alerta eleitoral ainda mais claro. Os eleitores destituíram o vereador John Perkins por uma margem de 68% a 32%, depois que ele apoiou um empreendimento proposto envolvendo a empresa de infraestrutura de IA Nebius. Outro apoiador do projeto perdeu uma disputa para prefeito depois que um adversário questionou o processo de aprovação e pediu uma votação pública. Esses resultados não estabelecem um consenso estadual, mas mostram o custo político de parecer desdenhoso. A reação local transformou a localização de data centers em uma questão de consentimento. Um projeto pode cumprir os procedimentos formais de zoneamento, enquanto os moradores ainda concluem que sua escala, suas demandas por recursos ou suas negociações receberam escrutínio insuficiente. Para empresas de tecnologia, essa distinção é crucial. Obter uma licença não é o mesmo que manter o apoio de uma comunidade durante toda a construção e operação. O debate sobre data centers de IA no Kansas agora começa nessa lacuna. Líderes estaduais criaram o incentivo, mas autoridades locais e moradores precisam lidar com as consequências práticas dos locais propostos. artigo.texto: The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors will consider a proposal Tuesday to develop a zoning amendment prohibiting large-scale data centers in unincorporated parts of the county, citing concerns about the energy and water demands and potential public health effects associated with facilities used to power artificial intelligence. The motion by Supervisor Hilda Solis would direct the Department of Regional Planning to begin drafting an amendment to the county’s zoning code establishing definitions for different types of data centers based on factors including acreage, square footage, energy use and water consumption. The proposed zoning amendment would distinguish hyperscale and artificial intelligence data centers from what the motion calls “beneficial use” facilities, including enterprise, accessory or sole-source data centers used for daily computational needs. The zoning amendment would prohibit all data centers meeting the zoning amendment’s definition of “large-scale” in every zone of unincorporated Los Angeles County. “Given the pressing concerns to immediately prevent the environmental and health effects of data centers powering AI from impacting unincorporated County residents, it is imperative that the Board of Supervisors act on the recommendations to prohibit these facilities expediently,” according to the motion. The proposal comes amid growing interest in the environmental effects of the computing infrastructure required for increasingly powerful AI systems. “Data centers servicing artificial intelligence (AI) consume high rates of energy, over-utilize water resources, contribute to environmental pollution, and impact public health in ways that are still being understood,” according to Solis’ motion. The motion states that the growth of artificial intelligence has fueled development of hyperscale or large-scale data centers that can be larger and consume more resources than facilities traditionally used to service computer networks and store data. It also points to opposition to proposed data centers in the San Gabriel Valley. According to the motion, the Board of Supervisors received 101 pages of public comments, primarily calling for a moratorium on data centers. The motion cites actions by Monterey Park, Montebello, Baldwin Park and El Monte to restrict or halt data center development and notes that Alhambra voters are scheduled to consider a similar ballot measure in November. The county began examining the issue in April, when the board approved a motion directing county departments to study the potential health, environmental and safety effects of data centers, along with their impact on electrical and water resources. A subsequent county report recommended amending Title 22 of the county zoning code to define data centers and prohibit hyperscale facilities in all zones. According to Solis’ motion, the county’s director of Regional Planning on Sept. 17 invoked existing authority under Title 22 to rely on the absence of a similarly defined land use to prohibit large-scale data centers while a comprehensive zoning amendment is developed. Tuesday’s motion would direct Regional Planning to inform residents in unincorporated communities about that action. It would also direct the Department of Public Health, working with County Counsel, to determine whether the county’s noise regulations should be amended to address “low frequency and continuous noise associated with large-scale data centers.” The county’s chief executive officer would be directed to identify funding needed to prepare and implement the zoning amendment, its required California Environmental Quality Act analysis and any changes to the county’s noise regulations. The motion additionally calls for Regional Planning and County Counsel to be prepared to introduce a moratorium if a proposed data center in an unincorporated area presents what the motion describes as a “current and immediate threat to public health, safety, and welfare.” Such a moratorium would target facilities posing a serious risk or nuisance involving health, safety or environmental resources, particularly water and energy resources. The item is scheduled to be considered when the Board of Supervisors meets Tuesday.

artigo.texto: EU Commits KSh590 Million to Back Kenya's Carbon Market Monitoring Framework The European Union is supporting Kenya with KSh590 million to develop a robust monitoring and validation system, aligning with the country's newly launched National Carbon Registry. The European Union has committed KSh590 million (approximately 4 million euros) to support Kenya in developing a robust monitoring and validation system for its rapidly expanding carbon market. This strategic financial backing comes at a critical juncture as Kenya seeks to position itself as a continental leader in climate finance, ensuring that the revenues generated from carbon credit trading are transparent, verifiable, and equitably distributed to local communities. Strengthening Market Integrity and Transparency The EU funding is specifically earmarked for the enhancement of Kenya's National Carbon Registry, a digital platform recently launched by the government to track the issuance, transfer, and retirement of carbon credits. As the global demand for high-quality, verified carbon offsets surges, the integrity of the underlying data has become paramount. The new monitoring system will utilize advanced satellite imagery, blockchain technology, and independent third-party audits to validate the actual emission reductions claimed by project developers, thereby preventing greenwashing and ensuring that buyers receive genuine climate impact. This investment aligns perfectly with Kenya's newly published Carbon Market Engagement Guide, which established a strict national carbon budget for international transactions. The government has capped the export of carbon credits at 10 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent through 2030, a move designed to ensure that Kenya retains sufficient mitigation capacity to meet its own Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. The EU-backed validation framework will be instrumental in enforcing this cap and managing the complex accounting required under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Empowering Local Communities A central pillar of Kenya's carbon market regulations is the mandatory sharing of revenues with the communities that host the projects. Under the Climate Change (Carbon Markets) Regulations, land-based projects such as reforestation and sustainable agriculture initiatives are required to allocate a minimum of 40 percent of their net earnings to local community development funds. The new EU-funded monitoring system will include a specific module to track these financial flows, ensuring that the promised benefits actually reach the intended beneficiaries and are used for agreed-upon development projects like schools, clinics, and water infrastructure. By guaranteeing fair distribution, the government aims to secure the long-term social license for carbon projects. Historically, some carbon initiatives in Africa have faced backlash from local populations who felt excluded from the financial benefits or whose land rights were compromised. A transparent, verifiable system of revenue sharing is therefore seen as essential for the sustainable scaling of the sector, attracting high-quality impact investors who prioritize social equity alongside environmental outcomes. Positioning Kenya as a Regional Hub The EU's financial support underscores the deepening climate partnership between Brussels and Nairobi. As the European Union implements its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which places a tariff on carbon-intensive imports, African nations are under increasing pressure to decarbonize their export industries. A well-regulated, transparent domestic carbon market provides Kenyan exporters with a mechanism to offset their emissions and remain competitive in the European market. Furthermore, Kenya is laying the groundwork for a formal, regulated carbon exchange, with plans to have the platform fully operational by early 2027. This exchange will move the country away from fragmented, over-the-counter bilateral deals towards a centralized, price-discovery mechanism that reflects the true value of high-integrity African carbon credits. The EU's technical and financial assistance is providing the foundational infrastructure necessary to make this exchange a reality, ensuring it meets international standards of governance and market surveillance. Future Outlook and Global Integration As Kenya refines its regulatory framework and deploys the new monitoring technologies, it is sending a clear signal to the global market that it is open for high-quality climate business. The combination of a strict national cap, mandatory community benefit-sharing, and EU-backed verification creates a premium product that is highly attractive to multinational corporations seeking to meet their net-zero commitments with credible offsets. The successful implementation of this KSh590 million project will not only safeguard Kenya's environmental assets but also serve as a blueprint for other developing nations navigating the complex intersection of climate finance, sovereign rights, and community development. By prioritizing transparency and equity, Kenya is demonstrating that the global carbon market can be a powerful engine for sustainable development, provided it is governed with rigor and accountability. artigo.texto: Linea Energy Closes Financing for 250 MW Mesa View Battery Storage Project in Texas Linea Energy has closed project debt and a preferred equity commitment for Mesa View, a 250 MW / 500 MWh battery storage project in Upton County, with commercial operation expected in 2027. Linea Energy, a renewables developer and independent power producer sponsored by EnCap Investments L.P., has announced the closing of project debt financing and a preferred equity commitment for Mesa View BESS. The standalone 250 MW / 500 MWh battery energy storage project is located in Upton County, Texas. The announcement was made on October 1, 2026. A three-part financing structure According to the company, the debt consists of a construction-to-term loan, a tax equity bridge loan and a letter of credit facility. Norddeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale (NORD/LB) acted as coordinating lead arranger, while Texas Capital participated as a syndicate lender. D.E. Shaw Renewable Investments (DESRI) provided the preferred equity commitment. Linea Energy did not disclose the amount of the debt or of the preferred equity commitment. This type of financing comes in a market where storage projects attract varied structures, as illustrated by CIP's investment in the Kilmarnock South battery storage project in Scotland. Company Linea Energy: company profile Partners already engaged with Linea Cassidy DeLine, Chief Executive Officer of Linea Energy, says the closing illustrates the maturation of the company's platform and its ability to repeatedly deliver investable opportunities to the market. Sondra Martinez, Managing Director at NORD/LB, states that the bank led another financing for Linea, following three previous transactions. Peter Koczanski, Head of Corporate Development at DESRI, notes that the new commitment follows the preferred equity commitment made on Duffy BESS. According to him, the partnership reflects DESRI's confidence in Linea's development platform and execution capabilities. Commercial operation expected in 2027 Mesa View BESS is expected to reach commercial operation in 2027. Once online, the project is to deliver 250 MW of dispatchable capacity into the ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas) market. Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP served as Sponsor counsel to Linea Energy. artigo.texto: Beaufort Co. planning commission recommends a temporary moratorium on data centers BEAUFORT COUNTY, S.C. (WTOC) - Beaufort County leaders are moving forward with a temporary moratorium on data centers. The county’s planning commission voted to send the proposed ordinance to the county council. They also asked council to consider extending the pause from nine months to 12 months. If passed, it would pause acceptance, processing, approval, or issuance of certain applications, permits, and approvals for data centers in the county. County leaders say the moratorium will give them time to define what a data center is and look at the potential impacts one could bring to the county. Several residents spoke during the public comment period, and they were all against the idea of data centers in Beaufort County. They also questioned where one would go. For the moratorium to pass, it will need to go through three different votes and a public hearing. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.
