artigo.texto: Plano de Supervisão de IA de Connie Chan Entra em Choque com Scott Wiener sobre Expansão de Data Centers Connie Chan transformou a supervisão de IA em uma linha divisória na corrida congressional de San Francisco ao exigir uma moratória nacional sobre novos data centers. Seu adversário, o senador estadual da Califórnia Scott Wiener, rejeitou essa suspensão abrangente durante o debate entre os dois em 1º de outubro. Ele argumentou que regras operacionais rígidas oferecem mais influência do que interromper a construção no país. O confronto foi mais do que uma divergência sobre desenvolvimento industrial. Chan quer que o Congresso desacelere a infraestrutura que sustenta a IA avançada até que existam padrões nacionais econômicos, ambientais e de segurança. Wiener quer que os data centers continuem se expandindo sob regras exigíveis que cubram segurança, custos de serviços públicos, uso de água e localização dos projetos. Ambos os democratas defendem uma regulamentação mais forte para a IA. A discussão diz respeito ao ponto em que a regulamentação deve intervir. Chan restringiria nova capacidade computacional enquanto os legisladores estabelecem proteções. Wiener regulamentaria empresas e instalações sem restringir amplamente essa capacidade. Essa diferença oferece aos eleitores uma escolha concreta sobre a estratégia de IA dos Estados Unidos. Ela também expõe um problema de política nacional que vai muito além de uma eleição em San Francisco. O Que Mudou Durante o Debate sobre IA em San Francisco O debate transformou um amplo apelo por regulamentação de IA em uma escolha direta entre pausar a infraestrutura e governar sua construção contínua. Chan e Wiener se encontraram na KQED em 1º de outubro, durante a campanha pelo 11º Distrito Congressional da Califórnia. O distrito inclui a maior parte de San Francisco, colocando a disputa próxima de muitas empresas que desenvolvem sistemas de IA de fronteira. O debate foi organizado pela KQED e pelo San Francisco Chronicle. Segundo a programação publicada do debate, ele abordou tecnologia, custo de vida, economia, imigração e política externa. Sobre IA, os candidatos partiram de premissas semelhantes. Ambos disseram que a tecnologia precisa de mais supervisão pública. Ambos rejeitaram uma abordagem que deixa as empresas fiscalizarem a si mesmas. Suas prescrições, então, se separaram de forma acentuada. Chan pediu uma moratória sobre data centers, maior supervisão das empresas de IA e uma desaceleração no desenvolvimento da superinteligência. Superinteligência descreve um sistema hipotético que supera as capacidades humanas em uma ampla gama de tarefas intelectuais. Wiener se opôs a uma moratória geral sobre data centers. Em vez disso, enfatizou a legislação de segurança de IA que aprovou na Califórnia e prometeu buscar proteções comparáveis em nível federal. A cobertura do debate também registrou a crítica central de Chan a Wiener. Ela argumentou que a medida de segurança aprovada por ele era mais fraca do que um projeto anterior vetado pelo governador Gavin Newsom. Wiener defendeu a lei aprovada como um compromisso viável. Ele disse que ela criou um modelo que outros governos podem adaptar, em vez de esperar por uma estrutura federal ideal. Essa troca importa porque nenhum dos candidatos defendeu o status quo regulatório. A disputa foi entre duas estratégias de intervenção, e não entre regulamentação e desregulamentação. A estratégia de supervisão de IA de Connie Chan começa com uma restrição temporária à infraestrutura. Sua lógica é que os data centers criam compromissos físicos e econômicos antes que as comunidades recebam proteções exigíveis. A estratégia de Wiener começa com regras para desenvolvedores e operadores de infraestrutura. Sua lógica é que uma pausa na construção poderia realocar investimentos sem reduzir a demanda subjacente por computação de IA. O debate, portanto, combina duas camadas de política pública que autoridades frequentemente discutem separadamente. Uma camada governa modelos de IA, práticas de segurança, comunicação de incidentes e denunciantes. A outra governa a eletricidade, a água, o terreno e os equipamentos necessários para treinar e operar esses modelos. Conectar essas camadas mudou o debate. Os eleitores já não ouviam apenas alertas abstratos sobre futuras capacidades da IA. Eles ouviam propostas concorrentes para os edifícios, sistemas de energia e custos locais que tornam essas capacidades possíveis. Por Que a Supervisão de IA de Connie Chan Começa com Data Centers Chan trata a infraestrutura computacional como o ponto de pressão em que o governo pode desacelerar a expansão da IA e negociar proteções mais fortes. Chan apoia uma moratória nacional sobre novos grandes data centers voltados à IA até que o Congresso estabeleça regras abrangentes. Essas regras tratariam dos efeitos econômicos, ambientais e de segurança da tecnologia. Sua posição reflete uma observação simples. A IA avançada não é apenas software distribuído a partir de servidores comuns de escritório. Treinar e disponibilizar modelos amplamente utilizados exige capacidade computacional concentrada, extensa infraestrutura elétrica, sistemas de refrigeração e conexões de rede. Uma moratória visaria essa capacidade antes que ela se tornasse operacional. Ela daria aos legisladores tempo para decidir quais instalações deveriam prosseguir e quais obrigações seus proprietários deveriam cumprir. Em um questionário anterior para candidatos, Chan disse que os Estados Unidos poderiam continuar líderes em IA sem transferir os custos para trabalhadores e comunidades. Sua posição completa, resumida pela Mission Local, vinculou a pausa na construção a regras nacionais, e não a uma proibição por prazo indeterminado. Essa distinção é importante. Chan não apresenta a moratória como uma política completa de IA. Ela a apresenta como instrumento de pressão para obtê-la. Sua abordagem se baseia em três preocupações interligadas. Primeiro, novos data centers podem aumentar

artigo.texto: Grid-forming capabilities support multiple grid-restoration functions The project plays an important role in supporting voltage and frequency stability at a key point in Cambodia's central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. Its grid-forming capabilities were put through a series of demanding system-restoration scenarios, demonstrating how energy storage can take on a more active role in supporting the power system. Key highlights include: - Large-scale black start from zero voltage: 516 grid-forming PCS units successfully energized the entire plant from zero voltage, establishing stable voltage and frequency across the system. - Restoration of a 240 km transmission network: The system supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations, while maintaining stable operation as the network was progressively restored. - Support for multiple generation sources: The system supported the start-up and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant, before the restored network was operated together with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, energy storage and loads. - Stable operation under challenging grid conditions: During restoration, the system remained stable through five transformer energization events, including a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stability when synchronizing different power sources under a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees, demonstrating its ability to handle challenging conditions during system recovery. - Extended islanded operation: The system operated independently for 3.5 hours, demonstrating that the energy storage system could continue supporting the local network even when separated from the main grid. - Seamless transitions: The project completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, with voltage deviation kept below 2% and transient frequency fluctuation within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. "This project demonstrates that the value of grid-forming energy storage goes far beyond storing electricity.When a power system faces disturbances or loses normal grid support, grid-forming technology can help establish and maintain stable voltage and frequency, support system restoration and keep the grid operating reliably," said Michael Ruan, Regional Director of Sungrow Southeast Asia and South Asia. "Through projects like this, Sungrow is helping turn energy storage into a more active grid-support asset and bringing proven grid-forming capabilities to the evolving power systems of Southeast Asia." Reducing Technical Risk and Ensuring Timely Delivery Faced with strict test protocols, complex power system scenarios, a compressed construction schedule and rainy‑season working conditions with ambient temperature up to 40°C, Sungrow's cross‑functional team covering pre-sales, on‑site delivery and R&D collaborated closely to deliver high‑quality project outcomes: - 20-day commissioning and testing: The on‑site team worked relentlessly under hot and humid conditions for two consecutive months. The team wrapped up hot commissioning plus three rounds of performance tests within 20 days to guarantee timely grid‑connection. - End‑to‑End Service Solution: Sungrow provides full‑lifecycle and one‑stop services spanning integrated design of storage and monitoring systems, EPC‑related support, equipment design, commissioning and O&M services, enabling the customer to fulfill customized grid‑level requirements with reduced management overhead. As Southeast Asia advances its energy transition, Sungrow will continue to bring proven energy storage technologies and solutions to the region, helping customers build more reliable and sustainable power infrastructure. artigo.texto: Créditos Fiscais de Data Centers da Meta Transformam Infraestrutura de IA em uma Disputa Tributária de US$ 6 Bilhões A Meta teria reduzido sua conta de impostos federais em quase US$ 6 bilhões após tratar novos data centers de IA como “modelos-piloto” experimentais. Os créditos fiscais dos data centers da Meta abrangeram chips especializados e equipamentos relacionados adquiridos durante 2024 e 2025. Esse tratamento transforma um boom de infraestrutura em um teste de alto risco para a política federal de pesquisa. A disputa não trata de saber se a Meta realiza pesquisa. Ela diz respeito a se campi de computação em escala de produção e seu hardware caro se qualificam como despesas de pesquisa experimental. A Meta afirma que o Congresso criou o crédito para incentivar investimentos domésticos como os seus. Críticos dizem que a empresa está reclassificando infraestrutura empresarial essencial como pesquisa, mesmo enquanto usa essa infraestrutura para operar produtos comerciais. A divergência continua sem solução. O Internal Revenue Service não anunciou publicamente que a Meta violou a lei nem emitiu uma decisão final rejeitando essas reivindicações. No entanto, os próprios registros regulatórios da Meta identificam créditos de pesquisa entre suas posições fiscais incertas mais relevantes. Essa divulgação torna a estratégia mais do que um argumento teórico de política pública. A Meta Transformou Data Centers de IA em Modelos-Piloto A mudança relatada não é um novo incentivo fiscal, mas uma aplicação extraordinariamente ampla de um crédito de pesquisa já existente. Segundo uma investigação sobre créditos fiscais, a Meta categoriza determinados data centers de IA como modelos-piloto para fins tributários federais. Essa classificação permite que a empresa inclua alguns custos de equipamentos no cálculo de seu crédito de pesquisa. Um modelo-piloto é uma representação ou modelo usado para avaliar um produto ou processo novo ou aprimorado. Ele pode se qualificar quando sua construção e uso fazem parte de uma experimentação genuína. A interpretação da Meta supostamente aplica esse conceito a grandes instalações de computação repletas de caros chips de inteligência artificial. A empresa diferencia esses campi de data centers convencionais que sustentam operações estabelecidas de armazenamento, publicidade e redes sociais. Os benefícios fiscais reportados chegaram a cerca de US$ 2 bilhões em 2024 e US$ 3,9 bilhões em 2025. Juntos, isso representa quase US$ 6 bilhões em dois anos. Esses valores descrevem benefícios fiscais federais reivindicados, não uma subvenção em dinheiro do governo. Eles também continuam sujeitos a análise, ajustes e possível litígio. A abordagem da Meta importa porque a infraestrutura de IA está se tornando uma das maiores exigências operacionais do setor de tecnologia. Aceleradores, sistemas de rede, equipamentos de resfriamento e infraestrutura de energia agora determinam com que rapidez as empresas podem treinar e implantar modelos avançados. Os créditos de pesquisa tradicionalmente se concentram em salários qualificados, suprimentos e pesquisa contratada. A estratégia da Meta supostamente coloca muito mais infraestrutura física de computação dentro do cálculo. A empresa não negou o uso do crédito de pesquisa. O porta-voz da Meta, Andy Stone, afirmou que a empresa é uma grande investidora americana em pesquisa e utiliza incentivos criados pelo Congresso para investimento doméstico. Essa defesa se baseia em um argumento direto. A Meta desenvolve novos modelos, sistemas, chips e projetos de data centers, portanto a infraestrutura que sustenta esses experimentos faz parte de seu programa de pesquisa. A questão sem solução é onde termina a experimentação e começam as operações empresariais comuns. Um campus de IA pode apoiar trabalho técnico incerto e, ao mesmo tempo, atender produtos usados por anunciantes, criadores e consumidores. Esse papel misto dá à Meta um argumento plausível, mas também cria a principal fragilidade de sua posição. Chamar um ativo de experimental não torna automaticamente todo custo associado uma despesa qualificada de pesquisa. O código tributário se concentra na atividade, finalidade, incerteza e experimentação envolvidas. Ele não pergunta simplesmente se uma empresa comprou equipamentos avançados para um negócio intensivo em pesquisa. Essa diferença explica por que as reivindicações reportadas atraíram escrutínio. A Meta está tratando a base física de sua estratégia de IA como parte do próprio experimento. Por Que os Créditos Fiscais dos Data Centers da Meta Enfrentam Escrutínio A disputa depende de saber se as instalações da Meta realizam experimentação qualificada ou se fornecem principalmente capacidade para um negócio comercial estabelecido. O crédito federal de pesquisa recompensa despesas qualificadas de pesquisa acima de um valor-base definido. Seu objetivo é incentivar trabalho técnico que as empresas talvez financiassem menos porque os resultados permanecem incertos. As regras de pesquisa do IRS aplicam uma estrutura de quatro partes. A pesquisa deve ser tecnológica, abordar incerteza, sustentar um componente empresarial aprimorado e envolver um processo de experimentação. Construir um sistema de IA pode satisfazer esses princípios. Pesquisadores não sabem antecipadamente qual arquitetura de modelo, método de treinamento ou configuração de hardware produzirá o resultado pretendido. A questão mais difícil diz respeito aos equipamentos usados durante esse trabalho. Empresas não podem transformar ativos empresariais padrão em despesas de pesquisa apenas conectando-os a projetos experimentais. O argumento da Meta parece tratar seus data centers de IA como sistemas experimentais integrados. Seus chips, redes, projetos de resfriamento e software operam juntos enquanto engenheiros testam novos modelos e métodos de infraestrutura. Críticos enxergam uma realidade econômica diferente. artigo.texto: Nevada AG Aaron Ford holds Boulder City town hall on data centers, utility bills LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford discussed data centers and their impact on utility costs in Boulder City. Ford, who is running for governor, held a town hall on Sunday in Boulder City focused on data centers’ impact on affordability and his plan as governor to protect Nevada families from higher utility bills. He also outlined his plan to protect taxpayer dollars and state resources. Ford has said he plans to pause new tax abatements and stop attempts to build data centers on federal land. He has also said he will audit data centers to verify whether they have delivered on their commitments. In a release sent to News 3, Ford's campaign claims, "Data Center Joe 'wholeheartedly' supports data centers and has handed them more than $240 million in taxpayer dollars while Nevadans struggle to afford to live in his failed economy. Meanwhile, Joe Lombardo’s campaign has taken $2 million from MAGA data center and Flock billionaires." News 3 reached out to Governor Lombardo's campaign for comment and is awaiting a response.

artigo.texto: Residents in Arkansas, Missouri unite against proposed Oregon County data center MAMMOTH SPRING, Ark. (KAIT) - A lot just outside of Thayer, Missouri, and minutes from Mammoth Spring State Park and the Arkansas state line, is open to potential data center development, prompting opposition from residents on both sides of the border. No developer has taken on the site yet, currently owned by Charles McCullough. Jeremiah Read, a protest organizer, said the area needs to be protected. He led a protest in Mammoth Spring Saturday against the potential data center investors. “Why should you care? I mean, we have an obligation to protect this beauty and not contaminate it for our children and future generations and for ourselves,” Read said. The proposed site sits about five minutes north of Mammoth Spring State Park, across the Arkansas-Missouri state line in Thayer. Read says that if a data center were to draw water from this state park, especially given the lower water table numbers due to the extended drought, it could put the state park in real danger. Thomas Sallings and Magic Keller, Alton residents and local business owners in Missouri, have been doing advocacy work opposing the data center in Oregon County. “This is a chance to use that momentum for people’s voices to be heard and for us to take a more active role in creating the world that we want,” Sallings said. A data center could have a major influence on the county based on the revenue it brings in, and those interests are not in the hands of the residents living close to it. “They’ll basically own 90% of the county and be able to make all the decisions for us,” Sallings said. “We want all the people’s voices to be heard, to develop our economy the way we want it to be developed.” Sallings and Keller propose maximizing taxes on potential developers, and inputting stricter pollution laws, many of which data centers would not meet. They said they hope these moves will keep potential investors away. Keller adds that many proponents tout the investment and value data centers bring to an area don’t amount to benefit for the local community. “The landowner, Charles McCullough, he’s been pretty straightforward,” Keller said. “He’s said—he’s just come out and said, like, this facility will bring in less than 10 jobs.” Romona Hampton, 72, lives minutes from the proposed site and owns a small farm nearby. “The water and the noise has got me bothered more than anything because it would direct me, I mean, it would affect me directly as close as I live to the farm that’s proposed,” Hampton said. Hampton believes the noise could disrupt her and her family, as well as local animal populations with a constant sound that can reach up to 105 decibels—the equivalent of a jet flyover. Additionally, she said a center could potentially heat up water drawn from the spring, which typically runs about 50°F, to temperatures 30-50 degrees higher. Hampton said she took to protesting not only because she feels like these centers are putting profits over people, but because she wants to make sure the future has a fair shake, too. “I have children and grandchildren, Hampton said. ”And I look at all these young people and I think, ‘Oh dear God, it’s up to us to protect them.’ It really is." artigo.texto: China has presented a goal of bringing all-solid-state batteries to an early stage of scaled application by 2030. However, CATL, the world's largest battery maker, is taking a cautious view, saying cost and mass-production technology issues remain and wider adoption will take more time. According to InsideEVs and other outlets, seven government bodies including China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology announced the "15th Five-Year Plan for the New Battery Industry". The plan includes a goal of realising early scaled application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030 and making breakthroughs in core technologies such as advanced electrode materials and new electrolytes. While the government is accelerating efforts to foster the industry, CATL is cautious about the commercialisation timeline. CATL Chairman Robin Zeng (쩡위췬) in June rated the technology maturity of all-solid-state batteries at level 4 out of 9. With level 9 representing mass-producible capability, he said a large technology gap remains. CATL is aiming for small-scale production and vehicle validation in 2027. However, Zeng forecast that "the possibility of scaling all-solid-state batteries to the point of being applied to millions of vehicles is very low before 2030". That is because manufacturing stability and cost, as well as performance, must be solved at the same time. LG Energy Solution offered a similar view. Robert Lee (로버트 리), head of LG Energy Solution in North America, said, "There are still difficulties in mass-producing large all-solid-state cells," adding that they are more likely to be commercialised first in smartphones or specialised uses before expanding to electric vehicles. Market forecasts are also cautious. BloombergNEF projected that "all-solid-state batteries will account for about 10 percent of global demand for electric-vehicle and energy-storage batteries even in 2035." In China, vehicles equipped with semi-solid-state batteries have already appeared, but it is difficult to view this as full-fledged commercialisation of fully all-solid-state batteries. Meanwhile, the Chinese government plans to foster next-generation technologies simultaneously, including sodium-ion and flow batteries, as well as long-life lithium batteries, in addition to all-solid-state batteries. It also set a goal of increasing the charge-discharge cycle life of long-life lithium batteries to 15,000 cycles by 2030.

artigo.texto: Panasonic Holdings plans to begin manufacturing humanoid robots by 2029, using its battery technology to power machines designed for factories and warehouses. Panasonic Holdings will enter the humanoid robot market by 2029, Chief AI Officer Akira Sakakibara told Nikkei Asia in an interview in Osaka. The Japanese electronics giant plans to deploy the machines in its own plants and warehouses first, drawing on its battery business to solve the power constraints that have limited robot mobility. Sakakibara said the company's battery technology gives it an advantage in developing robots that can operate for extended periods without tethering. Current humanoid prototypes from competitors typically run for two to three hours on a charge. Panasonic aims to exceed that significantly, though the company declined to specify target runtimes. The move places Panasonic alongside a growing cohort of Japanese manufacturers pursuing humanoid automation. Kawasaki Heavy Industries has said it will field a fully autonomous humanoid by 2030. Mitsubishi Motors plans to build humanoids for its auto factories. Toyota has committed to deploying 400,000 robots alongside factory staff. Japan's robotics push comes as the country faces a shrinking workforce. The working-age population has fallen 13% since its 1995 peak, according to government data. Companies are racing to automate tasks that conventional industrial robots cannot handle — jobs requiring two-legged movement, balance, and fine motor skills in spaces designed for humans. Panasonic's strategy differs from pure-play robotics startups. Rather than selling robots as standalone products, the company intends to integrate them into its own manufacturing and logistics operations first, then offer them to external customers. This mirrors the path Fanuc and Yaskawa took decades ago, when they automated their own factories before becoming the world's largest industrial robot makers. The humanoid market remains nascent. Goldman Sachs estimates global shipments will reach 1.4 million units annually by 2035, up from fewer than 10,000 in 2024. Most current deployments are pilots. Tesla's Optimus, Figure AI's Figure 02, and Agility Robotics' Digit have demonstrated warehouse tasks but have not reached volume production. Battery life remains a primary bottleneck. Humanoid robots carry their power source, adding weight that demands more power — a vicious cycle. Panasonic's energy division, which supplies batteries to Tesla and other automakers, produces cells with energy densities above 300 watt-hours per kilogram. Sakakibara said the robotics team is working directly with battery engineers to design custom packs shaped to the robot's torso and limbs. "We are not just buying batteries off the shelf," Sakakibara said. "We are co-developing the power system with the robot architecture." Panasonic has not disclosed investment figures for the humanoid program. The company spent 420 billion yen ($2.8 billion) on research and development in the fiscal year ended March 2024, about 4% of revenue. Robotics accounts for a small but growing share. Analysts say Panasonic's vertical integration — batteries, motors, sensors, and AI software all developed in-house — could accelerate development cycles. Competitors often rely on third-party suppliers for key components, creating integration delays. The first Panasonic humanoids will likely handle material transport and machine tending in the company's battery and electronics factories. Warehouse picking and packing will follow. Sakakibara said the robots must meet the same safety and reliability standards as Panasonic's industrial equipment before any external sales. "We have the luxury of being our own first customer," he said. "That lets us iterate fast without promising specs we can't meet." Panasonic shares rose 1.2% in Tokyo trading Monday following the Nikkei report. The stock has gained 18% this year, outperforming the Topix index's 9% rise. Source:asia.nikkei.com

artigo.texto: CIP invests over â¬270 million in Kilmarnock South battery storage project in Scotland Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners has taken the final investment decision for Kilmarnock South, a 350 MW, 1,400 MWh system. Under construction in southern Scotland, the site is due to enter service in early 2028. Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), through its fourth flagship fund Copenhagen Infrastructure IV, has taken the final investment decision for Kilmarnock South. The 350 MW, 1,400 MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) is located in South Ayrshire, southern Scotland. Construction has begun, and commercial operations are expected in the first quarter of 2028, the company said. A commitment of over â¬270 million CIP says the project represents an investment commitment of more than â¬270 million. UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks, for his part, refers to a battery worth GBP 232 million. With a four-hour duration, Kilmarnock South would become the longest-duration asset in CIP's UK storage portfolio. The system would store surplus Scottish wind power that would otherwise go unused and release it to the grid when the network has capacity. Such projects are part of a market where storage operators are multiplying across Europe, as illustrated by the energy storage contracts secured by ML System in Poland worth â¬4.1 million. Company Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners: company profile Four Scottish projects in total Kilmarnock South is CIP's fourth investment in transmission-connected BESS projects in Scotland. It joins Coalburn 1, which reached commercial operations in August 2026, as well as Coalburn 2 and Devilla. Once all four projects are fully commissioned, their combined storage capacity would reach 4.4 GWh, which CIP describes as the equivalent of almost a third of Great Britain's operational battery storage today. CIP's Scottish portfolio would have a total power capacity of 1.85 GW. According to the company, this capacity would match the electricity demand of over 5.5 million households over a two-hour period. Statements from officials Nischal Agarwal, Partner at CIP, says well-sited storage projects bring flexibility to the power system. In his view, they allow the full benefits of low-cost renewables to be captured, strengthen security of supply and help cut and stabilise consumer bills. Michael Shanks notes that a former coal mine at Coalburn is now home to one of Europe's largest batteries. He says these projects reduce the waste of locally generated power and strengthen energy security. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 % Other storage technologies are also advancing, such as the 12 MWh thermal storage system on which BrenX has started construction at the Wolfson hospital.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de comutadores de fibra óptica até 2035: demanda de data centers impulsiona o crescimento Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica entra em uma fase de expansão estrutural, sustentado pelo crescimento incessante da interconexão de data centers (DCI), pelas atualizações de redes de telecomunicações e pela mudança arquitetural em direção a sistemas ópticos abertos e desagregados. Os comutadores de fibra óptica — dispositivos eletro-ópticos ou optomecânicos que encaminham sinais ópticos sem conversão elétrica — são essenciais para gerenciar largura de banda, reduzir a latência e viabilizar redes definidas por software. A demanda se divide entre comutadores de alta confiabilidade e muitos recursos para redes de nível de telecomunicações e comutadores otimizados em custo e com alto número de portas para data centers de hiperescala. O controle sobre plataformas proprietárias de integração fotônica, como MEMS, PLC e fotônica de silício, determina desempenho e custo, enquanto a montagem e o encapsulamento continuam sendo gargalos. As compras são dominadas por relações diretas de design-in com fabricantes de sistemas ópticos, o que torna o sucesso dependente de roteiros tecnológicos plurianuais e de longos ciclos de qualificação. À medida que provedores de nuvem e operadoras buscam maior automação e programabilidade, o mercado migra de componentes isolados para soluções de subsistemas habilitadas por software. Este relatório analisa essas dinâmicas e apresenta uma previsão até 2035, com foco na demanda final, na lógica da cadeia de suprimentos e no posicionamento competitivo. O cenário-base para o mercado de comutadores de fibra óptica até 2035 pressupõe crescimento contínuo do tráfego global de dados, da computação em nuvem e da implantação de 5G/6G, impulsionando a demanda por comutação óptica tanto em telecomunicações quanto em data centers. Espera-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta anual (CAGR) de 8,2% entre 2026 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 220 (2025=100) em 2035. Essa perspectiva é sustentada pela transição em curso para redes ópticas abertas e desagregadas, que amplia o número de pontos de comutação e exige maior programabilidade. Nas telecomunicações, a implantação de CDC-ROADMs e OXCs sustentará a demanda por comutadores MEMS com alto número de portas, enquanto os operadores de data centers adotarão cada vez mais comutadores de circuito óptico para reduzir consumo de energia e latência. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico continuará sendo o maior mercado, impulsionada pela infraestrutura de telecomunicações da China e pelos data centers de hiperescala, enquanto América do Norte e Europa registrarão atualizações constantes. Restrições na cadeia de suprimentos, especialmente de ferramentas especializadas de fabricação e wafers eletro-ópticos, podem moderar o crescimento, mas as expansões de capacidade em andamento devem aliviar os gargalos. A pressão sobre os preços persistirá nos segmentos de menor número de portas, mas o valor migrará para subsistemas integrados com controle por software. O cenário-base não pressupõe mudanças tecnológicas disruptivas, e sim melhorias evolutivas na fotônica de silício e na confiabilidade dos MEMS. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Aumento da demanda por interconexão de data centers (DCI), impulsionado por cargas de trabalho de nuvem e IA - Atualização de redes de telecomunicações para 400G/800G e além, exigindo comutação óptica avançada - Migração para redes ópticas abertas e desagregadas, ampliando os pontos de comutação - Necessidade de menor latência e menor consumo de energia em data centers - Iniciativas governamentais de expansão de banda larga e implantação de 5G - Crescimento da computação de borda e da IoT, impulsionando arquiteturas de rede distribuídas Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Altos custos de qualificação e longos ciclos de design-in para comutadores de nível de telecomunicações - Gargalos na cadeia de suprimentos de componentes fotônicos especializados e ferramentas de fabricação - Erosão de preços nos segmentos de comutadores de baixo número de portas e de uso geral - Desafios técnicos para escalar a fotônica de silício para grandes números de portas - Tensões geopolíticas que afetam o comércio e o acesso à tecnologia, sobretudo entre EUA e China Estrutura da Demanda por Setor de Uso Final Telecomunicações (participação estimada: 40%) As operadoras de telecomunicações estão modernizando suas redes de transporte para lidar com o aumento do tráfego gerado por 5G, fibra até a residência e serviços corporativos. Os comutadores de fibra óptica são essenciais em nós ROADM e OXC para o roteamento dinâmico de comprimentos de onda, viabilizando grades flexíveis e arquiteturas incolores, sem direção e sem contenção (CDC). Até 2035, a demanda será impulsionada pela necessidade de maior número de portas, menor perda de inserção e velocidades de comutação mais rápidas. A transição para 400G/800G e, eventualmente, 1,6T exigirá comutadores com desempenho superior. Além disso, a busca por redes abertas e desagregadas aumentará o número de pontos de comutação, à medida que as operadoras procuram evitar a dependência de fornecedores. artigo.texto: I visit the hospital rooms of my family and church elders relatively regularly. I have never been to the hospital to visit any of my young cousins, but that changed a week ago. As a heat dome covered Memphis and the Mid-South, my 21-year-old cousin, Ra’Kelle Miller, was struggling to breathe after five minutes outdoors and was rushed to the emergency room. Neither her nebulizer nor asthma pump worked to open her airways. She lives a few miles away from Colossus I and only a couple of miles away from the Valero Oil Refinery. The pollution from these facilities, and the power plant with the illegal gas turbines in neighboring Southaven, are having a real impact on our community’s health now. Politicians and talking heads are leaving the people impacted by hyperscale data centers behind when discussing the “economic development” they think data centers can bring. Memphis is becoming a testing ground for the future of artificial intelligence. But before we rush into that future, we need to pause and ask: What will it cost the people who live here? SpaceXAI’s Colossus data center arrived in Memphis under the cover of NDAs and secret meetings that never included people from the community. That rush to secrecy and to market has led to tons of harmful pollutants being emitted into our air and lungs. SpaceXAI is raking in billions of dollars a month, and all we have to show for it is $30M in city and county tax revenue and temporary construction jobs filled by people from out of town. The tax money is a pittance compared to SpaceXAI’s value and profits. We should be ashamed, not celebrating how we are being treated. SpaceXAI’s Colossus data center has put extraordinary demands on Memphis for electricity, water and other infrastructure. To power those demands, SpaceXAI’s founder, Elon Musk, has relied on dozens of methane gas turbines that emit nitrogen oxides and other pollutants with well-documented health risks. The full health and environmental consequences for Memphis residents continue to worsen. The Memphis City Council has an opportunity to help us learn from this colossal mistake by pausing to think, learn and act in the best interest of the people of Memphis. The council is scheduled for a third reading and vote on Ordinance 5982 on Tuesday. The ordinance proposes pausing new large-scale data center development for 12 months to give Memphis time to study the impact of facilities like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, allow for community input on where they are built, and develop regulations that protect our air, water, land and jobs. There’s more than enough reason to pause and research this before expanding the existing facilities or allowing more. The environmental concerns are substantial. A recent Reuters report found that Musk’s company has installed many more gas turbines than it claimed, and without proper permitting. The majority of those turbines are in neighboring Southaven, near predominantly Black communities of Whitehaven and Westwood that already face elevated rates of respiratory illness. The five-mile affected area extends across the state line into Memphis, including John P. Freeman Middle School. The Reuters report calculated that 30 methane gas turbines with available emissions data could produce nearly 2,500 tons of nitrogen oxides, 4,000 tons of carbon monoxide, and 22 tons of formaldehyde annually, assuming they operate continuously at 80% capacity. The report says that the EPA states that these turbines typically operate around the clock at 80% capacity or more. The American Lung Association states that nitrogen dioxide, one of the nitrogen oxides produced by these turbines, increases toxic smog, which is proven to reduce lung capacity and increase airway inflammation, coughing and wheezing. Toxic smog also worsens asthma and can cause asthma in children, leading to hospital and emergency room visits. Carbon monoxide deprives the body of oxygen, and formaldehyde is a human carcinogen. Cancer rates in South Memphis are already more than 4 times the federal cancer limit. Memphis has become the sacrifice zone for a billionaire’s wealth and profit. An investigative report by ProPublica exposes that this highly elevated cancer rate is due to cancer-causing pollution from industrial sites. Beyond the proposed economic effects of this industrialization are the effects on the lives of the people living in Memphis. People like my cousin, Ra’Kelle. Further, Memphis residents are being asked to not only put themselves in harm’s way for these and future data centers, but also to accommodate this massive land use without the necessary regulation. The current Unified Development Code doesn’t specify regulations for these massive data centers that so heavily consume our water, burden our electrical infrastructure, and threaten our health. The real question isn’t whether Memphis should participate in the AI economy. It’s whether we should allow this unprecedented data center growth to continue under rules written before this technology existed and its adverse health effects were known. We need courage from our City Council to put people at the forefront of these policy decisions. Our lives matter more than hyper-scale data centers. I urge the council to pass Ordinance 5982, which identifies the regulatory gaps and would impose a temporary 12-month moratorium on specified permits for new and expanded data-center development while the city studies and develops permanent regulations. Tennessee is not alone in its quest to understand the impacts of these large-scale facilities before granting permits. Last month, Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared a halt on new data center construction until the state can conduct an audit of energy and water use and the burden on Texas’ electricity grid. Across the country and across party lines, 65% of Americans are opposed to the construction of new large-scale data centers in their communities. artigo.texto: ROX Capital Group Launches ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform Targeting UAE and Oman ROX Capital Group, a UAE-headquartered investor and developer of real assets, has introduced the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform, which will focus on utility-scale and commercial storage schemes across the UAE and Oman while also assessing prospects for regional assembly and manufacturing. The platform intends to assess multiple storage technologies, among them vanadium redox flow, lithium iron phosphate and sodium-ion batteries, plus long-duration options such as CO2 batteries, gravity-based storage, compressed-air energy storage and thermal storage. ROX aims to build alliances with chosen technology suppliers, judging them on their record of delivering large-scale storage projects, long-duration storage know-how where applicable, financial and operational strength, and ownership or control of core technology intellectual property. According to the company, preference will go to suppliers offering bankable systems, proven manufacturing capabilities and the capacity to provide long-term technical support, performance guarantees and warranties. Together with its partners, the platform will chase forthcoming energy storage tenders and evaluate local assembly or manufacturing prospects where commercially feasible. Robin Antony, Founder of ROX Capital Group, said the Gulf is developing some of the world's biggest solar projects, and the next hurdle is making sure clean power stays available after sunset and through peak demand periods. He observed that no single technology can satisfy every requirement, and that the platform is designed to pair the appropriate technology with each project's needs while, where feasible, backing the growth of local manufacturing capability. Antony further stated that lithium-ion batteries have reshaped energy storage and will continue to be a key part of the answer. Nevertheless, he noted that the Gulf's climate, load profile and energy-security priorities call for a wider mix of technologies. High summer temperatures can drive up cooling needs, while solar-heavy systems demand storage over longer stretches after dark. In his view, technologies such as vanadium flow batteries, CO2 batteries, gravity-based storage and thermal storage have a significant role to play alongside lithium-ion solutions. - 1. artigo.texto: Alabama regulators to decide how data center power deals protect customers MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WBMA) — As Alabama works to attract massive data centers, state regulators are preparing to answer a question that could eventually matter to every Alabama Power customer: Who pays for the electricity and infrastructure those facilities require? The Alabama Public Service Commission is scheduled Tuesday to consider new procedures for reviewing electric-service contracts between Alabama Power and large data centers. The proceeding does not decide whether a particular data center can be built. Instead, the PSC is establishing how it will review the power contracts for some of the state's largest electricity users — including whether the data center is paying the additional costs created by its demand and whether the agreement benefits other Alabama Power customers. The commission received 19 sets of initial comments and 10 sets of reply comments before developing the procedures scheduled for consideration Tuesday. What qualifies as a large data center? Under a new Alabama law, the process applies to a "large load data center customer" with an expected peak electricity demand of at least 150 megawatts at one or more contiguous parcels and meeting other requirements in state law. That threshold is important because the PSC says its existing process for reviewing special electricity contracts was developed long before today's large-scale data centers. Alabama Power's current Flexible Contract Rate, known as Rate FCR, dates to 1996 and applies to qualifying commercial and industrial customers. Under that process, contracts are deemed approved 10 days after filing unless the PSC disapproves them. The commission acknowledged in July that large data center contracts may require more time to review because they can require significantly more electricity capacity and energy than the types of customers contemplated when the existing system was established. Why should an Alabama Power customer care? At the center of the new law is a consumer protection. Before approving one of these contracts, the PSC must determine that its pricing and terms are expected to recover from the data center the incremental costs of providing its electric service and promote positive benefits for other retail customers. Incremental costs include additional expenses involving electricity generation, transmission and distribution that would not have been incurred without the data center, along with fuel costs and taxes. Put more simply: The regulatory framework is intended to determine whether a large data center pays the additional electric costs associated with serving it instead of shifting those costs to existing customers. State law also directs regulators to consider whether a data center agreement could lower costs for other customers, improve the efficiency of the power system and contribute to economic growth in the community where it is located. The PSC's action Tuesday does not itself change residential electric rates. More time to review contracts The PSC proposed in July replacing the existing process for qualifying data center contracts with a dedicated review system. Under the initial proposal, Alabama Power would have to provide regulators with the complete proposed contract and supporting information showing how the agreement complies with the new law. That would include evidence addressing the data center's incremental costs, effects on other customers' costs, power-system efficiency and economic-development benefits. The Alabama Attorney General would also receive an unredacted copy of the filing and supporting documents. PSC staff and the attorney general could then ask Alabama Power questions and request additional information. The proposed formal review period would increase from 10 days to 60 days. However, the original proposal contains an important provision: If the PSC does not issue an order rejecting the contract within those 60 days, the contract would be automatically deemed approved. No affirmative commission vote or approval order would be required. Whether that provision remains in the final procedures is one issue to watch Tuesday. Alabama Power says reviews already happen before contracts are filed Alabama Power told the commission in July that the existing 10-day approval period does not represent the entire review process. The company said it historically works with PSC staff before formally filing a contract and triggering the approval clock. According to Alabama Power, its most recent pre-filing review lasted nearly 60 days, while each of the two proposed contracts before it underwent review for several months. The company said that during the 30 years Rate FCR has existed, it has consistently waited to formally file a contract until it understood PSC staff had enough information to demonstrate that the proposal satisfied the existing criteria. Alabama Power temporarily agreed this summer to extend the formal review period for qualifying data center contracts from 10 to 45 days while the PSC developed permanent procedures. Those temporary changes lasted until the new state law took effect Oct. 1. How much will customers be allowed to see? Transparency also became an issue during the PSC proceeding. The commission's original proposal called for Alabama Power to file a public version of each proposed contract, with information redacted when necessary, while providing unredacted information to regulators and the attorney general. The PSC specifically asked commenters to address what information should be publicly available and what should remain confidential. Regulators also sought input on whether they should monitor contracts after approval to determine their actual effects on other customers and Alabama Power's system. One Alabama resident and ratepayer, Arie Lucille Kimble-Foster, urged the PSC to protect genuinely sensitive infrastructure information while keeping other information available

artigo.texto: Sand Batteries From Finnish Startup Offer New Renewable Energy Storage Option Polar Night Energies sand-filled silos show promise for load-balancing heating systems Builders are preparing the way to fill 2,400 tons of local sand into a silo under construction off a rural route between two large lakes in southern Finland in what will be, when finished, the second heat-storage battery for renewable energy operating in the region. Currently designed to power local district heating networks, the ‘sand battery’ is the brainchild of startup company Polar Night Energy. It now has two utility partners in the region deploying the technology. One sand battery has operated since 2025 in the town of Pornainen; the second is under construction about an hour’s drive away in the larger town of Vääksy. A sand battery is a large silo filled with an inert, non-combustible material that absorbs and retains heat from superheated air. The air circulates through a network of pipes and ducts coiled through the silo. This heat energy can come courtesy of excess electric power from renewable sources such as wind or solar. That power often arrives at the wrong time, creating a use-it-or-lose-it problem. This issue has stalked renewables for decades, spurring a hunt to develop creative energy-storage solutions. A sand battery uses electricity to power resistance elements (like a toaster, only bigger) that heat air flowing into the battery. The sand inside—or in the case of the Pornainen battery, the crushed soapstone recycled from a local fireplace manufacturer—can hold that heat. Internal temperatures can reach 500° to 600°C, or 930° to 1,100°F. The stored heat is then dispatched, on demand, via a heat exchanger. The output can be heated air, water, or steam, explains Annette Höglund-Dönnes, chief commercial officer at Polar Night Energy, based in nearby Tampere. The sand battery components include steel, piping, an electric fan and resistors, insulation, and a steel carriage. The idea came to Tommi Eronen and Markku Ylönen, now Polar Night Energy’s chief executive and chief technology officers, respectively, when they were students in the early 2010s. They developed it in a backyard. By 2022 they had a pilot battery running, successfully boosting runoff from a data center for heating purposes. Looking for quick answers on construction and engineering topics? Try Ask ENR, our new smart AI search tool. Ask ENR → That same year the utility Loviisan Lämpö, which is owned by a private equity firm, bought the heating business from a utility serving Pornainen’s 5,000 people. That’s when the town's mayor, Antti Kuusema, got a call. If the town was willing, Lämpö intended to install a 2,000-ton, 1 MW/100 MWh sand battery unit. It was in place by 2025, replacing the oil-and-wood-chip boiler the town used, along with biomass, to operate its district heating network. “Our experience has been very good. The idea for us as a small municipality has been to try to reduce carbon emissions in all operations,” Kuusela says. So far it’s meant a 60% to 70% reduction in carbon emissions in its district heating, and no more oil burning. District heating networks are specific environments: they are common in Scandinavia, less so elsewhere, but there are about 2,500 in the United States (including the steam tunnel system in Manhattan). They distribute heat from a central source, be it fossil, geothermal, or nuclear, through a spaghetti network of insulated pipes into surrounding residential or industrial areas. As of July 2026, the foundation was in place at the Vääksy sand battery site, which will be a 2MW/250 MWh facility, and construction was moving ahead for spring 2027 operation. Polar Night Energy recently inked a distribution deal to expand its reach into the Baltic states, partnering with US investors Solsiden Wangard Family Office and SIA Soldag, a construction firm based in Latvia. Plans call for the next sand battery to be even larger—perhaps 10 MW. The sand batteries are now being used for heat in cold weather, but the technology is not strictly tied to that, Höglund-Dönnes says. They could find industrial uses at a shipyard, university campus or in dairies for pasteurization. “You just need to have the need for heat,” she says.

artigo.texto: Godawari Power Gets Green Light For 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System In Maharashtra Godawari Power's subsidiary, Godawari New Energy, has received key environmental clearance from Maharashtra's SEAC-3 for a 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System building in AURIC. This critical milestone follows a cumulative capex of ₹501 crore already deployed into the BESS segment as of June 2026 and the recent incorporation of a dedicated clean energy EPC subsidiary. Market snapshot: Godawari Power & Ispat Limited's wholly owned subsidiary, Godawari New Energy Private Limited, has received fresh environmental clearance to construct an industrial building for its upcoming 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System. The greenfield facility is being developed at the AURIC Bidkin Industrial Area in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra, signaling major progress in the company's strategic pivot toward clean energy technology. Data Snapshot - Incurred ₹501 crore in capital expenditure for the BESS project as of June 30, 2026. - Subscribed to ₹150 crore in equity shares on a rights basis on July 3, 2026, taking total investment in subsidiary Godawari New Energy to ₹600 crore. - Reported Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue of ₹1,750.47 crore and a consolidated net profit of ₹222.37 crore. - Offered a 31.45-acre industrial plot at AURIC Bidkin Industrial Area for setting up its downstream Cold Rolling Mill project on September 24, 2026. What's Changed - GPIL's transition from cyclical steel manufacturing to a structural green energy platform is accelerating. The environmental clearance for Godawari New Energy's industrial building in AURIC clears the regulatory path for physical construction of the 20 GWh BESS facility. Parallelly, GPIL incorporated Godawari Energy Solutions on October 1, 2026, establishing a dedicated, in-house EPC and O&M vehicle to manage turnkey execution and capture integrated project margins. Key Takeaways - Environmental Clearance Secured: Godawari New Energy received environmental clearance from Maharashtra's SEAC-3, enabling structural construction of the 20 GWh battery storage facility in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar. - Robust Financial Backing: GPIL has already deployed ₹501 crore in BESS capex as of June 30, 2026, and scaled its equity investment in the subsidiary to ₹600 crore to fund project development. - Synergistic Land Infrastructure: Alongside the BESS facility, GPIL's downstream CRM project has secured a 31.45-acre land allotment at the same AURIC master-planned smart city, consolidating downstream manufacturing operations in Maharashtra. - EPC Ecosystem Integration: The newly incorporated Godawari Energy Solutions arm expands GPIL's capabilities to manage utility-scale clean energy installation and operations internally. SAHI Perspective GPIL's transition strategy is structured to build a highly captive energy storage value chain. By utilizing Godawari New Energy for battery integration and Godawari Energy Solutions for in-house EPC, the group is mitigating execution leakages. Securing environmental clearance for the 20 GWh BESS building is a crucial de-risking milestone that ensures civil works can proceed on schedule for a planned Q1 FY28 commercial launch. Furthermore, opting for AURIC—a master-planned smart city with ready plug-and-play utilities—bypasses the historical infrastructure and water allotment delays that have slowed the company's steel expansions in Chhattisgarh. Market Implications The clearance provides immediate medium-term visibility on GPIL's growth pipeline, which is key as traditional steel divisions remain subject to commodity price cycles. Investors are likely to react favorably to this tangible execution milestone, which validates the feasibility of GPIL's long-term clean energy initiatives. However, core profitability will remain driven by iron ore pellet realizations in the immediate quarters, with the BESS segment requiring further working capital deployment before generating meaningful margins in FY28. Trading Signals Market Bias: Bullish The regulatory clearance for the 20 GWh BESS building substantially de-risks GPIL's clean energy capex pipeline. With ₹501 crore already spent as of Q1 FY27 and the project on track for Q1 FY28 commissioning, GPIL is positioned as a rare first-mover in utility-scale industrial storage. Overweight: Clean Energy, Power Infrastructure, Industrial Engineering Trigger Factors: - Commencement of physical civil construction at the AURIC BESS site. - Operational setup and bagging of first EPC projects by Godawari Energy Solutions. - Formal registration and execution of land deeds for the 31.45-acre CRM plot at AURIC. Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months) Industry Context India's clean energy landscape is experiencing massive grid-scale storage mandates to balance renewable power supply. State and central agencies are aggressively bidding out gigawatt-hour battery storage contracts. GPIL's 20 GWh manufacturing facility—utilizing large-format Grade-1 LFP cells secured via supply deals with EVE Power—positions it strategically to capture early-stage tenders. The integration of its own CRM steel output into structural battery container manufacturing represents a compelling vertical integration play. Key Risks to Watch - Supply Chain Volatility: Dependance on imported lithium-ion cells from global partners exposes the project to geopolitical trade barriers and component pricing shifts. - Execution Timelines: Achieving the target Q1 FY28 commercial launch depends on smooth civil works execution and tech transfers without further regulatory bottlenecks. - Capex Pressure: While backed by solid cash generation (net profit of ₹222.37 crore in Q1 FY27), the overall transition is highly capital-intensive and could strain balance sheet liquidity if steel margins deteriorate. artigo.texto: Rox wagers on the Gulf’s storage gap Rox Capital Group, a Dubai-based asset manager focused on sustainability, is in talks with potential partners for a new energy-storage platform targeting utility-scale and commercial projects in the UAE and Oman, founder Robin Antony tells EnterpriseAM UAE. Rox’s plans will focus on storage technologies ranging from lithium-ion, flow, and sodium-ion batteries to longer-duration options such as thermal, gravity, and compressed-air storage, according to a press release. The plan includes jointly submitting bids for upcoming storage tenders. Depending on the project, Rox could invest directly, co-develop with partners, or broker contracts between technology providers, investors, and project owners, Antony said. The pitch is that Gulf projects need a mix of technologies: Summer heat raises cooling needs for batteries, and solar-heavy grids need storage that lasts longer after dark, Antony argues. Demand is building: Masdar and EWEC are developing a USD 6.1 bn Abu Dhabi plant that pairs 5.2 GW of solar with 19 GWh of storage, and Masdar’s Ibri III project is Oman’s first solar-plus-storage plant. Still no specifics: Rox hasn’t named partners, projects, or target tenders, and Antony declined to give a capital target or timeline. Following up on A:5 (xNF>AF) A UAE delegation was in Washington last week pushing for deeper tech ties, including follow-through on the US decision to ease export controls on the UAE. The trip was led by Omran Sharaf, assistant minister for advanced science and technology at the Foreign Affairs Ministry, according to a ministry statement. The delegation met White House science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios and Under Secretary of State for Economic Growth Jacob Helberg. Talks covered AI, cybersecurity, space, quantum computing, and post-quantum encryption. With the Commerce Department, the agenda covered trade facilitation and export management. BACKGROUND- Washington moved the UAE into Country Group A:5, its allies-only export tier, in July. That lets G42 and other approved firms buy advanced chips without a license, as we’ve reported. But G42’s access lapses in April 2027 unless it’s extended, and G42 is reportedly in exploratory talks about selling a majority stake to US firms to secure access beyond that date. The two countries are working together on a 5 GW UAE-US AI campus in Abu Dhabi, anchored by the 1 GW Stargate UAE cluster.

artigo.texto: Grid-forming capabilities support multiple grid-restoration functions The project plays an important role in supporting voltage and frequency stability at a key point in Cambodia's central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. Its grid-forming capabilities were put through a series of demanding system-restoration scenarios, demonstrating how energy storage can take on a more active role in supporting the power system. Key highlights include: - Large-scale black start from zero voltage: 516 grid-forming PCS units successfully energized the entire plant from zero voltage, establishing stable voltage and frequency across the system. - Restoration of a 240 km transmission network: The system supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations, while maintaining stable operation as the network was progressively restored. - Support for multiple generation sources: The system supported the start-up and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant, before the restored network was operated together with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, energy storage and loads. - Stable operation under challenging grid conditions: During restoration, the system remained stable through five transformer energization events, including a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stability when synchronizing different power sources under a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees, demonstrating its ability to handle challenging conditions during system recovery. - Extended islanded operation: The system operated independently for 3.5 hours, demonstrating that the energy storage system could continue supporting the local network even when separated from the main grid. - Seamless transitions: The project completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, with voltage deviation kept below 2% and transient frequency fluctuation within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. "This project demonstrates that the value of grid-forming energy storage goes far beyond storing electricity.When a power system faces disturbances or loses normal grid support, grid-forming technology can help establish and maintain stable voltage and frequency, support system restoration and keep the grid operating reliably," said Michael Ruan, Regional Director of Sungrow Southeast Asia and South Asia. "Through projects like this, Sungrow is helping turn energy storage into a more active grid-support asset and bringing proven grid-forming capabilities to the evolving power systems of Southeast Asia." Reducing Technical Risk and Ensuring Timely Delivery Faced with strict test protocols, complex power system scenarios, a compressed construction schedule and rainy‑season working conditions with ambient temperature up to 40°C, Sungrow's cross‑functional team covering pre-sales, on‑site delivery and R&D collaborated closely to deliver high‑quality project outcomes: - 20-day commissioning and testing: The on‑site team worked relentlessly under hot and humid conditions for two consecutive months. The team wrapped up hot commissioning plus three rounds of performance tests within 20 days to guarantee timely grid‑connection. - End‑to‑End Service Solution: Sungrow provides full‑lifecycle and one‑stop services spanning integrated design of storage and monitoring systems, EPC‑related support, equipment design, commissioning and O&M services, enabling the customer to fulfill customized grid‑level requirements with reduced management overhead. As Southeast Asia advances its energy transition, Sungrow will continue to bring proven energy storage technologies and solutions to the region, helping customers build more reliable and sustainable power infrastructure. Contact: Luly Wang, luly.wang@sungrow-hq.com Source: Sungrow Power

The global lithium silicon battery market is positioned for significant expansion through 2035, driven by escalating demand for higher energy density in electric vehicles and premium stationary storage applications. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries with graphite anodes, lithium silicon batteries incorporate silicon into the anode, enabling substantially greater energy capacity per unit of weight and volume. This technological advantage is critical for automotive OEMs seeking to extend driving range without increasing battery pack size, and for commercial and industrial storage operators where physical space is at a premium. However, market growth is tempered by challenges including silicon's volumetric expansion during cycling, which necessitates specialized binders, electrolytes, and mechanical designs, creating a high barrier to system integration. The supply chain for high-purity engineered silicon anode materials remains nascent, and qualification cycles for automotive and aerospace applications are lengthy. artigo.texto: A corrida pela inteligência artificial está criando uma infraestrutura gigantesca. Empresas de tecnologia estão investindo bilhões de dólares em data centers, chips, memória, redes e sistemas de energia para atender ao crescimento da IA. Agora, uma projeção coloca em perspectiva o tamanho desse movimento. Para sustentar o nível de investimento esperado nos próximos anos, o mercado de inteligência artificial precisaria chegar perto de US$ 6 trilhões em receita anual até 2031. O valor é uma estimativa baseada no ritmo projetado de expansão da infraestrutura, e não significa que US$ 6 trilhões serão gastos na construção de data centers. Investimento pode chegar a US$ 1,5 trilhão por ano A projeção considera que os gastos anuais com infraestrutura de IA podem alcançar US$ 1,5 trilhão em 2031. A conta inclui novos data centers, capacidade computacional e atualizações de equipamentos já instalados, como GPUs, memória e sistemas de rede. A estimativa utiliza uma hipótese de que os investimentos representariam cerca de 25% da receita do setor. Nesse cenário, uma infraestrutura anual de US$ 1,5 trilhão exigiria aproximadamente US$ 6 trilhões em receitas para ser sustentada. Boa parte dessa receita ainda não existe O problema apontado pela análise está na diferença entre o mercado que já existe e o tamanho necessário para sustentar a infraestrutura projetada. Aplicações voltadas ao consumidor, incluindo assinaturas e publicidade, poderiam gerar entre US$ 200 bilhões e US$ 400 bilhões por ano em 2031. Já soluções empresariais baseadas em produtividade e automação poderiam representar entre US$ 1 trilhão e US$ 1,4 trilhão. Juntos, esses mercados chegariam a algo entre US$ 1,2 trilhão e US$ 1,8 trilhão. Isso deixa cerca de US$ 4,2 trilhões que precisariam surgir de novas aplicações e mercados. Robôs e carros autônomos podem ajudar Entre as possibilidades estão veículos autônomos, automação industrial, robótica e outras aplicações conhecidas como IA física. Também aparecem áreas como descoberta de medicamentos, desenvolvimento de novos produtos, simulações e gêmeos digitais. A expectativa é que essas tecnologias criem mercados capazes de gerar receitas que ainda são pequenas ou inexistentes atualmente. Isso significa que o futuro financeiro da IA não depende apenas de chatbots e ferramentas de produtividade. Seria necessário que a tecnologia encontrasse aplicações comerciais muito maiores. Data centers estão ficando cada vez maiores A expansão também acontece em escala física. Segundo a projeção, o tamanho e o custo das principais instalações de IA estão crescendo rapidamente, com capacidade e investimento podendo dobrar em intervalos de aproximadamente 12 a 16 meses. O consumo de eletricidade acompanha esse movimento. A expectativa é que o consumo global dos data centers mais do que dobre até 2030, chegando a aproximadamente 945 TWh por ano. A inteligência artificial aparece como um dos principais motores desse crescimento. A conta depende do sucesso comercial da IA A projeção não afirma que o setor necessariamente alcançará US$ 6 trilhões em receita. O número representa o tamanho anual que o mercado precisaria atingir para sustentar o nível de investimento previsto dentro das premissas utilizadas. A questão central, portanto, não é apenas quantos data centers serão construídos. É também descobrir quais aplicações conseguirão transformar toda essa capacidade computacional em valor econômico. Nos próximos anos, a resposta deverá depender da capacidade da indústria de transformar a atual corrida por infraestrutura em produtos e serviços que encontrem demanda suficiente em larga escala. artigo.texto: GlobalFoundries brings massive solar array, battery storage online in Essex Junction ESSEX JUNCTION, Vt. (WCAX) - A massive new solar array and battery storage system are now online at GlobalFoundries’ Essex Junction campus to offset demand on the power grid and lower electric bills. With the flip of the ceremonial breakers, GlobalFoundries’ new on-site solar array and 16-megawatt battery energy storage system are now online, marking a milestone for the Green Mountain State. “It’s the largest battery ever installed in Vermont, right here behind our own meter,” said GlobalFoundries’ Dan Colello. The battery goes hand in hand with the solar array, which sits on more than 30 acres of already developed but underutilized land that includes an old parking lot and brownfield. The energy from the panels is then stored in the four-hour, or 16-megawatt-hour, battery energy storage system. Related Story: “The battery is positioned to be able to reduce peak. Over that four hours of duration, it will discharge to reduce the consumption by the facility in its footprint on the regional grid,” said Rory Jones, co-founder of Lightshift Energy. Gov. Phil Scott joined in on the celebration Monday, commending the project on saving Vermonters money. “In fact, it should reduce costs by more than $40 million over the next 25 years. That’s real money. The savings is important to GlobalFoundries, and the Vermonters that work here. It’s also important for all of us as ratepayers,” Scott said. The project, part of GlobalFoundries’ net-zero goals, won’t disrupt the company’s energy needs for manufacturing. “The project demonstrates how battery storage can be integrated into advanced manufacturing, while maintaining the quality our operations require. And it provides a valuable lesson about future projects across the whole of GlobalFoundries,” said GlobalFoundries’ CEO Tim Breen. Copyright 2026 WCAX. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Data centers, Flock cameras discussed in city council meeting adopting 2027 budget EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - City council members approved a 180-day moratorium on new data center development Monday night, pausing all related construction while officials study its potential impact on the city. City leaders say the pause gives them time to research effects on infrastructure, utilities and neighborhoods, and to finalize zoning rules before any new projects move forward. The moratorium can be extended if officials need more time. Council President, Ben Trockman said the decision followed sustained public pressure. “We had multiple conversations — I’ve heard in council quite frequently, and I think something that we see in our inboxes quite often as well, is that there is concern,” Trockman said. $152 Million Budget Approved for 2027 Council also adopted the city’s 2027 budget, totaling more than $152 million. Major allocations include: - ~$6 million for restoring 27 miles of city roads - ~$20 million for parks and recreation - ~$30 million for water and sewer projects - $182,000 for Flock Safety cameras — a line item that drew criticism from residents Flock Camera Funding Sparks Privacy Concerns Some residents like Philip Elpers say the automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras amount to an invasion of privacy and argue they were installed without public input. “There has to be a commitment in the budget that actually stops all of this in the future until we say it’s okay,” Elpers said. Police Chief Defends Flock Camera Use Evansville Police Chief Philip Smith addressed the concerns directly at Monday’s meeting, saying the department has strict procedures in place to prevent misuse. He pointed to the cameras’ role in solving crimes, including a 2022 child kidnapping case. Smith said the technology has not been found unconstitutional and defended the department’s track record. “Not one time, in not one courtroom in the United States has ALPR been ruled as a violation of the 4th Amendment,” Smith said. “We’ve had Flock here since 2021, and we’ve not had one officer violate the policy or procedure of Flock usage in Evansville, Indiana.” Officials say even though the budget was adopted, they can still bring up flock cameras in future meetings if needed.
