artigo.texto: In response to Dwayne Yancey’s “Data centers are creating blue-collar jobs. Are Democrats on the wrong side politically of these workers?”, September 29, 2026. Dwayne Yancey is right that the Munters plant in Botetourt County is making real things for real wages, and right that a moratorium would reach workers nobody in the moratorium debate is thinking about. He is also right that this is more complicated than a bumper sticker. I want to take that last point further than the column does, because the jobs number is softer than it looks and the rest of the ledger rarely gets added up. Start with where the numbers come from. The PwC study Yancey cites was commissioned by the Data Center Coalition, the industry’s trade association, and published on a website the Coalition runs. Those are the sources available, which is the problem. Read it as a party’s filing rather than a finding. The JLARC number is more interesting than either side has noticed. Yancey reports about 50 jobs for each 250,000-square-foot facility, citing JLARC’s 2024 study. What the study says is that “several data center representatives indicated” that figure, and that about half of them are contract workers: electricians, pipefitters, security. Fifty is also the number the statute asks for. To claim Virginia’s sales tax exemption a data center must invest $150 million and create 50 jobs at 150 percent of the local average wage, with lower thresholds in distressed localities. Virginia is not observing that data centers employ fifty people. Virginia is observing that they employ the number Virginia told them to employ. Then the measurement. No series publishes union membership annually for a single trade in a single metropolitan area, so far as I could find, so I built one from sixteen years of federal filings signed under penalty of perjury. Inside electrical construction membership in hyperscale data center metros grew 17.3 percent faster than in comparable metros through 2025. Covered employment in those same places, on the government’s own count, grew 9.1 to 11.9 percent faster. Both numbers are real and they are not the same claim. Some of what reads as job creation is a trade organizing work that was already there. That is a good thing for those workers, and it is different from hundreds of new jobs, and anyone arguing either side of a moratorium should know which one they are holding. Now Botetourt, since that is where the column starts. Google bought 312.55 acres of the county’s flagship business park at Greenfield in June 2025 for $14,055,406.37, plus $4 million for county initiatives, on an option signed the previous October. Eight weeks after that signature the county added “data center” to the permitted uses of the only zoning district that could host one and called it housekeeping. The staff report on the accompanying rezoning said “no use or concept is identified at this time.” The county had been hosting Google site visits since January 2024 under the code name Project Raspberry. The performance agreement caps the company’s effective equipment tax rate at $2.40 per $100 for twenty years per building. It binds the county and its development authority, on a records request reaching Google’s confidential information, to notify the company and help narrow or resist it. It assigns Google “all media and press relation services” concerning its involvement with the county. And it promises $1 billion and 50 jobs for each data center built. Fifty again. A local government signed away its own ability to talk about the largest transaction in its history. The noise standard it will hold the finished campus to asks only whether the sound is clearly audible fifty feet from the property line. None of that appears in a jobs count. Neither does the transmission. When a 765-kilovolt line is built in PJM, Schedule 12 splits the cost two ways: half by a zone’s share of regional load, half by a flow calculation. Neither half asks where the towers go. Dominion’s zone carries about 45 percent. The farmer whose fields the line crosses is not a stakeholder in any sense the proceeding recognizes. Once the line is certificated he is a landowner facing condemnation if he says no. Water is its own accounting. The Department of Environmental Quality simulated a three-million-gallon-a-day withdrawal, the published upper end for a hyperscale campus on evaporative cooling, at nine locations spanning the coastal plain. All nine failed the permitting criteria. That is the closest thing the commonwealth has to an answer about whether the eastern half of the state can physically host what it is approving. Then there is the subsidy, which is the part that should trouble anyone who cares what the money could otherwise do. Virginia’s exemption cost the commonwealth about $1.94 billion in forgone revenue in fiscal 2025 by operator self-reporting, or about $1.6 billion by state audit. JLARC’s own incentives table puts the return at 48 cents in state revenue for every dollar spent, against 41 cents for the average Virginia incentive, and says that on the state’s side of the ledger it does not pay for itself. The same table credits the exemption with 84 jobs per million spent against 58 for the average, which is the industry’s best card and a real one. It beats the average incentive on jobs and still loses money. What has never been measured for Virginia is how much of the investment the exemption actually caused. Georgia measured its own. The Carl Vinson Institute at the University of Georgia found that 30 percent of Georgia’s data centers could be attributed to the exemption, and that the other 70 percent would exist without it. The broader incentives literature points nearer 25 percent. Virginia is finally getting a number of its own. artigo.texto: A tática da Rússia envolve o uso de drones para atacar centros de dados e redes de telecomunicações ucranianas. Os ataques de drones russos contra centros de dados e telecomunicações ucranianos estão exercendo uma pressão significativa sobre as capacidades de defesa aérea e as redes de conectividade da Ucrânia. De meados de setembro ao início de outubro, as forças russas lançaram uma série de ataques contra importantes centros de dados e redes de telecomunicações na Ucrânia . Essa ofensiva marcou um aumento no uso de veículos aéreos não tripulados (VANTs) movidos a jato, representando um desafio significativo para a infraestrutura de tecnologia da informação e a rede de defesa aérea de Kiev. Alvos e frequência de ataques com drones a jato Na manhã de 27 de setembro, ataques de drones russos atingiram a sede da Kyivstar em Kiev, a maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia. No mesmo dia, o Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou um ataque a um centro de dados da rede de telecomunicações ucraniana Vodafone. Anteriormente, em 15 de setembro, o centro de dados da BeMobile foi afetado por um ataque aéreo, interrompendo diversos serviços que operavam na plataforma UCloud. Em 23 de setembro, a infraestrutura de dois provedores de rede, UTELS e Pavutyna, foi danificada, deixando aproximadamente 100.000 residências em Kiev e arredores sem conectividade à internet. Em 25 de setembro, o centro de dados da Datagroup em Solomianskyi, Kiev, também sofreu danos após um ataque com drone, obrigando a empresa a manter as operações a partir de locais de backup. O Ministério da Defesa russo afirmou que essas instalações foram alvejadas por desempenharem um papel no processamento e transmissão de dados de inteligência militar para a Ucrânia. Em contrapartida, o Ministro das Relações Exteriores ucraniano, Andrii Sybiha, rejeitou essa alegação, enfatizando que se tratava de infraestrutura civil essencial para a transmissão de alertas de mísseis e drones ao público. A campanha prosseguiu em 30 de setembro, quando a Rússia anunciou um ataque ao centro de dados De Novo, em Kiev, seguido por um ataque a um centro de dados em Odessa, em 4 de outubro. De acordo com a ex-vice-ministra da Defesa da Ucrânia, Kateryna Chernohorenko, a intensidade dos ataques com drones, incluindo os da série Shahed, contra instalações de dados, aumentou drasticamente. Você também pode gostar Limitações da infraestrutura em nuvem e da construção subterrânea Desde os estágios iniciais do conflito, a Ucrânia descentralizou proativamente sua infraestrutura digital. Em 17 de fevereiro de 2022, o Parlamento ucraniano aprovou a Lei de Serviços em Nuvem e, posteriormente, emitiu resoluções permitindo que órgãos estatais colocassem sistemas de informação e registros públicos em serviços de nuvem estrangeiros durante períodos de lei marcial. Por meio do dispositivo de armazenamento Snowball da Amazon Web Services (AWS), mais de 10 petabytes de dados de 42 agências governamentais e 24 universidades foram migrados para a nuvem. O PrivatBank, que atende aproximadamente 40% da população da Ucrânia, também concluiu a migração de seus sistemas para a nuvem. Embora o backup de dados no exterior ajude a minimizar o risco de perda permanente de dados caso a infraestrutura seja atingida, as soluções de computação em nuvem não podem substituir a infraestrutura física local. Redes de fibra óptica, fontes de energia e estações de retransmissão locais continuam sendo elos vulneráveis, fazendo com que os usuários percam a conectividade quando as estações de retransmissão são destruídas. A realocação de data centers inteiros para o subsolo também apresenta inúmeros desafios técnicos. Essas instalações exigem sistemas de alimentação de energia de alta capacidade, mecanismos de refrigeração especializados e manutenção contínua, o que torna a construção subterrânea dispendiosa e demorada. Por outro lado, análises de código aberto (OSINT) da Dnipro Osint indicam que a Rússia também está acelerando a construção de uma instalação subterrânea de produção de drones com uma área estimada em aproximadamente 42.000 m² na Zona Econômica Especial de Alabuga, no Tartaristão. A capacidade de interceptar drones e o desafio da manutenção do F-16. As variantes de UAVs movidas a jato apresentam maiores desafios de engenharia em comparação com os UAVs tradicionais movidos a hélice. Graças aos seus motores a jato, essas armas atingem velocidades mais altas e tetos de voo mais elevados do que os modelos Shahed convencionais. Você também pode gostar O presidente Volodymyr Zelensky afirmou que, durante o ataque de 28 de setembro, 90 dos mais de 120 drones russos utilizados eram movidos a jato. A taxa de interceptação apenas para esse grupo de alvos foi de aproximadamente 57%, significativamente inferior à média de 70% para drones convencionais. Para superar essa diferença, a Ucrânia está acelerando o desenvolvimento de aeronaves interceptoras especializadas e a produção nacional de motores a jato. O caça F-16 é considerado um dos interceptores anti-drones mais eficazes disponíveis atualmente em Kiev. No entanto, os procedimentos técnicos para a manutenção dessa frota enfrentam obstáculos logísticos. Segundo o Wall Street Journal, a inspeção técnica de rotina de um F-16 a cada 300 horas de voo pode levar até 40 semanas nas instalações belgas, em comparação com 2 a 6 semanas em condições normais. O porta-voz do Ministério das Relações Exteriores da Ucrânia, Heorhii Tykhyi, e a empresa belga Sabena Engineering afirmaram que os prazos de entrega estão sendo acelerados e que os relatos sobre uma prontidão de combate criticamente baixa são imprecisos. Embora a Bélgica, a Espanha e outros parceiros continuem comprometidos com a entrega de mais caças F-16 e munição, a pressão para manter as horas de voo, peças de reposição e pessoal técnico permanece crucial para a proteção eficaz de data centers contra as novas táticas de ataque da Rússia.

artigo.texto: Beaufort County commissioners holding public hearing & vote on data center moratorium The above video is our WITN+ livestream and may not reflect the content in this story. BEAUFORT COUNTY, N.C. (WITN) - Tonight, Beaufort County commissioners will hear public input and vote on a moratorium for data center developments. The public hearing on the one-year moratorium was originally scheduled for last month but was postponed so the community could have an additional opportunity to share input. Commissioners will then vote on the proposal following the hearing. The moratorium would pause building or expanding large computer facilities used to power artificial intelligence. The commissioners offered an informal hearing during last month’s meeting, where several residents spoke in favor of the moratorium. Residents voiced concerns about noise pollution, emissions and electricity costs from potential data centers. Several residents said they support a moratorium lasting longer than one year. The commissioners’ meeting will start at 5:30 p.m. at 136 W. Second Street in Washington. County commissioners say a public hearing sign-up sheet will be placed on the podium before tonight’s meeting. Copyright 2026 WITN. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Solid-state batteries by 2030: CATL readiness, Chery tests and China’s plan China has officially set 2030 as a target for the initial large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries. A 2026–2030 plan published by seven government departments calls for faster breakthroughs in electrode materials, new electrolytes and other key components, as well as the development of new battery systems. The wording does not mean that most electric cars will switch to the technology by 2030. CATL is also cautious about the outlook. Chairman Robin Zeng said solid-state batteries are only at level 4 on a nine-level technology-readiness scale, while level 9 corresponds to readiness for mass production. He does not expect an inflection point before 2030 and says commercial viability still has to be proven. CATL had earlier named 2027 as a target for producing small pilot batches. Industry forecasts do not point to an overnight revolution either. BloombergNEF expects solid-state batteries to account for about 10% of combined global battery demand from electric vehicles and stationary energy-storage systems by 2035. Analysts expect the technology to appear first mainly in expensive, high-performance vehicles. Chinese companies are already committing substantial money to the next technology step. Chery plans more than 10 billion yuan in total investment in advanced technologies, including all-solid-state batteries. Its Rhino S solid-state module has reached a claimed energy density of 400 Wh/kg, with the first vehicle-integration tests planned for 2027. For now, 2030 therefore looks more like the start of industrial scaling than the date when conventional lithium-ion batteries disappear from mass-market vehicles. artigo.texto: Noah Berger/Getty Images via Amazon Web Services Over the next five years, Amazon will invest more than $1 billion in education, energy and water conservation, as well as in infrastructure in communities that host their data centers, the company said last week. As part of its “Built Together” framework, residents of Amazon’s data center communities will receive free community college and hands-on workforce training to prepare them for in-demand career fields, such as HVAC, IT, health care, education, public safety and advanced manufacturing. When the initiative launches in a few months, Amazon will cover all out-of-pocket expenses that remain after a student receives financial aid. The company anticipates that the program will help some 300,000 students access degree programs over the next five years. In addition, Amazon is expanding the network of physical training facilities at and near its data centers. These facilities provide free skilled trade certification programs and direct pathways to jobs with Amazon and its construction partners. The company projects that by the end of 2028, they will train 100,000 workers a year “for real jobs in their hometowns—fully funded by Amazon,” Matt Garman, CEO of Amazon Web Services, wrote in the announcement. The announcement comes amid growing backlash against the AI-fueled proliferation of data centers over the past few years. According to a recent Gallup poll, 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their area, citing strained natural resources, cost-of-living increases, noise pollution and job losses, as well as general negative views about AI. But Amazon, which has at least 900 data centers across 50 countries, claimed in the announcement that many of those concerns stem from “misinformation” and “outright lies,” and that the United States can’t afford to fall behind on building more data centers. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run,” Garman said. “The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so.”

artigo.texto: Hermantown council unanimously passes AUAR review for proposed data center HERMANTOWN, Minn. (Northern News Now) - The Hermantown city council voted unanimously on Monday to approve an Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) for the proposed Google data center. Read: Heated data center debate results in pause to Hermantown city council meeting An AUAR is a state-authorized environmental review process used to study how different development scenarios could affect the environment before construction begins. The 2,700-page AUAR for the proposed Google Data Center includes comments from five government agencies and more than 200 residents. Public concerns listed in the AUAR include environmental impacts, wetlands and transparency to the public. Many data center opponents over the past year have pushed back on the AUAR, arguing it is not as comprehensive as an Environmental Impact Statement. Project leaders who presented at the meeting, including Kimley Horn and Mortenson Construction, said they addressed the public’s concerns in the AUAR. “Many of those items are the direct result of the public process the city facilitated through the AUAR, and demonstrate Google’s commitment to incorporating public input in the development of the project,” said Chris Bates with Mortenson. Public Comment Supporters at the meeting agreed, arguing that Google is acting in good-faith by making these changes, and that the AUAR is a comprehensive framework for the city. They also emphasized the economic benefits of the data center. “One thing I appreciate about the AUAR process is that it allows us to be excited about economic development while also doing the necessary work to understand its impacts,” said Hermantown Chamber of Commerce President Kim Parmeter. On the other hand, opponents of the data center pushed back on the AUAR, asking the city to instead do an Environmental Impact Statement, which they view as a more comprehensive review that would bring in an outside entity to complete it. “They can’t make promises for what’s happening in 5 years,” said Duluth resident Jim Klukkert. “How long has Google been in existence, and they want to tell you that they understand they are making a commitment of 20-25 years?“ MN DNR Letter Another big topic of conversation from both the public and presenters Monday night was the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources. The DNR sent a letter to the city in August asking for clarification and revision on the AUAR. That included mitigation plans and additional monitoring for impacts to wetlands from this project. Presenters on Monday said they made changes based on these letters, and that the DNR never formally objected to the environmental review Vote on Thursday The environmental review for Minnesota Power’s transmission line, which would power the data center, was also up for vote on Monday night. However, city leaders announced that due to the long public comment period on the AUAR vote, they moved for council to reconvene this Thursday. artigo.texto: City of Ozark, Mo., passes an ordinance that imposes restrictions on data center development OZARK, Mo. (KY3) - It’s about to be a lot tougher for data center developers to build in Ozark. On Monday night, the city’s board of aldermen voted unanimously to add more hurdles to data center development. Additions to the city ordinance tackle issues like water use and noise regulations, and others point to public input and transparency. “They would have to hold a mandatory neighborhood meeting for surrounding residents to allow residents to voice their opinions with regard to the development. They would have to submit ongoing noise monitoring and, in fact, maintain a public website,” said Ozark’s Mayor Pro Tem, Chris Aiken. “They will have to document and make public all complaints that they receive as well as their responses to those complaints.” Ozark resident Justin Wisdom says water consumption is towards the top of his list of concerns when it comes to data centers. “They do take a lot of water, and I’ve heard that water rights kind of get a little restricted when data centers are in your vicinity,” said Wisdom. “So, I mean, that’s kind of a pretty big worry.” Aiken says that the board of aldermen believes these changes to the city ordinance also address citizen concerns over potential data centers’ water and electricity consumption. “We’ve included design requirements within our ordinance to make sure that if there is a data center here, it’s using the most efficient cooling systems available,” said Aiken. “They actually have to submit a report from the utility company analyzing the impact that the facility would have on our electrical infrastructure.” Aiken says the city chose to add restrictions to the existing ordinance rather than impose a moratorium or outright ban on data centers. “I think our city determined that, legally, that was maybe a little more risky and that we’d be better off getting out ahead of these developments, placing reasonable restrictions on them so that they’re not going to constitute a nuisance for the people of Ozark,” said Aiken. “I think that’s a good strategy,” said Wisdom. “Make the companies just not even want to come around due to the restrictions and stuff. I think that’s honestly a good way to go.” To read the full ordinance, click here. The ordinance begins on page 105; new additions are in red. artigo.texto: Data centers are a hot-button issue right now, but many executives in Northern Virginia are looking beyond the controversy. Related stories - Despite skyrocketing rates, real estate agent says DC-area homebuyers still have ‘upper hand’ - How Alexandria hopes to transform Duke Street into a more unified corridor - From napkin drawing to final product, this Fairfax business helps inventors through the process A majority of D.C.-area business leaders now believe the centers will have a positive impact on the regional economy, according to a survey. A survey from the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce and Pinkston found 53% of top executives view data centers positively while 34% have doubts. One in eight leaders, 13%, had no opinion. “A majority of them see data centers as a positive economic force, but there is some concern,” Julie Coons, president and CEO of the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce, told WTOP News. “I believe that what business leaders see is that our economy today, and as it evolves into the future, the toehold we have here in Northern Virginia and the greater DMV is so important,” she said. “And data centers do enable those industries that we want to continue to keep here and attract here — cybersecurity, commercial space, quantum of the future. So they’re critical to our economic standing today and certainly in the future.” While many business leaders in the Northern Virginia region are embracing data centers, Tim Tkacz is a bit more guarded. The CEO of Blue Sky Innovators, a Reston-based defense and national security company, said he is “whole hog optimistic” about the technology behind data centers. “We need these,” Tkacz said. “But at the same time, we have to be responsible about the impact that they have on the local communities that they go into.” This was the first time the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce and Pinkston asked about the economic impact of data centers in their quarterly survey. They surveyed 169 CEOs, executives and business owners from companies based in Fairfax, Loudoun, Arlington and Prince William counties as well as the cities of Fairfax, Falls Church and Alexandria. Growing doubts about the economy The survey also found growing pessimism among business leaders about the economy, both nationally and locally. Thirty-six percent of executives expect the regional economy to grow in the next six months, down from 40% in the second quarter. Some 23% believe the local economy will decline slowly or significantly in the coming months. Coons said business leaders expressed a level of caution. “While they maintain high, high confidence in their own business capacity,” Coons said. “They do see regional headwinds.” Pessimism has swelled about the national economy in recent months too, with 47% of leaders now downbeat about the national landscape. That’s up from 38% in the second quarter. Only 34% are optimistic about the national economy. Almost half business leaders, 49%, said their companies are being hurt by President Donald Trump’s foreign policy decisions, led by international trade, tariffs and the war in the Middle East. Hiring and spending plans Two-thirds of business leaders are optimistic about their own company’s outlook. While strong, that’s still down from 77% in the last survey. This rise in pessimism about the local economy has business leaders moving cautiously as they plan for 2027. Some 40% do not plan to change their spending plans in the next six months while 37% plan to increase spending slightly. Only 6% plan to increase spending significantly. As for hiring, a third of business leaders in Northern Virginia, 32%, plan to increase their payrolls and add positions heading into the new year. Almost three in five, 58%, plan to keep staffing about the same. “Let’s watch how things go over the next year or so,” Coons said. Prof. Ashok Jhunjhunwala, Institute Professor, IIT Madras, and Chairman, ITEL Foundation, said collaboration between users, startups, manufacturers, and technology institutions can support the development and adoption of energy storage solutions in India. The collaboration comes as telecom operators and infrastructure providers increasingly look for reliable and efficient energy storage systems to support India’s expanding digital infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Amazon ends secret data center pacts and pledges $1 billion to host towns — AWS promises 30,000 home efficiency retrofits amid 100 proposed bans It will also invest more than $1 billion over five years in communities hosting its facilities. Amazon will no longer require nondisclosure agreements (NDA) with government agencies involved in its data center projects and will adhere to its new Data Center Commitment program designed to address mounting opposition to AI infrastructure, it disclosed on Friday in a blog post. The company also unveiled plans to invest more than $1 billion over five years in communities hosting its facilities. The announcements come as more than 100 data center moratoriums are being considered across the U.S., so AWS wants to make data centers more attractive to locals. No NDAs Amazon's decision to no longer require NDAs from government officials working with it is part of the company's newly announced Data Center Commitment program aimed at making data center building more transparent and somewhat less unpleasant to people living nearby. Among other things, the company vows to hold community open houses, disclose information about projects as early as possible, and listen to local concerns as development proceeds. Amazon also vows annual disclosure of its energy consumption and efficiency, water consumption and efficiency, and the proportion of electricity supplied by carbon-free sources. Speaking of power usage efficiency (PUE), Amazon reports a global PUE of 1.14 for 2025, compared with an industry average of 1.25 and 1.63 for on-premises enterprise data centers. It also says its facilities were 7x more water-efficient than the industry average and that it had reached 75% of its goal to become water-positive by 2030. Many concerns Also, new sites will use backup generators compliant with EPA Tier 4 emissions standards. While Amazon emphasizes that new sites will use backup generators meeting EPA Tier 4 emissions standards, the commitment is somewhat ambiguous in general, as the specification limits vary by engine power and generator classes, whereas Amazon does not specify the generator classes it intends to deploy. The company says an average U.S. data center consumes around 170,000 gallons of water per day, whereas an average Amazon facility uses less than 13,000 gallons, equivalent to 42 U.S. households. However, Amazon does not distinguish between the water consumption of a typical AWS data center designed for general-purpose cloud workloads and newly built AI data centers packed with power-hungry AI accelerators, which certainly have substantially different cooling requirements. In general, Amazon is trying to counter concerns about the resource requirements of data centers, although some of its comparisons remain rather ambiguous. When it comes to energy efficiency, the new Built Together initiative will add more than $1 billion to Amazon’s existing community spending. The company expects to provide more than 300,000 students with access to free community-college education over five years. It currently operates three Modular Training Centers, has six more under development, and plans another 16. Each facility can train roughly 2,000–4,000 people annually, with Amazon targeting as many as 100,000 trained workers per year by the end of 2028. Amazon also plans energy-efficiency upgrades for more than 300 schools and community buildings and 30,000 homes, targeting energy-bill reductions of 20%–40% and savings of approximately $700 per household annually. Separately, more than 65 contracted water projects are expected to return over 8 billion gallons annually, more than twice the water Amazon says its data centers consumed in 2025. artigo.texto: SAN FRANCISCO — As food delivery workers on e-scooters whizzed past a hulking tour bus parked next to Anthropic’s headquarters in downtown San Francisco on Monday afternoon, software engineers returning from their lunch breaks snapped pictures of a brash slogan bursting out of the bus’ idyllic Americana artwork of farmhouses and fields of grain. “AI Data Center Revolt,” the bus’ detailed wrapping declared, proclaiming its mission to rally communities against wanton data center construction efforts across the country. The bus and its small crew of conservative activists from a group called Humans First had just completed an over 8,000-mile whistle-stop marathon of a road trip on perhaps the most uniting theme today: anti-data-center sentiment. “This technology is being shoved down people’s throats,” said Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, admiring the bus’ artwork from a nearby sidewalk. She said the group aimed to push back against AI giants and their assumption that they can build billions of dollars of AI infrastructure without residents’ input. “That’s not the American way,” she said. Founded this year as a coalition of left- and right-wing activists who worry that the rush to embrace AI is being spearheaded by tech oligarchs steamrolling Americans’ ability to steer the technology, Humans First has since morphed into a conservative-only effort led by Kremer to advocate for better guardrails on data center construction and AI in general. Kremer, a veteran conservative organizer who played noted roles in the tea party and the organization that helped create the rally preceding the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol attack, has spearheaded cross-country bus trips to extol MAGA talking points and deny the outcome of the 2020 election. Composed of Kremer, her husband, her daughter and her dog, Lovie — “He’s been with me the entire trip,” Kremer said — along with staffers and security guards, the Humans First squad has made more than 35 stops in communities across the country over the past five weeks. The trip culminated in Monday’s visits to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta and Nvidia — widely regarded as the world’s largest and most influential AI companies. Kremer and her daughter, Kylie Jane Kremer, fielded questions from reporters about the tour’s goals and its accomplishments. FOR SUBSCRIBERSLatino voters feel buyer’s remorse in battleground Texas FOR SUBSCRIBERSWhat’s on the Supreme Court’s docket this term? FOR SUBSCRIBERSLatino voters feel buyer’s remorse in battleground Texas FOR SUBSCRIBERSWhat’s on the Supreme Court’s docket this term? “I want Big Tech to actually include the American people and allow them to have a seat at the table,” said Kylie Jane, a senior adviser at Humans First. She highlighted the organization’s Data Center Policy, a 13-point charter that emphasizes community control over data center planning, rejects data centers’ role in increasing electricity prices and decries any use of American data centers for unconstitutional surveillance, among other issues. “We’re not anti-AI, we’re not anti-tech, we’re not even anti-data center,” Kylie Jane said. Instead, the team touts a proud populist message: AI development must prioritize Americans, and the historic infrastructure buildout must benefit the communities hosting data centers humming with billions of dollars of business. Yet, during the monthlong tour, much of the nation’s AI discourse shifted dramatically from worries about data centers’ guzzling water to fears that the technology might wipe out billions of people — or the entire species — in the next decade. Recent worries about such risks were catalyzed by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s warning on X that leading AI companies are recklessly speeding toward technological disaster. Amy Kremer said AI’s potential existential threats had clearly struck a nerve with Middle America, with growing numbers of people at Humans First rallies bringing up AI’s risks to society beyond immediate data center impacts. “People across the country are definitely paying attention to the existential risk and what is coming out about that,” Kremer said. artigo.texto: Ukraine will receive $16.2 million to develop renewable energy and energy storage systems The Board of the Climate Investment Funds (CIF) has approved Ukraine’s $16.2 million investment plan. The funds will be directed toward the development of renewable energy, cross-border power interconnections, and energy storage systems. According to the minister, this funding is part of the “Renewable Energy Integration” (REI) program. “This will help accelerate the integration of the Ukrainian power grid into the European energy network and will also strengthen the transformation of the Ukrainian energy sector,” Shmyhal said. The implementation of the approved program involves both public and private sectors. As Denys Shmyhal noted, as part of the public sector component, an investment package with an estimated value of $200 million has been put together in collaboration with the World Bank and NPC “Ukrenergo.” It includes a number of important projects to strengthen the Ukrainian power grid. Specifically, the following are planned: - construction of the 400 kV Chernivtsi–Suceava cross-border interconnector; - the creation of additional transmission capacity of 880 MW toward Ukraine and 445 MW toward European power grids; - the modernization and reinforcement of five high-voltage substations; - providing engineering support for the implementation of investment projects; - modernizing the IT, telecommunications, and operational infrastructure of NPC “Ukrenergo.” The implementation of these measures is expected to contribute to the further strengthening of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and its integration with the European power system. The second component of the program focuses on attracting private investment into modern energy infrastructure. According to Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal, this component is being developed by the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Specifically, the plan includes: - support for private investment in energy storage systems; - the development of autonomous BESS systems, which are expected to provide 610 MW of battery storage capacity; - implementation of renewable energy generation projects in combination with energy storage systems; - the implementation of other distributed energy solutions. Thus, the investment plan approved by the CIF is intended to simultaneously support the development of renewable generation, electricity storage, and the expansion of Ukraine’s capacity to exchange electricity with European countries. This was announced on October 6 by Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal. As a reminder, Ukraine and Germany plan to expand cooperation in the energy and transportation sectors. Among the agreements are potential purchases of German equipment to restore the power grid and locomotives for Ukrzaliznytsia, which are intended to help offset losses caused by Russian attacks. Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi announced this following a conversation with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Ukraine and Germany have signed a series of agreements in the energy sector totaling more than 155 million euros. The agreements concern the restoration of damaged infrastructure, the supply of critical equipment, and the development of distributed generation. Separately, Germany announced a contribution of 250 million euros to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund.

artigo.texto: Data center emissions dispute prompts Virginia trip by Spartanburg officials Environmental group says public was misled on data center’s cancer-causing emissions SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - The Southern Environmental Law Center is asking the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services to reconsider its decision involving the Valara data center project in Spartanburg County, arguing the public did not have an opportunity to review updated information about the facility’s formaldehyde emissions. SELC sent a letter to DES on Oct. 1 asking the agency to reopen the public comment period for Valara’s air permit. Emissions estimates changed The dispute centers on formaldehyde emissions from natural gas-fired turbines planned for the data center. In its permitting documents, DES previously calculated controlled formaldehyde emissions at less than 10 tons per year. DES’ September permit sets a federally enforceable limit of less than 10 tons per year for any individual hazardous air pollutant, including formaldehyde. The permit also limits total hazardous air pollutants to less than 25 tons per year. SELC argues updated calculations put Valara’s controlled formaldehyde emissions at 10.58 tons per year. Frank Holleman, a senior attorney with SELC, said Valara’s original application relied on an emission reduction associated with technology the company was not using. “They reduced the estimates of that by using a reduction based on a technology they were not using and is no longer marketed,” Holleman said. DES later acknowledged that an incorrect emission factor had been used, according to SELC. The agency reviewed additional information provided by Valara and recalculated the emissions before issuing the permit. Holleman said the public has not been given enough information to independently review the updated calculation. “They also say they had some industry information that Valara provided, but they didn’t give the numbers. They didn’t show how they calculated it. And we’ve got this black box of additional information, all done behind closed doors,” Holleman said. DES says its permitting staff reviewed the application, supplemental information and public comments before issuing the Sept. 18 permit. The agency says it is required by law to issue the permit if an application demonstrates compliance with applicable state and federal regulations and the conditions of the permit. Why the 10-ton limit matters The permit places a limit of less than 10 tons per year on any individual hazardous air pollutant. Exceeding a permit limit could put the facility out of compliance and subject it to enforcement. Formaldehyde is classified as a known human carcinogen. Holleman said DES should give the public more information about how the updated emissions figure was calculated. “And what we’re saying is, no, no, no. The law doesn’t allow that. Simple fairness doesn’t allow it,” Holleman said. SELC is asking DES to reopen the public comment period. FOX Carolina reached out to DES for a response. The agency said it would answer questions the following day. Valara is also facing at least two active lawsuits, both led by the Southern Environmental Law Center. Valara had not responded as of the report. Spartanburg County officials travel to Virginia’s Data Center Alley The dispute comes as several Spartanburg County Council members and county officials travel to Loudoun County, Virginia, an area known for its concentration of data centers. According to a county travel notice, council members Monier Abusaft and Paul Abbott are traveling to Loudoun County from Sunday, Oct. 4, through Tuesday, Oct. 6. They are joined by county staff and others to learn from community leaders, utility executives and industry experts about Loudoun County’s experience with data center development. Monday’s schedule included a data center industry tour, discussions with Loudoun County supervisors and board members, a meeting with Amazon data center representatives and a session with other data center industry representatives. Tuesday’s schedule includes meetings with Loudoun Water, Loudoun County Economic Development and a state delegate. Loudoun County is about an hour and a half drive northwest of Washington, D.C. FOX Carolina reached out to county officials for comment but no one was available for an interview. Holleman, whose organization was told about the trip when it was announced Friday night, said he believes county leaders should hear from people who have raised concerns about data center development. “It really is yet another disgrace. And here they have county councilmen traveling up to Virginia. And if you look at their agenda, they’re meeting with one industry representative after another. Why are they not meeting with environmental advocates, community advocates, people who are concerned? Who do they represent? Do they represent the people of Spartanburg? Or do they represent the data center operators, owners, and investors and hedge funds in major corporations?” Holleman said. What Loudoun County says about data centers Loudoun County officials point to the tax revenue generated by the data center industry as a major economic benefit. According to Loudoun County, data centers generated $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue during fiscal year 2026, representing 39% of the county’s overall budget. The county’s adopted fiscal year 2027 budget projects $1.3 billion in data center revenue, or about 40% of the total budget. Loudoun County also says more than 17,000 direct and indirect data center-related jobs have been created. Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. artigo.texto: Tecnologia criada na FEEC utiliza células cilíndricas, eletrólito aquoso e circulação interna por turbina, elimina mangueiras e bombas externas e pode evoluir para sistemas estacionários de armazenamento conectados à rede Pesquisadores da Faculdade de Engenharia Elétrica e de Computação da Unicamp (FEEC) desenvolveram uma nova arquitetura de bateria de fluxo voltada ao armazenamento estacionário de energia em larga escala, com aplicação potencial em sistemas associados à geração solar e eólica. A solução chama atenção por abandonar parte da configuração tradicional dessas baterias. Em vez de placas empilhadas, mangueiras e bombas externas para movimentação do eletrólito, a tecnologia desenvolvida na Unicamp utiliza eletrodos cilíndricos, células seladas individualmente e uma pequena turbina instalada dentro da própria bateria. - Brasil já tem 35 GW em energia eólica, concentra 90% das turbinas no Nordeste e agora enfrenta o gargalo que pode limitar a expansão até 2035 - China coloca em operação nova unidade de 660 MW em Zhongwei para dar estabilidade a base de 13 GW de energia renovável no deserto de Tengger e levar eletricidade até Hunan - Europa inaugura complexo híbrido com 242 MW de energia solar e bateria de 773 MWh na Bulgária e prepara expansão com mais 250 MW em turbinas eólicas - Nordeste já produz energia solar e eólica para exportar ao restante do Brasil, mas expansão esbarra em falta de armazenamento, gargalos na transmissão e impactos sobre fauna, flora e comunidades Nos ensaios realizados em laboratório, o equipamento alcançou aproximadamente 400 ciclos de carga e descarga, além de cerca de 98% de eficiência de carga e 82% de eficiência energética. O projeto nasceu no grupo Brazilian Renewable Energies (BREnergies) durante o doutorado do engenheiro eletricista João Pedro Aguiar dos Santos, sob orientação de César Pagan e coorientação de Hudson Zanin, ambos da FEEC. A arquitetura já resultou em um pedido de patente depositado no Instituto Nacional da Propriedade Industrial (INPI), com estratégia conduzida pela Agência de Inovação Inova Unicamp. Eletrodos cilíndricos substituem pilhas de placas Nas baterias de fluxo convencionais, os eletrodos normalmente são organizados em placas empilhadas. O eletrólito circula por tubos e mangueiras ligados a bombas externas. Essa arquitetura funciona, mas aumenta o número de conexões hidráulicas e, consequentemente, os pontos em que podem surgir falhas ou vazamentos. A proposta desenvolvida pela Unicamp parte de outra geometria. Cada célula é selada individualmente e utiliza dois eletrodos posicionados de forma concêntrica: um deles forma um anel maior, enquanto o outro ocupa a região interna. Essas células podem ser ligadas em série sem necessidade de formar uma pilha convencional. A mudança não é apenas geométrica. Ela altera também a maneira como o eletrólito se movimenta dentro do sistema. Pequena turbina dentro da bateria elimina bombas e mangueiras externas Um dos diferenciais centrais da tecnologia está no sistema de circulação interna. Uma pequena turbina instalada dentro da própria bateria movimenta o eletrólito. Com isso, o projeto dispensa parte das bombas e tubulações externas utilizadas em sistemas convencionais. A ideia é reduzir componentes hidráulicos e simplificar a arquitetura. Esse foi também um dos maiores desafios do trabalho. Segundo João Pedro Aguiar dos Santos, a equipe não encontrou equipamentos comerciais capazes de atender à configuração pretendida. Foi necessário construir praticamente toda a estrutura experimental. “Durante os estudos, percebi que não existia nenhum tipo de design ou setup experimental que pudéssemos comprar para montar a bateria. Isso foi um grande desafio, porque tivemos que montar desde as células até os reatores maiores para fazer os experimentos no laboratório.” O pesquisador também destaca que o desenvolvimento exigiu conhecimentos de diferentes áreas. “Foi um sistema multidisciplinar, unindo engenharia mecânica, eletrônica e eletroquímica, e tivemos que construir tudo do zero.” Bateria chegou a aproximadamente 400 ciclos sem aditivos Nos testes de carga e descarga, a bateria de fluxo giratório chegou a aproximadamente 400 ciclos sem a utilização de aditivos no eletrólito. Segundo os pesquisadores, esse desempenho superou referências de sistemas semelhantes avaliados sob condições comparáveis, que alcançaram cerca de 100 ciclos. Um dos problemas encontrados nesses sistemas é o crescimento de dendritos. Essas estruturas podem se formar durante os processos eletroquímicos e, em determinados casos, provocar curto-circuitos e comprometer a bateria. No protótipo da Unicamp, o ensaio não terminou por falha eletroquímica. A interrupção ocorreu devido a uma limitação mecânica no anel coletor responsável pelo contato elétrico do eletrodo interno. Esse detalhe importa porque indica que a limitação observada não estava diretamente relacionada à química da bateria. A próxima etapa será justamente aprimorar esse componente. Pesquisadores querem superar 3 mil ciclos A equipe trabalha agora com a perspectiva de melhorar a durabilidade do sistema. Além da mudança no mecanismo de contato elétrico, o projeto prevê a utilização de aditivos no eletrólito. A expectativa dos pesquisadores é superar 3 mil ciclos de operação. Nos testes já realizados, a bateria apresentou aproximadamente 98% de eficiência de carga e 82% de eficiência energética. Em uma demonstração prática, o sistema conseguiu operar durante duas horas alimentando LEDs e um ventilador. O objetivo dessa etapa ainda não era demonstrar uma aplicação comercial em grande escala, mas verificar o comportamento integrado da bateria durante a operação. Sistema eletrônico acompanha até pH e formação de dendritos Os pesquisadores também precisaram criar um sistema próprio de gerenciamento. artigo.texto: Este encontro representa o próximo passo na concretização dos termos da cooperação entre as duas partes, com foco na modernização e digitalização da rede elétrica, no desenvolvimento de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias (BESS), no aumento da flexibilidade e confiabilidade do sistema elétrico, no compartilhamento de conhecimento e no desenvolvimento da capacidade nacional. Novos requisitos para a rede elétrica do Vietnã. No seminário de 30 de setembro, especialistas observaram que a crescente demanda por eletricidade, aliada à proporção cada vez maior de energias renováveis e fontes de energia distribuída, está impondo novas exigências à capacidade operacional do sistema elétrico. A localização e a finalidade de uso são fatores que podem determinar o valor que um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) pode agregar. Dependendo das necessidades de cada área, os sistemas de armazenamento podem ser implantados perto de centros de carga, em áreas com grandes fontes de energia renovável ou em pontos onde a rede elétrica está frequentemente sob alta pressão. Esse planejamento e operação determinarão como o BESS pode contribuir para o equilíbrio entre oferta e demanda, reduzindo a pressão sobre a rede e melhorando a eficiência da infraestrutura existente. Além disso, um dos principais requisitos é melhorar a "visibilidade da rede" — a capacidade de observar, coletar dados e entender o que está acontecendo na rede elétrica. Com o aumento do número de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), o desafio não é mais apenas instalar mais sistemas de armazenamento, mas também como monitorar e integrar múltiplos sistemas BESS à rede elétrica de forma eficaz. As empresas de serviços públicos de energia elétrica precisam de dados e ferramentas digitais para monitorar as condições da rede, prever mudanças e tomar decisões operacionais adequadas. Promover soluções digitais na gestão de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS). Para solucionar esse problema, a Global Energy Alliance está desenvolvendo uma plataforma centralizada de gerenciamento de energia e programação operacional para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS). A plataforma permite o monitoramento e a otimização de múltiplos sistemas BESS implantados em diferentes locais e níveis de tensão. Com base nas condições de operação da rede e em sinais como previsões de preços de eletricidade, a plataforma pode ajudar a determinar o momento e os métodos adequados de carga e descarga para cada sistema. Essa abordagem visa otimizar o valor operacional e a eficiência econômica dos sistemas de armazenamento distribuído, além de fornecer informações adicionais para o gerenciamento e a operação do sistema de energia. A plataforma é uma aplicação prática da tecnologia digital na gestão do armazenamento de energia e pode fornecer informações e experiência úteis para esforços mais amplos de aprimoramento da visibilidade do sistema, melhoria da flexibilidade operacional e suporte à integração eficaz de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) no sistema elétrico. “Os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) são mais do que apenas hardware. À medida que o número de sistemas de armazenamento aumenta, o software, os dados e os recursos de orquestração determinarão significativamente o valor que esses sistemas criarão para a rede elétrica”, disse Biswarup Ghosh, Diretor Global para Redes Elétricas do Futuro da Global Energy Alliance. Fortalecimento da capacidade nacional para o ecossistema de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS). Um dos tópicos relevantes discutidos na sessão foi a proposta de lançamento de um Centro de alta qualidade para iniciativas de BESS (Abastecimento de Energia Empresarial, Eficiência Energética e Segurança). Este centro serviria como plataforma para que agências, organizações, empresas e instituições de ensino vietnamitas pudessem aprender com a experiência e colaborar no desenvolvimento de capacidades e no acesso a financiamento para a implementação de iniciativas de transição energética. De acordo com as diretrizes delineadas na Sessão, se implementado adequadamente, o Centro poderá se tornar um polo de pesquisa, treinamento, testes e compartilhamento de conhecimento e experiência em tecnologia de armazenamento de energia, com base em resultados técnicos e em uma rede de partes interessadas formada a partir de atividades anteriores com sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS); além de apoiar o desenvolvimento de capacidades para agências de gestão, empresas de energia, empresas, universidades e organizações de pesquisa no Vietnã. A Autoridade de Eletricidade e seus parceiros continuarão a discutir detalhadamente o modelo operacional, o escopo de funções, os recursos e o roteiro de implementação do Centro, para garantir que esteja alinhado com as necessidades reais e os requisitos de desenvolvimento do sistema elétrico do Vietnã. “O papel crescente das baterias de armazenamento de energia cria a necessidade de maior especialização nacional em agências e organizações responsáveis pelo planejamento, gestão, implantação e operação desses sistemas. O Centro de Alta Qualidade será um local para desenvolver conhecimento especializado, compartilhar experiências e aprimorar as capacidades que o Vietnã precisa à medida que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) são implantados em uma escala cada vez maior”, afirmou o Dr. Hoang Anh, Diretor do Programa de Treinamento em Engenharia Elétrica da Escola de Engenharia Elétrica e Eletrônica da Universidade de Ciência e Tecnologia de Hanói . O Vietnã também precisa continuar pesquisando como os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) podem ser implementados. artigo.texto: Kinesis, a specialist project developer in the field of renewable energy, and NEDE, a developer of hybrid and sector-coupled energy projects, are planning the Afferde-Ost wind and solar park in Hameln-Afferde for the hybrid generation of renewable energy. At the end of September 2026, the Hameln City Council’s Administrative Committee approved the drafting of a project-specific local development plan for the project; the Afferde Local Council and the Hameln Urban Development Committee had previously also unanimously welcomed the project. About the planned Hamelin-Afferde hybrid energy site At the “Unter dem Schecken” site, a hybrid energy park is to be built, comprising two wind turbines with a hub height of 199 metres and a combined capacity of 13.6 megawatts, as well as two photovoltaic fields with a combined capacity of 24 megawatts. To make optimum use of the electricity generated and to buffer peak loads, a battery energy storage system (BESS) is also to be added to the park. The relevant land has been secured by the investors. A company has been set up by the project initiators to handle the project planning and operation. "This means our recently established partnership with NEDE is now gaining momentum," says Dr Janis Meyerhof, Managing Director of Kinesis, with delight. He continues: "The hybrid energy site planned here is very well thought out in its design, which has been approved by the local authorities. The combined generation of green energy from solar and wind power, together with integrated storage, forms a sustainable concept." Evan Gilroy, Managing Director of NEDE, on the project in Hameln-Afferde: “Now that the resolution to initiate the planning process has been passed, the next step is an early stage of public consultation for the preparation of the project-specific development plan. We anticipate that, once the resolution on the planning regulations has been passed, the project can be completed by our partners and ourselves within around 30 months.”

artigo.texto: A capital paulista recebe, entre os dias 6 e 8 de outubro de 2026, a edição de estreia do Data Center World Brasil, conferência internacional voltada à infraestrutura crítica de tecnologia da informação. Conforme anunciado pela organizadora Informa Markets, o congresso ocorre nas instalações do São Paulo Expo, funcionando em paralelo às atividades do evento Futurecom. O encontro reúne mais de 2.500 executivos e cerca de 300 congressistas com o objetivo de discutir os rumos da capacidade de processamento em larga escala no território nacional. Segundo informações divulgadas pela promotora, a agenda prioriza os impactos decorrentes da rápida expansão dos ecossistemas de inteligência artificial sobre a malha operacional brasileira. A programação foi estruturada para contrapor a crescente demanda por poder computacional aos desafios técnicos de suprimento elétrico, conectividade em hiperescala e segurança jurídica. A entidade promotora sustenta que os debates ocorrem em uma conjuntura na qual decisões regulatórias e logísticas moldarão a atratividade do país perante o fluxo global de capital intensivo voltado à computação em nuvem. Competitividade tributária e regime especial para infraestrutura De acordo com a programação detalhada pela Informa Markets, a rodada de abertura do congresso concentra-se nos instrumentos de atração de capital produtivo, com ênfase no debate sobre o Redata — regime especial de tributação formulado especificamente para o setor de processamento de dados. A organizadora aponta que o painel inaugural visa mapear os efeitos dessa política sobre a competitividade fiscal brasileira em um horizonte estimado entre cinco e dez anos. Especialistas escalados para a plenária avaliam como o alinhamento de diretrizes entre o Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) e as alíquotas estaduais de ICMS incide sobre a viabilidade financeira das construções civis e da importação de insumos tecnológicos de ponta. A promotora assinala que a discussão tributária transcende o escopo contábil e assume caráter geopolítico. Países vizinhos na América Latina disputam aportes de provedores globais conhecidos como hyperscalers, tornando a clareza nas regras de incentivo e desoneração de bens de capital um diferencial competitivo relevante. O cronograma do evento prevê a participação de lideranças do Ministério das Comunicações, do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (Brasscom) e da gestora Patria Investments para abordar entraves de funding, modelos de garantias e arquitetura de crédito de longo prazo. Restrições energéticas e viabilidade de suprimento elétrico A disponibilidade de potência elétrica desponta como o principal gargalo estrutural identificado pelos organizadores do congresso. De acordo com a Informa Markets, a transição para clusters computacionais dedicados a modelos generativos de inteligência artificial multiplicou o consumo por metro quadrado útil nos centros de processamento. A programação técnica inclui mesas dedicadas à análise da intermitência da matriz limpa, modelos de autoprodução de energia e sistemas avançados de armazenamento para garantir que as instalações sustentem contratos de nível de serviço com operação contínua e ininterrupta. O debate abrange as variáveis determinantes na seleção de sítios imobiliários industriais para a instalação dessas estruturas físicas. Conforme destacam os documentos informativos da organização, contratantes corporativos examinam indicadores de performance que exigem equilíbrio milimétrico entre proximidade dos anéis de transmissão, redundância de subestações e proximidade dos grandes polos consumidores para evitar perdas de transmissão e oscilações de voltagem. A busca por áreas com capacidade de expansão modular de megawattagem tornou-se premissa mandatória nos planos de negócios do segmento. - Segurança de suprimento: análise de interconexões com a Rede Básica do Sistema Interligado Nacional. - Contratos de longo prazo: estruturação de acordos bilaterais de compra de energia renovável certificada. - Sistemas de contenção de falhas: implementação de usinas de geração de backup e módulos de baterias químicas. - Arquitetura de missão crítica: redundância elétrica baseada em tolerância a falhas sem paradas programadas. Transformação da arquitetura térmica e expansão do resfriamento líquido A Informa Markets relata que a evolução de processadores gráficos e aceleradores de tensores provocou uma ruptura nos padrões tradicionais de engenharia predial. O diretor do Data Center World Brasil, Leonardo Benedicto, declarou na apresentação do fórum que a inteligência artificial exige repensar integralmente o ecossistema dos edifícios dedicados, articulando fornecimento energético, controle microclimático e flexibilidade modular para acomodar atualizações tecnológicas contínuas ao longo do ciclo de vida dos empreendimentos. Conforme sustentam os relatórios técnicos que embasam os painéis, a densidade energética por rack ultrapassou patamares históricos, forçando o abandono gradual dos sistemas convencionais de resfriamento exclusivamente por ar comprimido. O congresso programou demonstrações sobre o avanço de soluções de resfriamento líquido direto no chip (liquid cooling ou direct-to-chip) e tecnologias de imersão total. Essa migração técnica reduz substancialmente o indicador de eficácia no uso de energia (PUE), permitindo elevar a capacidade de cálculo instalada no mesmo espaço físico sem sobrecarregar os limites térmicos dos componentes semicondutores. artigo.texto: Yesterday morning we launched our National Data Center Tracker, and within hours we had a major new project to add to it, as well as legislation aimed at preventing projects like it from being built on federal public lands. The ground is moving fast. NPR reported Wednesday that nuclear startup Valar Atomics is proposing a massive data center complex on more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land near Price, Utah. The project, called Project Beehive, would include data centers powered by roughly 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and facilities for storing nuclear waste. According to company documents reviewed by NPR, the reactors would collectively produce around 9.6 gigawatts of electricity for the data centers, plus additional thermal energy for other industrial uses. Utah currently produces around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average, though its peak generating capacity can reach roughly 10 gigawatts during the summer. At almost the same time, Oregon Senator Ron Wyden introduced legislation that would prohibit the development, sale or transfer of federally owned public lands for new data centers and associated infrastructure nationwide. Project Beehive Valar’s federal proposal is still at the beginning of the process. BLM’s Utah office confirmed to NPR that it has received the company’s application and is reviewing it for completeness. The agency said that if the application moves forward through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, the public will have opportunities to weigh in. Valar is already laying out a timeline. Company documents call for non-nuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028. The 9,000-plus acres of BLM land are only part of the project. Utah state records show that Valar also sought a special-use lease covering roughly 640 acres of state trust land in Carbon County. The Trust Lands Administration Board unanimously approved the lease on September 17, according to KSL. The federal application is much larger. Project Beehive would spread across more than 9,000 acres near Price and combine the data centers, hundreds of reactors, nuclear fuel production and nuclear waste storage in a single proposed complex. And we’d already come across Valar before any of this surfaced. We’ve Seen Valar Before Our tracker already contained another Valar project near Green River, Utah. The company had applied for roughly 10,200 acres of BLM land for a data center co-located with small nuclear reactors before deciding not to pursue the site. We kept it in the tracker as withdrawn. That history looks a little more important today. A roughly 10,200-acre Valar proposal near Green River appeared in the federal record and was later dropped. Now another Valar proposal has surfaced near Price involving more than 9,000 acres of BLM land and hundreds of nuclear reactors. The Public Lands Fight Is Already Bigger Than Valar Our Public Lands tracker now has 16 data center sites sitting on land the public owns, each tied to a public document placing it there. South of Boise, Rhea Data’s Blacks Creek Campus would put a four-million-square-foot data center campus on 3,226 acres of BLM land beside Blacks Creek Reservoir. In Nevada, Copia Digital’s Bergen Data Center is proposed on 744 acres of BLM land north of Las Vegas. In Arizona, the Frontier Data Center would occupy 620 acres of BLM land in Pinal County, while the Harquahala Data Center would occupy another 275 acres in Maricopa County. All three remain proposed. The tracker also includes public-land projects that are much further along or have already run into trouble. Townsite Solar 2 outside Boulder City, Nevada was proposed on 89 acres of BLM land about 1.6 miles from Lake Mead National Recreation Area. Its approval was challenged, and BLM later asked the Interior Board of Land Appeals to set aside the agency’s own approval so the application could undergo additional review. Federal land controlled by other agencies is part of the buildout too. The tracker includes proposed or active data center projects at Energy Department sites in Kentucky, Ohio and South Carolina, along with projects on state-owned land and other BLM applications scattered across the West. And the 16 mapped sites still don’t capture everything sitting in the federal pipeline. BLM records also contain applications that don’t yet have enough public location information to map, including a Prometheus Hyperscale proposal in Wyoming involving rights-of-way for a road, telecommunications line and water pipeline, and another Valar nuclear-powered data center proposal in Utah whose public record still doesn’t disclose its size or exact location. The federal push behind these projects is coming from the top. President Trump’s July 2025 executive order directed federal agencies to make appropriate federal sites available for qualifying data center projects, and our tracker shows Interior later telling BLM state directors to identify public lands that could take data centers. Now there’s movement in the other direction. Wyden’s new legislation would prohibit the development, sale or transfer of federally owned public lands for new data centers and associated infrastructure. His office said the bill followed reporting that more than 17,000 acres of public land across Oregon, Nevada, Arizona, Idaho, Wyoming and Utah were being considered for data center development. None of that changes the law today. Valar’s application is still before BLM, the other proposed projects remain in various stages of the process, and Wyden’s legislation has only been introduced. But one day after launching the tracker, there’s already another 9,000-plus-acre project to follow and another major federal response to add to the record. artigo.texto: AI Energy Parks: From Speed to Power to Power That Lasts Why This Matters Up to 10 years. That's how long a large new grid connection can take in North America. So developers are chasing time-to-power, and they should be. But a site that gets power first and gets the architecture wrong has only traded one bottleneck for another. Every shortcut taken to energize on schedule becomes technology debt, and the bill comes due when the load changes, the technology moves, and the site has to be rebuilt while the data center is running. The alternative is the AI Energy Park. Think of it as a microgrid built for AI: a large, optimized, behind-the-meter power system designed for the scale, density, and dynamic load of AI data centers. It integrates grid supply, on-site generation, storage, power distribution, and controllable demand into one coordinated, software-enabled campus. But speed to power can’t be the only objective. Sites designed only to hit an energization date lock in today's assumptions: boundaries drawn around the first equipment, bespoke software, interfaces that fit one configuration. Over a multi-decade lifecycle, generation technologies, market rules, utility capacity, and AI load profiles will all change. An AI Energy Park should be treated as long-term infrastructure, not a temporary bridge to utility service. The goal is not to predict the next 20 years perfectly, but to build an architecture that can evolve without costly rip-and-replace cycles. So how do you get both: power on a credible schedule and an architecture built to last? Stop designing every site from scratch. A Repeatable Model for Speed and Certainty Custom designs add engineering effort, integration complexity, cost, and execution risk. They also force each project to repeat key decisions about system boundaries, operations, protection, procurement, and commissioning. Repeatability speeds delivery. Standard power blocks, controls, cybersecurity zones, data structures, and commissioning methods can be validated once and adapted to each site. This allows for earlier procurement and lets engineers focus on site-specific needs. Four principles make that model scalable and future-ready: - Connectivity links assets and systems, reducing integration effort and speeding commissioning. - Interoperability allows systems from different vendors to work together, preserving choice and simplifying expansion. - Visibility gives operators a real-time view of system health, capacity, risk, and performance. - Optimization uses that visibility to balance cost, reliability, emissions, and grid services. Design for Lifecycle Value Over a 20-year horizon, generation technologies, utility capacity, power density, market rules, software platforms, and renewable economics will all evolve. A future-ready design preserves options so the site can respond without rebuilding its core power architecture. That means designing for change through configuration and modular expansion. Standards-based interfaces, clear system boundaries, repeatable building blocks, and shared digital capabilities allow technologies and vendors to change without redesigning the entire system, reduce dependence on any single supplier, and allow capacity to be added as demand becomes firm. The objective is not a static design that is frozen on day one, but a durable framework that can absorb innovation over time. Reliability for AI Workloads A flexible Energy Park can operate in grid-connected, islanded, or hybrid modes; add generation, storage, and renewables without rebuilding supervisory controls; and actively manage demand. For AI workloads, coordinated controls across UPS, batteries, generation, and the grid provide load smoothing and fault ride-through. This protects compute uptime while preventing rapid load changes and grid disturbances from cascading across the campus. Reliability depends on coordinated system behavior, not just redundant equipment. The controls must detect changing conditions, protect critical loads, manage transitions between operating modes, and support predictable recovery. Validated sequences and clear visibility into available capacity help operators act before asset limits become campus-wide disruptions. Value Beyond the Fence Line A well-designed Energy Park can operate as a grid asset rather than an isolated private power plant: a flexible participant that can support both the anchor load and the broader energy system. For utilities, measurable curtailment, load shifting, and self-supply create more flexible interconnection options and can defer infrastructure during constrained periods. For communities, purpose-built infrastructure can strengthen local reliability, support future electrification, and provide measurable grid services. Community acceptance will depend on making those benefits tangible and transparent, while addressing concerns about local cost, reliability, land use, noise, emissions, water, and construction. Where market rules and utility agreements allow, these capabilities can also support demand response, reserve services, renewable balancing, and restoration. These remain secondary; the primary mission is reliable power for the data center. Power That Lasts Speed to power delivers the first megawatt. Power that lasts protects the investment over the decades that follow. A purpose-built Energy Park must absorb volatile AI loads, ride through grid disturbances, adapt as supply options and technologies change, and contribute measurable value beyond the fence line. A repeatable reference design and delivery model is how an Energy Park delivers both: power on a credible schedule, and an architecture built to last.
