artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov Oligarch Series on Oligarchy and the Historical Economics of Energy Storage Stanislav Kondrashov on oligarchy and energy storage The historical relationship between oligarchy and energy storage can be examined through a recurring economic question: who possesses the infrastructure, technical knowledge, manufacturing capacity, and organizational reach required to preserve usable energy for a later moment? Long before modern batteries, societies developed ways to retain energy indirectly through elevated water, mechanical systems, thermal methods, and other forms of storage. Modern electrical technologies have greatly expanded those possibilities. Key takeaway: energy storage matters economically because it changes the relationship between availability and time. Across history, technologies capable of preserving usable energy have required different combinations of infrastructure, engineering, manufacturing, specialist expertise, and coordination. Those requirements can influence where economic influence becomes concentrated and where new specialized participants can emerge. The Stanislav Kondrashov Oligarch Series examines this relationship without treating storage as a single technological category. Its history is instead a progression of methods for separating two moments that would otherwise need to occur close together: the moment when energy becomes available and the moment when it is needed. That ability has economic consequences. What Connects Oligarchy With the History of Energy Storage? The connection lies primarily in infrastructure, specialization, and scale. Storage technologies can require significant technical capabilities and extensive supporting systems. When those capabilities become concentrated among relatively few economic actors, storage can become part of a wider pattern of concentrated economic influence. The relationship is not automatic. Different storage technologies create different economic structures. Some depend heavily on large infrastructure. Others can operate at much smaller scales. Some require sophisticated manufacturing. Others depend more strongly on engineering, software, installation, maintenance, or integration with existing electrical networks. For this reason, the economics of storage cannot be understood simply by looking at the storage device. The surrounding system matters just as much. Energy Storage Existed Before Modern Batteries The basic principle of storage is much older than contemporary electrical technology. One of the simplest examples involves gravity. Water moved to a higher elevation contains potential energy that can later be converted into useful mechanical or electrical output as it moves downward. Mechanical systems provide another historical model. Energy can be retained through movement, pressure, or physical configuration and released later. Thermal storage follows a similar principle through temperature differences. The technologies differ considerably, but they share a common economic characteristic: they create a bridge between availability now and usefulness later. That bridge can be valuable whenever timing matters. Why Does Time Matter Economically? Electricity is unusual because generation and consumption traditionally require close coordination. Storage modifies that relationship. Electricity can become available during one period and contribute to activity during another. The economic importance of this capability becomes clearer when viewed through time rather than through the device itself. Storage can absorb electricity. It can retain it. It can release it later. This sequence creates flexibility. “The economic significance of storage begins with a remarkably simple transformation: something available at one moment can acquire additional usefulness because technology allows its availability to be shifted toward another moment,” Stanislav Kondrashov says. Time consequently becomes part of the infrastructure. Large Infrastructure Historically Favored Concentration Some forms of storage naturally operate at substantial scale. Large installations can require complex engineering, extensive construction, specialized equipment, and long-term maintenance. These requirements can favor organizations capable of coordinating numerous technical and industrial activities simultaneously. That is where the connection with oligarchic economic structures becomes particularly interesting. Economic concentration does not need to originate in the storage technology itself. It can emerge around the capabilities necessary to create and operate the wider system. Engineering expertise may become strategically important. Manufacturing can become highly specialized. Infrastructure can require substantial organizational capacity. Maintenance creates long-lasting technical relationships. The relevant economic structure therefore extends far beyond the physical storage installation. Batteries Changed the Geography of Storage Modern batteries introduced a particularly important characteristic: modularity. A storage installation does not necessarily need to exist at only one scale. Battery systems can appear in relatively compact configurations or become part of much larger electrical installations. This creates a different economic geography. Storage can exist closer to consumption. It can be integrated with buildings. It can support industrial facilities. It can participate within broader electrical networks. Different scales can coexist. That flexibility complicates traditional patterns of concentration. Large organizations may remain important in manufacturing and extensive infrastructure, while smaller specialized firms can participate in installation, engineering, software, maintenance, and technical services. artigo.texto: O Conselho de Meio Ambiente e Sustentabilidade da Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI) reuniu lideranças industriais, especialistas regulatórios e gestores públicos para estruturar a posição do setor produtivo frente à consolidação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE). O encontro deliberativo focou nos parâmetros de governança técnica, na harmonização de metodologias de mensuração e no escalonamento de investimentos em descarbonização profunda. A articulação visa assegurar que a transição para uma economia de baixo carbono preserve a competitividade industrial e estabeleça critérios objetivos de compensação e comércio de créditos. Durante os debates, foram enfatizados os mecanismos de monitoramento, reporte e verificação (MRV), além da compatibilização do arcabouço normativo nacional com as exigências internacionais, especialmente os acordos bilaterais no âmbito do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris e as diretrizes tributárias transfronteiriças da União Europeia. O direcionamento setorial busca consolidar a indústria nacional como polo receptor de investimentos verdes globais, mitigando riscos de bitributação ou barreiras não tarifárias ao comércio exterior brasileiro. Arquitetura regulatória e governança do mercado regulado A estruturação do mercado regulado de emissões impõe a definição clara de competências institucionais e limites de alocação de direitos de emissão. A proposta em acompanhamento pela CNI estabelece que empresas com emissões anuais acima de 25 mil toneladas de CO2 equivalente ingressem progressivamente no regime de cumprimento obrigatório, exigindo planos detalhados de inventário de gases de efeito estufa (GEE) submetidos a auditorias independentes. A governança exige a integração de sistemas digitais de registro que impeçam a dupla contagem de créditos e garantam a interoperabilidade entre o mercado regulado e os projetos voluntários de créditos florestais e agropecuários. Representantes do setor produtivo defenderam a alocação gratuita transitória de cotas (allowances) durante a fase de implantação do sistema, mecanismo fundamental para proteger indústrias intensivas em capital contra o risco de vazamento de carbono, no qual atividades industriais migram para jurisdições com legislações ambientais menos rigorosas. Desafios operacionais e convergência tecnológica nas cadeias fabris A transição para matrizes de baixo carbono requer aportes massivos em modernização tecnológica e eficiência energética nos processos de base. Setores como cimento, química, siderurgia, celulose e alumínio enfrentam o desafio de descarbonizar operações cujas emissões são inerentes às reações físico-químicas de transformação de matérias-primas. Nesses segmentos, a eletrificação direta é insuficiente, demandando combustíveis alternativos, biocombustíveis e hidrogênio verde. A incorporação de tecnologias de Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono (CCUS) figura como uma das principais fronteiras tecnológicas mapeadas pelos conselheiros industriais. O desenvolvimento dessa cadeia demanda a convergência de marcos legais específicos para injeção geológica de CO2, incentivos tributários para plantas piloto e desenvolvimento de redes de infraestrutura compartilhada para transporte do gás capturado. - Adoção de combustíveis derivados de resíduos e biomassa em substituição ao coque de petróleo e carvão mineral; - Implantação de programas avançados de eficiência energética térmica e recuperação de calor residual em processos contínuos; - Desenvolvimento e escala comercial de rotas de hidrogênio de baixa emissão para redução de minério de ferro; - Integração da cadeia de bioenergia com tecnologias de captura direta de carbono na fonte industrial. Competitividade externa e harmonização com padrões globais A sincronização do SBCE com mecanismos internacionais de precificação é condição central para a sustentabilidade econômica das exportações manufaturadas. A entrada em operação do Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira (CBAM) da União Europeia eleva a urgência de precificar o carbono em solo brasileiro, garantindo que os recursos arrecadados permaneçam na economia local para financiar a transição setorial em vez de serem retidos na forma de taxas alfandegárias europeias. A criação de mercados interconectados viabiliza a negociação de excedentes de cotas de carbono com nações que possuem metas mais agressivas e custos marginais de abatimento substancialmente superiores aos observados no Brasil. Esse diferencial de custos posiciona a matriz energética e produtiva brasileira como vetor atrativo para operações de descarbonização compartilhada entre corporações multinacionais. Financiamento e atração de capital para a descarbonização O aporte de capital estruturante constitui o principal elo para a execução física dos planos de descarbonização corporativa. Instrumentos financeiros sustentáveis, como debêntures verdes, títulos atrelados a metas de sustentabilidade (SLBs) e consórcios com agências multilaterais de desenvolvimento, tornam-se ferramentas operacionais indispensáveis para empresas sob o escopo regulatório. Paralelamente, a estruturação de linhas de financiamento de longo prazo com taxas compatíveis com o ciclo de retorno das tecnologias industriais limpas requer a coordenação entre bancos de desenvolvimento e agentes privados. A liquidez do mercado de carbono secundário servirá como balizador de precificação do risco climático, incorporando formalmente o passivo ambiental aos modelos de crédito corporativo. - Linhas de financiamento indexadas à redução comprovada da intensidade de carbono por unidade produzida; - Emissão de títulos verdes locais e internacionais com garantia de integridade metodológica ambiental; - Criação de fundos de coinvestimento público-privados para absorver o risco de tecnologias em estágio inicial; - Estruturação de contratos de compra e venda de créditos futuros para lastrear garantias de empréstimos. artigo.texto: Aplicações de inteligência artificial presentes no mundo físico, como carros autônomos, vão demandar baixíssima latência, o que deve incentivar a construção de pequenos data centers nas pontas das redes. Na opinião de Ivo Ivanov, CEO da DE-CIX, uma das maiores operadoras neutras de troca de tráfego de Internet, data centers modulares serão implantados por toda parte no futuro. Em entrevista para Mobile Time em Lisboa, durante o evento Atlantic Convergence, o executivo falou também sobre os planos da DE-CIX para o uso de satélites; processamento multiagêntico; capital digital distribuída; e a operação no Brasil. Mobile Time – Como a demanda por aplicações de IA física, de baixíssima latência, vai remodelar o mercado de data centers? Ivo Ivanov – Sim, a IA física, e especialmente a inferência de IA, ditará como a infraestrutura deve ser construída. Bilhões, provavelmente trilhões de dólares, estão sendo investidos mundialmente, não apenas em modelos de texto ou para produzir vídeos engraçados, mas em agentes treinados para realizar processos industriais em diversos segmentos. Eles têm uma característica em comum: são extremamente sensíveis ao tempo real. Isso significa que precisam de uma comunicação muito rápida entre o sistema de inferência e o dispositivo — seja um robô, um carro ou outro equipamento controlado por agentes de IA. A distância entre o sistema de inferência e o robô não pode exceder dois a três milissegundos. Isso equivale a cerca de 200 quilômetros. Essa é a realidade física; não podemos alterar a velocidade da luz. Portanto, a infraestrutura digital que atende a esses dispositivos precisa se aproximar deles. Os robôs não entrarão nos data centers; os data centers precisam se aproximar dos robôs, dos carros e das outras instalações. Teremos que desenvolver uma infraestrutura o mais próxima possível dos usuários, sejam eles seres humanos ou dispositivos. Então teremos mais data centers menores na borda (edge) das redes? Exatamente. Data centers modulares precisarão ser implantados literalmente por toda parte, suportados por tecnologias de transmissão como fibra ou redes móveis — o 5G Advanced já está em progresso e, em breve, esperamos o 6G —, além da conectividade satelital. Como a demanda por menor latência impactará o tráfego de internet, considerando que haverá mais agentes acessando a rede do que seres humanos? O tráfego será muito mais localizado. Ainda teremos deslocamento de tráfego devido ao treinamento e aplicações de interesse global — como telenovelas, que não podem ser restritas a um único país —, mas, na era da IA, o processamento precisa ser local. Isso é excelente para a soberania, pois mantém os dados protegidos dentro da jurisdição. Recentemente, a Anatel propôs para o leilão da faixa de 6 GHz, que as operadoras invistam em data centers de borda. Qual sua opinião sobre isso? É uma ideia excelente. Deve ser executada o quanto antes. Operadoras de telecomunicações frequentemente reclamam que a conectividade se tornou uma commodity, transformando-as em “dumb pipes”. Você acredita que elas poderiam reverter esse cenário com a IA? As teles poderiam ter um papel diferente nesta era da IA? Depende da gestão. É fácil reclamar; é melhor definir novas ideias. Os tempos de incumbência acabaram; hoje é a era da digitalização, dos serviços digitais, da colaboração e da parceria. O mercado exige ofertas complementares de valor agregado, combinando forças de diferentes parceiros. A ideia de que “eu sou o dono do mercado” era popular nos anos 70, mas não funciona mais. Clientes corporativos esperam agilidade e opções de conectividade de ponta que incluam inovações, novos provedores de serviços e de GPU. Um exemplo é a nossa oferta de acesso a provedores de GPU como serviço. Uma empresa automotiva ou um banco pode construir sua comunidade privada de GPU como serviço e treinar o quanto desejar, utilizando agentes em um ambiente privado. Chamo isso de “roteamento multiagente”, onde diferentes provedores de agentes podem ser combinados em um ambiente seguro com interconexão direta. É o novo multi-cloud. Você mencionou o roteamento multiagente em março. Essa solução já foi lançada ou implantada em algum lugar? O conceito e a tecnologia estão prontos e operacionais no Brasil. Estamos aguardando a entrada dos provedores de agentes e serviços. Estamos apenas no início desta nova era e queremos estar um passo à frente. Acredito fortemente que o Brasil possui todas as condições para se tornar um enorme universo de IA. Fale sobre os planos da DE-CIX para o uso de satélites. É uma nova esperança para aumentar a disponibilidade de serviços digitais, especialmente em regiões hoje subatendidas, onde é difícil implantar fibra. Acredito na conectividade via órbita também como uma solução redundante e complementar para mercados estabelecidos, protegendo a infraestrutura contra ataques ou desastres naturais, já que não há vento ou tsunamis no espaço. Além disso, é uma extensão relevante para soluções de defesa e segurança para governos e corporações que lidam com dados críticos. Nosso objetivo é construir o primeiro ponto de troca de internet no espaço, o “De-CIX Space-IX“, permitindo o roteamento entre diferentes operadoras em órbita, interconectando data centers espaciais com instalações de nuvem, inferência de IA e sinalização quântica. Quais satélites serão utilizados? Serão geoestacionários? Utilizaremos satélites em órbita baixa (LEO) e ultra-LEO. Não estamos falando de construir enormes fazendas de servidores no espaço, mas de módulos do tamanho de cabines telefônicas. Eles não servirão para treinamento de IA, mas são ótimos para inferência, que é mais leve, e para cache de conteúdo. A vantagem é a latência reduzida. Quando espera a primeira implantação? Dependemos da prontidão dos módulos de data center das empresas de satélite. Como há muitos projetos bem financiados, isso acontecerá muito em breve. artigo.texto: Tecnologia aparece como um pilar estratégico na corrida presidencial de 2026. O Olhar Digital analisou planos de governo de seis candidatos: Augusto Cury (Avante), Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), Renan Santos (Missão), Romeu Zema (Novo) e Ronaldo Caiado (PSD). A reportagem mergulhou nos documentos – todos disponíveis no site do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) – para checar o que os candidatos propõem em três temas: inteligência artificial (IA), data centers e soberania digital. A apuração também considerou dois mapeamentos – um feito por um centro de pesquisas e outro feito por uma consultoria. O ‘Brasil digital’ que seis candidatos à presidência da República propõem criar Existe um “núcleo comum” no qual propostas de candidatos distantes no espectro político se encontram. As convergências retratam o Estado “arrumando a própria casa”. E usando tecnologia para melhorar seus serviços. As divergências, por sua vez, aparecem quando os textos exploram regras de mercado, direitos digitais e atuação das empresas privadas. Confira abaixo os destaques sobre os planos de governo dos candidatos, organizados por tema: Inteligência artificial (IA) Os planos de governo analisados consideram a IA uma ferramenta decisiva para aumentar produtividade, modernizar serviços públicos e melhorar a saúde e a segurança do país. Ou seja: os candidatos concordam sobre a importância do tema. Mas discordam sobre como o Estado deve agir e regular a IA. Data centers Entre os planos de governo analisados, atração e expansão de data centers aparecem como consenso. Os seis candidatos consideram que o Brasil tem uma enorme vantagem em comparação a outros países. Isso porque o país tem energia limpa, renovável e abundante – ideal para alimentar esses galpões de supercomputadores. Todos querem trazer esse dinheiro para o Brasil. Mas divergem sobre as regras para esses investimentos. Uns exigem contrapartidas ecológicas e sociais. Outros preferem cortar impostos e burocracia para atrair empresas o mais rápido possível. Soberania digital Os planos de governo analisados abordam a soberania digital a partir de duas visões políticas. Uma delas é a soberania por meio da capacidade estatal e da regulação. Aqui, prioriza-se a criação de infraestruturas públicas soberanas (supercomputadores estatais, por exemplo), o controle nacional sobre dados e a imposição de regras e salvaguardas para empresas de tecnologia. A outra é a soberania via mercado e atração de capitais. Nesta visão, entende-se autonomia do país como a capacidade de se tornar produtor e polo atrativo para investimentos privados vindos de fora. Isso por meio de eliminação de amarras burocráticas. E aproveitando a energia limpa e os minerais estratégicos presentes no Brasil para desenvolver o setor. Quer entender no detalhe as propostas de cada candidato? Acesse esta reportagem exclusiva para assinantes do Clube Olhar Digital, que destrincha os planos de governo nos temas citados. Pedro Spadoni é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de Piracicaba. Já escreveu para sites, revistas e jornal.

artigo.texto: The U.S. power system ended 2025 with 43.6 gigawatts of utility-scale battery storage online. In just the first six months of 2026, operators added another 8.3 gigawatts, pushing total capacity to nearly 52 gigawatts. Over the prior three years, EIA data shows an annual average growth rate of 70 percent. Few segments of the energy industry are growing this fast, and few are being built on contract templates this unsettled. That gap between deployment speed and legal infrastructure is where the real risk sits right now, for developers, for the utilities and data centers buying storage capacity, and for the lenders financing it. What’s Actually Driving 52 Gigawatts Storage is being built for two different reasons that happen to be converging at the same time. The first is the traditional pairing with intermittent renewables, storage smooths out solar and wind output and lets a project sell power when prices are higher rather than only when the sun happens to shine. The second, newer driver is data centers. Standalone battery projects are increasingly being sited to manage congestion and reliability challenges tied to rapid data center load growth, particularly in interconnection markets that are already constrained. The industry expects roughly 24 gigawatts of new storage capacity in 2026 alone. A meaningful share of that is being financed and sited specifically around data center clusters, with ERCOT’s Dallas and Houston-area projects a leading example, positioned to capture both merchant revenue and behind-the-meter offtake arrangements with co-located facilities. The Revenue Structure Isn’t the Same in Every Market A storage contract that works in one market can be the wrong structure entirely in another, because the underlying revenue mechanics differ by region. ERCOT runs an energy-only market, so a battery there earns most of its money from arbitrage, charging when power is cheap and discharging when it’s expensive, with no guaranteed capacity payment underneath that strategy. California’s Resource Adequacy framework works differently: contracted capacity payments can represent 30 to 40 percent of a storage project’s annual revenue, a floor ERCOT projects don’t have. PJM’s recent capacity price spike signals its own acute need for dispatchable resources, changing the math again. A financing agreement or offtake contract built around one market’s structure doesn’t transfer cleanly to another. The Regulatory Gap FERC Is Still Closing The clearest sign that the legal framework hasn’t kept pace with deployment is a specific finding FERC made about PJM, the grid operator covering all or part of 13 states and the District of Columbia. FERC determined that PJM’s own tariff lacked sufficient rates, terms, and conditions of service governing co-located generation and load arrangements, the exact structure many storage-plus-data-center deals are built on. FERC ordered PJM to file a compliance filing by February 17, 2026, spelling out the specific terms an interconnection customer must follow to serve a co-located load, including how to designate the eligible customer that takes transmission service on the load’s behalf. That’s a regulator telling one of the country’s largest grid operators, mid-buildout, that its existing rules don’t actually cover the arrangements companies are already signing. Storage developers and their counterparties negotiating co-location deals in PJM territory right now are working against a rulebook that was still being written as of early this year. The FEOC Problem Nobody Priced In Two Years Ago Foreign entity of concern restrictions now affect eligibility for the investment tax credit and the Section 45X manufacturing credit that much of the storage industry’s financing model depends on. Battery supply chains run heavily through a small number of international manufacturers, which means FEOC compliance documentation has become a real part of deal timing and cost, not a formality. Industry guidance for 2026 now treats FEOC documentation protocols as something that needs to be ready at signing, not something to work out after a customer relationship is already underway. Companies that priced financing models two or three years ago, before FEOC rules were finalized, are discovering that the compliance framework underneath their tax credit assumptions has changed since the deal was structured. That’s the kind of gap that surfaces during due diligence on a financing round or an acquisition, not before. What This Means for Anyone Building or Buying Storage Four things are worth checking against current deals rather than assuming they were handled correctly when signed. Does the revenue structure match the market the project actually sits in, since an ERCOT arbitrage assumption built into a PJM capacity deal is a mismatch that eventually shows up in the financials. Do co-location and interconnection terms reflect the grid operator’s current tariff, not a template drafted before FERC forced operators like PJM to fill gaps in their own rules. Is FEOC documentation actually in place and current, given how much of the industry’s tax credit eligibility now depends on it. And have safety and siting requirements been checked against the newest state rules, since incidents at storage facilities have pushed several states toward new requirements that can affect permitting mid-project. The Pace Isn’t Slowing Down Nothing in the current data suggests this growth curve is flattening. Illinois enacted a wide-ranging energy law this year addressing battery storage payment structures and consumer protection requirements, one example among several states actively legislating in this space right now, and grid operators including the Southwest Power Pool have separately reformed their own interconnection queue processes to accommodate storage. artigo.texto: The Union Cabinet, an India-based executive body chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the third phase of the Green Energy Corridor, known as GEC-III. Under this scheme, 50 GWh of BESS will be deployed, and INR 50,000 crore (~ $5.19 billion) has been allocated to it. These batteries will be placed at renewable energy generator ends and at other locations of importance for grid flexibility. There, they are expected to ease intermittency, congestion and peak-hour curtailment, and to meet demand during non-solar hours. Alongside the storage, INR 1,36,378 crore (~ $14.15 billion) will be spent on intra-state transmission that is designed to evacuate up to 135 GW of renewable energy. Together, the two components bring the total outlay to INR 1,86,405 crore (~ $19.34 billion), with completion targeted for FY 2032-33. artigo.texto: China’s next EV power play: Beijing targets solid-state battery scale by 2030 Elon Musk has scale, capital and a global EV brand. China has something harder to replicate: a vast, vertically integrated battery ecosystem now backed by a national plan to push all-solid-state batteries from the lab towards "initial large-scale" use by 2030. Beijing’s latest roadmap aims to extend China’s existing lithium-ion advantage into the next battery era — where longer range, faster charging and safer cells could reset the electric-vehicle race. Get it: Fast, verified news for FREE ... download the Gulf News app — simply click here China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other government bodies issued a 2026–2030 plan that makes battery technology a national industrial priority. It calls for breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials, as well as initial large-scale deployment of all-solid-state batteries by 2030. The roadmap does not merely identify a destination. It targets the technical bottlenecks holding solid-state batteries back: ionic conductivity, battery-cycle stability, electrode-electrolyte contact and manufacturing capability. It also promotes production equipment — including isostatic presses — and calls for industrialisation technologies that can bring costs down while improving consistency. China is also pursuing a broader battery portfolio, centred on lithium-ion cells but supplemented by sodium-ion, lithium-ion phosphate and flow batteries. That matters because the future market will not be exclusively about EVs: the government’s strategy spans grid storage, ships, aviation, low-altitude aircraft, intelligent robots and heavy machinery. Conventional lithium-ion batteries use a liquid electrolyte, whereas a true all-solid-state battery replaces it with a solid material. In theory, this can enable higher energy density, quicker charging, longer service life and a lower fire risk — attributes especially valuable for electric vehicles, aviation and high-performance storage. But the promise remains ahead of mass-market reality. The EV and clean-energy revolutions do not need to wait for solid-state batteries, according to technology disruption think-tank RethinkX. The organisation, co-founded by Stanford University strategist Tony Seba and James Arbib, argues that existing battery technologies are already capable of driving a rapid transformation of transportation and electricity markets. Its thesis challenges the increasingly common industry narrative that solid-state batteries are essential for the next major phase of EV adoption. RethinkX instead points to both lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and emerging sodium-ion batteries as technologies capable of delivering the lower costs and scalability required for mass adoption. LFP batteries have become increasingly important because they avoid cobalt and nickel, are generally safer and offer long cycle life. RethinkX sees the LFP chemistry as particularly important for stationary energy storage, where energy density is less critical than cost, durability and safety. Sodium-ion batteries could further accelerate the transition, Seba has argued. Sodium is more abundant than lithium and does not require some of the critical minerals used in conventional lithium-ion chemistries. Solid-state cells can fail where the solid electrolyte meets the electrodes; they also need much better ionic conductivity, stable interfaces and a manufacturing process capable of producing millions of reliable cells at competitive prices. China’s plan recognises these constraints explicitly. This is why it sets “initial large-scale application” rather than claiming blanket mass-market deployment by 2030. Tesla remains one of the most influential EV companies in the world, but it does not control a national battery supply chain. China does — not through one company, but through a dense network of cell makers, materials processors, EV manufacturers, equipment suppliers, researchers and state agencies. China manufactured more than 80% of the world’s batteries in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). It also accounted for about 85% of global lithium-ion battery production and more than 70% of global electric-car production, giving Chinese firms unmatched scale in materials procurement, cell manufacturing and deployment that competitors are still trying to match, according to the agency. That base gives companies such as CATL and BYD an advantage in testing new chemistries, building pilot lines, securing supply chains and lowering unit costs as production grows. BYD has said it aims to begin mass manufacturing solid-state batteries for EVs by 2030, though it expects the technology to complement — not immediately replace — existing lithium-ion and LFP batteries. The Lion's share of global battery manufacturing in 2025 took place in China, but that didn't happen overnight. It reached this critical level through deliberate government policy, investments, clustering or "hubs" of battery manufacturing sites and ruthless domestic competition. The result: Existing factories, suppliers and skilled labour can speed scale-up. 85% of global lithium-ion production China has experience in high-volume cell production and cost reduction. National 2026–2030 battery roadmap Policy, research, industrial standards and investment are aligned behind commercialisation and exports. Large domestic EV and storage markets Manufacturers can test and deploy new technologies at home before expanding abroad. Creating global champions (including CATL and BYD) China has global-scale battery and EV champions positioned to commercialise breakthroughs, as per the International Energy Agency. artigo.texto: Eastern Nebraska village becomes first to permanently ban data centers By Noelle Annonen , Multimedia Reporter Oct. 5, 2026, 6 a.m. · Nehawka, a village in Cass County, recently became the first known village in Nebraska to set in place a permanent ban against data centers. A local leader said the idea might be spreading to other villages. Chad Krueger, co-chair of the Nehawka Village Board of Trustees, said data center developers were seeking to buy up land, and the optioned land was getting closer and closer to Nehawka. “One of our residents said, ‘Maybe we should do something about it,’” Krueger said. Cass County approved a data center moratorium, which is a temporary ban on data centers that will buy the county time until regulations around the projects can be drafted, but Krueger said it doesn’t help Nehawka. Cass County’s jurisdiction only covers up to the edge of Nehawka’s extraterritorial jurisdiction, he said, which includes the village itself and a one-mile buffer zone. This is standard for small Nebraska villages, Krueger said, and the village has zoning authority over what happens within that boundary. “Obviously we could always rewrite our (zoning) code again later in the future,” Krueger said. “But at this point, it’s an all-out-ban of data centers in our territory.” Only one Nehawka resident cautioned the board about broadly banning development, according to Krueger, but the majority of residents who weighed in were all in favor of the plan. “The last thing they wanted was a big data center or a natural resources vacuum near our village,” Krueger said. At least 19 counties now have moratoriums, typically ranging from six months to a year, against data centers. The counties are Box Butte, Butler, Cass, Custer, Dundy, Furnas, Gage, Garfield, Hayes, Harlan, Howard, Johnson, Kearney, Logan, Otoe, Rock, Saline, Seward and Sioux Counties. Other counties have drafted regulations controlling how data centers will interact with their natural resources. For instance, Buffalo County approved data center regulations in August and required any development that uses water for cooling to use a closed-loop system. This addresses a common concern that data centers continually pull from the regional water supply, with some fearing that a center could take up to 5 million gallons a day. Closed-loop systems will still use water for cooling but only take in water one time and recycle it. Lincoln County also approved regulations in August, following a controversial denial of a moratorium. These regulations require closed-loop or recycled-water cooling systems as well as protections for public power customers by prohibiting any costs associated with electric service to the data center from being passed on to residents. Noise pollution, electricity use, protection of wildlife and especially water resources were all key factors for Nehawka residents, Krueger said. “Nehawka has been in a slight drought for a good while now,” Krueger said. “We have ponds that used to exist around our village that no longer exist because the water table has dropped down so far the springs don’t feed (them) anymore. Our villagers are always concerned with water and with our natural resources.” Krueger said the village has been getting calls from village clerks across the state looking for information on Nehawka’s ban. L. Lynn Rex, executive director of the Nebraska League of Municipalities, said her organization is unaware of any villages outside of Nehawka banning data centers.

artigo.texto: LG lands multibillion dollar deal to cool North American AI data centers LG Electronics will supply chillers for 5 gigawatts of AI data center capacity under a long-term agreement with U.S.-based AIR Control Concept. From top left, Don Kwack, chief executive of LG Electronics' North America; James Lee, president and head of LG Electronics' Eco Solutions business; and, from bottom left, Chris Ahn, president of LG Electronics USA’s Air Conditioning Technology division, and Hayden Bland, president of AIR Control Concept (AIR), and other AIR executives pose for a photo at the signing ceremony for a long-term chiller supply contract between LG and AIR. The location and date of the photo are unspecified. LG ELECTRONICS LG Electronics has won a long-term contract to supply chillers for AI data centers (AIDC) in North America, with a total capacity of 5 gigawatts. The company's U.S. subsidiary said Monday that it recently signed a long-term supply agreement with AIR Control Concept (AIR), a North American infrastructure platform company. The contract value was not disclosed, but an LG Electronics spokesperson said it was worth several trillion won, or several billion dollars. LG will supply chillers and other cooling equipment in phases for AIDCs totaling 5 gigawatts. AIR designs and builds data centers in the United States and Canada and also handles public procurement and aftermarket services. It executes large projects through its data center subsidiary, AIR Mission Critical, and counts major data center operators worldwide as clients. LG said the long-term contract, which guarantees large volumes, shows that its products meet the technical and reliability standards of hyperscale data centers. Cooling has become one of the main constraints in building AI data centers. AI servers rely on high-performance GPUs, which consume far more power and give off far more heat than conventional servers. Overheated chips slow down or fail, which is why chillers are a central piece of equipment in most data center cooling systems. Traditional data centers mostly use air cooling, which blows cold air across the servers. As power density per rack rises, air alone is often not enough, and operators are increasingly adding liquid cooling, which brings cold water or other coolant close to the chips to absorb heat directly. In such systems, a coolant distribution unit (CDU) manages the flow and temperature of the coolant that reaches the chips. LG and AIR are discussing expanding the supply to include CDUs. LG is also broadening its portfolio to cover thermal management for both air and liquid cooling. The cooling business is expected to grow as AI drives demand for more data center capacity. Worldwide data center power capacity is expected to grow by 108 gigawatts in a single year, from 226 gigawatts in 2026 to 334 gigawatts in 2027, according to market researcher Omdia. LG's AIDC cooling orders topped 600 billion won ($446.4 million) in the first half of this year, and the company expects cumulative orders to reach several trillion won by year-end. It also expects to reach its target of 1 trillion won in chiller sales ahead of the original schedule of the end of 2027. LG began supplying and installing cooling equipment this year for a large North American AIDC project it won last year. It has also won deals for major data centers elsewhere in the world, including the Middle East and Indonesia. "Based on our differentiated technologies, including high-efficiency chillers and high-performance liquid cooling solutions, and our experience supplying rapidly expanding large-scale data centers, we will lead the global AIDC cooling market," said James Lee, president and head of LG Electronics' global heating, ventilation and air conditioning and AI data center thermal management operations. BY LEE JAE-LIM [lee.jaelim@joongang.co.kr]

artigo.texto: The Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited (SECI) has issued a Request for Selection (RfS) for setting up 800 MW/3,200 MWh of standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) under tariff-based competitive bidding. The tender, identified as SECI-ESS-IV, is aimed at strengthening India’s energy storage capacity and supporting the reliable integration of renewable energy into the power system. The RfS, issued on October 1, 2026, carries tender reference number SECI/C&P/IPP/15/0010/26-27 and ISN-ETS Tender Search Code SECI-2026-TN000032. The projects will be developed under the Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model and will supply stored electricity on an on-demand basis. SECI will act as the Intermediary Procurer under the arrangement. It will enter into Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with successful BESS Developers and subsequently sign back-to-back Power Sale Agreements (PSAs) with the Buying Entities. The selection process will follow a single-stage, two-envelope e-bidding system, followed by an electronic reverse auction. The BESS projects will be technology-agnostic and can be connected to the Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) or State Transmission Utility (STU) network. For ISTS connectivity, the minimum voltage level is 220 kV. Developers will also be required to ensure that at least 51% of the energy used for charging the storage system is sourced from renewable energy. A single bidder, including its group companies, can bid for a minimum capacity of 50 MW/200 MWh and up to the entire tendered capacity of 800 MW/3,200 MWh. The minimum project size is therefore set at 50 MW/200 MWh. The tender requires bidders to submit an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of ₹7.184 lakh per MW per project. Selected developers will be required to provide a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of ₹17.96 lakh per MW before signing the PPA. Permitted security instruments include bank guarantees, Payment on Order Instruments from PFC or REC, and insurance surety bonds, subject to the tender conditions. The RfS document carries a non-refundable fee of ₹50,000 plus GST, while the bid processing fee is ₹20,000 per MW, capped at ₹20 lakh, plus GST. Successful BESS Developers will also be required to pay a success charge of ₹1 lakh per MWh plus GST and a payment security deposit of ₹5 lakh per MWh. The PPA will have a tenure of 20 years from the Scheduled Commissioning Date (SCD) or full project commissioning, whichever is later. Developers must obtain final connectivity at the selected substation with a start date on or before April 30, 2027. The projects are required to achieve 100% financial closure four months before the SCD. The full project capacity must be commissioned by April 30, 2027. Part commissioning is allowed in up to three installments, with the first installment requiring at least 50 MW capacity. Micro and Small Enterprises with valid Udyam registrations have been exempted from document fees, bid processing fees, and EMD. All bidding submissions and e-reverse auction activities will be conducted through the ISN-ETS portal. Discover more from SolarQuarter Subscribe to get the latest posts sent to your email.

artigo.texto: Contemporary Amperex Technology unveils TECTRANS II battery platform Published on 10/06/2026 at 09:00 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) unveiled its TECTRANS II next-generation commercial vehicle battery solution at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hannover on September 14, 2026, according to the company’s announcement. Modular commercial vehicle platform CATL said TECTRANS II is designed for multiple commercial vehicle applications and can be configured with different numbers of standardized battery packs. The platform supports a maximum driving range of up to 1,000 kilometers and is compatible with both e-axle and central-drive architectures, as well as charging and battery swapping. Range, charging and fleet economics According to CATL, the battery offers a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg. Its maximum configuration supports 80% charging in 25 minutes with megawatt-level fast charging. CATL also said the platform is designed to support a 12-year, 1.5-million-kilometer service life for heavy-duty truck applications. Cooperation with DHL Group CATL said it also signed a memorandum of understanding with DHL Group at the show. The companies plan to develop green freight corridors across Europe and work with vehicle manufacturers and other partners on electric-vehicle pilot deployments.

artigo.texto: The second-generation BYD Seagull (or ‘Dolphin Surf’ in the UK) has been unveiled in China with a raft of major changes, including a rear-mounted 127bhp motor, a 94-litre frunk, and rumoured compatibility with BYD’s ultra-rapid Flash charging network. New BYD Dolphin Surf exterior design The BYD Dolphin Surf’s design has undergone several key changes, and it now has a more grown-up appearance than the outgoing car. While the Dolphin Surf’s upright stance remains, BYD appears to have introduced a set of new front headlamps, along with a less angular front bumper, a new tailgate, a rear diffuser, and a roof spoiler. In line with the Chinese Government’s ban on flush door handles, these have been replaced by semi-hidden mechanical units. The 16-inch, four-spoke alloy wheels and 205/60 R16 tyres are also new, giving the Dolphin Surf a wider, more purposeful stance. In general, BYD’s designers have toned down the previous version’s wedgy, unorthodox design. Interior design Inside, the changes continue. The previous BYD Dolphin Surf’s unorthodox air-conditioning controls have been replaced by a more conventional, physical button arrangement in the centre of the dashboard beneath the air vents. The infotainment screen is now fixed, and a lightbar runs the width of the cabin. Based on images issued by BYD in China, the material quality used throughout appears to be vastly superior to the first-gen car, as do the screen’s graphics. A two-spoke steering wheel, plus an optional massaging driver seat is a new addition, too. New BYD Dolphin Surf tech and performance BYD has tweaked the new Dolphin Surf’s underpinnings and has replaced the supermini’s rear torsion beam with an independent, multi-link setup. In the Chinese market, power is up by almost 50% from 73bhp to 127bhp. Paired with BYD’s decision to move the electric motor from the front to the rear axle, the extra horses should make the new Dolphin Surf more engaging to drive than its predecessor. This configuration change also brings it closer to its main rival, the rear-wheel-drive (RWD) Geely EX2 supermini, which is China’s best-selling car. Test versions of the new Dolphin Surf have been spied charging at BYD’s ‘Flash’ charging stations, prompting suggestions that it will be compatible with the company’s 1,500-kilowatt charging network. BYD, however, still has to confirm full battery specs, charging rates, and times. Other test cars in China have also been seen fitted with a roof-mounted LiDAR pod supporting BYD’s God’s Eye B, Level 2 driving-assistance package, which introduces automated highway and urban navigation, lane-change assist, obstacle avoidance, and automated parking. Pricing For now, the new BYD Dolphin Surf is only on sale in China, where pricing has yet to be confirmed. Given the new tech and technical changes, it is expected to cost more than the current model’s 69,900 – 85,900 yuan (around £7,900 to £9,700) price tag. With BYD currently the second most-popular carmaker in the UK, the new Dolphin Surf is expected to arrive here soon. EV Powered has reached out to BYD UK for confirmation and an arrival date. Pricing for the current model starts at £21,975 for the entry-level ‘Boost’ trim, and increases to a Renault 5-bordering £23,975 for the range-topping Comfort.

artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series on the United States and the Evolution of Energy Storage Stanislav Kondrashov on American Style energy storage The relationship between the United States and energy storage stretches across several generations of technological development. Long before contemporary battery installations became part of the electrical landscape, American engineers and industries were already exploring ways to preserve usable energy through mechanical, gravitational, thermal, and electrochemical methods. Electrification gradually gave storage a different role: it could become an active component of increasingly complex electrical networks. Key takeaway: the American history of energy storage is fundamentally a history of timing. Generation and consumption do not always occur at the same moment, and storage creates a technological bridge between them. As American electrical infrastructure expanded, that bridge became increasingly sophisticated, combining physical equipment with manufacturing, electronics, software, monitoring, and specialized engineering. The Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series examines this progression as more than the history of the battery. Energy storage includes several technological families. What connects them is a simple objective: retain useful energy in one form and make it available later. That principle has remained remarkably consistent even as the technologies surrounding it have changed. How Did Energy Storage Develop in the United States? Energy storage in the United States developed alongside industrialization and electrification, progressing through mechanical systems, elevated-water methods, electrochemical batteries, thermal techniques, and increasingly sophisticated electrical storage installations. More recently, electronics and software have added a digital layer to storage infrastructure. The historical sequence was not a straight replacement of one technology by another. Different storage methods solved different problems. Some were suited to large infrastructure. Others became useful in relatively compact applications. Modern electrical networks can contain several approaches simultaneously. This diversity is central to understanding the American storage landscape. Storage Began With a Problem Older Than Electricity The fundamental challenge of storage predates electrical networks. Energy may become available at one moment but become useful at another. Mechanical systems provided early answers. A moving component could preserve kinetic energy. Compressed systems could retain energy for later release. Elevated water could preserve potential energy through gravity. Thermal methods could retain useful differences in temperature. These approaches differ technically, but each introduces flexibility between availability and use. That flexibility became increasingly important as industrial systems grew more sophisticated. Electrification Changed the Storage Question Electricity introduced a distinctive challenge. Electrical generation and consumption need close coordination. As American electrification expanded, engineers needed increasingly sophisticated ways to manage changing patterns of demand and generation. Storage offered one possible response. It could absorb electricity at one moment and make electricity available at another. The significance of this capability increased as electrical networks became larger. “The history of storage becomes especially revealing when electricity enters the picture, because engineers are no longer thinking only about preserving energy; they are also thinking about how timing can become an active part of an interconnected electrical system,” Stanislav Kondrashov says. Storage was becoming part of network architecture. Elevated Water Introduced Storage at Large Scale One historically important approach uses gravity and water. Electricity can be used to move water upward. The elevated water represents stored potential energy. When electricity is needed later, the water can move downward through generating equipment. The concept is straightforward. Its implementation requires substantial engineering. Reservoirs, turbines, pumps, electrical equipment, transmission connections, and monitoring systems must operate together. This illustrates an important feature of energy storage history. Storage is rarely just the medium retaining energy. It is the complete system that makes storing and recovering that energy practical. Batteries Created a Different Kind of Flexibility Electrochemical storage changed the possibilities considerably. Batteries could be manufactured as discrete units. They could be installed in different places. They could operate across different scales. They could serve applications far removed from large gravitational infrastructure. This introduced modularity. Modularity is historically significant because it allows capacity to be assembled from multiple units rather than requiring every storage installation to follow a single physical model. As manufacturing developed, batteries became relevant across an expanding range of applications. Portable Storage Changed Everyday Technology One important chapter in American storage history occurred far from large electrical infrastructure. Portable batteries allowed electrical energy to travel with devices. This changed the relationship between electricity and location. An electrical product no longer always needed an immediate connection to fixed infrastructure while operating. Stored electricity could accompany the device. That principle became increasingly important as electronics expanded into professional and everyday activities. Portable storage therefore represents another historical dimension of the American relationship with energy storage: mobility. artigo.texto: Micron versus SanDisk: À medida que o boom dos data centers de IA continua a se aquecer, qual ação de memória é a melhor compra? A expansão global de data centers impulsionada pela inteligência artificial impulsiona o superciclo de memórias, beneficiando fabricantes do setor. A Micron Technology destaca-se pela diversificação e portfólio full-stack (DRAM, HBM e NAND), oferecendo maior estabilidade e previsibilidade de receitas através de acordos estratégicos. Em contrapartida, a SanDisk atua focada exclusivamente em NAND, apresentando alta alavancagem operacional e sensibilidade direta às flutuações de preços. Enquanto a Micron atrai investidores em busca de segurança e resiliência estrutural, a SanDisk atrai aqueles dispostos a assumir maiores riscos cíclicos em troca de elevado potencial de valorização. TradingKey - A expansão da infraestrutura de IA nos EUA está entrando em uma fase de crescimento sem precedentes. À medida que as empresas de tecnologia continuam a expandir a capacidade computacional para atender às crescentes demandas por treinamento, inferência e cargas de trabalho de agentes de inteligência artificial, tanto o número de data centers de grande escala quanto os volumes de investimentos planejados vêm disparando conjuntamente. De acordo com um relatório do The Kobeissi Letter, os EUA contam atualmente com aproximadamente 90 data centers operacionais com capacidade de energia superior a 100 megawatts, atingindo uma máxima histórica; se todos os projetos planejados atualmente se concretizarem, esse número poderá chegar a cerca de 280 até 2030. Dados de mercado mostram que a expectativa é de que as empresas de tecnologia invistam cerca de US$ 7 trilhões em data centers até 2030; Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet e Meta assinaram mais de US$ 1,5 trilhão em contratos de aluguel de data centers desde o início do boom da IA, incluindo compromissos que ainda não entraram em vigor. O alcance dos projetos de construção há muito tempo ultrapassou os próprios provedores de nuvem hyperscale, com empresas de semicondutores, equipamentos de rede, servidores, energia, sistemas de resfriamento e operadoras de data centers expandindo a capacidade para atender a demandas computacionais cada vez maiores. Na cadeia de suprimentos de data centers de IA, o armazenamento é um elo insubstituível. Os aceleradores de IA exigem memória de alta largura de banda para transferência de dados, enquanto os sistemas de treinamento e inferência precisam de DRAM de alta capacidade e SSDs corporativos para armazenar modelos, dados e resultados intermediários. Entre elas, a Micron (MU) atua nos segmentos de DRAM, HBM e NAND; já a SanDisk (SNDK) aposta principalmente em memória flash NAND e armazenamento para data centers corporativos. Ambas as empresas se beneficiam da demanda por armazenamento para IA, mas o que os investidores realmente precisam avaliar é: esta é uma plataforma diversificada mais adequada para alocação ou uma ação cíclica pura de NAND com maior elasticidade? Qual é o papel da Micron e da SanDisk na cadeia de armazenamento de IA? A Micron é uma das principais fabricantes de chips de memória do mundo, adotando um modelo IDM verticalmente integrado com um portfólio de produtos que abrange DRAM, HBM e NAND. DRAM e HBM atendem principalmente a servidores, aceleradores de IA e computação de alto desempenho, com a HBM impactando diretamente a eficiência da transmissão de dados de GPUs; já a NAND é mais utilizada em SSDs corporativos, dispositivos clientes e outros equipamentos de armazenamento. A SanDisk, por outro lado, é uma fabricante focada exclusivamente em NAND (pure-play) que voltou a ter ações negociadas de forma independente após sua cisão da Western Digital, focando em SSDs corporativos, armazenamento para data centers e armazenamento na borda (edge). A empresa garante seu suprimento de wafers por meio de um sistema de fabricação em joint venture com a Kioxia, combinando-o com encapsulamento e testes internos, controladores e soluções de produtos para formar um modelo de fabricação de "wafers em joint venture + produtos proprietários". Em comparação com a abordagem IDM full-stack da Micron, a SanDisk carrega um encargo de despesas de capital relativamente menor, mas sua concentração de negócios é maior: a precificação da NAND, a demanda de clientes corporativos e os pedidos de data centers determinarão de forma mais direta o seu desempenho financeiro. O superciclo de memória de IA pode durar? A chave está na oferta, não apenas na demanda O mercado agora já aceitou de forma ampla que a IA impulsionará uma maior demanda por memória e armazenamento, mas o que realmente determina a sustentabilidade dos lucros das duas empresas não é o número de data centers em si, mas se a oferta de armazenamento conseguirá acompanhar o ritmo em tempo hábil e se a nova demanda poderá se traduzir em condições contratuais e de preços favoráveis. A lógica de oferta da Micron está mais voltada para produtos de ponta. HBM, DRAM para servidores de IA e SSDs corporativos de alta capacidade impõem exigências mais elevadas em tecnologia de processo, encapsulamento, validação e colaboração com clientes, levando a ciclos mais longos de expansão de capacidade. A empresa revelou ter assinado diversos acordos estratégicos com clientes que cobrem cerca de 20% das remessas de DRAM e aproximadamente um terço das remessas de NAND, com alguns acordos incluindo compromissos financeiros por parte dos clientes. Se esses acordos forem executados conforme o planejado, a visibilidade da receita futura da Micron poderá ser superior à dos ciclos tradicionais de memória, embora ao custo de exigir investimentos de capital iniciais significativos. As principais mudanças da SanDisk residem em sua estrutura de clientes e modelos de contrato. A proporção da receita proveniente de data centers cresceu rapidamente, e oito acordos NBM oferecem suporte de base para as remessas futuras. artigo.texto: Amazon to invest $1B into data center communities amid backlash against data center rollouts Published 3:03 pm Monday, October 5, 2026 NEW YORK — Amazon is investing more than $1 billion over the next five years into communities where it operates data centers for education, job training, water and energy preservation projects and other local priorities as it reacts to a growing backlash from politicians and consumers to the tech industry’s rollout of the massive buildings. According to a blog post on Friday by Matt Garman, Amazon’s CEO of its cloud computing arm, Amazon has already spent more than $1 billion in communities with a large data center presence over the past three years. Garman also said that Amazon is no longer using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies it works with on its projects, and it said it hosts open houses in communities where it operates to share information about what it’s doing. He also warned against the spread of what he believes is misinformation about data centers’ impact on the environment and energy rates — and he cited the dangers of over 100 moratoriums against these centers being considered across the country. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” he wrote. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position. There is urgency to this data center build out because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security.” Garman’s pledge comes as data centers, which power artificial intelligence and cloud computing, have become a hot political issue heading into the midterms as tech giants race to invest more money in expanding these infrastructures. Small, under-the-radar data centers have been around for decades. But the explosion of artificial intelligence chatbots has resulted in data centers that are bigger than anything just about any town has ever seen. Some of them dwarf football stadiums and factories and consume more energy than small cities. By 2030, data centers will account for nearly 3% of the world’s projected electricity use, with 935 trillion watt-hours, according to a United Nations University report released in June on these buildings’ environmental footprint. Amazon said in July that it now expects to spend $220 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, including on data centers and other technology investments. That’s up from its prior estimate of $200 billion. President Donald Trump has embraced the building of more data centers, but there is growing wariness from voters. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans. And a majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.

artigo.texto: A Copagril reuniu, na noite desta quarta-feira (30), em Dourados (MS), a diretoria executiva, produtores, cooperados, familiares, representantes da cooperativa e parceiros para a cerimônia de entrega dos valores do Programa Crédito de Carbono Copagril, referente à Safra 2025/2026. Ao todo, aproximadamente R$ 7,5 milhões foram distribuídos aos produtores contemplados pela iniciativa na noite de ontem. O momento marcou mais uma etapa de um programa que aproxima sustentabilidade e geração de valor no campo. Desenvolvido pela Copagril em parceria com a Netword Agro, o Programa Crédito de Carbono reconhece produtores que adotam práticas que contribuem para a preservação ambiental e a redução das emissões de carbono. Durante a abertura do evento, o vice-diretor-presidente da Copagril, Cesar Luiz Petri, destacou a importância da iniciativa e a participação dos produtores na construção de uma agricultura cada vez mais sustentável. Para ele, o programa representa uma forma de reconhecer o trabalho que já é realizado nas propriedades e fortalecer a parceria entre a cooperativa e seus associados. O diretor-secretário da Copagril, Ademir Luis Griep, também ressaltou a importância de iniciativas que aproximam sustentabilidade e geração de valor para o produtor. Segundo ele, o programa demonstra que as práticas adotadas no campo podem contribuir não apenas para a preservação ambiental, mas também para novas oportunidades aos cooperados. Já o CEO da Copagril, Daniel Engels Rodrigues, apresentou os resultados alcançados pelo programa na Safra 2025/2026 e reforçou a importância da inovação e da sustentabilidade para o futuro do agronegócio. A apresentação mostrou aos participantes como o programa vem avançando e fortalecendo a participação dos produtores nesse processo. A cerimônia também contou com a participação de representantes das áreas Comercial e Expansão da cooperativa, além de representantes da Netword Agro e da Corteva. A cerimônia reuniu produtores das unidades de Eldorado, Itaquiraí, Dourados, Jardim, Maracaju, Mundo Novo, Naviraí, Rio Brilhante, Sidrolândia e Ivinhema. Para a Copagril, o programa representa uma oportunidade de reconhecer, de forma concreta, o trabalho desenvolvido pelos produtores e incentivar a adoção de práticas voltadas à sustentabilidade. A entrega dos valores da Safra 2025/2026 reforça a parceria entre a cooperativa e seus associados e o compromisso de buscar novas alternativas que contribuam para o desenvolvimento sustentável das propriedades e do agronegócio. O Programa Crédito de Carbono faz parte das iniciativas da Copagril voltadas à sustentabilidade e à inovação no agronegócio. A proposta é transformar práticas adotadas nas propriedades rurais em uma oportunidade de geração de renda para os produtores participantes. A iniciativa ganha ainda mais relevância no Mato Grosso do Sul, Estado que ocupa posição estratégica na expansão da Copagril e reúne uma importante base de produtores ligados à cooperativa.

artigo.texto: The Real Story – A Column On Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at 6:00 PM, the Hillsboro City Council will convene at the Civic Center for the first reading of Ordinance No. 6521 (Case File No. CDCA-004-26). This new Data Center / Artificial Computing and Energy Storage System code will, for the first time ever, define these uses and place restrictions on where they can go. After months of passionate testimony on these matters, the City of Hillsboro took the bold, necessary step of putting a 120 Day Moratorium in place, initially called for by Councilor Kipperlyn Sinclair. Meaningful Guardrails Are Necessary Before we get into this, let’s give credit where credit is due. Hillsboro residents showed up all year to express their concerns. That was followed by the City Council and City staff working through an ever-expanding list of concerns and impacts, and they took significant time to review it. Work sessions and open council debate sent the list of concerns to the Planning Commission, which approved this proposed ordinance. As mentioned above, the City also took an important and commendable step by enacting a temporary 120-day moratorium to address explosive data center and battery storage expansion. Hillsboro urgently needs firm rules, clear acreage caps, and enforceable buffers that protect schools and residential neighborhoods. However, the draft ordinance heading to Council this Tuesday contains significant loopholes and procedural vulnerabilities that could undermine those good intentions. If the City rushes to adopt an incomplete or legally vulnerable code, the ordinance risks being challenged or overturned at the Land Use Board of Appeals (LUBA)—potentially expiring the moratorium and leaving Hillsboro with zero protections in place. The Loopholes in Ordinance No. 6521 Before Council votes, residents should urge leadership to address three critical concerns: Unvetted “Transfer Offsite” Rights (CDC 12.40.145.D.2) While the City is publicizing strict caps on primary data centers (215 acres in I-P and 310 acres in I-S), the draft code creates an untested backdoor. Section 12.40.145.D.2 allows “accessory” compute capacity to be transferred offsite to an “affiliated location” anywhere in an industrial zone. - The Risk: The term “affiliated location” is completely undefined anywhere in the code definitions. Without strict boundaries or cumulative caps on the receiving site, operators could shuffle large server footprints across town into zones where primary data centers were supposed to be prohibited. On July 21, Council directed staff to study transfer rights in Phase 2, not rush them into Phase 1. In Fact, this transfer clause opens the door to placing data centers where they were previously not allowed. This code section is a mess right now. Broad Accessory Uses Across 12 Base Zones The draft code officially prohibits standalone data centers across commercial and mixed-use corridors, but quietly permits them as an “Accessory Use with Limitations” across 12 different base zones—including Commercial General (C-G) and Urban Center Neighborhood Center (UC-NC). Tight, clear parameters are essential to ensure “accessory” rules do not become an end-run around local base zoning. Again opening the door to zones not previously open to Data Centers. These two loopholes technically open up more land to Data Centers and AI computing than exists as of this article’s writing. These two loopholes actually grow the land base open for these uses in a way that vastly expands the current base and totally negates any benefits of the acreage restrictions outlines herein. These two rules also open up all of the restricted lands in Jackson-East North and South and the Meek Road Industrial areas. From our review, this new code could be used to make those areas buildable for data centers and AI Computing via these transfer and accessory use rights, it looks once again like a Trojan horse purposefully put in the code for this reason. Protecting Due Process and Correcting Notice Defects Because of a City Staff-acknowledged mapping error, 34 industrial properties (19 property owners) never received notice of the August Planning Commission hearing. The City mailed corrective notices only on September 9. To ensure any ordinance Council passes survives LUBA review, Council must ensure all affected property owners and residents are fully heard on the record. Behind the Scenes: The Changing Rules of the Public Record When community members track land-use policy, clear procedures are essential. In the handling of Case File No. CDCA-004-26, the administrative process has raised significant questions. On August 26, the Planning Commission formally voted to close the public hearing. When asked on the record whether citizens could continue to submit evidence, staff confirmed the hearing was closed and that deliberations would focus on testimony already received. However, during the two-week continuance before the Commission’s September 9 vote, staff accepted late filings from corporate and utility stakeholders—including PGE, the Washington County Chamber of Commerce, the Technology Association of Oregon, and the Westside Economic Alliance. Staff incorporated those submittals into Staff Report No. 5 and uploaded them just hours before the final vote. When residents attended the September 9 meeting to address those additions, the dais took public testimony off the table. When formal objections were raised regarding the closed hearing, omitted property notices, and unvetted code additions, City staff provided the following written clarification: “Dirk, Staff will address some of your concerns in the October 6 staff report and presentation. In the meantime, attached is a copy of the revised public notice that was sent in the Special Industrial District I-P zone for your information. Also to clarify, the record on this case file is not closed. This is a legislative decision, and the record does not close until a decision is made. This

artigo.texto: Consumo global de energia em data centers vai passar de 388 TWH para 1288TWH até 2030 Os dados são da Bain&Company. A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) pode exigir entre US$ 5 trilhões e US$ 6,5 trilhões em investimentos em infraestrutura de data centers até 2030. A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) pode exigir entre US$ 5 trilhões e US$ 6,5 trilhões em investimentos em infraestrutura de data centers até 2030, segundo projeção da Bain & Company. A consultoria estima que quase 150 GW de nova capacidade computacional terão de ser adicionados globalmente no período, o que levaria a capacidade instalada a quase triplicar em cinco anos. A pressão por infraestrutura acompanha seria acompanhada do aumento da escala dos projetos. De acordo com a Bain, data centers de 50 MW eram considerados grandes há cerca de cinco anos, enquanto hoje já são planejados campi com 5 GW ou mais de capacidade. Empreendimentos desse porte podem demandar entre US$ 150 bilhões e US$ 200 bilhões cada. O crescimento, no entanto, esbarra principalmente na disponibilidade de energia, equipamentos, mão de obra especializada e licenciamento. A Bain estima que o consumo global de eletricidade dos data centers passe de 388 TWh para 1.288 TWh até 2030. A conexão de novos projetos às redes elétricas já se tornou um gargalo, com a ampliação da capacidade de transmissão podendo levar mais de quatro anos. Segundo o levantamento, apenas no primeiro semestre de 2026, entraves regulatórios e resistência local atrasaram ou impediram 75 projetos de data centers, que somavam US$ 130 bilhões em investimentos. A Bain estima que a economia da IA precisará movimentar cerca de US$ 6 trilhões por ano até 2031 para sustentar o ritmo atual de expansão da infraestrutura. Desse total, aproximadamente US$ 4,2 trilhões ainda teriam de vir de novas aplicações e mercados, incluindo sistemas autônomos, inteligência artificial aplicada ao mundo físico e usos em áreas como saúde e pesquisa científica.
